Children's development examined across cultures and in the context of the various social institutions and settings within which they live.

sections.note: Class Description: Poetry in English has been written by Asian Americans for a century and a half in this country, even if the term ”Asian American” itself dates from the late 1960s. This course will be a broad survey of various styles of Asian American poetry in English from the late nineteenth century to the present, with an emphasis on more “experimental” writing in recent decades. Students will learn how to close-read poems but always with an eye to the broader political, historical, and social contexts of the writing, which are themselves reflected in the poetry’s aesthetics. No prior knowledge of poetry required.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ HIST 14) Survey of African history from the early nineteenth century to the present. courses.title: Introduction to Africana Studies
courses.desc: A wide-ranging survey of the history, culture, and politics of people of African descent on the African continent and in the diaspora. Issues of colonialism, migration, slavery, revolution will be emphasized. The formation and growth of black communities in the New World and in the former colonial capitals.

courses.title: Seminar - Black Power/Red Power
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Class Description: Heeding recent scholars' calls to place Black Studies and Native American and Indigenous Studies in more active dialogue with each other, this seminar examines the Black Power and Red Power movements. Students will engage both primary and secondary sources and attend to the ways in which these movements rejected the possibility of Black and Indigenous incorporation into the American polity and instead called for self-determination and political autonomy. Rather than limiting our consideration of Black Power and Red Power to the late 1960s and 1970s, we will take a “long movement” approach to thinking about these movements. Broad topics covered will include sovereignty and self-determination, and and community control, revolutionary violence and self-defense, gender and sexuality, and solidarity.

courses.title: Seminar - Scenes of Revision
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Examination of revision in African American literature within the contexts of enslavement, surveillance, material scarcity, and racial violence during slavery and Reconstruction. Analysis of texts revised, sometimes repeatedly, by authors including Phillis Wheatley, John Marrant, William Wells Brown, Hannah Bond, and Frances Ellen Watkins Harper. Attention to the material effects of revision and questions of authorship, agency, print culture, and archival recovery. Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Introduction to AI and Society
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 40) Introduction to how AI systems are developed, deployed, and managed in a broader societal context. Technical foundations relevant to discussions and critiques of AI systems. History of AI and computation and their roles in society, with a focus on social issues such as privacy, the environment, and labor. Technical foundations include principles of computing and programming such as data representation, problem decomposition, and algorithm design.

courses.title: Understanding AI: Systems, Tools, and Applications
courses.desc: A holistic overview of how AI systems are built, deployed, evaluated, and managed in a variety of domains, with a focus on generative and data-driven AI methods. Foundational principles of computing and programming such as data, problem decomposition, and algorithmic thinking. Understanding differing perspectives on the definition of AI and how various users use AI systems. Evaluating situations when AI based approaches may be warranted compared to traditional software. Economics and resource requirements of AI software solutions, such as comparing in-house solutions with third-party providers.

courses.title: Dissent and Democracy: American Literature to 1900
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ ENG 23 & CVS 31) Literature survey focused on "dissent" and "democracy": two major thematic and formal concerns of early American writing. Readings include exploration narratives, settlement propaganda, sermons, autobiographies, political pamphlets, philosophical essays, poetry, short fiction, and novels. Brings together Native American, white European American, African American, Latinx, and Asian American voices to think about the construction of literary history, the politics of representation, and why this matters today. 
Authors studied include Phillis Wheatley, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Frederick Douglass, Emily Dickinson, Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Sui Sin Far, and Zitkála-Šá.

sections.note: Fulfills English major survey requirement.

courses.title: Special Topics - Literature of The American Sixties
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to graduate and advanced undergraduate students.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
Interdisciplinary examination of literature produced in and about the American Sixties. Readings associated with the Beat and Black Arts movements, New Journalism, second-wave feminism, anti-war activism, psychedelic and blues-folk poetry, and popular culture. Attention to experimentation with literary forms, the incorporation of non-literary discourses, and connections among literature, music, and other arts. Comparative reading of seemingly disparate works, including SCUM Manifesto, Soul on Ice, The Whole Earth Catalog, Play It as It Lays, The Bluest Eye, In Cold Blood, and The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test. Exploration of how these works challenge familiar interpretations of the period and how their formal and narrative innovations helped shape contemporary autofiction and writing concerned with identity. Authors may include Thomas Pynchon, Bob Dylan, Joan Didion, Chuang Hua, Alice Walker, and Toni Morrison.

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.desc: Intercultural consideration of how people understand what it means to be human in their own particular social settings and environments. Topics include difference and belonging, relationship, exchange, expression, and technology. Emphasis on the use of ethnographic interviewing, participant-observation, and other qualitative methods in holistic and critical analyses of power and meaning-making.

courses.title: Global Cities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 20 and UEP 20) Introductory-level urban anthropology class exploring cities as intersections of people, ideas, capital, and the physical environment. Themes include anthropological understandings of space and place-making; utopic and dystopic urban visions of the city; urban mobility; cities as nodes in global environments, economies, and networks of people and production; sensory experience and expressive culture in cities; urban "nature" (e.g., parks); difference and inequality in urban landscapes; the growth of urban populations and megacities; and tensions between the city as planned or conceptualized and the city as a lived experience.

courses.title: Kinship: Living in Relation
courses.desc: Gateway sociocultural anthropology course introducing basic concepts in anthropology of gender, sexuality, reproduction, and power, and feminist and queer anthropology. Explores what it means to be related to another person,what “family” is, and what that means or meant to people in different times and places. Kinship as a foundational yet diverse aspect of social life; “the family” as a site for expression of power and reparative world-making. Kinship in relation to culture, gender, law, science, politics, and activism. Topics include marriage diversity, kinship dissolutions, property, reproductive technologies, adoption, relational ecologies, activism, and ruptured and repaired kinship amid historical trauma.

courses.title: Primate Social Behavior
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/BIO 44) Introduction to social lives of primates. Uses experimental and observational studies to teach students how to understand and engage with scientific literature and method. Covers ecological, physiological, and developmental bases of primate social behavior, with attention to evolution of social interactions among individuals of different age, sex, relatedness, and status. Topics include competition and cooperation, dominance and territoriality, sex and mating, parenting, cognition and conservation. Includes a weekly lab where students will learn primatological methods. No pre-requisites.

courses.title: Introduction to Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 30). Survey of human culture from the earliest paleolithic hunters and gatherers to the formation of states and the beginnings of recorded history. Course provides an introduction to archaeological methods, a worldwide overview of prehistoric ways of life, and a more detailed analysis of cultural development in the New World.

courses.title: Soundworlds of North Africa
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MUS 42) Anthropology of music approach to North African soundworlds—the sonic spaces where music, culture, and social action intersect. Centering the voices of North African scholars, musicians, and listeners of the contemporary Maghreb region (Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara, and their borderlands and diasporas). Topics may include the role of music in Amazigh rights and Sahrawi independence movements, spaces of Islamic-Jewish convergence, ritual healing and the recuperation of sub-Saharan heritages, traumas of migration, the Arab Spring, and mythmaking about North Africa by foreign and local powers. How to relate anthropological and social theory to public and “hidden” meanings embedded in the sounds of diverse musical genres.

courses.title: Archaeology Methods, Ethics, and Dilemmas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 116) Archaeological methods for understanding the past. Includes ethical considerations, new technologies, conceptual dilemmas, postcolonial critiques, and collaborative work. Best practices in archaeological methods and current debates about ethical dilemmas. Impact of methodology on descendant communities, stakeholders, rightsholders, and the public.

courses.title: Technologies of Enchantment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 123) Mid-level course in anthropological theory: examines technologies made to entice, lure, and persuade, in a social and cultural context. Compares the design, use, and reception of techniques ranging from animal trapping to user experience design. Topics may include hunting, machine gambling, scams, advertising, magic, art, hospitality, persuasive design, behavioral addiction, and algorithmic recommender systems. Recommendations: One prior course in cultural anthropology.

courses.title: Archaeology, Museums, and Colonialism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 129) Connections between archaeology, museums, and colonialism. Insights on colonialism offered via archaeology and museum collections. Considers how the ruins of colonialism shed new light on the contemporary world. Investigates how histories of archaeology and museum collecting are implicated in colonialism and what this means for the future of these disciplines. Examines new forms of archaeology and museology that engage with colonial legacies, with particular attention to Indigenous and other community-based forms of research and knowledge dissemination.

courses.title: Palestinians & Israelis: Ethnographies of Justice
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with RCD 143 and CST 143) Ethnographic approaches to the study of Palestinians and Israelis with various legal statuses and cultural and religious backgrounds; migrants in Israel; Palestinian refugees in the Middle East and beyond. Comparative analysis based on concepts of race, colonialism, diaspora, and indigeneity. Analysis of mobilizations for justice for Palestinians and Israelis, primarily but not exclusively in the Middle East.

courses.title: Sex and Money: Anthropology of Sex Work
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with WGSS 147) Intersections between sex (and other forms of intimacy) and money (and other forms of exchange). Reading of ethnographies about sex workers and those who seek to regulate, profit from, or “help” them. How neoliberalism has shaped ways of earning a living throughout the world in ways that changed gender roles and intimate relationships. Topics include ethical concerns with studying sex workers; their relationships with family members, pimps, and clients; moral panics about “white slavery” and “sex trafficking;” the whore stigma; sex tourism; criminalization and legalization; transactional sex; and the eroticization of perceived racial difference.

courses.title: Selected Topics - Agribusiness Dreamworlds
courses.desc: Current Topics in Anthropology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course applies cultural anthropology and visual studies approaches to deconstruct the histories and ideals of agribusiness on a global level. We cover agriculture as a possible means for land occupation with colonial aims; theoretical aspirations to standardization, order, modularity, and control; university contributions to shaping modern agriculture; rural aesthetics and experiences as foundations for national, gender and racial identities; ideal cities and adventure parks informed by farming utopias. Also, we consider resistance and critiques of agribusiness models, including worker organizing and protest, worker expertise and rights, pluriversal approaches to farming, artistic responses and consumer awareness efforts.

courses.title: Selected Topics - Contraptions
courses.desc: Current Topics in Anthropology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: “Contraptions” are a weird kind of technology: they may work, but they don’t work right. This course is a workshop in the anthropology of technology, dedicated to exploring the figure of the contraption in social and cultural context. How do people decide that a technology is complicated, or too complicated for a particular use? Why do some technologies seem to barely work, and how do we know what it means for a technology to work in the first place? How do people respond emotionally to technologies, finding them funny, pathetic, or even liberatory? Topics will range from early anthropological debates about technical and social complexity to contemporary concerns about the programming behind AI agents. We’ll talk about how hacks, kludges, and workarounds of all kinds might change the way we think about how technology works and why it works the way it does. Alongside course readings and discussion, students will collaborate with a team from the School of Engineering to build and critique contraptions of their own.

courses.title: Biopolitics & the Body: Life, Power, Knowledge
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 152 and WGSS 151) Theories and ethnographies of biopolitics and biopower. What happens when biological life (including that of humans) becomes a site for power and management? Reading of conceptual and ethnographic texts at the intersection of science, medicine, the state, and capital. Topics include neoliberal governmentality, hegemony of interventionist biotechnologies, bioethics, biosecurity and management of risk, biocapitalism, necropolitics, logics of social abandonment and disposability, political rights, and projects of biological and social enhancement.

courses.title: Fieldwork Methods in Music, Sound, and Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MUS 184) Experiential and critical approach to ethnographic field research in the arts and humanities. Hands-on learning assignments in project design, participant-observation, field note taking, interview techniques, audio-visual documentation, and ethnographic writing. Ethics of knowledge production, complexities of self-other relations, and awareness of implicit bias. Decolonial, collaborative, and multimodal methodologies. Strategies for creating written, visual, and multimedia representations of music, sound, and embodied cultural expressions, and their entanglements with social issues. Recommendations: Major or minor in Anthropology or in Music, Sound, and Culture, or graduate standing, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Music, Trance, & Consciousness
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with MUS 159) Cross-cultural approaches to relationships between music and altered states of consciousness, ranging from high-arousal trance states in healing rituals to low-arousal, individual experiences of deep listening. Ethnographic case studies of music-driven spirit possession, mysticism, shamanism, rave culture, and mobile individual listening practices from Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Interdisciplinary approach with material from ethnomusicology, anthropology, psychology, religious studies, and neuroscience.

courses.title: Practicing in Food Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ENV 190) Project-based course designed to integrate academic learning with application in a range of food systems settings. Focused observation exercise culminating in a jointly produced useable report for a community partner. Emphasis will be on balance between process and product. Readings, discussion, and field research will be split between the specific content focus of the group project and general issues arising from planning and carrying out interdisciplinary team projects; developing productive relationships with communities, clients, and stakeholders; addressing ethical concerns in collaborative and public research. Preference will be given to students who have declared the Food Systems and Nutrition minor or the Food Systems, Nutrition and Environment major.

courses.title: Human Evolution
courses.desc: Reconstruct 10 million years of human evolutionary history using evidence from genetics, the fossil and archaeological records, primatology, and ethnographic research. Discuss adaptations that define our lineage and distinguish humans from other apes. Topics may include the origins of bipedalism, big brains, cooking, hairlessness, menopause, language, cumulative culture, and art. Prerequisites: ANTH 0040 or ANTH 0126, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Thinking with Plants: Plants, People, and Society
courses.desc: Explores use of plants as material resources (food, medicines, licit/illicit drugs, infrastructure) and as symbolic resources. Topics include circulation of plants; colonial cultivation, extraction, and power; place of plants in different lived environments and symbolic ecologies; plants, capitalism, and commodity chains; indigenous knowledge, tourism, and biopiracy; commercialization, criminalization and legality; multi-species approaches to living with and among botanicals.

courses.title: Current Topics In Anthropology - Violence, Pleasure, & Value(s)
courses.desc: Detailed analysis of a selected issue in contemporary sociocultural anthropology, linguistics, physical anthropology, or archaeology. Open to advanced undergraduate majors and qualified graduate students.

sections.note: This upper-level seminar examines anthropological theories of value and will try to understand them on their own terms as well as apply them to thinking about the value(s) of pleasure, especially but not exclusively sexual pleasure, in relation to violence. We will spend the first five weeks of the semester reading anthropological approaches that center economic value, semiotic value, and their intersections, as well as approaches that define value as that in which people see as worthwhile to invest their time and energy. We will then spend the rest of the semester applying those ways of framing value to texts from a variety of disciplines (mostly by Black, Latina, and Latin American feminist, queer, and trans scholars and activists) that grapple with the co-existence of violence and pleasure, covering topics such as: BDSM, pornography and postpornography, sex work, femicide and transfemicide, and countersexuality.

courses.title: Current Topics In Anthropology - Mystery of Beasts: The Nature
courses.desc: Detailed analysis of a selected issue in contemporary sociocultural anthropology, linguistics, physical anthropology, or archaeology. Open to advanced undergraduate majors and qualified graduate students.

instructors: J Michael Reed, Zarin P. Machanda
sections.note:
BIO 196-05/ ANTH 149 Mystery of Beasts: The Nature of Scientific Evidence
Humans throughout history and across cultures have a tendency to believe in fantastical creatures that sometimes defy the laws of science. With the rise of social media, the rate at which these stories spread greatly exceeds the rate that scientific information is disseminated. In this course, we will investigate the nature of scientific evidence through the lens of cryptozoology - the study of mysterious creatures. Topics will include understanding species distribution maps of bigfoot and how they overlap with North American bears, ecological constraints on lake ecosystems and how this would impact the presence of the Loch Ness Monster, the human psychology of fear and myth, and the the discovery that some mysterious creatures turn out to be real. Each week we will discuss the evidence or lack thereof that examines the existence of a new cryptid, using primary literature, popular media, indigenous knowledge, and class discussions.
sections.req: Completion of one BIO Group C course or Bio Anthro course (not including BIO 14)

courses.title: Classical Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HAA 19, CLS 27, and ILVS 27.) Survey of ancient Greco-Roman civilization spanning c. 3,100 BCE to 565 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: sculpture, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, sociopolitical organization, and artistic technique. Examination of the development and collapse of the Bronze Age civilizations of the Aegean and Italy. Exploration of the evidence of cultural transformations driven by trade, colonization, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the city-state in archaic Greece and Italy, then to the Greek-speaking kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, and finally to the inclusion of the Latins, Etruscans, Greeks, Egyptians, and others within a single multicultural state: the Roman Empire. Assessment of the renegotiation of identities and historical narratives as polytheistic religions were supplanted by Christianity within the Roman state. Field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Ancient China, Korea, and Japan
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 28 & ILVS 28) Survey of the ancient cultures of China, Korea, and Japan from g . 2,100 BCE to 907 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: social rituals, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Excursions into sociopolitical organization, religion, diplomacy, philosophy, writing systems, and artistic technique. Evidence of cultural transformations and renegotiations of identity driven by trade, colonization, diplomacy, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the state in ancient China, and finally to the evolution of a world system that interconnected the kingdoms and peoples of East Asia, as well as the many cultures linked by the Silk Routes: from the Yangshao culture to the Shang state, the first unification of China under the Qin emperor, to the Han and Tang periods, Gojoseon, Goguryeo, then the Jomon, Yayoi, and Kofun period Japan. Includes a field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Introduction to Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 50.)Survey of human culture from the earliest paleolithic hunters and gatherers to the formation of states and the beginnings of recorded history. Course provides an introduction to archaeological methods, a worldwide overview of prehistoric ways of life, and a more detailed analysis of cultural development in the New World.

courses.title: Special Topics In Archaeology - Medieval Ruins + Relics
courses.desc:
Exploration of special topics in archaeology through a lecture course or seminar. Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: ARCH/CLS 27 or ARCH/ANTH 30.

sections.note: No additional costs. Full title: Ruins, Relics, Remains: Vibrant Matter from the Middle Ages

courses.title: Archaeology Methods, Ethics, and Dilemmas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 116) Archaeological methods for understanding the past. Includes ethical considerations, new technologies, conceptual dilemmas, postcolonial critiques, and collaborative work. Best practices in archaeological methods and current debates about ethical dilemmas. Impact of methodology on descendant communities, stakeholders, rightsholders, and the public.

courses.title: Archaeology, Museums, and Colonialism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 129) Connections between archaeology, museums, and colonialism. Insights on colonialism offered via archaeology and museum collections. Considers how the ruins of colonialism shed new light on the contemporary world. Investigates how histories of archaeology and museum collecting are implicated in colonialism and what this means for the future of these disciplines. Examines new forms of archaeology and museology that engage with colonial legacies, with particular attention to Indigenous and other community-based forms of research and knowledge dissemination.

courses.title: Introduction to Geospatial Humanities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 125 and UEP 103) Geographic Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods, and technology for applications in the humanities in past and present settings. Topics include GIS data creation and data structures, geodesy, spatial analysis, and cartographic visualization. Includes extensive laboratory exercises to apply concepts presented in the lectures using a variety of GIS software and tools. Assignments concentrate on application of concepts covered in lectures and exercises and include a final project that applies GIS to each student’s field of interest.

courses.title: Senior Honors Thesis In Archaeology B
courses.desc:
Intensive investigation designed and carried out by the student, culminating in a written thesis and oral defense under the supervision of a thesis adviser. Usually two semesters. Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: Archaeology major and permission of instructor.

courses.title: From The Big Bang To Humankind
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CHEM 6 and BIO 6). An exploration of the origins of the Universe, the formation of Earth and its structure, the chemistry of life, the development of complex organisms, and the development of modern humans including evidence for the various ideas presented, the scientific method used by scientists, and how the community of scientists evaluate the evidence. This course does not fulfill pre-med requirements for a lab-based chemistry course.

courses.title: Concepts Of The Cosmos
courses.desc:
A general course on the cosmos aimed at an introductory understanding ofthe concepts and science of modern astronomy. Topics include gravity, light, matter, telescopes,properties and evolution of stars, normal and active galaxies, cosmic distance measurements,super-massive black holes, structures of galaxies and their growth, galaxy formation andevolution, dark matter, dark energy, expansion and fate of the universe, the Big Bang, andinflation. Lectures are supplemented by outside readings, as well as projects and problem setsrequiring analytic reasoning. Students are expected to solve simple quantitative problems.Intended for undergraduate students not planning to major in the physical sciences.
Recommendations: An understanding of algebra and plane trigonometry.

courses.title: Galactic and Extragalactic Astrophysics - Galactic and Extgalact Astphys
courses.desc: Key radiative processes in astrophysics, the Milky Way galaxy, normal and active galaxies including quasars, formation and evolution of galaxies, and observational cosmology. Will include assignments involving the use of computers. Intended for students with a background in physics and/or astronomy and mathematics, and a strong interest in astronomy. May be used to satisfy the concentration requirements for majors and minors in the department of physics and astronomy. Prerequisites: Physics 11 and 12, or by instructor consent.

courses.title: Astrophysics Laboratory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ AST 151) Aims at developing and strengthening data analysis skills and expertise through astronomy-based projects. Practical applications of numerical methods (root finding, interpolation, integration, random number generation), statistics and probability (Bayes’ theorem, probability distributions, Bayesian inference, Monte Carlo generators), error analysis and propagation, and data fitting. Projects in astronomy using data from major national facilities and computer analysis of data. For students with a background in physics and/or astronomy and/or mathematics and/or computer sciences. Prerequisite: Math 34. Recommendations: Introductory course to computer science, or consent from instructor. May also be taken at the 100 level.

courses.title: Biochemistry of Gene Expression & Signal Transduction
courses.desc: This course covers the molecular mechanisms of gene expression and signal transduction. The fundamental mechanisms underlying transcription, RNA processing, translation, and DNA replication are highlighted, and the integration of these fundamental mechanisms into molecular and cellular regulation of proliferation and signal transduction is discussed. Current literature is emphasized.

courses.title: Biochemistry of Gene Expression
courses.desc: The fundamental mechanisms underlying transcription, RNA processing, translation, and DNA replication are highlighted in this course. Current literature is emphasized. This course represents the first part of Biochemistry 230 and may be taken as a separate course.

courses.title: Biochemistry of Signal Transduction
courses.desc: The integration of fundamental mechanisms into molecular and cellular regulation of proliferation and signal transduction is discussed. Current literature is emphasized. This course represents the second part of Biochemistry 230 and may be taken as a separate course.

courses.title: Drug Design

courses.title: Plants And Humanity
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 10.) Principles of botany accenting economic aspects and multicultural implications of plants, their medicinal products, crop potential, and biodiversity. Emphasis placed on global aspects of this dynamic science, with selected topics on acid rain, deforestation, biotechnology, and other applications. Also covered are medicinal, poisonous, and psychoactive species, as well as nutritional sources from seaweeds and mushrooms to mangos and durians. Three lectures.

courses.desc: Required for biology majors. Selected topics in ecology, physiology, and evolution with examples from across the tree of life. Two lectures and one laboratory each week.

courses.title: Primate Social Behavior
courses.desc: (cross-listed w/Anth 44) Introduction to social lives of primates. Uses experimental and observational studies to teach students how to understand and engage with scientific literature and method. Covers ecological, physiological, and developmental bases of primate social behavior, with attention to evolution of social interactions among individuals of different age, sex, relatedness, and status. Topics include competition and cooperation, dominance and territoriality, sex and mating, parenting, cognition and conservation. Includes a weekly lab where students will learn primatological methods. No pre-requisites.

courses.title: Cell Biology
courses.desc: Basic concepts of cellular organization, function, and regulation. Emphasis on molecular/biochemical research methods used in the study of protein structure and function, gene expression and regulation, signal transduction, intracellular transport, and cell communication. Credit cannot be received for both BIO 46 and BME 33. Prerequisites: BIO 0013 or permission of instructor. Recommendations: Completion or co-enrollment in BIO 0041.

Gene cloning, recombinant protein expression, protein biochemistry, and immunochemistry are emphasized for teaching state-of-the-art laboratory skills and for reinforcing basic concepts of modern molecular biology. One laboratory session per week plus one discussion period. Requires completion of BIO 0013 (or equivalent).

courses.title: Biology of Aging
courses.desc: An introduction to the biology of aging. Focus on molecular, cellular, and physiological changes that occur during the aging process in humans and other organisms. Major topics include theories of aging, genetic regulation of longevity in model systems, and therapeutic modulation of the aging process. Prerequisites: Bio13 and Bio14 or their equivalent, or consent.

courses.title: Immunology
courses.desc: Concepts of modern immunology and their importance in biology. Topics include humoral and cellular immune responses, antibody structure and biosynthesis, antigen-antibody interactions, cellular immunology, immunological tolerance, autoimmunity, and tumor immunology. Prerequisite: BIO 13 or BME 33; and sophomore standing. Recommendation: BIO 41.

Molecular mechanisms of DNA replication and repair, recombination, transcription, and protein synthesis are emphasized. Advanced topics including regulation of gene expression during development, transposition, and regulation of chromatin structure are based on current literature.

courses.desc: A survey of the structures and functions of microbes, including bacteria, archaea, viruses, and eukaryotic microbes (fungi, protists). Topics include microbial genetics, physiology, cell biology, diversity, evolution, ecology, and the human microbiome. BIO 107 (Microbiology Lab) is not required but may be taken concurrently. Requires completion of BIO 0013, BIO 0014, and BIO 41 or graduate standing. (Group A or C.)

courses.title: Microbiology Lab
courses.desc: Examination of microbial diversity and function using laboratory techniques to isolate, identify, and manipulate microbes. Introduction to microscopy, sterile technique, microbial cell culture, microbial physiology, sequence-based microbial identification, and antibiotic susceptibility testing. One laboratory session per week. Must be taken concurrently with BIO 106 (Microbiology Lecture). Prerequisite: BIO 0013, BIO 0014, and BIO 0041, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Plant Development
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ENV 108.) Structural and physiological aspects of plant development. Genetic and environmental influences on development as these pertain to germination, root and shoot growth, and plant sexuality and flowering. Information on corn, bean, and tobacco systems will be extended to diverse groups such as cacti, ferns, bromelaids, water plants, parasitic and carnivorous plants.
Recommendations: BIO 13 and 14, or equivalent.

courses.title: Physiology – Endocrine, Neural, and Digestion
courses.desc: Normal functioning and pathophysiology of selected systems – endocrine, neural, and digestive – from the level of the cell to the level of the organism. Emphasis on critical thinking, integration, and application. BIO 115 is not required for this course. Requirements: BIO 14 or instructor permission. Recommendations: BIO 013 or instructor permission.

sections.req: Completion of Bio 13 and Bio 14 or equivalents.

courses.title: Physiology of Movement
courses.desc:
Introduction to the physiological basis of human and animal movement. Topics include biomechanics, kinesiology, muscle and bone physiology, biological materials, and locomotion. (Group B or Q).
Prerequisites: Bio 14 and Physics 1 or 11; or permission of instructor

sections.req: Requires compltetion of Bio 14 and Physics 1 or equivalent.

courses.title: Regeneration in Biology: From Nature to Medicine
courses.desc: Exploration of diverse organisms and their ability to regenerate their bodies and tissues in response to damage. Topics range from regenerating animals in their ecological settings to biomedical endeavors in human regenerative medicine, including vision restoration and human-machine interfaces. Survey of diverse systems ranging from the molecular to whole-organism level. Fulfills the group B requirement for the Biology major. Prerequisites: BIO 13 and BIO 14, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Completion of Bio 13 and Bio 14 or equivalents.

courses.title: Molecules, Medicines, and Markets
courses.desc: How biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies develop new drugs, from target identification and validation through preclinical optimization and testing, clinical trials, regulatory approval, and commercialization. Additional topics include R&D decision-making by drug developers and investors and the impact of new and emerging technologies, economic factors, and government policies on drug development. Prerequisites: BIO 14, 41, and at least one BIO course numbered above 41; or graduate standing in Biology; or instructor consent.

sections.req: BIO 14, 41, and at least one BIO course numbered above 41; or graduate standing in Biology; or instructor consent.

courses.title: Animal Behavior
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ENV 130.) An examination of ethological theory: the development of behavior, orientation, migration, communication, and social behavior. Particular emphasis will be placed on the functioning of animal societies.
Recommendations: BIO 13 or 14, or equivalent or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Ecological Statistics & Data w/Lab
courses.desc: Probability and likelihood, fitting simple statistical models to data, and using these models to make predictions. Examples come from ecology, emphasis on monitoring plant and animal populations and forecasting how these populations will respond to changing environments. Includes use of discrete probability distributions (binomial and Poisson), building mixed and compounded probability distributions, an introduction to Bayesian statistics, and use of the open-source statistics program, R. (Group C or Q). Students should have a good working knowledge of high school algebra and an interest in ecology.

courses.title: Neurobiology
courses.desc:
Biology of nervous systems. From the biophysical basis of neuronal function, through synaptic interactions and signal processing in neural circuits, to behavior, learning, and memory. Examples from both vertebrates and invertebrates.
Recommendations: BIO 13 or BME 33 and 14, plus one Group A course in biology or PSY 103.

courses.title: Evolutionary Biology w/Lab
courses.desc:
Examines hypotheses for patterns of biological diversity and for the apparent good fit of organisms to the environment. Topics include the genetic and developmental basis of evolutionary change, processes at the population level, the theory of evolution by natural selection, concepts of fitness and adaptation, rates and long-term trends in evolution, extinction, biogeographical patterns, determinants of conflict and cooperation, the evolution of sex and life history, modes of speciation, and coevolutionary dynamics. The laboratory will familiarize students with evolutionary genetics methods. Topics include genotype-phenotype relationships, DNA sequence assembly and alignment, gene and gene pathway function, estimation of population demography and phylogenetic relationships, and hypothesis testing. (Group A, C, or Q.) Recommendations: BIO 13 and 14, or equivalent.
Recommendations: BIO 13 and 14, or equivalent.

courses.title: Computational Laboratory in Population Genomics
courses.desc: Evolutionary processes such as natural selection and genetic drift generate patterns in genomic sequence data that are often interpreted with computational analyses. Research-driven course exploring an open problem in population genomics through analysis of open access data, modeling of evolutionary processes, and/or simulation. Development of computational genetic research and scientific writing skills. Prerequisites: BIO 35 OR BIO 133 OR (BIO 143 and any computer science course)

courses.title: Molecular Biotechnology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BME 162 and CHBE 162.) Key concepts of molecular biology and engineering aspects of biotechnology. Molecular biology, recombinant DNA techniques, immunology, cell biology, protein purification, sequencing, gene therapy, and bioethics with review and discussion of primary literature. Comprehensive technical paper on an emerging topic. Students may not receive credit for both BME/CHBE/BIO 162 and BME 33.
Recommendations: CHEM 1.

sections.req: BIO 13 and (Junior or Senior standing), or Graduate Standing

courses.title: Marine Biology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 164.) An intermediate-level introduction to the biology of marine organisms. Detailed survey of major marine animal and plant groups; food web dynamics; physiological and ecological adaptations to key marine habitats, including the deep sea, coral reefs, estuaries, and the intertidal zone. The impact of global warming, ocean acidification, and overfishing on marine communities and fisheries. Prerequisites: Biology 13 and 14, or equivalent. (Group C.)

courses.title: Advanced Genetics: DNA Repair and Genome Editing
courses.desc: Combined lecture and seminar. Current state-of-the-art knowledge of DNA repair pathways that the cell uses to maintain a stable genome and consequences of inappropriate repair for cell health and cancer initiation. Genome editing technologies that rely on DNA repair pathways, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and variants, and how they are employed in the lab and in the clinic. Emphasis on research techniques and analysis of journal articles. Prerequisites: BIO 105 or graduate standing.

courses.title: Seminar In Conservation Biology
courses.desc:
Advanced topics in conservation biology. Readings and discussion of the current literature emphasized. Topics will change each year; example topics are landscape ecology, dynamics and conservation of small populations, and restoration ecology. Please see departmental website for detailed semester course descriptions.
Recommendations: Upper level Group C course in Biology

BIO 51, 130, 142, 143, 144, 164, 181, 183 or graduate student.

courses.title: Seminar in Field Endocrinology
courses.desc: Advanced seminar explores the mechanistic role of endocrine systems in coordinating how animals survive, breed, and adapt to the ever-changing natural environment. Emphasis on wild animals in natural conditions with focus on student-led discussions of primary scientific literature surrounding a core text.

sections.req: Requires the completion of one Biology Group B course or graduate student

courses.title: Seminar In Molecular Biology And Genetics
courses.desc:
Current topics in molecular biology, genetics and genomics, studied through readings from the original literature. Focus will be on studies recognized by the Nobel Prize Committee as pivotal to modern molecular biology and genetics. These studies and current research directions that follow from them will be covered using a combination of lectures, class discussion, and presentations. Selected topics of current interest to be covered include genome structure and polymorphisms as related to human disease, RNA functioning in the regulation of gene expression, and cell cycle regulation and cancer.
Recommendations: BIO 41 and junior standing or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Requires completion of BIO 0041 and junior standing or graduate student.

courses.title: Protein Structure and Function
courses.desc: The intricate relationship between protein structure and biological function. Molecular mechanisms underlying the folding, stability, and function of proteins, including enzymes, receptors, and protein complexes. The dynamic nature of proteins, the effects of disease-causing mutations, and their implications for drug targeting. Evolution of protein structures and functions, highlighting the molecular adaptations that contribute to biological diversity. Integration of theoretical knowledge through lectures with real-world examples through critical analysis of primary literature. Fulfills the group A requirement for the Biology major and the elective requirement for the Biochemistry major. Prerequisites: BIO 152 or CHEM 171, or graduate standing.

sections.req: CHEM 0171 or BIO 0152 or graduate standing

courses.title: Independent Research in Biology
courses.desc: Academic credit for students participating in continued biology research. Students must find their own research positions, either within or outside of Tufts, and consult with potential faculty supervisors prior to enrollment. Students should demonstrate autonomy in literature reading, experimental design, and data collection/analysis. Undergraduates should have prior research in a related project and written science communication experience equivalent to Bio 93; graduate students without prior research experience should be familiar with literature in the field prior to enrollment. At least 225 hours (roughly 15 hours/week per week in the academic semester) of research involvement and participation in research group meetings, culminating in a research paper and presentation. Confirmation of project eligibility and consent of supervising research mentor required at the start of the term. Prerequisites: Sophomore standing or higher and BIO 93 or BIO 193, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Chromatin, Epigenetics and Gen
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
BIO 196-02 Chromatin, Epigenetics and Gene Expression
 An introduction to the multiple mechanisms of gene regulations and how this contributes to transcription. Concepts include DNA/histone/RNA modifications, transcription factors, 3D chromatin architecture, non-coding RNA, and condensates. Goal of this course is to understand these regulatory mechanisms and their contribution to development, diseases, and aging.
sections.req: Completion of BIO 41 and juniors or seniors

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Microbiome and mucosal immunity
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
BIO 196-03 Microbiome and mucosal immunity
Our body’s mucosal surfaces are occupied by an ecosystem of microbes that influence host immune responses to disease. This course will survey immune responses across the nasal, oral, gut, skin and vaginal mucosa. We will do this through the lens of different bacterial, viral and fungal infections and evaluate existing vaccine strategies to boost immunity at barrier surfaces.
sections.req: Completion of BIO 104 or Graduate Standing

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Introduction to Bioinformatics
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
BIO 196-04 Introduction to Bioinformatics -
The computational analysis of large-scale biological data, from sequencing output through biological interpretation. Topics include sequencing platforms and genome assemblies, read alignment, bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, metagenomics, variant calling and translational applications, AI models for structural biology, and using AI agents in workflows. The bioinformatics toolkit and public data resources are integrated throughout. Course format is lecture and discussion based with interspersed computational workshops. No prior programming experience assumed.
sections.req: Completion of BIO 41 or graduate standing

sections.note:
BIO 196-05/ ANTH 149 Mystery of Beasts: The Nature of Scientific Evidence
Humans throughout history and across cultures have a tendency to believe in fantastical creatures that sometimes defy the laws of science. With the rise of social media, the rate at which these stories spread greatly exceeds the rate that scientific information is disseminated. In this course, we will investigate the nature of scientific evidence through the lens of cryptozoology - the study of mysterious creatures. Topics will include understanding species distribution maps of bigfoot and how they overlap with North American bears, ecological constraints on lake ecosystems and how this would impact the presence of the Loch Ness Monster, the human psychology of fear and myth, and the the discovery that some mysterious creatures turn out to be real. Each week we will discuss the evidence or lack thereof that examines the existence of a new cryptid, using primary literature, popular media, indigenous knowledge, and class discussions.
sections.req: Completion of one BIO Group C course or Bio Anthro course (not including BIO 14)

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Big Data for Living Systems: A
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Bio 196-06 Big Data for Living Systems: Analysis and Visualization

This course will introduce and explore quantitative and computational tools with applicability across the full range of biological scales, from molecules to the biosphere, with a heavy focus on data interpretation and visualization. Although these different scales of life are usually studied in isolation from each other, living data can challenge our basic statistical training in many of the same ways like context dependence, nonlinear interaction, temporal sequencing, and spatially explicit patterning. This class will hone the problem-solving skills to navigate these biological realities, while learning some advanced statistical and machine learning tools to help no matter the scale of investigation.
Prerequisite: Requires Bio 132 or Bio 133 or Math 070 or Biostatistics for Bioinformatics (Bio 196-23) or Graduate standing

sections.note:
**This course meets on the BOSTON campus.**

BIO 296-07 Interdisciplinary Studies in Antimicrobial Resistance
The objective of this interdisciplinary course is to train the next generation of leaders working to understand and combat the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, well-prepared to contribute to novel and improved treatments.  This course covers content related to antimicrobial resistance and antibiotics, including modes of action and mechanisms of resistance to existing agents, new anti-infective strategies, the role of diagnostics and stewardship in combating AMR, and how new agents are discovered.  During the course, students will learn about and reflect on major challenges related to the antimicrobial resistance crisis, including the impact of AMR infections in clinical practice, the need for innovative approaches, why the antibiotic development market is different from other drug development, and challenges in equal distribution of medicines.

sections.note:
BIO 196-08 Applied Bioinformatics
Applied Bioinformatics is a practical course in analyzing biological data through reproducible computational workflows. Students will spend a majority of the course working on guided, hands-on sessions using real datasets. Topics include genomics, bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, and microbiome and metagenomics analysis. Students will learn to run bioinformatics pipelines, organize projects with Git and GitHub, and interpret and communicate results clearly. Brief lectures introduce key concepts before each hands-on analysis. During the final four weeks, students complete a project to reproduce selected analyses and findings from a published paper, leaving with practical skills.

Diffuse optics, near-infrared spectroscopy, and photoacoustic imaging. Emphasis on experimental design, selection of imaging parameters, data acquisition and interpretation of results using state-of-the-art instrumentation. In-class exercises and projects reinforce the students' understanding of the lecture material and provide practical design experience. Students use computer-based prototyping tools to model and demonstrate their design solutions. Frequent guest lectures by user-interface design specialists from industry.

sections.note: This course explores the fundamentals of cardiovascular physiology, the pathophysiology of cardiovascular diseases, and engineering-based solutions for diagnosis and treatment. courses.title: Special Topics - Quantitative Cardio Biomechanics
courses.desc: Guided study of an approved topic. Please see departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Students will learn to model blood flow and mechanical forces in the cardiovascular system. After a brief review of cardiovascular physiology and fluid mechanics, they progress from small-scale steady flow to small-scale pulsatile flow to large-scale, complex pulsatile flow. Students also calculate mechanical forces on cardiovascular tissue and cells (endothelial cells, platelets, red and white blood cells) and their effects, and learn methods for modeling cardiac function. Concepts are applied to medical devices such as heart valves, ventricular assist devices, and artificial lungs. 
Recommendation: Students should be comfortable in fluid mechanics, solid mechanics, and multivariable calculus.

courses.title: Special Topics - Immunoengineering
courses.desc: Guided study of an approved topic. Please see departmental website for details.

sections.note: Principles and applications of engineering approaches to understand, manipulate, and therapeutically control the immune system. Topics include fundamental immunology and engineering strategies for cancer, infectious disease, autoimmunity, transplantation, and regenerative medicine, with emphasis on protein, cellular, nucleic acid, and biomaterial engineering. Prerequisite: Immunology at the level of BME 44 or equivalent; junior, senior, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Wind Turbines
courses.desc: Combined aerodynamic, electromechanical, and structural behavior of wind turbines. Betz's momentum theory, fundamental aerodynamic parameters and criteria governing efficient turbine operation. Analysis of turbine subsystems such as blades, drive trains, generators, towers and foundations to develop an integrated understanding of the overall turbine as a unified entity. Static and dynamic behavior described using simplified analytical models. System interactions interpreted through Campbell diagrams for rotating components. Review of component failure statistics and emerging technological innovations with emphasis on their potential to reduce capital and operational costs.

Approximate analysis methods will be discussed. Design of elements including steel and pre-stressed concrete beams, abutments, piers, joints, and bearings using AASHTO code (LRFD) will be covered.

courses.title: Data Science for Sustainability
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ DS 143 and ME 173). Emerging topics in data science and statistical learning with applications to the three pillars of sustainability (environmental, economic, and social). Building, estimating and interpreting models used in energy and environmental decision-making with emphasis on social justice. Development of critical consumers and responsible producers of data-driven analysis through: learning a suite of data-driven modeling and prediction tools; building the programming and computing expertise to use those tools; and, developing the ability to formulate analyses to answer questions pertaining to sustainability.

sections.req: (ES 2, CS 10 or CS 11) and (ES 56, CEE 156, EE 24, EE 104, BME 141, MATH 166, or ME 102); OR graduate standing

courses.title: Foundation Engineering
courses.desc: Foundation engineering design, with emphasis on bearing capacity and settlement for shallow (footings) and deep (pile) foundations. Design of footings, rafts, piles, and piers subjected to axial and lateral loads; building code requirements for design; and evaluation and selection of foundation types and alternatives. Case studies.

sections.req: Requires the completion of CEE 42 or graduate standing

courses.title: Principles Epidemiology
courses.desc:
Methods that quantify disease processes in human populations. Topics include study design, sources of inaccuracy in experimental and observational studies, the methodology of data collection, and an introduction to the statistical evaluation of epidemiological data.
Cannot receive credit for both CEE 154 and CEE 54

courses.title: Biostatistics
courses.desc: Statistical methods for analysis and interpretation of data generated by biomedical, environmental health, and public health studies. Descriptive statistics for continuous and categorical data, probability, hypothesis testing, correlation, analysis of variance, linear and logistic regression, multivariable regression, and non-parametric methods. Foundations of probability and statistical theory, and how to apply concepts by analyzing data.

sections.req: Prior completion of MATH 42 or graduate standng

courses.title: Occupational And Environmental Health
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ENV 158 ) An examination of current topics in the area of occupational and environmental health, with particular emphasis on the types of materials that produce human health effects. Both clinical and epidemiologic data will be used to assess the public health importance of environmental pollutants and to evaluate the effectiveness of control strategies
Recommendations: Senior standing or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Resilient and Equitable Infrastructure
courses.desc: Influence of uncertain extreme weather events on infrastructure. Framework for designing, evaluating and tracking risk-based equitable adaptation strategies to ensure the resiliency of infrastructure under current and future climates. Students will select an infrastructure sector, use open data to examine current technical and equity challenges, and identify climate adaptation strategies that are technically and environmentally sound, socially just, and economically practical.

courses.title: Environmental Law
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 207 and ENV 109) This survey course explores the evolution of environmental and natural resource law and examines if, where, and how it addresses climate change among several other pressing environmental threats. The course also reveals the challenges presented by the intersection of environmental issues and our political process and the critical role played by planners and policy makers. The course is designed for those considering careers in environmental science or engineering, environmental management, and those looking to participate (professionally or personally) in the political or regulatory process related to environment and climate issues.

courses.title: Environmental And Water Resource Systems
courses.desc: Mathematical models of water resource and environmental systems are presented in combination with optimization procedures, decision theory, and environmental applied statistics to generate an integrated approach to the planning, design, and management of complex water resources systems. Water resources systems applications are formulated as decision problems where an optimal solution is sought, yet cost, safety, environment, and technology appear as competing constraints. Applications include regional water quality management; siting treatment plants; reservoir system operations; and design, irrigation, flood control, and watershed planning.

courses.title: Off Shore Wind Structures
courses.desc: Design and analysis of structures that support wind turbines. Topics include steady state & turbulent winds, drag & inertial effects from waves, turbine rotor induced loadings, aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, turbine control, dynamic response, metocean conditions, and seabed properties. Focus placed on a hand-based process for the selection, design, and assessment of offshore wind turbine support structures. Validation of designs using computational models.

courses.title: Laboratory And In-situ Measurement Of Soil Property
courses.desc:
In-depth study of various laboratory and in-situ tests used to measure the shear strength, compressibility, and permeability of soils. Laboratory work includes index, consolidation, and triaxial tests. Field tests discussed include SPT, cone, vane, pressuremeter, and dilatometer. Discussion of methods used to process laboratory and field data. Report writing and hands-on laboratory testing.
Recommendations: CEE 42.

courses.title: Energy and Marine Infrastructure
courses.desc: Consideration of engineering, permitting, policy, and market concepts relevant to the development of a U.S. offshore wind energy supply chain. Case studies include ports, vessels, and manufacturing facilities for both fixed and floating offshore wind turbines.

courses.title: Corporate Management Of Environmental Issues
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as UEP 265 & ENV 265 ) Students in this course will explore the ways corporations interact with the environment, with the goal of understanding the processes, pitfalls, and tools for preventing/addressing environmental issues or disasters. Using case studies, students will critique the ways corporations have
managed real environmental challenges, and discuss the alternatives that may have been available. Students will also be introduced to approaches used by companies to envision and prepare for environmental problems. They will also focus on the perspectives of various stakeholders who have an interest in corporate environmental management, including shareholders, boards, corporate leaders, community members, governments, and activists/NGOs, and unravel the tensions that often exist among these groups.

courses.title: Master’s Project
courses.desc:
A project under the guidance of a faculty adviser that addresses an engineering topic
related to the student’s program of study. Students who are practicing engineers are
encouraged to consider projects relevant to their own work. Topic, scope and SHUs
must be approved by department. See departmental website for details.

courses.title: Graduate Seminar
courses.desc:
Weekly seminar series covering contemporary topics in civil and environmental
engineering.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: Supervised, independent study of topics related to civil and environmental engineering. Departmental consent required

courses.title: Introduction to Ceramics
courses.desc:
An introduction to sculptural, painterly, and functional approaches to ceramics. Explores techniques in wheel-throwing and construction for hand-building and examines the basic use of fire, glazes at low and high temperatures, and raku. No prerequisites. 

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Intro to Ceramics: Wheel
courses.desc: Introduction to wheel throwing as an integral part of the ceramics process. Learn to create forms on the wheel, including bowls, cups, vases, plates, and enclosed forms. Explore various surface design, glazing, and firing techniques to create both functional and expressive objects and learn to incorporate these techniques into an individual art practice. Non SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

sections.attrs: BFA Introductory Studio|BFA Studio Art|LA-Distribution-Arts|MFA Studio Art|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Arts
sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Ceramics Technical: Glaze
courses.desc:
An in-depth approach to the materials and methods of glaze development, testing and firing. Students will learn approaches to either design glazes from scratch or learn to understand what is needed to alter color, surface or melting temperature of glazes. The course is broken up into a mixture of lecture, personal research, and lab time. This course offers students with the skill sets that are necessary to operate a personal studio, or be a viable contributing member of a community studio or institution. While this is a methods based course students will be encouraged to apply their knowledge to their ongoing body of studio work. Critiques will be scheduled on an as needed basis.

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.
sections.req: One previous Ceramics studio course or permission of instructor.SMFA students only

courses.title: Ceramics II
courses.desc:
Intermediate-level studio course in ceramics emphasizing individually developed, proposal-driven projects. Students work through wheel throwing, handbuilding, sculptural, or combined approaches while developing their abilities in form, surface, material, process, and content. Research, experimentation, demonstrations, individual meetings, and critique support an independent artistic direction. Projects build on previous experience and challenge students to extend their work through greater scale, complexity, refinement, or conceptual depth.

Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Advanced Studio Projects
courses.desc: Intermediate and advanced Ceramic Studio course. Discussion of ceramic-based installations to inspire the final project, a complete ceramic-based installation for a gallery or site-specific space. Visiting artists, slide presentations, and examination of historical and contemporary ceramic art with emphasis on how to make a body of work flow together for a final exhibition. Prerequisites: CER 102, CER 137, CER 151, CER 133, CER 132, and CER 120.

courses.title: Introduction To Community Health
courses.desc: Examines the relationship between health, health care, and community. Considers the determinants of health and illness in contemporary society. Major emphasis on how communities define and try to resolve health-related problems explored through case studies.

courses.title: Introduction to the U.S. Healthcare System
courses.desc: Problems and issues encountered in the planning, organization, and regulation of health services. Health policy formation and its implications for service delivery. Health care financing; health insurance; the changing role of physicians; technology; poverty and health; the mix of planning, regulation, and competitive strategies; and consumer organizations. Problems of implementation and administration; federal, state, and local interests.

courses.title: Public Health Engineering
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 0027 and CEE 0052). An introduction to public health engineering. Elements of waterborne disease control, hazardous materials management, occupational health and safety, and environmental interventions. Applications to environmental engineering and environmental engineering science.

courses.title: Introduction to Global Health
courses.desc: Introductory course in global health. Focus on health in low- and middle-income countries. Principles of global health along with additional topics such as health determinants and disparities, socioeconomic status and health, human rights, culture and health, maternal and child health, water and sanitation, parasitic diseases and the Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs).

sections.attrs: BFA-Language/Culture|BFA-Social Science|LA-Distribution-Social Sciences|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Social Sciences|World Civilization Requirement

courses.title: Current Topics in Community and Public Health - Public Health in Culture and Society
courses.desc: Explores current and emerging topics in community and public health, with an emphasis on discussions of interdisciplinary perspectives and issues affecting individuals, communities, and populations. Topics may include contemporary public health challenges, emerging research, timely debates, policies, and practices.

courses.title: Community Health Methods
courses.desc: Fundamentals of research on population-level health and development of skills important for understanding and improving community, public, and global health. Emphasis on accessing and critically evaluating public and community health research; developing research questions and hypotheses identifying appropriate research designs; addressing ethics in research; conducting measurement and sampling; applying qualitative and quantitative research methods; and disseminating findings.

courses.title: Health Policy Analysis
courses.desc: Introduction to the field of health policy analysis and the basic theories, concepts, and methods for conducting policy analysis in the fields of community health and health care. Examples from a variety of community health and health care policy areas to learn about different analysis techniques. Prerequisites: Sophomore standing or above, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Sophomore Standing or Graduate StudentsCH 2

courses.title: Race, Ethnicity, And Health
courses.desc: Examination of racial and health disparities. The nature of racial and ethnic categories, data issues, current health status of various populations, and approaches to resolving disparities including the concept and practice of cultural competence.

sections.req: Requires the completion of CH 1 and 2 or permission

courses.title: Drugs, Society, and Public Health
courses.desc: Overview of substance use within a public health context, drawing on socio-ecological and intersectional frameworks. Critical evaluation of public health approaches to substance use and their differential impacts across populations. Examination of historical and contemporary contexts of drug use, harm reduction, theories of ‘addiction’, community-led advocacy, and public health responses to substance use within a rapidly changing social and policy landscape.

courses.title: Health Economics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ EC 48) An examination of major topics in the economics of health and health care, both in the United States and abroad, using the basic theoretical and empirical tools of economics. Covers the medical and nonmedical determinants of health, markets for medical care services and health insurance, and proposed ideas for health care reform. Prerequisites Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Built Environment and Community Health
courses.desc: Influences of built environment on human health. Explores key arenas of community health study, including , physical activity, nutrition, air quality, injury, water, mental health, and social capital, as well as promising built environment interventions to improve health outcomes, such as active transport, healthy housing, contact with nature, climate resilience. Use of behavioral and ecological models to think critically about the specific contexts and populations for which health is most strongly affected by the environment. Prerequisite: CH 0001.

courses.title: Introduction to Epidemiology
courses.desc: Introduction to the principles of epidemiology, including an overview of the field's history and its modern applications such as outbreaks and surveillance. Descriptive and analytic measures of disease frequencies in populations and comparisons of different study designs. Examination of validity and reliability, effect modification, and sources of bias, including confounding and information bias.

sections.req: CH majors, Undeclared sophomores, or first years

courses.title: Principles of Biostatistics
courses.desc: Deriving meaningful conclusions from complex health data. Development of the statistical toolkit required to evaluate and conduct high-quality population health research. Analytical methods, including study design and probability theory, hypothesis testing and categorical data analysis, and multivariable techniques such as general linear models and logistic regression. Connection of conceptual theory and technical execution through hands-on application using Stata.

sections.note: completion of CH 1 or instructor permission

courses.title: Disability and Difference in Children
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 190) Overview of some of the special needs of preschool and elementary-age children who show a variation in physical, sensory, emotional, cognitive, and social development, through the lens of a positive model of identity. Focus on educational implications, family support, and adaptations to promote inclusive environments. Class lectures, observations of children, media portrayals, hands-on adaptations of materials, and visiting speakers.

courses.title: Analysis of Medical and Health Data
courses.desc: Programming in Stata (statistical software) and guidance on data management strategies for health-related research. Command-based programming for modifying/managing data and statistical analyses. Navigating software, creating datasets, and accessing and using existing datasets for research projects.

courses.title: Internship in Community, Public, & Global Health
courses.desc: Structured and supervised community health work in a health organization, government agency, community group, or healthcare-related company that 1) provides opportunities to gain professional skills and experience, 2) facilitates application of community health curriculum and 3) provides exposure to community, public, and global health career possibilities. Students select Boston area sites in the public or private sector and at the local, state, or federal level. Class meetings with Internship Administrator and department faculty. Prerequisite: Major in Community Health, second semester junior standing and consent of department.

sections.note: CH major with pre-requisites, Dept Consent required
sections.req: CH 1, CH 2, CH 30 & CH 36 or instructor permissionCH Majors

courses.title: Community-Based Participatory Research Fieldwork
courses.desc: Theoretical orientation to and training in community-based participatory research with the intent of nurturing student-community partnerships and promoting ongoing collaborative research, evaluation, and needs assessment work in Tufts host communities. Practical experience in interpersonal communication, partnership development, group facilitation, qualitative and quantitative research methods, team work, grant-writing, and community and academic dissemination.

courses.title: Beyond the Food Desert: Access, Health and Justice
courses.desc: Critical inquiry into the theories, measures, and policies that influence how we think about and define "healthy food access." Predominant models of food access in the US, evaluations of place-based policies to improve food access, and structural and historical factors that influence the food environments of today. Engagement with active policy discussions about the future of food access in the US through class discussions and debates. Prerequisite: CH 1.

courses.title: Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics
courses.desc: Thermodynamic concepts - first and second laws, heat, work, energy, entropy, equilibrium, reversibility, equations of state - are introduced in process contexts. Phase equilibria, chemical potential, fugacity, and colligative properties are also discussed.

courses.title: Transport Phenomena I
courses.desc:
Fundamentals of fluid mechanics and their applications to the design and understanding of flow phenomena in industrial and biological processes.
Enrollment requirement: CHEM 2, PHY 11, and MATH 51 (concurrent or completed)

sections.req: CHEM 2, PHY 11, and MATH 51 (concurrent or completed)

courses.title: Chemical And Biological Separations
courses.desc: Design and analysis of separation processes. Equilibrium-staged processes, stagewise separation processes, mass transfer operations, and rate-controlled separations. Fundamental study of distillation, extraction, adsorption, membrane separation & chromatography processes.

courses.title: Chemical And Biological Engineering Laboratory
courses.desc: Open-ended laboratory projects in an area of applied and industrial interest of chemical and biological engineering. Students work in groups and choose one project for the whole term. They are asked to not only analyze the results of a given experiment but also decide what are the important experiments to perform as part of their overall plan to bring their project to a successful conclusion Oral presentations and written reports are an integral part of this laboratory course.

courses.title: Product & Process Design
courses.desc: This is a capstone design course covering the principles of design and economic evaluation through the preliminary design of a commercial project related to a product or a process. Working in groups on assigned or selected portions of the overall project , students are required to make integrated use of a wide variety of fundamentals and principles gained from previous courses. Computational laboratories are supplemented by lectures. Use of design software.

courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: Preparation of a report based on personal research, design, or experiment.Please see departmental website for specific details.
