courses.title: Honors Thesis Research B
courses.desc: Supervised research in chemical and biological engineering leading to the completion of the undergraduate honors thesis. Please see the Departmental website for specific program details and qualification requirements.

instructors: Ayse Asatekin, Bin Wang, Daniel F Ryder, David L Kaplan, Graham Leverick, Hyunmin Yi, James Van Deventer, Kyongbum Lee, Manolis Tzanakakis, Matthew Panzer, Milo David Koretsky, Nathaniel Eagan, Nik Nair, Prashant Deshlahra, Qiaobing Xu, Soha Hassoun
sections.req: Requires completion of CHBE 0096 sequence A.

courses.title: Internship In Chemical & Biological Engineering
courses.desc:
A mentored professional experience in engineering at an off-site organization. The internship must conform to all the requirements of the School of Engineering Internship Program. The department will grant course credit for internships if all of the following conditions are met: 1) The project is approved in advance by the department, 2) a faculty mentor has supervisory and technical control of any work that receives credit, and 3) a written report is submitted that is evaluated by the faculty adviser and the outside institutional supervisor.
Recommendations: Junior or senior standing.

instructors: Ayse Asatekin, Bin Wang, Daniel F Ryder, David L Kaplan, Hyunmin Yi, James Van Deventer, Kyongbum Lee, Linda M Abriola, Manolis Tzanakakis, Matthew Panzer, Nik Nair, Prashant Deshlahra, Qiaobing Xu, Soha Hassoun

courses.title: Reactor Design
courses.desc: Treatment of chemical reaction equilibrium and kinetic fundamentals and application of them to the design of reactors. Topics include interpretation of reaction-rate data, establishment of reaction mechanism and rate-controlling steps, sizing, and optimization of reactors. Use of personal computer software is encouraged.

courses.title: Thermal-fluid Transport II
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ME 151) Multi-dimensional conduction. Transient conduction including moving boundary problems. External forced and natural convection. Internal forced and natural convection. Developing flows and transition to turbulence. Condensation and boiling heat transfer. Radiation and conjugate heat transfer involving radiation. Temperature and heat flux measurements. Numerical techniques.
Recommendations: ME 111 Thermal-Fluid Transport I or equivalent.

courses.title: Composite Materials
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ ME 116 & MSE 172) Fundamentals of design, manufacture, and analysis of composite materials. Fiber materials such as glass, kevlar and carbon fibers along with state-of-the-art thermoplastic and thermoset matrix materials. Rules of mixtures (ROM) to calculate transverse isotropic properties in laminae. Classical Lamination Theory (CLT) and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to calculate stress and strains in laminates. Case studies in aerospace. Hands-on experiences, such as vacuum bagging to manufacture and test composites. Team project.

courses.title: Protein Purification
courses.desc: Methods of purifying proteins at a large scale for therapeutic or industrial uses. Focus on unit operations found in a typical process flowsheet including centrifugation, membrane filtration, most modes of chromatography, and lyophilization. Topics include introduction to protein chemistry and analytical methods, effects of production host choice, and protein stability. Process economics, GMP operations and validation, and case studies of biotechnology industry separations.

courses.title: Molecular Biotechnology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BME 162 and BIO 162.) Key concepts of molecular biology and engineering aspects of biotechnology. Molecular biology, recombinant DNA techniques, immunology, cell biology, protein purification, sequencing, gene therapy, and bioethics with review and discussion of primary literature. Comprehensive technical paper on an emerging topic. Students may not receive credit for both BME/CHBE/BIO 162 and BME 33.
Recommendations: CHEM 1.

sections.req: BIO 13 and (Junior or Senior standing), or Graduate Standing

courses.title: Biomolecular Engineering and Design
courses.desc: Protein and nucleic acid engineering and design for applications in basic research, diagnostic and therapeutic development, and sustainable chemical production. Methods and theory including directed evolution, high throughput screening, antibody engineering, genetic code manipulation, nucleic acid nanotechnology, and computational strategies.

courses.title: Upstream Bioprocess Engineering
courses.desc: Mammalian cell cultivation for biomanufacturing of recombinant proteins, viral vectors and cells for therapies. Topics include cultured cell metabolism, genetic engineering and cell line development, media formulation, stoichiometry and kinetics of cell growth, nutrient consumption and product formation, oxygen transfer in bioreactors, cell culture data analysis, bioreactor scale-up, and bioprocess design. Recommended for those interested in combining basic biological knowledge and application of engineering principles to cellular biotechnology.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Drug Product Formulation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as BME 185) Fundamental concepts of proteins' physical and chemical stability as applied to developing dosage forms for clinical studies. The role of analytical assays and elements of Quality by Design.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Special Topics - Heterogeneous Catalysis
courses.desc: Guided individual study of an approved topic to develop the art of self-teaching. Appraisal of the student's knowledge in the approved area will be based on a written and/or oral examination. Arrangements with a department member are required by the student prior to registration in the course. For master's degree candidates. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Heterogeneous catalysts are essential for improving sustainability in chemical processes, reducing energy, waste, and costs. In this course we focus on understanding how these materials work, the tools we use to characterize them, and the use of kinetic modeling to bridge understandings of atomistic events in model systems to macroscopic behaviors in true reactors. We endeavor to span ranges of complexities with these methodologies, providing context for catalysis development across chemistry, chemical engineering, and broader disciplines. Students are expected to have prior basic knowledge of reaction kinetics, thermodynamics, and differential equations. Basic knowledge of programming in Python is ideal but not essential.

courses.title: Special Topics - Electrochemistry for Energy
courses.desc: Guided individual study of an approved topic to develop the art of self-teaching. Appraisal of the student's knowledge in the approved area will be based on a written and/or oral examination. Arrangements with a department member are required by the student prior to registration in the course. For master's degree candidates. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Introduction to the principles of electrochemistry and their application to energy storage and conversion devices such as batteries, fuel cells, and electrolyzers. Starting from basic circuit concepts, the course explains the operating voltage of a device in terms of its thermodynamic equilibrium voltage and the voltage losses from reaction kinetics, mass transport, and ohmic resistance. Students then apply this framework to interpret electroanalytical measurements, such as chronoamperometry, cyclic voltammetry, and impedance spectroscopy, and to analyze efficiency and degradation in practical devices. This course prepares students for research or industry careers in electrochemistry, with emphasis on applying fundamental knowledge to analyze and improve device performance.

courses.desc:

courses.title: General Chemistry I with Lab
courses.desc: Atomic and molecular structure, chemical nomenclature, the relation of structure and bonding to physical and chemical properties of matter, patterns of chemical reactions, stoichiometry, and thermochemistry. Two lectures, one laboratory, one recitation each week. Only one of CHEM 1, 11, or 16 may be counted for credit.

courses.title: General Chemistry II with Lab
courses.desc: Intermolecular forces and states of matter, properties of solutions, chemical kinetics and thermodynamics, physical and chemical equilibria, aqueous equilibria (acid-base, precipitation, and complex formation), electrochemistry, and introduction to organic chemistry (families of organic compounds and nomenclature). Additional topics may include environmental, nuclear, and coordination chemistry. Three lectures, one laboratory, one recitation each week. Prerequisite: CHEM 1, 11, 16, or instructor consent. Only one of CHEM 2 or 12 may be counted for credit.

courses.desc:
Introduction to chemical research. Discussion of current research in chemistry and related fields; suited for introductory chemistry students. Weekly presentations by different Tufts faculty members and guests.
Pass-Fail grading. Prerequisite: concurrent or prior enrollment in Chem 2 or 12.

courses.title: From The Big Bang To Humankind
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as BIO 6 and AST 6). An exploration of the origins of the Universe, the formation of Earth and its structure, the chemistry of life, the development of complex organisms, and the development of modern humans including evidence for the various ideas presented, the scientific method used by scientists, and how the community of scientists evaluate the evidence. This course does not fulfill pre-med requirements for a lab-based chemistry course.

courses.title: Chemistry Workshop
courses.desc: Small group working session for students enrolled in CHEM 1 led by a trained Learning Assistant. Students are invited to enroll after completing a diagnostic test in CHEM 1. Corequisite: CHEM 1

courses.desc:
Topics covered are the same as in Chemistry 2, but are discussed in greater detail and mathematical depth. For interested students who seek to engage deeply with chemical thinking. Three 75 min lectures; required co-enrollment in Chem 4 (Frontiers in Chemistry), one laboratory, one recitation.
Prerequisites: Chem 1 or Chem 11. Only one of Chemistry 2 or 12 may be counted for credit.

courses.desc: Advanced concepts in physical chemistry. Topics include reaction kinetics, with a focus on rates, mechanisms, and transition state theory and an in-depth study of quantum mechanics and its applications to spectroscopy and the determination of atomic and molecular structures. Prerequisites: CHEM 2 or 12; MATH 34; and PHY 2 or 12; or instructor permission. Physics may be taken concurrently.

sections.req: Chem 2 or 12, AND (Math 34 or equivalent) AND (PHY 2 or 12 or SOE). Physics may be taken concurrently.

courses.title: Physical Chemistry Lab II
courses.desc:
Advanced course providing opportunities for guided original research. Small group work to propose, develop, and perform research related to one of the four core areas of physical chemistry: quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, or kinetics and dynamics. Prerequisite: CHEM 31,
CHEM 32 or concurrent registration in CHEM 32, or instructor permission.

sections.req: CHEM 31, CHEM 32 or concurrent registration in CHEM 32, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Biophysical Chemistry
courses.desc: Fundamental principles of modern physical chemistry, applied to the structure and dynamics of biomolecules. Molecular thermodynamics, kinetics, and statistical mechanics; protein structure and stability, protein folding, molecular binding processes; and experimental and computational techniques used to study biomolecular systems. Note that CHEM 35 can be used to satisfy requirements only for the Biochemistry Major, but not for the ACS-Certified Chemistry, Chemistry, or Chemical Physics Majors. Prerequisites: CHEM 2 or 12, MATH 32, and PHY 1 or 11, or instructor permission.

sections.req: CHEM 2 or 12, MATH 32, and PHY 1 or 11

courses.title: Quantitative Analysis
courses.desc:
Introduction to the methods and scientific basis of quantitative analysis including sampling, error & statistical analyses, data treatment & presentation, basic concepts and operation of chromatographic, electroanalytical, and spectroscopic instrumentation. For chemistry and life science majors, as well as students enrolled in environmental studies and engineering. The course will provide students in chemistry or any related discipline with the necessary foundation, understanding, and basic tools for doing good science. Two lectures, two laboratories. One and one-half courses.
Requires completion of CHEM 0002 or CHEM 0012.

courses.title: Organic Chemistry I
courses.desc: Structure, bonding, conformational analysis, functional groups, and stereochemistry. Organic reactions, synthesis, and mechanisms including acid/base reactions, nucleophilic substitutions and eliminations, reactions of alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and their derivatives, and amines. Additional topics may include tools for structure determination: nuclear magnetic resonance and infrared spectroscopy. (Note: The laboratory course, CHEM 53, is normally taken concurrently with CHEM 51.) Prerequisites: CHEM 2 or 12.

courses.desc: Continuation of CHEM 51. Structure, properties, and reactions of alkenes, alkynes, ethers, epoxides, conjugated unsaturated systems, and aromatic compounds. Radical reactions. Additional topics may include the chemistry of carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids, nucleic acids, and organometallic reactions. (Note: The laboratory course, CHEM 54, is usually normally taken concurrently with CHEM 52.) Prerequisites: CHEM 51

courses.title: Atomic Scale Structure and Properties of Surfaces
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ MSE 128) Foundational concepts relevant to surface and interfacial chemistry, with a focus on solid surfaces. Topics include surface and adsorbate structure (both geometric and electronic), adsorbate bonding motifs (including chemisorption and physisorption), thermodynamics, kinetics and dynamics of adsorption and reaction, heterogeneous catalysis, and impacts of surface modification on reactivity. Prerequisite: Chemistry 31 or instructor's consent.

courses.title: Instrumental Analysis
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with MSE 124) Theory, operation, and application of principal instruments used in chemical analysis and research. Selected special topics such as molecular, atomic, and mass spectroscopies; electrochemistry; and chromatography. Designed to acquaint the student with modern laboratory techniques used in all areas of chemistry. Student-designed projects incorporating analytical metrics of precision, accuracy, selectivity, and sensitivity as well as experimental design and hypothesis development that relate theory to experimental data. Recommendations: CHEM 31, 41 or 43, and 51, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Advanced Analytical Methods
courses.desc: Student-led case studies of modern analytical instrumentation and its application to chemically-related problems in a broad variety of research areas such as environmental, materials, biomedical, etc. In-depth oral and written presentations based on recently published literature. Recommendations: Chemistry 41, 43, or 141, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Advanced Organic Synthesis
courses.desc: Techniques and strategies for the synthesis of complex molecules. Mechanism and scope of new bond-forming methods and functional group transformations. Can be taken independently, concurrently, or in sequence with CHEM 0150. Prerequisite: CHEM 0052 or graduate standing.

courses.title: Molecular Medicine
courses.desc: Molecular mechanism and structural analysis of compounds useful in human medicine. Introduces the biochemistry of a system relevant to a particular disease indication, then focuses on the detailed interaction of chemo(bio)therapeutic agents with the biological system. Material drawn principally from the primary literature. Topics may include antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal agents; anti-cancer compounds; and molecules affecting immunity, inflammation, metabolic syndrome, and neurodegenerative conditions. Prerequisites: CHEM 171 and CHEM 52, or graduate standing.

sections.req: CHEM 171 and CHEM 52, or graduate standing

courses.title: Organometallic Chemistry

courses.title: Professional Skills in Chemical Research, Training and Learning
courses.desc: This two-semester course provides instruction and training in "soft skills" critical to students' professional success in chemical research and teaching. Topics include: successful TAing, selecting a research group, finding mentors, scientific writing, efficient experimentation strategies, public speaking, approaches for study topic and original proposal success, literature management, thesis preparation, communication of science to the public, careers in science, involvement in the local scientific community and outreach. Responsible conduct of research (RCR) issues such as: conflicts of interest, responsible authorship and peer review, research misconduct, collaborative science, and data acquisition and management are also covered as part of this course. These topics are discussed in the context of chemistry research and the Tufts Chemistry Doctoral Program. Assessment includes Q&A sessions and case study based quizzes. Chem 291 (Fall) and Chem 292 (Spring) comprise a two-semester course sequence required for all Chemistry doctoral students.

The student must satisfy the CIS board that the topic falls outside the purview of any department or interdisciplinary program and that significant course work and/or faculty directed research relevant to the thesis topic has been accomplished. The student must assemble a committee of three faculty readers with expertise in the disciplines involved, one of whom is designated as the chair of the committee and who is responsible for submitting a grade and designating the amount of credit for the thesis course work.One member of the committee must be from a department or program in which the student is majoring. The topic must be approved by the CIS board no later than the end of the first week of classes in the first semester of the student¿s senior year. Students who would like to be recommended for degrees with honors by departments that require a thesis should be aware that these departments require a thesis within their own department and a CIS thesis will not usually count as a substitute. However, students may apply for a CIS thesis to count as an honors thesis in the Thesis Honors Program like a thesis in any other discipline by assembling a thesis committee and filing the appropriate paperwork. If the CIS thesis is to qualify as an honors thesis, the chair of the thesis committee must be from a department or program in which the student is majoring.For more detailed information, please visit the Web site http://ase.tufts.edu/cis/.

The student must satisfy the CIS board that the topic falls outside the purview of any department or interdisciplinary program and that significant course work and/or faculty directed research relevant to the thesis topic has been accomplished. The topic must be approved by the CIS board no later than the end of the first week of classes in the first semester of the student¿s senior year. Students who would like to be recommended for degrees with honors by departments that require a thesis should be aware that these departments require a thesis within their own department and a CIS thesis will not usually count as a substitute. However, students may apply for a CIS thesis to count as an honors thesis in the Thesis Honors Program like a thesis in any other discipline by assembling a thesis committee and filing the appropriate paperwork. If the CIS thesis is to qualify as an honors thesis, the chair of the thesis committee must be from a department or program in which the student is majoring.For more detailed information, please visit the Web site http://ase.tufts.edu/cis/.

courses.title: Classical Archaeology - Civilizations of Mediterranean
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 27, HAA 19, and ILVS 27.) Survey of ancient Greco-Roman civilization spanning c. 3,100 BCE to 565 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: sculpture, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, sociopolitical organization, and artistic technique. Examination of the development and collapse of the Bronze Age civilizations of the Aegean and Italy. Exploration of the evidence of cultural transformations driven by trade, colonization, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the city-state in archaic Greece and Italy, then to the Greek-speaking kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, and finally to the inclusion of the Latins, Etruscans, Greeks, Egyptians, and others within a single multicultural state: the Roman Empire. Assessment of the renegotiation of identities and historical narratives as polytheistic religions were supplanted by Christianity within the Roman state. Field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Ancient China, Korea, and Japan
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 28) Survey of the ancient cultures of China, Korea, and Japan from g . 2,100 BCE to 907 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: social rituals, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Excursions into sociopolitical organization, religion, diplomacy, philosophy, writing systems, and artistic technique. Evidence of cultural transformations and renegotiations of identity driven by trade, colonization, diplomacy, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the state in ancient China, and finally to the evolution of a world system that interconnected the kingdoms and peoples of East Asia, as well as the many cultures linked by the Silk Routes: from the Yangshao culture to the Shang state, the first unification of China under the Qin emperor, to the Han and Tang periods, Gojoseon, Goguryeo, then the Jomon, Yayoi, and Kofun period Japan. Includes a field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Roman Literature: Texts and Contexts
courses.desc: A survey of Latin literature in translation, with particular attention to its origins, generic forms and their socio-political function, and the way literature helps define and reflect—but also challenge—Roman cultural identity.

courses.title: History Of Ancient Rome
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 51) The history of ancient Rome, tracing Rome's rise from an insignificant Italian community to the ruler of the Mediterranean world, and ending with the transfer of the imperial capital to Constantinople in A.D. 330. Emphasis on the interaction of Rome with various foreign peoples, and examination of literary and documentary sources.

courses.title: Paradoxes and Dilemmas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 40) Introduction to fundamental themes in logic, epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. Paradoxes and dilemmas are frequently associated with moments of crisis and groundbreaking developments in the history of philosophy, as they lead to questions about basic presuppositions. Analysis of famous cases in the history of Western thought from Antiquity to the present including Meno’s paradox (knowledge), Zeno’s paradoxes (space, time, motion, and the infinite), the Euthyphro dilemma (justification), the liar paradox (truth), the Heap (vagueness), the Ship of Theseus (identity), Antigone (moral conflict), the voting paradox (choice), and the prisoner’s dilemma (action).

courses.title: Greek And Roman Comedy
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 29.) Study of plays of Aristophanes, Menander, Plautus, and Terence and the contexts in which they are performed. (May be taken at the 100-level.)

courses.title: Introduction to the New Testament
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as REL 22) Study of the origins of Christianity and the evolution of its earliest beliefs and practices, as reflected in the writings ultimately selected for its canon. Jesus and his interpreters, Paul and his letters, beginnings of the church, interaction between Christians and their jewish and Greco-Roman enviroments, women's paticipation in the shaping of early Christian history. Occasional readings from non-canonical literature to add perspectives.

courses.title: Passion, Power, & Piety: The Voices of Byzantium
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 156) Evolution of Byzantine history and literature through the voices of the Byzantines themselves, in their histories, novels, hagiographies, the great heroic epic Digenes Akrites (the Two-Blood Border Lord), the amusing if somewhat ribald Amazing Tale of Quadrupeds, and others, from the 4th century AD to the end of the empire. How Byzantine literature draws from Greek, Roman, Christian, Near Eastern, Islamic, and Judaic influences to construct a new identity, a world view neither "Eastern" nor "Western" but rather a complex fusion.

courses.title: Empresses, Saints, & Scholars: The Women Of Byzantium
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 157). Examination of the themes of political legitimacy, spirituality, education, gender roles, the spread of Byzantine culture, and the evolution of Christian theology through a careful study of the lives of various women of the Byzantine world. This will include examination of the lives of women of the Byzantine Empire, Southeastern Europe, Russia, Western Europe, the kingdoms of Armenia and the Ottoman Empire.

courses.title: Introduction to Geospatial Humanities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 175, HIST 179, and UEP 103) Geographic Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods, and technology for applications in the humanities in past and present settings. Topics include GIS data creation and data structures, geodesy, spatial analysis, and cartographic visualization. Includes extensive laboratory exercises to apply concepts presented in the lectures using a variety of GIS software and tools. Assignments concentrate on application of concepts covered in lectures and exercises and include a final project that applies GIS to each student’s field of interest.

courses.title: Epics of the Ancient World: A Comparative Approach
courses.desc: A comparative study of ancient epics from Greece, Rome, the ancient Near East, India, and Tibet exploring the narrative qualities and socio-political functions that define the epic genre. Epos and oral poetry, bards and sacred poets, epic as history, epic and national identity, heroes and heroines, wives and enchantresses, fate and gods, epic and anti-epic, and their reflection in modern movies and video games. Readings may include selections from Gilgamesh, The Iliad, The Odyssey, The Epic of Gezar, Ramayana, The Aeneid, Shahnameh, and Cú Chulainn's.

courses.title: Greeks And Barbarians
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as HIST 149). Exploration of the unsettling and stimulating cross-cultural encounters of Greeks with other peoples of the ancient world, leading both to the Greeks' discovery of themselves-the formulation of a Greek "cultural identity"-and to expanding knowledge of the wider world. Attention to contacts and conflicts with Cretans, Trojans, Phoenicians, Egyptians, and Romans, with emphasis on the seminal, two-century-long, encounter of the Greek city-states with the mighty Persian Empire. Sources include the accounts of Greek poets, historians, explorers, and playwrights, documents from the Persian Empire, and images of ancient artifacts and sites such as Athens, Persepolis, and Alexandria.
Recommendations: CLS 31 or 37.

courses.title: Women In Greek Mythology
courses.desc: Study of legendary and mythical female figures with emphasis on identifying characterizations and roles for these figures and assessment of how their representation enhances female stature, as it informs and supports cultural identity at various historical times. Exploration of how ancient authors and artists represent the female experience generally: matriarchy, misogyny, martyrdom, marriage, gender-specific cults, athletics, and election in various vocations.

courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Ancient Christianity
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ WGSS 160 and REL 160) Examination of gender and sexuality in the ancient Mediterranean, with special attention to how issues of gender and sexuality are treated in the New Testament, in early Church Fathers, Hebrew Bible, martyrdom accounts, and hagiography (saints’ lives). courses.title: Natural Language Processing and the Human Record
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as DH 130) Review of state-of-the-art research in the Digital Humanities and development of collaborative research projects. Emphasis on how new technologies can engage a diverse and multilingual global audience with the past, with a particular focus on the applications of natural language processing and a range of visualization techniques to the human record. Course projects combine code with an analysis of its impact. Programming skills required. Prerequisites: CS 10 or CS 11 or CLS 161, or instructor permission

courses.desc: North Africa (the Maghreb) from the Bronze Age to the end of Antiquity. New perspectives on the social, economic, cultural, and political history and archaeology of North Africa.

courses.title: Principles of Epidemiology and Inferential Statistics II
courses.desc: This course introduces the fundamentals of biostatistics with mindful integration of epidemiologic concepts. Using peer reviewed publications as a starting point, you will learn these concepts by deconstructing the results and exploring the underlying concepts, mechanisms, and techniques. And then, to further strengthen our understanding, together we will practice by replicating the analyses using the statistical software, Stata, and real-world data sets. Through a blend of theory and practical application, you will develop the essential skills needed to critically analyze health-related data, understand the design, interpretation, and reporting of epidemiological studies, and make evidence-based decisions in public health research.

courses.title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
courses.desc: Negotiation is a strategic means of managing differences or arriving at consensus among two or more willing parties with the goal of arriving at a mutual agreement. This course will begin with separate overviews of negotiation and conflict resolution - in the workplace and beyond. After the introduction, the first 3 sessions will focus on conflict resolution. This includes conflict in the workplace, in school, and within the home and community. Conflict theory will be combined with in-class practice. Sessions 4 through 7 will focus on negotiation skills as a means of both resolving conflict but also conducting business. In all sessions, we’ll address the common themes of effective communication, emotional intelligence, and meticulous preparation. Every session will integrate practice with theory. A final paper will be based upon an understanding of strategies for building strategic skills that can be applied broadly.

courses.title: Case Studies in One Health
courses.desc:
This course examines the interconnected health and sustainability challenges of our time, including emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and climate change, through a One Health lens. Using case studies and interactive breakout sessions, students will apply a socioecological perspective to explore the interdependence of human, other animal, and environmental health, with an emphasis on systems thinking and transdisciplinary collaboration to solve complex challenges. 

Students will be introduced to current discourse on One Health governance and practical analytical tools, including stakeholder analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis, fuzzy cognitive mapping, and gender analysis. Students are evaluated through a variety of methods, including class participation, a One Health blog post, and group presentation.

courses.title: Ebb and Flow of Public Health and Healthcare in Maine
courses.desc: This course is designed to help MD/MPH students explore the public health landscape in Maine and its overlaps and gaps with the healthcare landscape in Maine. The course is spread out over the 2nd and 3rd years of training. Each semester, students will participate in a series of approximately monthly sessions facilitated by the faculty instructor. Some sessions may include guest speakers. In between the monthly sessions there may be homework assignments to prepare for the next in-person session. This homework may involve reading articles, reviewing websites, watching recorded webinars, and/or posting to the course discussion post on Canvas. There will also be 1-2 graded assignments per year. Collectively, the in-person sessions, homework, graded assignments, and guest speakers are designed to expose students to intersections of public health and healthcare in Maine.

courses.title: Minority Women's Reproductive Health
courses.desc: This course focuses on the critical evaluation of key research and issues surrounding minority women's reproductive health. The course content is strategically designed to highlight and examine historical factors shaping the well-being of minority women. Students will engage with historical perspectives to better comprehend the roots of existing health disparities and their lasting impacts on minority women's reproductive health. Emphasizing racial and ethnic disparities, the course delves into the intricate intersectionality of race, ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status, providing a comprehensive exploration of the factors influencing reproductive health outcomes for minority women in the United States.

courses.title: Talk Less, Listen More: Understanding Personal & Population Perspectives Through Qualitative Methods
courses.desc: This course prepares future physician leaders to use qualitative methods to understand the needs and experiences of individuals and communities and to apply those insights to the design, implementation, evaluation, and improvement of health services and public health programs. Through learning how to gather and analyze stakeholder perspectives, students will develop skills for identifying barriers to service utilization, understanding community priorities, evaluating program implementation, and designing interventions that are acceptable, accessible, and effective. Emphasis is placed on the gathering and application of qualitative data to better decision-making in public health practice and as part of health services research, program evaluation, and health system improvement. Examples will mostly draw on research done outside the USA, to emphasize understanding unfamiliar perspectives such as those of immigrants. However, the course is intended to be of use for students working with any different or unfamiliar population. This course will be offered in-person, over 3 full days (Friday, Saturday, and Sunday) in a workshop format. All students, including Maine-track students, are required to attend in-person.

courses.desc: This course will explore the application of leadership skills in the community health setting. This course helps physician leaders move from diagnosing isolated problems to leading complex systems. Each session will begin with a realistic healthcare dilemma. Learners will define the decision, analyze the organization, weigh trade-offs, recommend action, and design implementation. During each session, learners will apply a relevant leadership framework to the case. Learners will complete the course with a toolkit of skills that they can use as a clinical leader in the future. This course will be taught by current MD and MD/MPH practicing clinicians and will also aim to demonstrate the practical application of public health concepts as a physician leader.

courses.title: Machine Learning via Sequential Interaction
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as EE 140) Introduction of machine learning as a sequential and interactive game technically referred to as 'online learning'. In online learning, the learner aims to minimize the regret: loss incurred for not playing the best strategy (in hindsight) averaged over time. This framework generalizes the traditional statistical learning set-up in a non-trivial manner to cases where the examples are not independent, are supplied only sequentially, and possibly in an adversarial manner. Topics include: general set-up of sequential learning with examples, online convex and online linear optimization, online-to-batch conversion, multi-armed bandits, contextual bandits, practical algorithms and their analysis with provable guarantees. Connections with and extensions to reinforcement learning will be highlighted. Prior programming experience is recommended.

courses.title: Special Topics - Randomness and Computation
courses.desc: Content and prerequisites to be announced. sections.note:
In this course we will explore the role of randomness in computations with an emphasis on theoretical aspects of computer science. We will develop foundations in discrete probability, including conditional probability and expectation, and introduce the probabilistic method. We will study concentration inequalities and their applications to algorithm analysis and computational complexity, as well as basic concepts from information theory. The course will also introduce pseudorandomness and derandomization: how deterministic constructions can reproduce useful properties of randomness, and when randomness can be eliminated from computational procedures.

This course is suitable both for students who have not taken a probability course and for those who have taken an introductory probability course. From the beginning of the course, we will explore topics and applications that go beyond standard introductory probability courses, while developing the necessary probability foundations.

Prerequisite: CS/MATH 61 or graduate standing or permission by instructor. 

MATH 70 is recommended. CS 160 and CS 170 are helpful, but not required.

courses.title: Special Topics in Data Infrastructure and Systems - Anonymous Communications Theor
courses.desc: A special topics course in data infrastructures and systems, suitable for fulfilling requirements of the Bachelor of Science in Data Science.

sections.note: We know how to communicate a message so that only the recipient can read the message. (We can encrypt the message.) But how can we communicate over the Internet without anyone learning who we are communicating with? Anonymous channels can help the Iranian protester who wishes to inform the world what is happening in the streets of Tehran by tweeting videos and the netizen in Moscow who wants to read the BBC news (currently banned in Russia). We could use Tor (i.e., “The onion router,” inspired by Chaum's onion routing idea) or VPN, but both are easily blocked, and neither guarantees privacy from the adversary with a full view of the network traffic (e.g., a standard model for a resourceful ISP- or AS-level adversary). In this course, we present cryptography-style definitions of anonymity and study state-of-the-art techniques for achieving provable anonymity.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computational and Theoretical Aspects of Data Science - Generative AI for Social Impact
courses.desc: A special topics course in computational and theoretical aspects of data science, suitable for fulfilling requirements of the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science or Bachelor of Science in Data Science. Refer to the Class Notes for the description and prerequisites (if any) for each specific section of this course.

sections.note:
This course examines the growing role of generative AI in addressing critical social challenges, including healthcare, accessibility, education, development, and civic engagement, with a particular focus on marginalized communities. Through case studies and real-world applications, students explore when and whether AI can meaningfully address these challenges, the risks it introduces, and who benefits or is harmed.

Students develop a working understanding of generative AI technologies, including prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic workflows, and guardrails, alongside practical approaches to designing, customizing, and evaluating AI applications. The course emphasizes human-centered design and evaluation, examining both the technical performance of AI systems and their impact on individuals and communities.

The course follows a studio-based format, combining hands-on activities, mini-projects, peer feedback, and a semester-long group project involving needs assessment, iterative design, and evaluation. Projects will address real-world challenges, with opportunities for students to collaborate with external partners, including community organizations, nonprofits, and public agencies. The recommended programming language for projects is Python.
Prerequisites: CS 15 or equivalent programming experience for the Developer Track; no programming prerequisite for the Evaluator Track.

Developer and Evaluator Tracks. The course welcomes students from diverse academic backgrounds through two complementary tracks. Students in the Developer Track focus on designing and implementing generative AI applications, while those in the Evaluator Track focus on assessing their capabilities, limitations, risks, and real-world impact. Both tracks engage with the same core concepts and are held to rigorous expectations appropriate to their learning objectives. Students are encouraged to collaborate across tracks on their final projects, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of developing AI for social impact.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computational and Theoretical Aspects of Data Science - Multi-agent Systems
courses.desc: A special topics course in computational and theoretical aspects of data science, suitable for fulfilling requirements of the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science or Bachelor of Science in Data Science. Refer to the Class Notes for the description and prerequisites (if any) for each specific section of this course.

sections.note:
Everyone's hyping ""Agentic AI"", but most can't even define what an agent is. This course cuts through the buzz, giving you the foundations and frontiers of multi-agent systems: from game theory and multi-agent planning to LLMs as agents, theory of mind, and intelligent disobedience. By the end of this course, you should be able to: 1. Define a multi-agent system problem in a new domain and offer suitable solution approaches. 2. Identify to what extent an ""Agentic AI"" is truly agentic, and how it might be improved. 3. Implement various frameworks of multiple agents.
Prerequisite: Prior completion of CS 131

courses.title: Special Topics in Computational and Theoretical Aspects of Data Science - Reasoning Theorem Proving & AI
courses.desc: A special topics course in computational and theoretical aspects of data science, suitable for fulfilling requirements of the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science or Bachelor of Science in Data Science. Refer to the Class Notes for the description and prerequisites (if any) for each specific section of this course.

sections.note:
Full title: Reasoning, Theorem Proving & AI
Modern AI systems are radically changing software engineering and programming. They can generate massive amounts of code in seconds —- but how do we know it is correct? This hands-on seminar course explores how proof assistants, automated reasoning, and modern AI can help us build reliable software. We will learn the Lean programming language and proof assistant, which supports precise and mechanically verifiable reasoning. We will also study the “good old-fashioned AI” algorithms behind automated theorem provers, including algorithms for Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). Finally, we will explore how AI/LLM agents can support and amplify rigorous, mechanical, and automated reasoning in various domains. Using these tools, we will reason about program behavior and develop programs with correctness guarantees.
Pre-reqs: CS 105 and CS 61 highly recommended

courses.title: Special Topics in Social Context of Computing - Algorithmic Auditing
courses.desc: ABET CAC requires us to include more social context in our curriculum, and this course provides a vehicle for such interaction, by allowing us to cross-list specific courses in A&S and Fletcher as satisfying that requirement via this number. Thus, this number can be used to change the description of the BSCS to include social context courses as required by ABET. We desire both undergraduate-only and undergraduate/graduate numbers for this option, depending upon course level.

sections.note: What does it mean for an algorithm to be racist? Is it possible to prevent chatbots from promoting emotional dependency? Can we even reasonably audit frontier AI models? This course explores the intersection of law, public policy, and algorithmic harm. We will explore the meaning of the phrase “anti-discrimination policy” in hiring, insurance, credit, or housing in the age of algorithms, and we will design AI regulation from the perspective of an enforcement agency. Recommendations: Basic knowledge of Python and statistics.

courses.title: How Systems Fail
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ DHP D293) Graduate version of CS 27. Failure of computer systems within the larger context of complex systems, including the power grid and aviation. Failures of algorithms and protocols, engineering and implementation, systems and applications, people and culture. Attacks, attack recovery, security, privacy, and attribution. Case studies of failures and attacks, including distributed denial of service, Meltdown, Spectre, and spear-phishing attacks.

courses.desc:
Part one of a two-course, hands-on, and project-based culmination to
the Master of Science in Computer Science Online program. Application of principles, strategies, methods, and tools for requirements analysis and design of a programming project, including project planning, project management, and proof of concept prototyping. Science in Computer Science Online program.

Presentation of final project results and documentation. To be taken in the last term of the Master of Science in Computer Science Online degree. Not available to students outside that program. 
Prerequisites: CS 288, and enrollment in the Master of Science in Computer Science Online program.

courses.title: Introduction to Child Study and Human Development
courses.desc: A survey of child development from infancy through adolescence. The course covers the major cognitive, physiological, emotional, and social changes that occur during this period. Midterm and final exams; observation and testing reports. Required for majors.

courses.title: Children, Nature, and the Development of Earth Stewards
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 34, CVS 32, ED 34, and CSHD 234) Understanding how children and youth develop as earth stewards in the 21st century in the context of environmental breakdown, environmental injustice, and widespread disconnection from nature. Focus is on frameworks, methods, and programs for fostering ecological literacy and earth stewardship among children and youth.

courses.title: Inquiry and Analysis in Child Study and Human Development
courses.desc: Introduction to the logic and processes of inquiry in health, well-being, and development as it relates to developmental science research and to clinical and educational settings where clinicians, teachers, and other practitioners puzzle about particular children and families needing help. Provides students with an opportunity to consider in depth the questions that guide any systematic inquiry related to the health, well-being, and development of children and families. Required for majors.

sections.req: CSHD majors and minors only-NON CSHD students need Instr. Permission.

courses.title: Senior Thesis Workshop
courses.desc: Course open to all senior thesis writers, aiming to create a supportive community at all stages of thesis work. Idea exchange, strategies, and peer support throughout the process, complementing guidance from thesis advisors. Prerequisite: Approved Senior Thesis proposal and instructor permission.

courses.title: Childhood Across Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/AAST 62 and LST 62) Intermediate-level study of child development, with emphasis on cultural perspectives integrating psychological and anthropological theory. Children's development examined across cultures and in the context of the various social institutions and settings within which they live.

sections.attrs: BFA-Language/Culture|BFA-Social Science|LA-Distribution-Social Sciences|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Social Sciences|World Civilization Requirement

courses.title: Community Field Placement
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 88) Work and study in programs serving children, youth, and families, including programs addressing environmental education, children’s media, children’s mental and physical health, juvenile justice, child advocacy, and special education. Prerequisite: Consent. Fall/Spring.

courses.title: Autism Across the Lifespan
courses.desc: How the social model of disability impacts care and stigma for neurodivergent and autistic individuals from birth through old age; accessibility of services and systems. Majority of readings and guest lectures by self-advocates. Prerequisites: CSHD 01, PSY 01, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Completion of CSHD 0001 or PSY 0001 or Grad Standing

courses.title: Children, Arts, and Media
courses.desc: A foundation for understanding how various forms of art (visual arts, music, poetry, dance, theatre, literature) and media literacy can play a central role in supporting children’s development, in helping children thrive even in challenging circumstances, and in making for a more just and inclusive world for children.

courses.title: Assessment of Children
courses.desc:
Practicum seminar on applied comprehensive, developmental assessments of children. Testing procedures, clinical observations, interview techniques, and written reports. Topics such as learning disabilities, autism, ADHD, mental health and the impact of disabilities on education with case examples and practice assessments. 
Prerequisite: graduate status or permission of instructor

sections.req: Graduate students only; undergraduates require instructor permission

courses.title: Working w/Communities: Research-Practice Integration
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 142) Working in partnership with communities is a different approach than working in communities. Explores frameworks for socially just research and practice conducted in collaboration with ethnoculturally diverse communities and responsive to the community issues and needs identified by members of that particular community.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Exploring Deaf Communities
courses.desc: An introduction to the diverse Deaf communities, exploring their cultural, linguistic, and social foundations. Enduring strengths and persistent challenges faced by these communities. Topics include cultural identity; language and communication; history and milestones; social and political issues; educational perspectives; arts and contributions; and technology and accessibility. Analyzing cultural conflicts from multiple perspectives. Skills needed to be effective allies and partners with Deaf, DeafBlind, and hard-of-hearing individuals. No prerequisites.

courses.title: American Sign Language I
courses.desc: The first in a series of courses on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL), the language that is widely used by Deaf and DeafBlind Americans. Immersion approach to language learning Emphasizes basic expressive and receptive conversational skills. Includes basic ASL vocabulary, grammatical structures, and conversational behaviors, storytelling, and an introduction to American Deaf culture and DeafBlind communication. Attendance at events in the Deaf and DeafBlind communities is required. High demand (see "class notes" for signup procedure).

courses.title: American Sign Language II
courses.desc: Second in a series of courses on the use and study of American Sign Language (ASL). Emphasizes basic expressive and receptive conversational skills through active student participation. Storytelling is included. Special emphasis on developing more awareness of the cultural values and beliefs shared by the Deaf and DeafBlind Communities. Attendance at events in the Deaf and DeafBlind communities is required. Prerequisite: ASL 124 or ASL Placement Test or instructor permission.

courses.title: American Sign Language III
courses.desc: Third in a series of courses on the use and study of ASL. Includes intermediate ASL vocabulary, grammatical structures, storytelling, and conversational behaviors. Students will develop ASL presentations to increase communicative fluency. Special emphasis on awareness of the cultural values and beliefs shared by the Deaf and DeafBlind communities. Attendance at events in the Deaf and DeafBlind communities is required. Prerequisite: ASL 125 or ASL Placement Test or instructor permission.

courses.title: Introductory Statistics for Developmental Science
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LEAD 273) Foundational statistics concepts and procedures including measures of central tendency and dispersion, relationships between continuous and categorical variables, and hypothesis specification and testing. Use of computer programs for analysis, data interpretation, and reporting results. Prerequisites: Junior, senior, or graduate status or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Research Methods and Design for Developmental
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LEAD 261) Introduction to research design and field and laboratory methods relevant to research in developmental science. Topics may include designs for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods research; measurement of behavior; reliability, validity, and generalizability of findings; and ethics. Analysis and evaluation of research studies and preparation of a literature review and a research proposal. Prerequisites: Senior or graduate status or permission of instructor.

courses.desc: Group seminar study of an approved topic that is not covered by a regular course in the department. Please contact the department for detailed information.

courses.title: Special Topics - Dev. in Digital Contexts: AI
courses.desc: Group seminar study of an approved topic that is not covered by a regular course in the department. Please contact the department for detailed information.

courses.desc: Group seminar study of an approved topic that is not covered by a regular course in the department. Please contact the department for detailed information.

courses.title: Physiology of Human Development
courses.desc: Biological and physiological processes that underlie human development with emphasis on childhood and adolescence. How children’s nervous systems, hormones, immune systems, and brain functioning are in part shaped by their environmental experiences and play a role in shaping their development across time. Prerequisites: CSHD 0001 or graduate standing. Recommendations: CSHD 061 or 161.

sections.req: CSHD 0001 or PSY 0001 or grad student.

courses.title: Evidence-Based Interventions with Children and Youth
courses.desc:
Examines the science of evidence-based prevention and intervention, including theoretical underpinnings, implementation, assessment, transportability and generalizability to other populations. Covers interventions targeting problems such as such as poor parenting, developmental delays, conduct problems, bullying, substance abuse and others. 
Recommendations: CSHD 191 and grad/senior status or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Children's Television Project Research Lab
courses.desc: Representation in current children’s animated programming through participation in the Children’s Television Project (CTV), a research program in the Eliot-Pearson Department of Child Study and Human Development. Training in CTV coding instruments prepares students to code, cleaning, and analyzing the data sample of the CTV project. Bibliographic research and discussions about children’s televisual media and its importance in the development of children’s attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors. Examines representations of race, ethnicity, gender, age, and other demographic characteristics across popular children’s television shows. Offered for either two or three credits. Students who enroll in the course for three credits will complete a final written project. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Development Of Language
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LING 155). Human language is examined as a form of communication and compared with animal signal systems. Other topics are phonological, syntactic, and semantic development; language, culture, and thought; language and social class; and language and bilingualism.

courses.title: Advanced Personal-Social Development
courses.desc: This course deals with personality and social development from infancy through adolescence. Topics to be covered include continuity in development, attachment, sex-role development, empathy and friendship, social cognition, and moral development. A combination chronological/topical approach will be followed.

sections.req: Completion of CSHD 0001 or PSY 0001 or Grad Standing

courses.title: Creating Children’s Media
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 141 and CVS 184) Exploration of book-to-film transitions, creation of scripts for children’s television programs, podcasts for children, development of storyboards for ad campaigns, and proposals for apps, and other digital content for children. Application of child development, media literacy and civic engagement theories, and strategies for storytelling in children’s media content across media platforms. Student projects on pitching, scriptwriting, and other topics.

courses.title: Introduction to Art Therapy
courses.desc: Overview of the history, theory and practice of art therapy from an intersectional perspective. Understand the integration of the creative and therapeutic processes. Explore the complexity of human life and behavior within a historical, cultural, social, and personal context. Analyze case studies of diverse populations and engage in doing art to examine the process of how tools, media, and expression impact healing, resilience, self-awareness, identity, social justice, and transformation. Use drawing materials, papers, paints, collage materials, assemblages, 3D materials, fibers, carving, and casting and their applications to real life, including specific clinical and community settings. Study the dimensions of form, shape, color and texture of various materials that stimulate, structure, and organize artistic expression. Integrate personal practice and experience with assigned readings, discussions, and hands-on activities, fostering self-awareness and an understanding of others and the surrounding world.

courses.title: Children's Literature
courses.desc: Analysis of literature for children from preschool age to early teens from developmental-learning and literary perspectives. Final project: story or book for children, or critique/analysis of some genre or issue of children's literature.

courses.title: Child Art
courses.desc: The nature and developmental implications of the art of the young child, with emphasis on the ways in which cognitive and expressive factors influence the artistic process. Consideration of appropriate materials and activities for preschool and elementary-school-age children. Studio work is an integral part of the course.

courses.title: Advanced Seminar in Resilience: Children, Youth and Trauma
courses.desc: Seminar focuses on resilience in development; the potential for children, families, and communities to do well in the context of trauma and the responsibility of communities to provide resources that foster resilient functioning in meaningful ways. Topics include neurological basis of adaptation in the context of adverse and protective experiences; and individual, family, school, neighborhood, community assets that foster resilience. Will include discussion of prevention and intervention programs and policies. PREREQUISITE: Graduate Students and junior and seniors.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Social Policy For Children And Families
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ UEP 282) Intersection of child development and social policy. Case studies of processes through which social problems are defined, policies formulated and implemented. Models for analyzing existing and proposed policies and for interpreting program evaluation results. Topics may include child abuse and neglect, family leave, maternal and child public-health policy, child care, early-childhood education. Special attention to policies affecting disadvantaged and minority populations.

Upper level of dual-level course with expanded readings and more advanced assignments.

Recommendations: CSHD 1 or PSY 1.

courses.title: Youth Activism, Civic Identity, & Moral Development
courses.desc: Explores critical questions about civic engagement and pressing moral issues facing us today, like raising children to be engaged moral citizens. Analysis of significant moral issues within historical and contemporary political and social contexts. Historical exploration of racism in the US, spanning from Reconstruction to contemporary civil rights movements. Consideration of the role of youth activism in the context of civic identity and moral development. Theoretical framework derived from literature on moral and civic identity development, and anti-racist materials.

courses.title: Promoting Positive Youth Development: Applying Developmental Science In The Community
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CVS 155) The positive youth development approach views children and adolescents as possessing strengths and emphasizes the role of families and communities as key resources. It highlights the importance of aligning individual and contextual resources across time and place to support youth thriving. How these principles can inform efforts to support marginalized youth and promote social justice and equity. Emphasis on the experiences of youth affected by adversity, trauma, and systemic inequities related to racism, privilege, and social determinants of well-being. Guest lectures from scholars and community leaders discuss strategies that foster positive development among diverse youth.

courses.title: Homelessness In America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 161 and UEP 181) Multi-disciplinary course examining the social, economic, and political dimensions of homelessness in the United States. Overview of causes, historical responses, and current conditions. Analysis of housing and welfare policies, mental health and substance abuse issues, economic and employment concerns. Volunteer work at shelters and organizations addressing homelessness required.

sections.note: Prospective students must complete a survey that will be used to select a group that meets criteria for a successful learning experience for all: Your commitment to applying what you have learned in prior coursework life experience to your own and fellow students' learning. Your interest in building on the learning in this course for your future studies at Tufts. Your interest in applying the learning in this course in your future career, education, and social change work after you graduate. Priority will be given to seniors and juniors. Selection will also aim to create a class composed of students with a variety of interests and experiences. Deadline for submission of the survey November 25 for first round of selection.

courses.title: Human-Animal Interaction in Childhood and Adolescence
courses.desc: Interdisciplinary course exploring mutually beneficial human-animal relationships: the role of animals in promoting positive development in childhood, adolescence and across the life-span, animal-assisted therapy, the role of animals in mental and physical health, animals in the family setting, animal policy and welfare, and animals in educational and programmatic contexts.

courses.title: Disability and Difference in Children
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CH 121) Overview of some of the special needs of preschool and elementary-age children who show a variation in physical, sensory, emotional, cognitive, and social development, through the lens of a positive model of identity. Focus on educational implications, family support, and adaptations to promote inclusive environments. Class lectures, observations of children, media portrayals, hands-on adaptations of materials, and visiting speakers.

courses.title: Pediatric Psychology
courses.desc: Research, clinical practice, and public policy focusing on children's health. Application of child development theories, methodologies, and empirical database to problems in health care. Focus is biopsychosocial and multidisciplinary, aiming at comparison and integration of perspectives of researchers, clinicians, advocates, and policymakers. Topics chosen from psychosocial stress and illness; adaptation to chronic illness including diabetes, childhood cancer and pediatric AIDS; mental health in primary care; behavioral and developmental pediatrics; schools as health-care delivery agents; prevention and health promotion; adolescent pregnancy.

sections.req: Juniors or Seniors and completion of CSHD 1 or PSY 1, OR CSHD graduate students

courses.title: Contemporary Families in the 21st Century
courses.desc: Overview of changing family patterns, changing attitudes toward ‘non-traditional families,’ and parenting aspirations among diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. A wide variety of family configurations in Western and semi-Western contexts with an intersectional focus, including foster and adoptive parents, families headed by lesbian mothers, families created via assisted reproductive technologies (in vitro fertilization, donor conception, and surrogacy), single mother and gay-parented families, and families headed by bisexual, polyamorous, transgender, and LGBTQ+ immigrant parents. Reflection on the methodological difficulties posed by research on non-traditional families. Prerequisites: CSHD 1 or PSY 1, or graduate standing.

sections.req: Completion of CSHD 0001 or PSY 0001 or Grad Standing

courses.title: Community Field Placement
courses.desc: Graduate equivalent of CSHD 99. Work and study in a variety of programs serving children and families. Placements include child advocacy programs, museums, hospitals, children's media, social service centers, and government agencies. Placements are supervised in a seminar or in consultation.

courses.title: Doctoral Pro Seminar B
courses.desc: Professional development seminar for doctoral students. Discussion of doctoral program and presentation of individual reports on basic topics to a seminar group for discussion and criticism.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.req: First and second year PhD students only.

courses.title: Graduate Internship Seminar B
courses.desc: This bi-weekly seminar is designed for MA-Applied students and is taken in fall and spring of the second year. It is a forum for the hallmark of Eliot-Pearson: the integration of theory, research, and applied work. courses.title: Cultural Sensitivity In Child And Family Research/practice

Centered on children and families, there are two foci: 1) cultural sensitivity in research, and 2) cultural sensitivity in practice. The focus on research examines culture as a contextual influence on human development and briefly addresses issues in conducting culturally sensitive research, including theory, methodology, analyses and interpretation. With various media, primarily audio-visual, the focus on practice will examine specific cultural constructs (e.g., race, ethnicity, religiosity) and their impact on interpersonal interactions. sections.note: Class Description: Heeding recent scholars' calls to place Black Studies and Native American and Indigenous Studies in more active dialogue with each other, this seminar examines the Black Power and Red Power movements. Students will engage both primary and secondary sources and attend to the ways in which these movements rejected the possibility of Black and Indigenous incorporation into the American polity and instead called for self-determination and political autonomy. Rather than limiting our consideration of Black Power and Red Power to the late 1960s and 1970s, we will take a “long movement” approach to thinking about these movements. Broad topics covered will include sovereignty and self-determination, and and community control, revolutionary violence and self-defense, gender and sexuality, and solidarity.

courses.title: Real World Evidence
courses.desc: This course serves as an introduction to topics in the use of real world evidence (RWE) to inform healthcare decision making. While randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard for establishing treatment efficacy, RWE offers many advantages including the availability of timely data at reasonable cost, large sample sizes that enable analysis of subgroups and rare outcomes, and increased generalizability to real-world clinical practice and more representative patients. Enthusiasm for RWE is tempered by concerns including those related to misclassification or data quality, the lack of randomization and other biases, and spurious data-driven findings. This course will introduce the foundational study designs and analytic approaches that are integral to the valid and efficient analysis of RWE, including those relevant to “big data.” RWE frameworks and approaches to be discussed will include limiting bias in observational big data, harnessing RWE for predictive analytics, identification of heterogeneity of treatment effects, pragmatic trial designs and the role of RWE for various stakeholders, including regulators. The potential role of RWE for the regulatory approval of novel therapies will also be discussed. Topics will be illustrated through the use of contemporary case studies representing both the promise and limitations of using RWE to inform healthcare decision making.

courses.title: Introduction to Health Technology Assessment
courses.desc: This course describes the practice of health technology assessment, as conducted by major agencies and other organizations in the United States and elsewhere, and introduces the technical tools used to project health benefits and costs. For the United States, the course reviews guidelines promulgated by the Second Panel on Cost Effectiveness Analysis in Health, and value assessment frameworks developed in the United States, with a focus on the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER). The review of HTA in other countries focuses on the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and also reviews approaches used by agencies in other countries. Finally, the course introduces the use of computer simulation to estimate value when empirical data alone will not suffice.

courses.title: Dissent and Democracy: American Literature to 1900

Readings include exploration narratives, settlement propaganda, sermons, autobiographies, political pamphlets, philosophical essays, poetry, short fiction, and novels. Brings together Native American, white European American, African American, Latinx, and Asian American voices to think about the construction of literary history, the politics of representation, and why this matters today. Authors studied include Phillis Wheatley, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Frederick Douglass, Emily Dickinson, Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Sui Sin Far, and Zitkála-Šá.

courses.title: Special Topics - Literature & Assessing Value
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
"In what kind of life do I want to invest my time, money, and spirit? What kind of career do I want to have, and what kind of pay am I aiming for? How will I find fulfillment in what I do? How will I want my classmates to perceive me at reunions? These are personal questions for students. They are also economic and social questions, because they are about navigating the social, financial, and spiritual tradeoffs one will face in life.


This reading group is organized around six central questions (one question for each class meeting), which are intended to help you frame your own value definition process. Rather than using textbook definitions of value (e.g., “exchange value”), this course invites you to consider the complicated ways in which we construct value for ourselves, with the help of classic literature. Accordingly, each meeting will pair literary primary texts with a contemporary essay that illustrates one possible framework for approaching the week’s central question."

Faculty and staff are also welcome to join.

Some of the main transformations of political thinking that characterized the Enlightenment: the possibility of scientific thinking and reasoning as the basis for human freedom.
