courses.title: Future of Global Institutions (EPIIC)
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 81) Education for Public Inquiry and International Citizenship (EPIIC) explores the role of global institutions in contemporary world affairs, beginning with a critical examination of theoretical concepts and debates about global institutions and global governance. Origins of the UN in the aftermath of the Second World War. Overview of the African Union and other regional organizations. Leadership role of executive heads of international organizations, especially the UN Secretary-General. Appraises the substantive work of global institutions on peace and security, sustainable development, human rights, the rule of law, humanitarian affairs, and the environment.

sections.note:
The Future of Institutions: The Politics of the Past: Memory and Historical Narrative

“The ways in which the memories of past events are interpreted, misinterpreted, or even manipulated in public discourse create the context that shapes international relations.” -- from Power and the Past: Collective Memory and International Relations
 
How do people(s) construct a sense of the past, and what are the implications of how that history is told? Can there be shared cultural knowledge when there are competing narratives, especially as a result of traumatic events? Why do some pasts triumph, while others fail, and how do those decisions affect future decisions and power relations? This class will explore the connections between the cultural, political and historical aspects of memory, as well as the connections between representation and social experience.

This year marks the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Declaration of Independence, a set of ideas that became a transformative, global event. How has the memorialization of those ideals manifested in today’s partisan politics? Rwanda faces a bifurcation between those that continue to be defined by the 1994 genocide and those ready to be defined by the country’s current accomplishments. Memory attached to land is a powerful driver, from Israel/Palestine to the Field of Blackbirds to the legacies of partition in South Asia. What some call “memoryscapes” are often deep-seated historical, cultural and emotional attachments driven by violence, displacement, dispossession. 

What is a national memory? How are national and international events memorialized and how are those memorials experienced by current and future generations? 
 
What is the influence of collective and/or competing memories on foreign policy formation? How is the cultural made political? How are historical narratives being used from Ireland to Russia to define territorial boundaries? 
 
This yearlong class is organized with frequent guest lecturers where students have the opportunity to organize and enact an international symposium.

courses.title: Communication for Social Change
courses.desc: Examines how civic actors communicate to inform and persuade others. Develops verbal, written, and digital communication skills including relational meetings, small group facilitation, public speaking, policy memos, op-eds, social media communications, and webcasts.

sections.note:
Communication for Social Change

Examines how civic actors communicate to inform, persuade, and inspire while providing students with opportunity to develop verbal (relational meetings, small group facilitation, public speaking), written (policy memos, op-eds), and digital (social media, webinars) communication skills in a supportive learning community. Throughout the course, students will interact with leading practitioners; learn strategies for communicating authentically while demonstrating understanding of different identities and perspectives; and explore ethical issues including the difference between persuasion and manipulation along with how to recognize misinformation and disinformation. Students will leave course with a portfolio of communications related to a social change issue of their choosing.

courses.title: Civic Identity, Reflection, & Action: Tisch Scholars Foundation Seminar B
courses.desc: Explore the connections between identity and systems of privilege, power, and oppression, and apply learning directly to fieldwork and vice versa. Learn to apply an asset-based approach to community-based work and develop skills in effective communication and collaboration. This is a two-part course that is the foundation for the Tisch Scholars Program. Scholars will take this course while concurrently working 8 hours per week at a community-based placement. Course open only to students participating in the Tisch Scholars Program.

sections.note: Tisch Scholars only

courses.title: Tisch Scholars Fieldwork Practicum
courses.desc:
Learn about Tufts partner communities and forge meaningful, reciprocal
partnerships with community members through service and collaboration at a community-based placement 8 hours per week. Course open only to students participating in the Tisch Scholars Program.

sections.note: Tisch Scholars only

courses.title: Internship-Social Change
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as GRA 100) Supervised fieldwork in a wide range of community, peace, justice, and social change organizations. Readings, guided group discussions, and written reports to integrate analysis and experience.
Recommendations: PJS 1, one intermediate course each from core areas A through D, and one intermediate course from core area E which may be taken simultaneously.

sections.note: Enrollment in this course is by application only.

courses.title: Sociological Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with SOC 103) Examination of major theoretical traditions and their critical challenges in sociology. Explores diverse frameworks that address systems of power and oppression (e.g., racism, misogyny, capitalism, colonialism, adultism, and their intersections). Sociological discussions focusing on modernity, evolution of society, community and division, domination; approaches to highlighting past and contemporary social divisions and imagining social visions for alternative futures.

sections.req: Requires the completion of at least one Sociology course.Sociology Majors and Minors only

courses.title: Seminar: Hannah Arendt
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 157 & JS 157) Hannah Arendt (1906-1975) personally experienced some of the great events of the 20th Century, interacted with many famous contemporaries, and offered challenging arguments about totalitarianism and democracy, migration and human rights, Jewishness and Israel, modernity and science, feminism, activism, and the role of intellectuals. Critical discussion of her texts, her life, and her context. Comparison of her ideas to those of other thinkers and issues of the present.

sections.req: Requires the completion of one PHIL course or graduate standing

courses.title: Who Owns the Past? Art, Heritage, and Global Conflicts
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ILVS 164 and HAA 164) Cultural heritage as a subject of identity and ownership. History of museum collections and preservation programs in the context of nationalism and colonialism and the aftermath of these developments on the basis of selected case studies from different parts of the world. From heritage and the process of nation-building to the debate on heritage in the Anthropocene era.

sections.note: No additional costs.

courses.title: Evangelicalism in America
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as REL 121, AMER 121, and HIST 126) History of evangelical Christianity in North America from the 17th century to the present. Attention to issues of theology, race, class, gender, culture, politics and globalization. Consideration of relationships among evangelicalism, fundamentalism and pentecostalism. 
Recommended: One lower level course in the history of Christianity (REL 12 or 63) or one lower level course in American religious history (REL 42, 47, 48, 49), OR permission of the instructor

courses.title: Topics In Economic Development
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed with EC 136) Selected major current problems in various developing countries. Students will be asked to utilize and extend the theoretical insights from Economics 35 by applying them in specific cases. Topics will include problems in energy, agriculture, balance of payments, and industrialization. Elements of benefit-cost analysis will also be covered.
Prerequisites: Economics 11 and 35; Economics 13 suggested.

sections.note:
Course includes Research Paper.
Course is designated as a seminar course.

courses.title: Working w/Communities: Research-Practice Integration
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CSHD 121) Working in partnership with communities is a different approach than working in communities. Explores frameworks for socially just research and practice conducted in collaboration with ethnoculturally diverse communities and responsive to the community issues and needs identified by members of that particular community.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Special Topics - Social Movts & Amer. Pol Inst.
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: Social movements are important drivers of institutional change. The American constitutional system influences how these movements emerge – and whether or not they are successful. In this class, we explore theories of how social movement mobilization, followed by an overview of the American political system, focusing on the intersections between movements and institutions in multiple venues. We conclude with an analysis of movement-state interactions from the 1960s to present, focusing on how progressive and conservative movements have reshaped the political order through the party system, tracing movement-state development from the Civil Rights Movement to the MAGA and Democratic Socialist movements of the 2020s. Students will engage with scholarship from sociology, political science, and history in this fast-paced and rigorous course that asks students to consider how change occurs in the American political system. The final product of this course is a 15-20-page original research paper on a case of the student’s interest, including a research presentation to the class.

courses.title: Special Topics - Nonviolence in Theory and Practice
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Nonviolence in Theory and Practice

Students in this course will examine the non-violence as a theoretical concept in Peace Studies and the movements that it has inspired over the course of the 20th century. Students will learn to articulate the nuances of non-violent movements as strategic choices in the interests of resolving longstanding issues of historical harm. Students will collectively choose case studies to investigate how different movements have approached the strategy of non-violence from different cultural, religious, and political backgrounds and towards what ends. We will take a special interest in how religious movements have used non-violent tactics to promote peaceful practices and just relations (peace movements, provision of care for the poor and sick by religious orders and communities, peaceable co-existence and cooperation with religious and ethnic others, liberation and justice movements). Students will be able to articulate how non-violent methodology can be used to promote social change and will deepen their understanding of peace studies terminology such as just peace and structural violence while simultaneously questioning whether violence is ever an effective strategy in creating a peaceful society.

courses.title: Special Topics - Dialogue Facilitation Lab
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
From Conflict to Connection: A Dialogue Facilitation Lab

This course provides an opportunity to learn and practice the skills needed to facilitate meaningful and constructive dialogue across differences. Upon completion of the course, students will become a part of the larger dialogue facilitation community at Tufts gaining access to a Community of Practice and facilitating programs across the institution. Students will gain skills in curiosity, inquiry, generous listening, question design, multipartiality, adaptability, intercultural agility, perspective-taking, and affirming & reflecting experiences. These skills can be used in any professional or personal setting to build trust, communicate across differences, and encourage collaboration. Through practice, reflection, and feedback, students will learn to design and facilitate dialogues in a variety of educational, professional, and community settings.

courses.title: Special Topics - Gender and Literature
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Gender and Literature

"How have ideas about gender and about ""femininity"" and ""masculinity"" changed over time? In what ways do social and cultural influences affect our understanding and embodiment of gender, specifically with respect to race, sexuality, and socio-economic status? And what does it mean to say, as many do today, that gender is performative? By analyzing gender, how might we come to understand it in the context of social justice rather than simply as unchanging biological fact? In doing so, might we embrace “theory” and literary interpretation as the praxis of enacting gender in ways that restore justice and repair harm for so many who have suffered (indeed, for all) under the ideological regime called gender? 

 This course will incorporate some canonical texts of gender theory. Simultaneously, students will consider literature that treats gender as matters of life and love, enabling us to approach the theoretical questions as embodied and thus fully relevant for all. By examining some of the theories contributing to the gender debates in the west, students will gain a new frame through which to interpret a variety of literature and develop a deeper understanding of gender identity, especially attending to how it is influenced by distinctions of race, class, desire, and ethnicity."

courses.title: Special Topics - War on Drugs
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
War on Drugs

This course will enable students to foster a deep understanding of the challenges of administering justice in a democratic society. Extensive readings by Elizabeth Hinton, Michelle Alexander, Sam Quinones, and Sam Kelley will provide students with an historical framework for understanding this history of the “war on drugs,” with specific attention to the opioid and crack “epidemics.” A central aim of this course will be to develop a keen eye for understanding better the effects of language and representation on the very practices related to drug use and drug policy that impact individuals and communities. A look at several case studies will further expand students ability to re-formulate their own philosophies of justice and ideas about past and current practices in the realms of contemporary jurisprudence and community-based interventions.

courses.title: Special Topics - Women, Power & Leadership
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Women, Power & Leadership: Gender, Conflict, and Change

"What does it mean to be a woman and a leader in a world shaped by conflict, political change, social expectations, and unequal systems of power?

This interdisciplinary course explores women’s leadership in societies experiencing conflict, political transformation, social change, and cultural tension. Using case studies from the Middle East and other regions of the world, students will examine how women navigate formal and informal power, challenge gender stereotypes, build influence, and create change in environments where traditional structures may limit their opportunities.

The course looks beyond the idea of leadership as simply holding a formal position. Students will explore different forms of power including positional, relational, cultural, and informal power. The course is grounded in more than 20 years of the instructor’s experience in women’s leadership, journalism, and conflict environments, bringing real-world cases and field experiences into the classroom."

courses.title: Special Topics - Community Co-Creation Lab
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Enrollment restricted to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

An immersive, interdisciplinary, and collaborative course focused on developing technical and conceptual expertise in participatory research methodologies, community-based art practices, and the ethics of engagement. Partnering with a Boston-based nonprofit, students will co-design, co-create, implement, and reflect on impactful art projects. Students work alongside unhoused artists at Saint Francis House to co-create artworks that reflect shared stories of resilience, care, and belonging. The first four weeks emphasize context, ethics, and preparation; the remaining nine weeks center on collaborative making, critique, and public presentation. Through workshops, technical training, assignments, readings, and discussions, students will gain practical skills in conducting participatory research on social justice issues, using digital and analog tools to collect oral histories and interviews, applying fiber arts for community engagement, exploring performance art as a medium for empowerment and storytelling, and utilizing multimedia platforms to amplify engagement and documentation. This hands-on course prioritizes co-creation, collaborative knowledge production, and meaningful partnerships, preparing students to co-produce art projects that authentically represents community voices and concerns. Open to all skill levels. Locations: SMFA + Saint Francis House Art Studio (alternate visits).

courses.title: Special Topics - Democratic Resilience
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: This course examines how democracies confront both perennial and acute challenges to their institutions and principles. Themes include theories of democratic origins and survival, the role of civil society and the media in times of crisis, and patterns of protest and collaboration. Cases include countries from around the world and across time, but there is a particular focus on the contemporary United States

courses.title: Special Topics - Generative AI for Social Impact
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
This course examines the growing role of generative AI in addressing critical social challenges, including healthcare, accessibility, education, development, and civic engagement, with a particular focus on marginalized communities. Through case studies and real-world applications, students explore when and whether AI can meaningfully address these challenges, the risks it introduces, and who benefits or is harmed.

Students develop a working understanding of generative AI technologies, including prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic workflows, and guardrails, alongside practical approaches to designing, customizing, and evaluating AI applications. The course emphasizes human-centered design and evaluation, examining both the technical performance of AI systems and their impact on individuals and communities.

The course follows a studio-based format, combining hands-on activities, mini-projects, peer feedback, and a semester-long group project involving needs assessment, iterative design, and evaluation. Projects will address real-world challenges, with opportunities for students to collaborate with external partners, including community organizations, nonprofits, and public agencies. The recommended programming language for projects is Python.
Prerequisites: CS 15 or equivalent programming experience for the Developer Track; no programming prerequisite for the Evaluator Track.

Developer and Evaluator Tracks. The course welcomes students from diverse academic backgrounds through two complementary tracks. Students in the Developer Track focus on designing and implementing generative AI applications, while those in the Evaluator Track focus on assessing their capabilities, limitations, risks, and real-world impact. Both tracks engage with the same core concepts and are held to rigorous expectations appropriate to their learning objectives. Students are encouraged to collaborate across tracks on their final projects, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of developing AI for social impact.

courses.title: Promoting Positive Youth Development: Applying Developmental Science In The Community
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CSHD 185) The positive youth development approach views children and adolescents as possessing strengths and emphasizes the role of families and communities as key resources. It highlights the importance of aligning individual and contextual resources across time and place to support youth thriving. How these principles can inform efforts to support marginalized youth and promote social justice and equity. Emphasis on the experiences of youth affected by adversity, trauma, and systemic inequities related to racism, privilege, and social determinants of well-being. Guest lectures from scholars and community leaders discuss strategies that foster positive development among diverse youth.

courses.title: American Conservatism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 193) An interdisciplinary, social science approach to the study of American political conservatism. Drawing from philosophy, psychology, political science, and economics, study works of contemporary conservative thinkers as well as social science research that are emphasized by conservative thinkers. Examination of what conservatives think and the assumptions and values that underlie their perspectives. Topics include both public policies (e.g., family, religion, affirmative action, taxation) and conservative worldviews about the role of an individual, a community, and a nation.

courses.title: Homelessness In America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 181 and CSHD 186) Multi-disciplinary course examining the social, economic, and political dimensions of homelessness in the United States. Overview of causes, historical responses, and current conditions. Analysis of housing and welfare policies, mental health and substance abuse issues, economic and employment concerns. Volunteer work at shelters and organizations addressing homelessness required.

sections.note: Prospective students must complete a survey that will be used to select a group that meets criteria for a successful learning experience for all: Your commitment to applying what you have learned in prior coursework life experience to your own and fellow students' learning. Your interest in building on the learning in this course for your future studies at Tufts. Your interest in applying the learning in this course in your future career, education, and social change work after you graduate. Priority will be given to seniors and juniors. Selection will also aim to create a class composed of students with a variety of interests and experiences. Deadline for submission of the survey November 25 for first round of selection.

courses.title: Developing Leaders in a Civic Context
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 180 & ENT 170) Integrates and applies concepts from adult development and learning, leader(ship) development, and organizational behavior to build capacity for social change. Creating effective strategies to develop individuals, teams, and organizations to address complex challenges. Pre-requisites: CSHD 1 or PSY 1 or Junior standing or instructor permission.

courses.title: Social Justice, Advocacy, and Music
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MUS 152) The role of music in movements for social change and in models of advocacy in scholarship, research, educational programming, and communities. Case studies include the role of music in the Civil Rights movement and LGBTQ+ advocacy in the US, and in the struggle against apartheid in South Africa. Using music as a tool for activism, and the role of music in developing successful social justice initiatives. No prerequisite.

courses.title: Creating Children’s Media
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 169 and FMS 141) Exploration of book-to-film transitions, creation of scripts for children’s television programs, podcasts for children, development of storyboards for ad campaigns, and proposals for apps, and other digital content for children. Application of child development, media literacy and civic engagement theories, and strategies for storytelling in children’s media content across media platforms. Student projects on pitching, scriptwriting, and other topics.

courses.title: Spanish In The Community
courses.desc:

Focus on the history, literature, and politics of Puerto Ricans on the island and the mainland and the experiences of Salvadorans and Mexicans in their native countries and in the United States. Minimum of four hours of volunteer work per week. In Spanish. Prerequisite: At least two courses above SPN 0022 or consent. Native Spanish-speakers require
consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Entrepreneurship for Social Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as AMER 141, TCS 141, and ENT 141) Learn how to address systemic social and environmental problems and generate financial returns. Choose a problem based on your why. Form a diverse team and interview stakeholders. Harness AI for marketing and product development. Execute a pilot project with real users. Create and present a pitch deck. Interact with impact entrepreneurs and investors. Emerge as a more confident leader with valuable career skills, a broader network, and maybe even an impact venture.

courses.title: Capstone Seminar - Civic Knowledge
courses.desc: The relationship between knowledge and democracy. Examines what counts as a fact, how valid knowledge is created, and the relationship between theory and practice. The nature and importance of local knowledge and the roles of science and other ways of knowing, including stories and narratives, in the communication of knowledge. Readings, discussion, and a collaborative research project with the Community Action Agency of Somerville (CAAS), a Tisch College community partner. Prerequisites: junior standing.

sections.note:
CVS Capstone: Civic Knowledge

Explores and examines the relationship between knowledge and democracy. What makes something a fact? How is valid knowledge created? Is science distinct from other ways of knowing and, if so, how? What’s the relationship between theory and practice? What’s the ideal role for stories and narratives in the communication of knowledge? What is the difference between research and advocacy? In addition to theoretical readings and discussions, course culminates in a collaboration with a Tisch College community partner. The goal is to “create” knowledge with our community partners that people in Somerville can use.

courses.desc:
Introduction to the power of data across the arts, humanities, and sciences. How data is created, interpreted, visualized, and sometimes misused, evaluating real-world information with a critical eye. Hands-on labs to develop practical data analysis skills in Python and visualization skills in Tableau. Machine learning techniques, including clustering, regression, and classification trees. Emerging trends in data analytics. Prepares students to apply data-driven thinking in any field.
Open to Arts & Sciences and Engineering Undergraduates.

courses.desc: Modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) employs a variety of modalities, including image, audio, and text. Introduction to deep learning and its domain-specific applications from computer vision and Large Language Models (LLMs) to audio and speech recognition. Hands-on experience building deep learning models (CNN, RNN, Transformers, etc.) and AI systems using frameworks such as PyTorch and Tensorflow Keras. Survey of State-Of-The-Art literature on multimodal AI such as CLIP (Language-Image) and CLAP (Language-Audio). Opportunity to carry out a mini AI research project following industry standard practices. Students should have proficiency in Python; and familiarity with probability, linear algebra, and calculus prior to enrollment.

courses.title: Introduction to Digital Humanities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 161) Computational methods to study humanistic disciplines (literature, history, politics, art, music, social media, etc.). Introduction to methods such as web scraping, Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), topic modeling, Named Entity Recognition (NER), network analysis, mapping, and the programming language Python. Assignments analyze primarily text-based sources in English, and the methods can be applied to a wide range of languages, ancient and modern. No programming skills are assumed.

courses.title: Uncovering the Past: Historical Soc in Digital Age
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with SOC 118 and HIST 100) Compares sociological and historical approaches to uncovering and interpreting traces of the past. Examines challenges of research in a digital world, including the ethics and politics of archives. Focuses on critical reading, analytical writing, and research strategies: locating and analyzing primary documents and oral histories; leveraging text recognition, retrieval, and data cleaning; conducting press reviews in the era of AI; and using big data to measure culture and trends. Introduces tools and methods for organizing and analyzing qualitative data. Considers the future of historiography and historical sociology in a globalized, digital world.

courses.title: Natural Language Processing and the Human Record
courses.desc: Review of state-of-the-art research in the Digital Humanities and development of collaborative research projects. Emphasis on how new technologies can engage a diverse and multilingual global audience with the past, with a particular focus on the applications of natural language processing and a range of visualization techniques to the human record. Course projects combine code with an analysis of its impact. Programming skills required. Prerequisites: CS 10 or CS 11 or CLS 161, or instructor permission

sections.req: CLS 161 or CS 11 or CS 10 or permission

courses.title: Maritime Geopolitics: Maritime Security, Global Trade, Energy and Environmental Issues at Sea
courses.desc: Over 90% of international trade is carried by sea – the lifeblood of globalization. The world’s oceans also present a myriad of opportunities and challenges in international affairs, such as territorial disputes, opening Arctic sea routes, piracy, terrorism, strained fisheries, mineral and energy extraction, marine disasters, whaling, maritime security and technological advances in maritime domain awareness. The course will explore these issues and other maritime topics based on individual student interests. Course format is lecture and discussion. Writing and speaking skills receive considerable attention. No prerequisites other than a lively curiosity.

courses.title: International Humanitarian Response
courses.desc: Taught jointly by faculty from the Harvard Humanitarian Initiative and the Feinstein International Center, this course offers insight into the complex issues involved in humanitarian work and provides training in the practical field skills needed to engage in effective responses. Key topics include: humanitarian community and history; sphere standards; rapid assessments; humanitarian clusters: protection; shelter; camp coordination and management; food security; early recovery; water, sanitation, and hygiene; health; nutrition; education; logistics; and emergency telecommunications; program design, budgeting, and monitoring and evaluation; field security; civil-military relations; media skills; mental health and responder resilience; localization and diversity; ethics and accountability. Over the semester, the course will also explore questions about how the current model of humanitarianism needs to evolve in a changing world. It culminates with a mandatory, three-day intensive field simulation. The fee to cover camping gear, food, and other equipment is still to be determined, but in past years has been in the range of USD 300.

courses.title: International Public Diplomacy in the Digital Age
courses.desc:
This introductory course provides an overview of Public Diplomacy in the current context of a
highly digital world, including both theory and practice. It provides an overview of the elements of public diplomacy, its relationship with national strategy, the roles of technology, the major challenges to public diplomacy, and comparisons of the public diplomacy practices of different countries throughout the world. In some classes we will be joined by guest participants who are former Fletcher students now working in public diplomacy for different countries. Course material includes the work of researchers and practitioners in the field, and from many different countries. Student participation and interaction is essential to learning in this class. No prior background in or knowledge of the professions and fields that comprise Public Diplomacy or related to it is required.

courses.title: International Mediation
courses.desc: Mediation is one of many international intervention approaches to prevent, resolve, or recover from political violence. It is practiced by individuals, international and transnational organizations, small and large states, and in bilateral or multilateral contexts. This seminar focuses on the ways in which mediators in the international arena carry out their third-party roles. Topics to be covered include: gaining entry; developing a strategy; gaining and using leverage; and managing complexity. The seminar relies on detailed, extensive case study analysis to understand how international mediators operate in real-time, complex environments. Open to students who have completed D220 or equivalent.

sections.note: Completion of DHP D220 or an equivalent negotiation is highly recommended

courses.title: Humanitarian Action: Past, Present and Future
courses.desc: This is a course about global humanitarian action. It looks at the historical roots of what has become today’s humanitarianism, including differences in humanitarian thought, the development of the UN and NGO systems, donor behavior and initiatives and organizations that are outside mainstream humanitarian architecture. This course centers and privileges the experience of crisis-affected communities, including their own responses to crisis, and how the formal humanitarian system supports, ignores, or hampers these responses. We take a look at the laws, principles, and ethical codes of conduct underpinning the humanitarian enterprise, as well as dilemmas humanitarians face in applying these norms, principles and codes, historically and presently. We examine various types of humanitarian responses from prevention to emergency responses, to “medium-term” and “long-term” prevention. We learn how to evaluate information coming from the sector, and conduct our own inquiries. Importantly, this course is taught with a continuous critique of the politics and norms underlying the sector, whether formally acknowledged or not. With this in mind, two cross-cutting topics will be taught throughout the course: local responses to humanitarian action and neo-colonialism in humanitarianism.

courses.title: Nutrition in Complex Emergencies: Policies, Practice and Decision-making
courses.desc: The course will introduce students to the concept of Public Nutrition and examine its central role in complex emergencies. The implications of the Public Nutrition approach for assessment and analysis, policy development, program design and implementation will be examined. This will provide an understanding of; the causes and nutritional outcomes of humanitarian crises and complex emergencies (malnutrition, morbidity and mortality). The course has a field oriented focus based on a wide range of recent and past food and nutrition crises ranging. The course reviews international response strategies, nutrition programmes and relevant policies; and incorporates relevant applied research. The course provides the opportunity for active class participation drawing upon the actual work experience of the students and applying a range of up-to-date case-study materials based on current humanitarian crises. This course is cross-listed with the Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy.

courses.title: Climate and Migration
courses.desc: Explores the ways in which people are displaced by the destruction of our environment, the role of financial capitalism in that destruction, and the consequences for climate change and global migration. Through the lens of global supply chains, we explore the connections between economic development and global capitalism, environmental impact, human mobility and climate change. Through case studies we explore different supply chains, and the interaction of their links with the environment, migration, and climate change and consequently, human security and justice. The course provides a perspective on the fast-growing body of research on climate change and migration, and explores the associated challenges of human security and environmental justice. The course explores potential policy responses and technological solutions, including positive interventions in supply chains, and ends with a perspective on pandemics response at the national and international level. Participants will gain an exposure to academic and non-academic literature and case studies from different regions. Flexible course assignments will offer students an opportunity to delve deeper into topics of their interest.

courses.title: Case Study Methods Research
courses.desc: Explores the use of case studies from a theoretical, methodological, and practical perspective. The goal is to understand the advantages and disadvantages of the case study method and its place in a mixed methods research design. We examine the tasks and problems involved in all stages of case study development. The goal of the course is to equip students with the knowledge and skills to implement a sound case study, either as part of a capstone or a PhD dissertation.

courses.title: Livelihoods, Food Security and Nutrition in Crisis-Prone Contexts
courses.desc: Livelihoods are a strong determinant of food security and poor food security is a strong determinant of poor nutrition, even under-nutrition. Nutrition studies are often limited to the immediate drivers of undernutrition, ignoring the larger, more systemic factors. This class will examine how livelihoods function within systems, and how the structure of these systems may drive poor food security. We will also look at how poor food security can lead to poor nutrition, especially among young children, adolescents and the elderly. We will look at each of these components individually and as they interact. The approach we take to these topics will be equally applicable to students interested in high-resource settings like the US and to students interested in international humanitarian and development studies.

courses.title: Famines and Severe Food Insecurity
courses.desc: For people who live in a country with abundant resources, famine may seem like a surreal topic in distant lands. For others, it is all too real. These terrible episodes in human history can have a lasting effect on the people who experience them, changing the norms of society, relationships between nations and between a people and its government. Some 20 years ago, we thought we had seen the last famine. Sadly, though we now have the technical capacity and resources to prevent famines and severe food insecurity, these are becoming increasingly common. There are many different types of catastrophes in the world, but famine is somehow unique – it involves not an isolated group of individuals within a society, but in one way or another, everyone in that society as a large part of the population struggles day to day just to stay alive, sometimes across multiple years, and many are not successful. This class will examine famines not as events, but processes and systems manipulated by humans, though often aggravated by natural hazards, market failures, epidemics and other factors. We will look at these systems from the highest, conceptual, theoretical levels down to the experiences of individuals simply trying to get enough food to keep their families and themselves alive.

courses.title: Existential Environmental Politics
courses.desc: The contemporary challenges arising from global environmental change, such as climate change, land degradation, loss of biodiversity, freshwater scarcity, toxic contamination and energy scarcity, are important issues for scholars from not only the natural and social but also the human sciences. As a result of increasing concerns about global environmental change, over the last decade a new scientific field of research has emerged, the Environmental Humanities (EH). Whereas scholarship on issues of environmental change was formerly dominated by the natural, economic and social sciences — and by technological approaches to problem-solving — this relatively new and rapidly growing field is constituted by the work of scholars from a wide variety of disciplines within the Humanities, including history, literature, philosophy, cultural studies, religion studies, arts, architecture, and linguistics. These scholars are investigating how the human and human agency are to be understood in the age of the Anthropocene –the era in which humans have become a geological force with devastating potential (Croetzen and Stoermer, 2000). Emergent transdisciplinary fields, such as the environmental humanities and global health, reflect a growing awareness that responses to contemporary environmental dilemmas require the collaborative work of not only diverse scientists, medical practitioners, and engineers, but also more expansive publics, including artists, urban and rural communities, social scientists, and legal fields. Environmental Humanities thus marks an effort to explore and channel the creative synergy that is possible when scholars from the humanities, social sciences, and sciences talk across disciplines about the environment and environmental problems. Central to our concerns are the unequal access to resources as well as the unequal exposure to risk during a period of widening economic disparity. The readings in this course have been selected to help us discuss questions that span the disciplines and the globe: What does it mean to be human in a time of global environmental change? What should environmental ethics look like? How are political, social, and economic structures—and inequities—intertwined with ecological realities? How has our understanding of the relationship between culture and nature shaped our conservation efforts? How do our concepts of nature and of environmentalism need to change in response to our current situation? Scholars in the environmental humanities ask and seek to answer these questions, and to develop more equitable ecologies.

courses.title: Nationalism
courses.desc: Nationalism is having a resurgence. It is almost impossible to talk about world politics today without referencing nationalism. From China’s nationalist project, the far-right ethnonationalist parties destabilizing Europe, environmental nationalism in climate change debates, to the specter of lost nationhood in the Russia-Ukraine and Gaza conflicts, nationalism is everywhere. Yet nationalism is an idea and phenomenon that suffers from many misconceptions. This course will survey the major debates and questions within nationalism studies. What is a nation? How does it differ from an ethnic community? Why is nationalism sometimes utterly destructive and other times invaluably constructive? Is strong nationalism more compatible with authoritarian regimes? We will answer such questions from the primary lens of comparative politics, using theories and cases drawn from across the world. By the end of the course, you will have a strong grasp of nationalism as an ever-shifting political force and be able to critically discuss both its powers and pitfalls.

courses.title: Corruption: Concepts, Causes, Consequences, Countermeasures
courses.desc:
Corruption exists in almost every country in the contemporary world. It is common ground that
corruption harms the rule of law, demoralizes the society, and inhibits economic growth, as there
is a strong interaction between corruption and political and economic development. This raises
the question of how to successfully contain and counter corruption. The institutional/legal,
political, economic and even cultural contexts, within which corruption appears as a
phenomenon, in the form of human behavior, constitute an constantly changing framework, at
international and national level, that sets always new challenges – as new forms of corruption –
throughout the globe. Addressing these challenges in a manner, both at international and
national/comparative level, that will explore corruption’s dimensions (its concept, causes, forms,
and consequences) allows for the identification of the possible anti-corruption measures in a
preventive and/or a punishing approach.

courses.title: Conflict Management in a Fragmented World Order
courses.desc: We live in a ‘multiplex’ world order where conflicts have become more diffuse and fragmented. Conflict management has equally become distributed, complex, and fuzzy. A wide array of actors, including governments, states, organizations as well as informal actors seek to shape conflict outcomes and intervene at different stages of the conflict resolution (CR) process. Against this backdrop, how do these actors’ strategies compete, interact, and intersect at the same time? The course examines the changing nature of multilateral conflict management. It offers a range of case studies that explore multi-actor interventions in violent/armed conflict, negotiations in peace processes, and multi-scalar peacebuilding initiatives etc. Additionally, it reflects on the role that organizations such as the European Union (the EU), the Arab League (LAS), the African Union (AU) and UN agencies can play in the management of geopolitical conflicts. The course offers a variety of interactive activities, such as in-class discussions, group work, guest lectures and a final role-playing exercise in which students simulate ‘fog and friction’ in a conflict scenario rooted in a real-world event.

courses.title: Peace and Democratization Processes: Cross-Comparative Perspectives
courses.desc: This course is about peace governance and the twin processes of peacebuilding and democratization in post-conflict societies. It examines patterns of governance after conflict, and their complex relationship with the quality of democracy, authoritarian resilience, and sustainable peace. The course addresses the following questions: How do post-conflict societies navigate the complex journey of peace and democratization? What are the trade-offs between peace and democratization? What role do various actors play in shaping peace and democratization outcomes? Lastly, how do practitioners go about sequencing peacebuilding activities? Students will gain analytical and conceptual tools to analyze peace governance and learn their application through various case studies and post-conflict scenarios. They will also acquire insights into practical missions such as electoral monitoring or designing town hall meetings in post-conflict societies.

courses.title: U.S.-China Security Relations
courses.desc: China’s rise is arguably the most important development of the 21st century and relations between the United States and China touch on every aspect of international affairs, from addressing climate change and responding to global pandemics to limiting the spread of nuclear weapons and promoting economic development. Relations between these two countries have the potential to touch every element of international affairs. In recent years, U.S.-China relations have become increasingly “securitized,” meaning that security considerations dominate. This course provides a survey of these relations today. While the course includes historical elements and considers how both China and the United States interact with the rest of the world, this course is strongly focused on contemporary security issues in the bilateral relationship.

courses.title: How Systems Fail
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/CS 203) Failure of computer systems within the larger context of complex systems, including the power grid and aviation. Failures of algorithms and protocols, engineering and implementation, systems and applications, people and culture. Attacks, attack recovery, security, privacy, and attribution. Case studies of failures and attacks, including distributed denial of service, Meltdown, Spectre, and spear-phishing attacks. Prerequisites: COMP 13 or consent of instructor.

courses.title: U.S. Foreign Policy, 1898 to Present
courses.desc: This course will examine major themes in United States foreign relations, including isolationism, humanitarianism, and imperialism; the link between domestic politics and foreign policy; and the debate about American exceptionalism. Key topics will include the expansion of US power in the early 20th century; the diplomacy of the World Wars; the Cold War and the construction of the U.S. alliance system; and the challenges to the U.S. backed order.

courses.title: Supply Chain Statecraft
courses.desc: This course examines how global manufacturing supply chains formed, who captures power and profit within them, and how states have weaponized them. Starting with the historical and geographic origins of fragmented production, the course examines the rise of contract manufacturing in Taiwan, the distribution of value in supply chains like Apple's, and the conditions under which suppliers escape dependence. It then turns to the state: industrial policy, and the weaponization of critical inputs (rare earths, semiconductors) and production equipment (lithography tools, Cold War machine tools, oilfield technology). The course will also test the analogy that economic interdependence functions like nuclear deterrence against classical strategic theory (Schelling, Jervis, Wohlstetter, Kahn), asking whether supply chain coercion can produce anything like stable "mutually assured economic destruction," and whether escalation between economic powers can be controlled.

courses.title: Art, Heritage, Diplomacy and Global Conflicts
courses.desc: From antiquity and into the present, conflicts of all kinds have impacted art and heritage. Objects of art and visual culture have been destroyed, looted, or reinterpreted; monuments and sites have been targeted or have sustained collateral damage; and archives and collections have been threatened. This course explores the impact of conflicts (especially armed conflicts) on art and heritage through explorations of particular case studies ranging from Greek, Roman, and medieval conquests, the Byzantine iconoclastic controversies, the Napoleonic campaigns, the World Wars, and more recent conflicts in the Balkans, the Middle East, Armenia, and Ukraine. In addition to documenting, understanding, and analyzing instances of destruction, the course engages with the layered meanings of art and heritage (both tangible and intangible), the ideological motivations behind the destruction or protection of certain objects and monuments in times of crisis, preservation and reconstruction efforts, the legal and ethical aspects of cultural property in global conflicts, as well as the opportunities and challenges of heritage diplomacy today.

courses.title: Revolutions: Theories and Histories
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 279) Revolutions have been responsible for some of the greatest political, social, economic, and cultural changes in human history. But what is a revolution? What sort of change does it induce, and what are its causes? What leads a revolution to fail? This course explores the history and meaning of revolutions by taking a theoretical and comparative historical approach. Students will first explore different sociological theories of revolution before studying a series of case studies in order to develop their own views about how to define and understand revolutions. The course is intended to provide students a framework through which to understand revolutions, as well as to encourage them to apply these frameworks to various historical and contemporary case studies.

courses.title: War and Society in the Middle East in Historical Perspective
courses.desc:
Wars do not merely destroy societies; they remake them. They create new states, new refugees, new forms of citizenship, new humanitarian institutions, and new collective memories. This seminar examines the social history of war in the modern Middle East from the First World War to the ongoing war in Gaza. Rather than approaching war through campaigns, diplomacy, or military strategy alone, it asks how wars transformed societies and how ordinary people experienced these transformations.

Drawing on history, anthropology, sociology, geography, memory studies, legal studies, and genocide studies, the seminar explores war as a social process. It examines mobilization, displacement, occupation, humanitarianism, gender, disability, veteranhood, urban destruction, reconstruction, and memory across six major conflicts: the First World War, the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, the June 1967 War, the Lebanese Civil War, the Iran-Iraq War, and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Throughout the semester, students will work with an unusually diverse range of sources, including military archives, soldiers' letters, oral histories, memoirs, humanitarian reports, photographs, films, maps, legal documents, epidemiological studies, and digital evidence. The seminar emphasizes comparative analysis, asking how similar social processes recur across different conflicts while remaining attentive to the historical specificity of each case.

Rather than treating Middle Eastern wars as exceptional, the course places them in dialogue with broader debates in the social history of war, historical sociology, and genocide studies. Students will examine both classic historiographical interventions and recent interdisciplinary scholarship while developing their own comparative research projects.

courses.title: South Asia in the World: Political and Historical International Relations
courses.desc: South Asia has a long history of international engagement, whether in the form of transnational anti-colonial mobilization, diplomatic encounters with states and international organizations, or the movement of South Asian peoples and cultures across the world. This course explores South Asia’s significance in global politics, with a particular historical focus on the twentieth century. It examines a number of case studies in which national, regional, and international political impetuses have intersected, placing emphasis on South Asians as key actors who have played leading roles in defining the parameters of nation-state politics and global governance in the era of decolonization and the Cold War. In so doing, it uses South Asia’s history to offer a history of international relations from a Global South perspective.

courses.title: Analytic Frameworks for International Public Policy Decisions
courses.desc: Introduction to the basic tools of policy analysis and decision making, providing students with analytic skills to make policy decisions in many types of organizations. The course includes an introduction to public policy objectives, decision making, and the role of analysis. Students then learn powerful analytic decision-making techniques, including decision trees, Bayes theorem, utility theory, prospect theory, game theory, benefit-cost analysis, and tipping models. Case studies are used to learn the policy analysis tools while applying them to real world policy problems. Cases come from developed and developing countries, and cover many different policy fields. No background in economics or statistics is required.

courses.title: GIS for International Applications
courses.desc: This course introduces students to geographic information systems (GIS) with a specific focus on their applications in various international settings and topics. The primary objective of this course is to equip students to explore geospatial technology and related tools, including ESRI ArcGIS Pro, for data creation, management, analysis, and visualization. Throughout the curriculum, students will delve into the dynamic field of GIS through a combination of assignments and interactive discussions, which are organized into modules. This approach enables students to develop an understanding of how geospatial technologies can be utilized across different fields and disciplines. The course also includes a practical component, where students will work on a final project with guided activities. By the end of this course, students will have acquired a relevant skill set that can be readily applied in a wide range of professional contexts. It is worth noting that this course is specifically designed to fulfill the quantitative analysis requirements for both the Master of Arts in Law and Diplomacy (MALD) and the Master of Global Affairs (MGA) programs. Enrollment is limited to 24 students. For more information, visit: https://bit.ly/49cNV1A

courses.title: Political Economy of Development
courses.desc: This class offers a survey of some of the key debates and issues in the political economy of development. First, we examine alternative approaches to development and how they have informed policies in developing countries since the 1950s. Second, we compare different patterns of interaction among the state, political parties, interest groups, and civil society and examine how they have affected development outcomes. Third, we address current topics such as the rise of China and India, new approaches to poverty alleviation, and the impact of global financial crises on developing countries.

courses.title: The Arts of Communication
courses.desc: Today’s leaders must have the ability not only to analyze thoughtfully but also to communicate clearly and persuasively. This full semester course is intended to turn you into a significantly more persuasive and effective public speaker—someone who speaks with the ease, confidence, clarity, and modes of persuasion that are critical in today’s corporate, nonprofit, policy, and diplomacy worlds. We will cover a range of speaking scenarios, from podium speeches on values to simulations of a press conference or media interview on camera. The course is intended to help you develop your own personal style by deepening your understanding of the persuasive tools, recommendations, refutations, modes of analysis, and variations in audiences that motivate listeners to turn business, policy and diplomacy ideas into action. The full semester course will take a deeper and wider dive into the world of public speaking relative to the module course, and include sessions on debating, ceremonial speeches, as well as more detailed sessions on facing the camera and press, impromptu speaking, and elevator pitching. Approximately one-half of the course will be devoted to classes that introduce students to strategies of spoken communication and to models of public presentation. The other half will consist of speech delivery sessions in which students will hone their skills in public speaking.

courses.title: Privacy in the Digital Age
courses.desc: This course examines the evolving threats to and protections for privacy in the digital age, considering challenges from both the public and private sectors on a global scale. We will explore key questions such as: Who values privacy, in which contexts, and why? What roles do anonymity and security play in privacy? How can we assess the benefits and drawbacks of privacy-enhancing technologies? What factors influence the choices people make about their online privacy? The course will integrate technical knowledge with insights from social science literature, drawing on fields such as law, economics, and political science to provide a multifaceted understanding of privacy issues. Topics will include encryption policy, privacy threat models, location tracking, first- and third-party data collection by private entities, government threats to privacy, regulations, and cross-cultural perspectives on privacy norms and values.

courses.title: Modern Military Power
courses.desc: Could the Arab states have defeated Israel in 1967? Could Iraq have resisted the United States in 1991? Could Russia have successfully conquered Ukraine in February 2022? Every one of these questions, which had significant effects on policymakers’ decisions before each conflict, hinge on estimates of military power and the potential outcomes of a military campaign. This class will provide students with the analytical tools to evaluate historical, ongoing, and potential military operations and to predict their potential outcomes. We will begin by discussing the organization of modern militaries and the political and social drivers of military strategy and military effectiveness. Next, we will consider the challenges to military analysis created by friction and the fog of war, looking at historical campaigns to better understand these limitations. Then, we turn to studying the campaign analysis framework for assessing military operations, and apply it to land campaigns, air campaigns, naval campaigns, counterinsurgencies, and humanitarian intervention, looking at both the broad variables and models needed to analyze these problems and specific case studies of military operations in the recent past. Finally, we consider two potential future conflicts, on the Korean Peninsula and over Taiwan, and consider the most likely outcomes of those possible future wars.

courses.title: Terrorism and Counterterrorism
courses.desc: This course examines the nature of terrorism; the spectrum of terrorist motivations, strategies, and operations; the socio-political, economic and other factors that can enable terrorist group activities; the unique threat of WMD terrorism; and the internal vulnerabilities of terrorist organizations. Students will examine current and classic research on terrorism, and explore many of the puzzles that remain unanswered. Finally, the course will analyze these critical issues within the context of policies and strategies for responding to the threat of terrorism with increasing sophistication and success.

courses.title: Civil Resistance
courses.desc: Offers an in-depth primer on civil (nonviolent) resistance waged by ordinary people to bring about substantive political, economic, and/or social change. The course begins with a brief history of nonviolent struggle over the last century, the theoretical foundations of resistance, and common misperceptions. The course then turns to the historical record to study how and why nonviolent resistance movements succeed at double the rate of armed struggles even when waged against oppressive regimes. Students learn several of the core skills taught by practitioners and leading academics in assessment, strategy and planning, tactics, mass mobilization, and organization, and apply these frameworks to case studies throughout the course. Next, the course examines the dynamics that often emerge within nonviolent struggle such as how violent repression can backfire, how to maintain resilience and discipline within the movement, and the role of external actors and assistance. The course ends with students’ assessment of several ongoing civil resistance movements and the prospects for achieving enduring political, economic, or social change.

sections.req: Jr and Sr IR and PS Majors

courses.title: Strategy and Grand Strategy: Theory, Art and Practice
courses.desc: This course aims to build students’ understanding of the theory and practice of strategy and grand strategy and their influence on policy. It is a course designed for practitioners in which students are asked to think critically and creatively about today’s geopolitical environment, potential strategies, their implementation and their consequences. The course begins by examining the nature of strategy and how it is defined across the literature. It explores the historic origins and modern foundations of the field, introduces the concepts of power and statecraft, and considers critiques of strategic planning. Next, the course turns to a discussion of strategic art - the assessment, formulation, and implementation of strategy including the use of diplomatic, economic, and military tools of statecraft. The course concludes by considering the influences of culture, national values, and institutions on contemporary cases of strategy in the United States, China, Russia, and the NATO Alliance. Emphasis throughout the course is primarily focused on nation-state behavior but students are strongly encouraged to apply the course frameworks to other actors in the international system including intergovernmental organizations, non-governmental organizations, the private sector, and other non-state actors.

sections.req: Jr and Sr IR and PS Majors

courses.title: International Cyber Conflict
courses.desc: As a domain and instrument of competition and conflict, cyber space enables a range of global actors—including dissidents, terrorist organizations, and states with varying levels of offensive and defensive cyber capabilities—to assert influence, project power, and conduct activities in the increasingly ambiguous areas between war and peace. This course will explore the role of cyberspace in international conflict, including through the use of espionage, disinformation campaigns, and attacks; the course will examine the policies, strategies, and governance structures of key actors that operate within the cyber domain. We will also study why the development of international norms in cyberspace has proved so elusive.

courses.title: Global Water Security Perspectives
courses.desc: This is a seminar-style course to introduce students to the concept of water security. Water security is a relatively new term in the field of water science and policy, and it is a concept with multiple interpretations. One definition by the Global Water Partnership is “Water Security, at any level from the household to the global, means that every person has access to enough safe water at an affordable cost to lead a clean, healthy, and productive life while ensuring that the natural environment is protected and enhanced.” Since the early 2000s, the term has been used in increasing popularity often as justification or informing technical or policy solutions to the world’s water challenges. How the term is applied in these situations depends on its interpretation, making a solid understanding of the underlying concepts of water security important for decision-makers. Ultimately, water security is a concept that allows us to consider the risks associated with water, such as the risk of a lack of access, risk of poor quality, or risk of flood, and to develop solutions to address these risks, thereby ensuring one’s water security. However, water security is often conflated with the idea of securitization, which has the potential to encourage a securitized approach to water resources management, when interdependence and cooperation are often what is needed to ensure water security for all. This course will take a deep dive into the main concepts and theories underlying the term water security. We will use the Web of Water Security (Zeitoun 2011) as a framework for understanding how water relates to climate, energy, food, human, and national securities, plus consider the economics of water and address environmental water needs. This course aims to help students build an understanding of water security as a concept so that they can use it as a tool to evaluate and inform sustainable and equitable water solutions to the global water crisis we are currently facing.

courses.title: International Energy Policy
courses.desc: Energy affects every dimension of human society ranging from basic living conditions, mobility, and economic prosperity. Energy, primarily derived from fossil fuel sources, has powered industrialization globally since the onset of the industrial revolution, resulting in a substantial rise in economic growth. Nevertheless, energy is at the heart of some of the most intractable environmental problems, national security challenges, and economic-development strategies. Energy is also central to addressing each of these challenges. This survey course explores energy-related challenges and opportunities issues among countries. The policies of major energy consumers and producers are compared. International energy policy topics such as the geopolitics of oil and gas, energy markets, energy access and equity, energy and health, energy technology innovation, and international cooperation and competition are covered in this survey course.

courses.title: Contemporary South Asia
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ HIST 145) Organized along both historical and thematic lines, the course surveys politics, economy, and society in late colonial India and offers a comparative historical analysis of state structures and political processes in post-colonial South Asia, particularly India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Among the themes considered are the reasons for the partition of 1947, the nature of the colonial legacy, the origins of democracy and military authoritarianism, history of development, the shifting balance between central and regional power, the ongoing clash between so-called secular and religiously informed ideologies, and the impact on interstate relations in the subcontinent.

courses.title: 21st Century Intelligence and National Security Seminar
courses.desc:
This seminar on intelligence in the 21st century is designed to give students a sophisticated grounding in what intelligence is, what it is not, and how it is changing rapidly. The focus will be on intelligence in the national security context, but the curriculum is relevant to anyone who in their professional lives will gather, assess, and convey information and insight to others--which is to say almost every professional setting. 

The seminar will convey the key functions of intelligence, including collection, analysis, counterintelligence, covert action, and paramilitary operations. At the same time, the class will attempt to bust the many myths surrounding intelligence—sustained by inaccurate portrayals of the business in popular culture. The instruction and readings will place special emphasis on how intelligence functions have played out in the real-world of US foreign and national security decision making. The seminar will be enhanced by outside experts who will speak directly about their professional experiences in intelligence.

courses.title: Information Technology and Politics in China
courses.desc: This course will explore the relationship between information technology and politics in China, a subject that has consistently challenged and reshaped conventional theories in political science and international relations, especially in the context of U.S.-China technological and ideological competitions. Early cyberpolitical theories posited that the advent of the internet would catalyze democratic changes in China, fostering greater openness and freedom of expression. Contrary to these predictions, the Chinese government has not only adapted to the digital era but seems to have also mastered the art of controlling the internet. Through sophisticated information control tactics, the state has successfully manipulated public opinion, fostering pro-regime sentiments and stifling dissent. These instances underscore the complexity of understanding the interplay between information technology development and the authoritarian regime in China. Grasping this dynamic is not only academically intriguing but also crucial for the United States and the international community to effectively respond and adapt to the multifaceted challenges and opportunities presented in this field.

courses.title: Identity Politics of East Asia
courses.desc: As the axis of global competition shifts eastward, understanding East Asia is ever more important. East Asia is a region that defies many expectations. Remarkable post-war developmental trajectories co-exist with thriving democracies and stable autocracies in neighboring states. The premise of this course is that you cannot get East Asia right without understanding its identity politics: how countries in the region think of their national identity, define their national interest, narrate their past, and imagine their future place in the world. We will explore how identity issues condition cooperation and conflict in the region, shaping everything from diplomacy, military strategy, party politics, democracy, and development. New and seasoned students of East Asia will walk away with a more nuanced understanding of what drives East Asian politics.

courses.title: Advanced GIS
courses.desc: GIS and Spatial analysis offer a unique and insightful perspective on our world, serving as a distinctive lens through which we explore events, patterns, and processes that unfold on or near the Earth's surface. At its core, spatial analysis resides at the crossroads of human insight and computational power, combining the art of interpretation with the precision of spatial data analysis, modeling, machine learning, deep learning, and AI. This fusion of human expertise with advanced technologies is pivotal in shaping decision-making processes, enabling us to unravel complex spatial phenomena and make informed choices that drive progress and innovation. This course is designed to immerse professionals in training in a rich learning experience, blending lab sessions with hands-on activities and engaging lectures and discussions through a holistic approach. The course not only covers spatial data science but also delves into the intricate realms of machine learning, deep learning, and AI. Participants will gain the knowledge and skills needed to apply these cutting-edge technologies to spatial analyses and decision-making processes. Throughout the course, the emphasis is on practical, real-world applications, including topics such as modeling, suitability analysis, pattern detection, deep learning, neural networks, dynamic visualization, and the nuanced examination of complex spatial datasets. This ensures that students are well-equipped with various quantitative methods, from descriptive to geostatistical methodologies. Finally, decision-making methods and visualization techniques are embedded to ensure we equip students with the practical skills to effectively interpret and communicate complex spatial data. These skills help bridge the gap between data analysis and real-world applications, fostering a deeper understanding of spatial relationships and their impact on decision outcomes. GIS for International Applications is a prerequisite to enroll, and the class is limited to a maximum of 24 students. For more information, visit: https://bit.ly/3u2xki8

courses.title: Migration and Transnationalism in Latin America
courses.desc: This seminar will examine the implications of international migration, migrant remittances, and transnationalism for development and politics in Latin America. The first section addresses alternative theories of migration and reviews global patterns of migration in both sending and receiving countries. The last two sections focus on the impact of international migration and remittances on economic development and politics in sending countries, primarily in Latin America but with some comparative data from other developing countries.

courses.title: Power in World Politics
courses.desc: Power is the defining concept in the international relations discipline, and yet there is no consensus about what that concept means. This is a problematic state of affairs. The need for a better conceptual and empirical understanding of power should be obvious. This seminar will confront these conceptual and empirical problems head-on. Through an array of scholarly readings and case studies, we will aim for a better understanding of what power means, its myriad dimensions, how it is perceived over time, and how it is exercised by actors in world politics.

courses.title: Introduction to Digital Media
courses.desc:
Explore creating art with computers: digital video, 3D, still images, and audio.
Introductory course focused on core concepts and practical techniques. Understand file formats, binary representations, computer hardware, compositing modes, alpha channels, video compression, data rate, digital audio techniques, AI image generation, and principles of creative coding. Learn the skills to prevent “computer problems”, by understanding the under-the-hood workings of hardware and software. Learn the software of today, and become well-prepared for the hardware and software of tomorrow. Small weekly assignments leading to a larger final project. No experience is necessary. Open to all levels.
Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Thinking Machines and Automata
courses.desc:
Explore the creative use of artificial intelligence and autonomous machines. Learn basic and necessary skills in electronics, physical computing, digital fabrication, and creative coding to bring their ideas to fruition. Develop proficiency in beginner-friendly tools that encourage creative exploration, such as the Arduino microcontroller, Teachable Machine simplified machine learning, and prompt-based AI applications like Dall-E 2 and ChatGPT. Through readings and discussion, we examine the philosophical and ethical discourses regarding the nature of intelligent machines and their use in society. No experience in digital media required.
Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Poetic Data
courses.desc:
Studio/seminar course explores data and storytelling. Learn to work with data to create art and design projects: 2D and 3D data visualizations, immersive Augmented Reality applications, mixed-reality experiences. Through software tutorials, creative in-class activities, and critique of student work, we explore the potential of data as a medium for creative expression. Develop the required skills for a solid basis for future data-driven art and design works. Examine, subvert, and reimagine “data” in relation to the cultural and conceptual associations that surround it, and learn to appreciate the poetic possibilities within data.
Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.
