courses.title: Programming for Visual Thinkers
courses.desc:
Develop software using visual modules instead of code, similar to plugging guitar pedals into one another. Concepts of visual programming, including instantiation, matrix math, lookup tables, and parametric design. Applications to a variety of disciplines including image making, installation, lighting, interactive video, graphic design, projection mapping, VJing, and data visualization.
Develop unique software tools for creating real time interactive 3D scenes, generative 2D images, and audio reactive systems.
Recommendations: Some experience with Photoshop, Premier, After Effects or equivalent image manipulation software is expected. Open to all levels.

courses.title: Virtual Reality
courses.desc:
Hybrid studio/seminar. Practice and theory of Virtual Reality as contemporary fine art form. Uses the software Unity3D to create immersive interactive audio-visual environments to be viewed with VR headsets, mobile phones, or as video art. Build custom VR projects. History of philosophical, aesthetic, and ethical dimensions of mimetic representation. Differentiates and expands on what makes a virtual reality experience a work of art, as opposed to a game or a tool. Appropriate for students who have some experience with video, and who are comfortable engaging with critical concepts. Contact the instructor with any questions.

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: America Imaginaria
courses.desc: Use Blender, open-source 3D animation software, and various animation and sculpting tools, to explore the theme of monstrosity with special emphasis on the “American Bestiary”. Throughout history encounters with fictional beings have been described in terms of our fears and prejudices. Explore the abandoned narratives of these so-called monsters and recreate them using 3D Animation Software. In-class exercises use motion capture to create short films that reclaim the notion of monstrosity as a tool for understanding ourselves. No previous experience required.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Advanced 3D Animation
courses.desc:
Advanced 3D Animation employs an experimental approach to address concepts, tools, and problems of current computer animation. As an advanced course, introductory knowledge of concepts such as rigging, texturing, and keyframes is expected in order to develop projects that use Blender 3D to experiment with Python Scripting, mechanical rigs, and other animation procedures useful in creating more elaborate artistic projects involving animation. The coursework involves technical challenges in character animation, motion graphics, scripting, and a final unit centered on the expressive possibilities of using CG for Video Installations. 3D animation experience expected. Intermediate/advanced level.

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Art / Archives / AI
courses.desc:
Studio/seminar course explores forgotten archives and hidden datasets as critical sites of artistic inquiry. By addressing both the archive and the dataset as technologies of power, it considers art's potential to propose counter-histories and new poetics of redress. Key topics include: feminist shadow archives (Halberstam), archives of feelings (Cvetkovich), critical fabulation (Hartman), Afro-fabulation (Nyong’o), AI data bias (Crawford). Technical workshops (video/editing/coding), and in-depth analysis of relevant case studies and theoretical texts (critical theory, queer, postcolonial, and critical race studies) will provide students with the necessary skills and intellectual understanding to develop their own archive/dataset-based artworks.
Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Ballet II
courses.desc: For students with fundamental experience with ballet, continuing with traditional barre and center work on an advanced beginning level. Creative applications of ballet techniques and movement vocabulary in short compositional assignments. Supplemental study of ballet history and comparative styles. Recommendations: DNC 12: Ballet I or equivalent recommended but not required.

courses.title: Ballet IV
courses.desc: For students with advanced training in ballet. Technical emphasis on accuracy, aesthetic differentiations in ballet styles and continued detail to musical phrasing and interpretive performance. Continuing with traditional barre and center work on an advanced beginning level. Continued compositional assignments and advanced analysis of historic repertory and artistic interpretation.For students with substantial dance training in modern and/or ballet. Modern-oriented technique, combinations, and creative studies. Aesthetic context addressed in additional assignments. May be repeated.

courses.title: Modern III
courses.desc: Intermediate or lower modern techniques, adapted for those with basic training in a movement discipline such as modern, ballet, jazz, or another cultural form. Coaching of performance qualities such as musicality and group dynamics. Creative opportunities and appreciation of performance. For students with intermediate to advanced dance training in modern and/or ballet. Modern-oriented technique, including introduction to extended combinations, repertory and creative/improvisationalstructures. Experiential exposure to differing historic forms and styles. May be repeated.

courses.title: Hip Hop: Introduction to Breakin' Culture/Practice
courses.desc: Introduction to Breakin’, the original dance of Hip Hop, combining movement and written work. Development of foundational skills in toprock, downrock, and other styles of movement through tools of dance. Exploration of self-expression and community through practice and exchange within street dance pedagogy. History of Hip Hop (globally and locally) and engagement with its social, political, and spiritual dimensions. Includes readings, videos, weekly reflections, discussions, and written assignments. No previous dance experience required.

courses.title: Hip Hop II: Study Through the Cypher
courses.desc: Exploration of relationship between movement practice and written/spoken word, including lyricism of Hip Hop emcees, poetry, and philosophical readings. “The Cypher” as a space of research and communication. Study of self and society through street dance pedagogy, based on the movement vocabulary and practice of Breakin’. Engagement with local Hip Hop culture and economic history. Includes readings, videos, weekly reflections, discussions, and written assignments. Recommendations: DNC 0030 or previous experience with Breakin’ or other Hip Hop dance forms.

courses.title: Contemporary Jazz Dance
courses.desc: Contemporary jazz fuses elements of pop culture with modern dance and ballet, underscored by principles of hip-hop. Emphasis on personal expression through movement to become a confident and eclectic dancer. Assignments include short viewings; readings and written work; and performance viewing and response. Appropriate for more advanced dancers and dance minors.

courses.title: Tap Dance: Practice, Performance, and Survey
courses.desc: Tap dance techniques and historical tap dance repertoire. Explores a variety of dances, their cultural contexts, and strengthens technical skill. Emphasis on improvisation within the form provides a deeper connection with the material.

courses.title: Tap Dance II
courses.desc: Refinement of tap dance technique and continued study of historical tap dance repertoire. Various dances are learned, with a focus on exploring their cultural contexts and strengthening technical skill. Emphasis on improvisation within the form provides a deeper connection with the material.

courses.title: Afro-Haitian Dance
courses.desc: Historical influences of the traditional dance and rhythms of Haiti, including Yanvalou, Ibo, Banda, and Congo. Experiential course, which also includes short viewings, discussions of readings, and written assignments. No previous dance experience required.

courses.title: Dance Production Practicum
courses.desc: Logistics and rigor of producing dance performance. Prepares dancemakers for transitioning into the role of dance choreographers and directors. Participation as crew and/or staff in the production of Dance Program events. Entails approximately 15-hours, concentrated during load-in, tech, dress, and performance schedules for events. Required for Dance minors. May be repeated once.

courses.title: Dance Performance Practicum
courses.desc: Reserved for students participating as performers or a full-semester stage manager for Senior Dance Minor capstone projects and dance faculty performance projects. May be repeated once. Prerequisite: Consent of instructor.

courses.title: Dance Movement And Creative Process
courses.desc: Fundamental principles of speed, weight, dynamic force, momentum, spatial composition, and body articulation through individual and group movement. Collaborative and improvisational exploration of non-verbal communication, giving and receiving weight, and creative problem-solving. Includes video viewings, readings, discussions, and short written assignments. Designed for students of all levels. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Dance on Camera
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/FMS 27 & DNC 177 & ILVS 29) Inter-disciplinary course designed for any dancer, artist or student interested in film & video production with dance or movement as a medium. Participants will take dance and movement concepts outside of studio walls and into the community through site-specific collaborative video projects. Through storyboarding, shooting, editing, and choreographing/directing, students will learn basic video production techniques and advanced camera work in this hands-on course. Development of movement ideas as well as non-linear editing skills will be explored. Work culminates in end of semester public screening and online video sharing. Open to all. No dance or film/video experience necessary.

courses.title: Dance and the Hollywood Musical
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with FMS 26) The role of dance in the film musical genre over the past century. Explores how bodies, movement vocabulary, and choreography can reinforce, oppose, and/or comment on contemporary society and our “collective” cultural identity. How do parallel developments in cinema and art impact the way we view dance? How are race, gender, and nationality portrayed? How do we define and view this genre today? Viewings, readings, movement experiences, discussions, and independent projects. Focus on developing literacy and critical research skills in dance. No previous dance or film background required. Recommendation: Art History and/or critical studies course in the arts.

courses.title: Special Topics - Beyond the Ballroom
courses.desc: Guided independent study of an approved topic or courses not yet in the curriculum. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://dramadance.tufts.edu/

sections.note: Beyond the Ballroom asks us to interrogate our own relationship with social dancing, and how we show up and engage as members of the partner dance community. Students will learn a variety of beginner/intermediate level patterns in a selection of partnered social dance styles including foxtrot, waltz, swing, hustle, bachata, salsa, & merengue. Weekly reading assignments in dance studies will support a broader understanding of the historical lineage of each dance style; the geopolitical forces that have shaped their global movement and appropriation; and how the ballroom dance industry has codified and commodified these forms. Alternatively, we will explore how local dance practitioners build and sustain dance communities beyond the ballroom dance industry. Prereq: DNC-67, DNC-64, or permission from the instructor.

courses.title: Special Topics - House Dance
courses.desc: Guided independent study of an approved topic or courses not yet in the curriculum. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://dramadance.tufts.edu/

sections.note: This course explores the rich history, foundational techniques, and cultural significance of House dance from its origin to its global evolution. Students will learn house steps and variations while working toward developing freestyle expression and musicality, and examining how social dance reflects broader socio-political contexts. Includes readings, viewings, and discussions. Open to all, including beginners and experienced dancers of any style are welcome.

courses.title: Dance on Camera

Participants will take dance and movement concepts outside of studio walls and into the community through site-specific collaborative video projects. Through storyboarding, shooting, editing, and choreographing/directing, students will learn basic video production techniques and advanced camera work in this hands-on course. Development of movement ideas as well as non-linear editing skills will be explored. Work culminates in end of semester public screening and online video sharing. Open to all. No dance or film/video experience necessary.

courses.title: Experiential Anatomy
courses.desc: An internal study of the body through an exploration of anatomical, physiological, and biomechanical systems and principles. Each week, a different area of the body and/or body system is studied and physically explored in individual and group movement experiences. Design and in-class facilitation of movement explorations. Reading, viewing, and written assignments will draw from both scientific and experiential movement studies. No prerequisites, but a background and/or keen interest in body science and/or movement is highly recommended. Meets Occupational Therapy (OT) elective credits. Does not meet anatomy and kinesiology requirements for OT.

courses.desc: Comprehensive introduction to drawing techniques, strategies and materials. Gateway course for all students interested in interpreting and responding to the world through drawing. Students build strong technical and perceptual skills through direct observation and rigorous practice. Drawing is also a way of thinking with the body and as a conceptual practice it overlaps many areas of art activity. Through projects and prompts, evolve an understanding of the unique opportunities for transformation and expression that drawing provides. Coursework includes demonstrations, presentations, exercises and assignments. Introductory course open to all levels. Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

As the semester continues students build supportive habits as they develop individual projects large-scale in size or quantity. Materials include pencil, paper, ink; additional media optional. Class occasionally meets outdoors. Sources include historical and contemporary art spanning meditative, spiritualist and conceptual, and readings on mindfulness and distractions of contemporary culture. Ideal for students wanting to expand their practice and develop strong habits, and suitable for any discipline. Open to all levels.

Combine visual accuracy and conceptual expression in student work. Lectures and readings on contemporary figurative artists working in a range of media add to visual understanding of the body inside and out. courses.title: Special Topics - How the Brain Perceives Art
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: Examines how the brain converts the projected image of the world into our perception of it. Teaches how perceived contrast, lines and edges, simple shapes, and movement make an interpretation of reality tied to our lived experience. Illustrates these mechanisms using artwork throughout history that empirically tapped into them. Required: an art project in drawing (dry or water-based media), and a presentation on how neural principles increase the impact of your work. Extreme cross-disciplinary course with required intro level courses and appreciation of art-science interface an advantage.
sections.req: DRW 18, DRW 51 or PAI 3 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Art As Process
courses.desc: Introduction to art-making through process. Explore multiple mediums to develop an artistic practice and enrich visual awareness. Emphasis on experimentation, ideation, and thinking critically about creative practices and developing a personal voice. Explore multiple discourses, including drawing, graphic, paint, and sculpture. Experiment with abstraction, realism, and conceptual approaches in the context of historical, cultural, and contemporary issues. Individual and collaborative exercises to broaden awareness of beliefs, concepts, and autobiographical content.. Not a foundations course in any specific medium. Open to all levels.

courses.title: Drawing: Foundation
courses.desc:
Drawing is an ancient and universal practice as well as an aspect of visual thinking. Working from direct and indirect observations, students will develop the confidence to evaluate shape, line quality, value, composition, and how the critical choice of materials will impact an idea. Drawing Foundations introduces drawing as a practice of observation. We approach the illusion of space and form through formal analysis and subjective interpretation. Foundations examines the multiple functions of drawing across time and culture as well as emphasizing the breadth of the drawing experience and its application across disciplines. The course provides a format for a focused exploration of drawing practice as an instrument of communication, a source of ideas and an opportunity to risk and move beyond one's current abilities and notions.

This course is open to all LA + EN undergraduate students.

courses.title: Drawing: Mixed Media
courses.desc: Builds on the historical traditions of drawing while introducing a variety of artists and approaches to the processes of drawing. Tailored to the individual’s sensibilities and natural inclinations, students experiment with pencil, pen, charcoal, color pastels, and water-based paints (gouache, watercolor or acrylics). Produce a body of work with a personal vision. Includes virtual and/or in-person visits to local art museums. Designed for students at all levels and a desire to experiment with the language of marks and stains while exploring a variety of dry and wet materials. Open to all LA + EN undergraduate students.

courses.title: Perspective Drawing
courses.desc:
This comprehensive course in basic perspective drawing is open to all levels and is devoted to drawing from observation. Still lives in the studio and some field trips to outside locations will provide our subject matter and sources of inspiration. Through various methods for creating the illusion of realism we will utilize the elements of line, shape, texture, value, composition and the techniques of western perspective design to convincingly portray 3D volume and space on a 2D surface. Towards the end of the course these tools will be used to design and create your own ideas and structures; drawings, houses, monuments, memorials, autos, objects and sculptures, etc. of your choosing. Our exploration and work will provide insight into what has given this discipline its time honored visual appeal and help us to create new and unique perspective drawings and designs. Materials include charcoal, graphite, erasers, rulers, sumi ink and paper.

This course is open to all LA + EN undergraduate students.

courses.desc:
Application of mathematical methods common to both micro- and macroeconomics. Applications include: systems of equations and comparative statics, e.g., supply and demand equations and models of strategic interaction; consumer constrained utility maximization; firm profit maximization and cost minimization; dynamic equilibria (difference and differential equations) and dynamic optimization techniques. 
Prerequisites: Economics 11; and Mathematics 34 or above.

courses.title: Review of Statistics for Quantitative Economics
courses.desc: Mathematical statistical techniques that are used in econometric analysis and provide a foundation for students pursuing the quantitative economics major track. Topics may include probability theory, discrete and continuous random variables and their joint distributions, sampling and estimation, hypothesis testing, rudiments of statistical programming, and brief introduction to the theory of linear regression. Students who have taken Economics 13 and want to take Economics 14, must enroll in Economics 17 for credit. Economics 13 and Economics 14 may not both be taken for credit. Prerequisite: EC 13

courses.title: Quantitative Intermediate Macroeconomic Theory
courses.desc: Analysis of the determinants of national income, basic concepts and accounting, aggregate consumption and investment behavior, and implications for public policy, with mathematical illustrations. Required for all quantitative economics majors who have not completed Economics 205. In no case may a student receive credit for both Economics 18 and 12.

courses.title: Review Of Quantitative Macroeconomic Theory
courses.desc: Review of EC 18 for Quantitative Economics majors who have taken EC 12. Prerequisites: Economics 16.

courses.title: Game Theory
courses.desc:
Introduction to game theory and how it is used to understand strategic interactions among individuals, firms, governments, and countries. Topics include credible threats, signaling, principal-agent problems, auctions, arbitration, voting, implications of asymmetric and incomplete information and collusion. Not open to students who have taken or are currently taking EC 119 or its equivalent.
Prerequisites: Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Environmental Economics
courses.desc:
An examination of the uses and limitations of economic analysis in dealing with many of the environmental concerns of our society. Public policies concerning the environment will be evaluated as to their ability to meet certain economic criteria.
Prerequisite: Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Economic Development
courses.desc:
Problems in the growth of underdeveloped economies. Emphasis on quantitative models of economic growth at low levels of income and on the testing of various hypotheses proposed to explain underdevelopment. Consequences of market structures, population growth, externalities, institutions, and political factors for economic development.
Prerequisites: Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Health Economics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CH 112) An examination of major topics in the economics of health and health care, both in the United States and abroad, using the basic theoretical and empirical tools of economics. Covers the medical and nonmedical determinants of health, markets for medical care services and health insurance, and proposed ideas for health care reform. Prerequisites Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Introduction to Finance
courses.desc:
An introduction to fundamental ideas of corporate finance and their connection to economic principles through basic theory, cases and applications. Not open to students who have taken or are currently taking Economics 150 or its equivalent.
Prerequisite: Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: International Economics
courses.desc:
Analysis of the economic effects of trade among nations. Determination and stabilization of exchange rates; regulation of commerce through various commercial policies; the United States' balance of payments; the impact of international trade on price, incomes, and employment in the participating nations; and international agencies and agreements affecting world trade. Custom unions and common markets, world liquidity problems. Not open to students who have taken or are currently taking EC 161 or its equivalent.
Prerequisites: Economics 5 or Economics 8.

Topics include least squares estimation, instrumental variable estimation, panel data techniques, and time-series techniques. EC 15 and 107 may not both be taken for credit.

courses.title: Behavioral Economics
courses.desc: Analysis of economic decision making which incorporates the effects of social, emotional, and cognitive issues. Topics considered include loss aversion, risks, time preferences, learning, and social preferences. A familiarity with taking derivatives and using calculus is expected. Prerequisites: EC 11. Recommendations: EC 0024, EC 0119, EC 0170, or PHIL 0038.

courses.title: Quantitative Games & Information
courses.desc:
The strategic role of information, or who knows what and when they know it. Application of game theory to understanding how revealing and concealing information can be the basis of strategic behavior in economics. Games of perfect, imperfect, and incomplete information, and development of the corresponding solution for each type of game. Examples include games of asymmetric information that have been applied in economics to a wide range of fields including industrial organization, finance, labor, and development economics. No previous course in game theory is required.
Prerequisites: EC 13 or EC 14, and EC 16; or EC 201 and 203.

courses.desc: Introduction to the economic analysis of cities and regions. Topics include land use, transportation, urbanization, housing, inequality and discrimination, and public finance and services. Prerequisites: EC 11 and Statistics (EC 13, 14 or 201, or ES 56, or MATH 166). Recommendations: Econometrics (EC 15 or 107).

courses.title: Economics Of Energy Markets
courses.desc:
Analysis of energy markets and policy issues arising from our production and consumption of energy. Topics considered include the theory of depletable resources, measurement of energy externalities, market power in energy production, climate change and energy security.
Prerequisites Economics 11; Economics 13 suggested.

sections.req: Requires the completion of EC 11 or graduate student.

courses.title: Topics In Economic Development - Topics In Economic Development
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed with CVS 133) Selected major current problems in various developing countries. Students will be asked to utilize and extend the theoretical insights from Economics 35 by applying them in specific cases. Topics will include problems in energy, agriculture, balance of payments, and industrialization. Elements of benefit-cost analysis will also be covered.
Prerequisites: Economics 11 and 35; Economics 13 suggested.

courses.desc: Research seminar for students who wish to pursue health economics beyond the level of Economics 0048. Emphasis on how economists use causal inference methods to answer health economics questions. Topics may include the effect of health insurance on outcomes such as health care utilization, preventive health behaviors, financial well-being, and the effect of pollution on health. Prerequisites: EC 11 and either EC 15 or EC 107. Recommendations: EC 48.

courses.title: Economics of Sports
courses.desc:
The world of sports is used to illustrate the application of core concepts from microeconomics and econometrics. The main topics covered are the industrial organization of sports, the public finance of sports, the labor economics of sports, and college sports. Each section will begin with an overview of contextual information and will then show how the appropriate tools from economics can be applied. Each section closes with discussion of recent research on the topic of the section. 
Prerequisites: Economics 11 and Economics 15 or Economics 107.

courses.title: Financial Economics
courses.desc:
Application of economic theory and statistics to the analyses of corporate investment and financing decisions and the equilibrium prices of financial instruments. Topics include the time value of money, structure of interest rates, evaluation of investment projects, the advantage of portfolio diversification, asset pricing models, corporate capital structure, dividend policy and the valuation of options and futures.
Prerequisites: Economics 11 and either Economics 12 or Economics 18.
In no case may a student receive credit for both Economics 150 and Economics 159.

sections.req: EC 11 and either EC 12 or EC 18

courses.title: Monetary Economics
courses.desc:
Overview of the U.S. financial system with an emphasis on basic monetary theory, the structure and regulatory environment of financial institutions, the conduct of monetary policy, and international linkages.
Prerequisites: Economics 11 and either Economics 12 or Economics 18.

sections.req: EC 11 and either EC 12 or EC 18

courses.title: Sustainable Finance and Investment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with EIB B248) Effects of environmental, social, and governance factors on financial decision-making. Key themes and developments in regulation, financial reporting, sustainability assessment (or ratings), investment analysis, and capital sourcing across a range of financial markets and asset types, including public equities, public debt, private equity, and infrastructure. Examination of financial strategies and vehicles as tools to advance sustainability and impact objectives whether at the investor, state, or multinational level. Introduction and use of a variety of analytic tools to understand the basic decision models of sustainable and impact investing. A&S prerequisites: EC 50 or EC 150; Fletcher prerequisites: EIB B200 and one of EIB B221 or B229.

courses.title: Topics in Finance and Entrepreneurship
courses.desc:
Topics covered include: the financial life-cycle; corporate liquidity; small-firm financing options; organizational constituencies--founders, shareholders, employees--and their goals; conflict and cooperation in constituent goals; and strategic modeling. Individual and/or team projects. Capstone course for the Finance Minor.
Prerequisites: Ec 50 or Ec 150 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: International Trade
courses.desc: Investigation of why countries trade with each other, using theories of comparative advantage, factor abundance, and product differentiation. Topics may include trade and imperfect competition, trade policy, and trade wars. Each topic and model followed by real-world application and discussion of recent trends and regulation. Prerequisite: Economics 11.

sections.req: Requires the completion of EC 11 or graduate student.
Requires the completion of EC 11 or graduate student.

courses.title: International Finance
courses.desc:
Macroeconomic and monetary aspects of international economics. Topics include foreign exchange markets, income and price determination under flexible and fixed exchange rates, theories of the exchange rate and of the balance of payments, stabilization policy in the international economy, international capital movements, and the institutional arrangements of the international monetary system. Not open to students who have taken or are currently taking EC 169 or its equivalent.
Prerequisite: Economics 12 or Economics 18.
In no case may a student receive credit for both Economics 162 and Economics 169.

courses.title: Industrial Organization
courses.desc:
Examination of the strategic interaction of firms in the marketplace and how this affects the way markets are organized. Different models of oligopoly are studied in order to understand how firms strategically set price, choose output, choose product quality, invest in capacity, and engage in R&D. Use of government policy and antitrust laws to influence the ways in which firms compete with each other.
Prerequisite: Economics 11.

sections.req: Requires the completion of EC 11 or graduate student.

courses.title: Law And Economics
courses.desc: Economic analysis of the common, legislated, and constitutional law and the process of each with primary emphasis on the impact of legal rights and duties. Topics chosen from products liability, malpractice, tort, contracts, property, financial, family, discrimination, environment, corporate, antitrust, employment, and regulatory vs. common law remedies for the abuse of market power. Prerequisites: EC 11 and either EC 13 or EC 14; or instructor consent.

sections.req: Completion of EC 11 and either EC 13 or 14

courses.title: Number & Size Of Nations
courses.desc:
The number of sovereign states has increased dramatically from 74 in 1945 to almost 200. They come in all sizes with China at 1.2 billion people and Tuvalu, the smallest country with a seat at the United Nations, at less than 11,000. This advanced seminar examines what determines the number and size of nations and how borders change over time, how a country's size matters for economic prosperity, and how the formation and breakup of nations depend on democratization, economic integration, international conflicts and wars. These questions are addressed using the tools of economic analysis, while also taking into account insights from other disciplines, such as history and political science.
Prerequisites: Economics 11 or 16 and Economics 12 or 18.

The class complements and does not substitute ongoing meetings with thesis advisor(s). (Only open to second-year research-based MS students and not appropriate as a general graduate elective).

courses.title: Research Seminar II
courses.desc: This course is a required course for all first year candidates in the Economics and Public Policy Ph.D. program joint between the economics department in Arts and Sciences and the Fletcher School. Course requirements include mandatory attendance at the weekly seminar series in the economics department. The schedule and date for the seminars may be found at: https://ase.tufts.edu/economics/events/seminarseries.htm. These seminars typically last for 1.5 hours and will cover a broad spectrum of topics. You should make sure to read the paper before the seminar and come prepared to participate in the discussion of the paper being presented.

courses.title: Doctoral Seminar in Research Approaches and Methods
courses.desc: One of the primary challenges for any researcher is taking a promising research question, refining and testing estimation strategy, and shaping the results into a paper (and associated presentation). This is what we will work on in this course. (The preceding companion course covers identifying a strong research question, data and methodology.) The objectives of this course are to provide PhD students with tools to rigorously analyze data and to craft research output (papers and presentations) from the resulting estimates; and to provide constructive feedback on others' work. We will cover current topics in modern applied econometrics such as difference in difference, regression discontinuity, randomized controlled trials, shift-share designs, inference, missing data, and others. This course is the second part of a two-course sequence in the joint Fletcher-Econ PhD program.

Students present their ongoing research and receive feedback from their peers, the instructor, and other faculty. Students will also meet with the instructor individually to hone their research and presentation skills. The class is open to all students in the Economics and Public Policy PhD program and enrollment is required for students in the 3rd year and beyond. The course meets once a week for 1 hour and 15 minutes; the instructor will hold office hours for the EPP enrolled students once a week.

courses.title: Intro to the Earth, Resources, and Environments
courses.desc: Introduction to the dynamic system of the solid Earth and the changes it undergoes on timescales ranging from seconds, to millennia, to eons. Topics include plate tectonics, origin and composition of the Earth, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, critical minerals and geologic resources, mountain building, weathering, sea level shifts, and interactions between solid Earth, oceans, and climate. Emphasis on skills to critically evaluate diverse datasets to understand Earth’s evolution and habitability. Co-enrollment in the lab, ECS 2, is strongly encouraged.

courses.title: Introduction to Climate Science
courses.desc: Introduction to the physical and chemical workings of Earth's climate system including sources of energy, the greenhouse effect, carbon cycle, and redistribution of heat through the atmosphere and ocean. Provides a fundamental scientific context for understanding the causes and impacts of past, current, and future climate change.

courses.title: Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology
courses.desc: Classification, occurrence, and origin of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Laboratory emphasis on hand specimen and microscopic identification and interpretation. Prerequisite: ECS 11 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Sedimentology and Stratigraphy
courses.desc: Processes of sedimentation in environments ranging from continental to marine settings; tectonic, climatic, and oceanographic processes, control sedimentation patterns in these environments, and their relative importance. Observational and interpretational skills in sedimentary rock description and classification through study of sedimentary structures, statistical analysis of sediment grain parameters, and diagenetic textures. Correlation techniques using litho- and biostratigraphy applied to depositional basins in case studies. Prerequisite: ECS 1. Recommendation: ECS 2.

courses.title: Geochemical Cycles
courses.desc: Cycling of chemical elements through the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere, with a focus on processes at and near the Earth’s surface. Topics include the chemistry of natural waters, carbonate chemistry and the carbon cycle, nutrient cycles, trace metal pollution, and soil chemistry. Emphasis on interactions with climate and biological processes. Prerequisites: ECS 1 or ECS 3, and CHEM 1 or CHEM 11, or instructor permission.

sections.req: ECS 1 or ECS 3, and CHEM 1 or CHEM 11

courses.title: Paleoclimate
courses.desc: Examination of climate changes that took place on Earth during the last ~4 billion years with a focus on the proxy evidence for those changes and understanding of the mechanisms that caused them. This journey begins with the wrongly perceived “hell” of the Hadean and ends with Quaternary glaciations, the Holocene, the “Hockey Stick,” and a glimpse into the near future. Prerequisite: ECS 3 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Physical Oceanography
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ECS 56/256) Introduction to physical properties and dynamics of the ocean, with an emphasis on the ocean’s role in climate. Builds upon fundamental principles to develop the equations that describe fluid motions in the ocean. Topics include ocean circulation, heat transport, waves, atmosphere-ocean interactions, and connections between ocean physics and its biology and chemistry. Prerequisites: Physics 1 or 11 and Math 32, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Physics 1 or 11 and one of Math 32, 34, 39, 42, or 44

courses.title: School & Society
courses.desc: Role and purpose of schooling in the United States. Focus on the desegregation and resegregation of schools in the last fifty years; proposals for school reform.

courses.title: Teaching and Learning in K-12 History and Social Studies
courses.desc: History and social studies education are often at the center of crucial debates about national identity and civic engagement. What are history and social studies as disciplines in K-12 schooling? How have they become what they are now? How is it decided what should be taught, why and how? What epistemological and curricular frameworks shape responses to these questions? And what does it mean for K-12 students to do history?

courses.title: The Global Educator: Education in Post Colonial Africa
courses.desc: Essential educational issues from a global perspective. History, economics, and cultures of developing African nations. How the current (or developing) educational system is influenced by these issues. Case study illustrating aspects of working to build and sustain a school in Rwanda. Connections between education and citizenship from a global perspective.

courses.title: Social-Emotional & Civic Learning in Schools
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 46) Explore how fostering social-emotional development and ethical civic learning in K-12 schools helps to advance the civic mission of public education. Study intersecting fields of civic education, moral education, and social-emotional learning (SEL). Consider research on and cases involving culturally responsive social-emotional learning. Interactive seminar. School site visit required. Culminating projects guided by students’ questions and interests.

courses.title: Seminar for Learning Assistants in STEM
courses.desc: Addresses theories of learning and instruction; the nature of STEM disciplinary Practices and understandings; and diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice (DEIJ). Trains undergraduate Learning Assistants (LAs) to facilitate student learning. Prerequisites: Enrollment in the Tufts LA Program and permission of instructor.

courses.title: Children, Nature, and the Development of Earth Stewards
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 34, CVS 32, ED 34, and CSHD 234) Programs and methods being used around the world to connect children and teens to the natural world and nourish their development as earth stewards. Forest schools, wilderness programs, environmental education, urban gardening, children’s books related to earth stewardship, and teen protests for climate action. By permission of instructor, open to graduate students as CSHD 234

courses.title: Behavior Management In The Classroom
courses.desc: Theory, research, and practice of creating a positive classroom climate and working with challenging students. Introduction to practical and empirically derived classroom-based interventions intended to have beneficial effects on the academic, behavioral, social, and emotional functioning of children and adolescents. An iterative, problem-solving approach to intervention will be emphasized.

courses.title: Pedagogies

Explores the connections between and among culture, institutional structure, policy, and pedagogy through an emphasis on praxis. 
Junior, Senior, Grad, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Senior Capstone
courses.desc: Senior Capstone Seminar provides an academic space for seniors majoring in Education to share and reflect on their learning in education and their co-major culminating in a Capstone project. Capstone projects may include, but are not limited to, long term investigative projects, internships, or field work that culminate in a final product, presentation, or performance. Prerequisite: Declared Education major, instructor permission, and permission of student’s major advisors.

courses.title: Resource-based Models of Learning in STEM Disciplines
courses.desc: Research on learning, across STEM disciplines, social sciences and humanities, tends to focus on misconceptions and developmental limitations, barriers students must overcome. This seminar focuses on models of productive intellectual resources - aspects of students' knowledge, reasoning abilities, inclinations that are beginnings of expertise.

courses.title: Pre-Practicum Seminar
courses.desc: Supervised field experience seminar on professional practice in school psychology during the pre-practicum year. Emphasis on integrating National Association of School Psychologists (NASP) domains including data-based decision-making, consultation and collaboration, mental and behavioral health services and interventions, safe and supportive schools, assessment, and legal and ethical practice. Emphasis on developing skills in culturally responsive practice.

instructors: Emily Joyce Sostek, Noelle P. Roop

courses.title: Mste Proseminar
courses.desc: First and second year MSTE students are required to take an ongoing Program Seminar (Proseminar). The course meets biweekly, is attended by interested faculty and researchers and by all first and second year students, focuses on issues of current interest, and constitutes a forum for outside speakers, students and faculty in the program to present their ongoing research and to discuss papers of outstanding relevance for those in the program. Students in the more advanced years of the program will be invited to use the proseminar as a forum to present and receive feedback on their dissertation work at various points during its development.

courses.title: Practicum In School Psychology
courses.desc: Supervised field experience focuses on professional practices including assessment, consultation, counseling, informal assessment, and academic and behavioral interventions. The school-based practicum is accompanied by a seminar designed to provide students with additional supervision and didactic training. The seminar focuses on implementation of problem solving models for identifying and addressing students' academic and social/emotional/behavioral needs and on supporting all aspects of professional practice, including participating in effective site-based supervision. Students complete a minimum of 600 hours of supervised field experience in a school setting during the year, and the requirements of a weekly seminar. Students submit a portfolio and present their work to members of the department as evidence of their growth and professional development. Two courses. Prerequisite: consent

courses.title: School Based Mental Health
courses.desc: A public health model emphasizing prevention in the broader context of a comprehensive, coordinated continuum of interventions. Preventive interventions encompassing areas such as social and emotional learning, health and mental health promotion, wellness, positive school and classroom climate, skills training, bullying, family-school partnering, trauma sensitivity, and greater community involvement in schools as public institutions. Recognizing the significant evidence that exists to support such interventions as critical for academic success, this course will consider the challenges to effective implementation of mental health services in schools.

courses.title: Assessment Of Cognitive Abilities
courses.desc: The purpose of this course is to provide knowledge and skill in the area of cognitive and intellectual assessment. The course is designed to (a) introduce students to the process of standardized intellectual assessment, (b) develop skills for administering and critically evaluating the results of standardized measures of cognitive and intellectual functioning, (c) evaluate and integrate information obtained during the assessment process with other sources of information about the child's learning and behavior, (d) communicate assessment findings in both written and oral formats in a clear manner to a variety of audiences, and (e) consider the role that cognitive and intellectual functioning play in the classification and programming for students with disabilities.

courses.title: Assessment And Intervention For Learning Problems In The Classroom
courses.desc: This course will further students' knowledge of learning disabilities focusing upon assessment, classification, identification, collaboration, and intervention planning within a problem-solving framework. Through field-based case studies, students will: a) enhance their assessment and intervention planning skills for students with learning problems; b) compare traditional and RTI models of identification and intervention planning; c) consider student learning problems within the broader contexts of schools, communities, and local and national policies.

courses.title: Developmental Psychopathology In Educational Settings
courses.desc: An ecological, multicultural, and developmental approach to understanding, assessing, diagnosing, and developing interventions for childhood psychopathology.

courses.title: Professional Practice, Ethics, And The Law In School Psychology
courses.desc: Contemporary roles and functions of the psychologist in schools within the historical, ethical, and legal framework of the profession. Particular emphasis on systems level change and educational policy.

courses.title: School-based Consultation
courses.desc: The purpose of this course is to provide students with the knowledge and skills necessary for a broad-based and pragmatic approach to collaborative consultation and problem-solving within a school context. We will explore collaborative consultative processes, drawing from current perspectives on consultation practices and issues. The complex dynamics of the consultant-consultee relationship as well as the evaluation of the process and outcomes within a problem-solving model of consultation will be examined through course readings, course consultation experiences, and a field-based consultation.

courses.title: Advanced Internship In School Psychology
courses.desc: The year-long internship and seminar are designed to provide students with an opportunity to integrate and apply their knowledge of school psychology (a minimum of 1200 hours, of which at least 600 must be completed in a school setting; the remaining hours may be completed in a clinical setting). Supervised field experiences address all aspects of school psychology practice including assessment, consultation, counseling, informal assessment, and academic and behavioral interventions and program design in a multi-tiered system of support. The internship is accompanied by a bi-weekly seminar focusing on legal, ethical, and professional issues in the delivery of culturally responsive services within a problem solving framework. Students submit a culminating portfolio and present their work in an open forum. Two courses. Prerequisite: Education 231, 232, and consent.

courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: Guided experience in an approved educational setting with supervision. Each student is expected to work in an approved facility for at least 150 hours over the course of one or two semesters. Please contact the department for detailed information.

courses.title: Museum Education for K – 12 Audiences
courses.desc: Museums offer school groups unique experiences that enhance classroom learning and instill the skills of life-long learning. This course explores ways in which museums create on and off-site programs for the K -12 community of pupils, teachers and parents, as well as home-schooled students, scouts, and other learning communities. Students will examine Common Core Standards and other frameworks and will develop outcome-based curricula that make use of museum resources. Partnerships with teachers and schools and professional development programs for teachers will also be addressed. Guest speakers and field trips connect classroom experience to current issues and practices in the field. Prerequisites:ED/FAH/HIST0285 and ED0280.

courses.title: Proseminar In Museum interpretation
courses.desc: All visitor experiences in museums are mediated by the choices museum professionals make in the selection, interpretation, contextualization, and presentation of collections in exhibitions and programs. Students will interpret scholarship for a variety of audiences, examine strategies for interpreting difficult topics, and consider interactives that stimulate meaning-making. Students will also delve into strategies for facilitating community conversations and sharing authority in the creation of exhibitions, programs and projects. Because this is a seminar, a forum for discussion that prepares students for the professional world, we may modify the topics to suit student interests, needs, and expertise. Prerequisites: ED/FAH/HIST0285 and ED0280.

sections.req: Museum Studies Certificate Students or ARCS, ED, AH, HI, MCON grad students

Prerequisites: A minimum of three Museum Studies courses, one of which must be FAH/HIST/ED0285, must be completed before beginning the internship

courses.title: Inclusive Practices in Art Education
courses.desc: Visual culture and art-making in the inclusive classroom. Role of the art educator in asking what counts as art, who counts as an artist, and what is knowledge in the context of art. Focus on accessible high-quality art engagement opportunities for all. Explores learning differences through current research in psychology, sociology, and anthropology. Ways of adapting and modifying lessons to accommodate all learners in the context of special education law. A Disability Studies view of ability/disability in the context of culture, society, and politics. Open to all BFA students; with priority registration given to BFA students who intend to apply for the MAT program.

courses.title: Seminar In Student Teaching In Art, Grades Pre-k - 8
courses.desc:
The course is designed to support student art teachers in their practicum fulltime internship in a school art classroom for grades PK-8. Emphasis is placed on developing the artist/researcher/teacher identity with a critical view on the role of art education in visual culture and multicultural education. The role of teaching philosophy, social justice issues, student voice & activism, public school culture, and curriculum development are studied. Strategies and organization for meeting state requirements to achieve teacher licensure are offered through the standards presented in the state Dept of Education's Pre-service Performance Assessment. Professional practices and career launching strategies are explored. Lifelong learning as a community leader in art education is modeled through an exhibit and gallery talk at the culminating event, the Art Education Festival.
Recommendations: MAT students only .

sections.note: Remote component Thursday 4:00-5:30 PM.

courses.title: Seminar In Student Teaching In Art, Grades 5-12
courses.desc:
The course is designed to support student art teachers in their practicum fulltime internship in a school art classroom for grades 5-12. Emphasis is placed on developing the artist/researcher/teacher identity with a critical view on the role of art education in visual culture and multicultural education. The role of teaching philosophy, social justice issues, student voice & activism, public school culture, and curriculum development are studied. Strategies and organization for meeting state requirements to achieve teacher licensure are offered through the standards presented in the state Dept of Education's Pre-service Performance Assessment. Professional practices and career launching strategies are explored. Lifelong learning as a community leader in art education is modeled through an exhibit and gallery talk at the culminating event, the Art Education Festival.
Recommendations: MAT students only .

sections.note: Remote component Thursday 4:00-5:30 PM.

courses.title: Art Education Curriculum, Pre-k-8
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). This course focuses on curriculum development for elementary and middle school art programs. Emphasis is placed on lesson and unit plan writing, curriculum design, and critical study of existing art curricula. Discussion topics include: curriculum development for diverse student populations, integration of art with other subjects, the application of national and state standards to curriculum, evaluation criteria and procedures, and studies of contemporary art and visual culture in art curricula. Instructional methods, assessment strategies, art media, and technologies will be explored through student projects and presentations.
Recommendations: MAT students only unless granted special permission.

courses.title: Art Education Curriculum, 5-12
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). This course will guide students in formulating a standards-based curriculum for a yearlong high school or middle school course. Methods and examples will be reviewed, evaluated and discussed so students can compose their own goals, objectives, units and lessons that reflect the National Standards and the Massachusetts Frameworks. This course strives to help students understand the definition, purpose, and variety of different curricula and the role of curriculum in the art classroom. The course fosters the development of sequential units, guided by enduring understandings and essential questions. Lessons will reflect the knowledge and practice of differentiated instruction and reflect a strong academic tradition and sensitivity to the developmental growth and personal uniqueness of all learners. Multicultural education and postmodernism will be included in curriculum perspectives. Written reflections and presentations on curriculum ideas, and assessment revolving around the facets of understanding are important components of the course. Guest speakers will include former students who will share their teaching experiences as well as an evaluator for the Advanced Placement program who will discuss the requirements and assessment rubrics of the AP program.
Recommendations: MAT students only unless granted special permission.

courses.title: Embedded Systems
courses.desc: Embedded system hardware, basic concepts of embedded software, and interfacing concepts of an embedded microprocessor; embedded programming, memory management, memory allocation, efficient hardware-aware algorithms; registers and memory; mixing assembly and high level language; real-time deadlines and timers; interrupt hardware and software systems; input/output in an embedded system; embedded application software design and analysis.

courses.title: Electronics I W/lab
courses.desc:
Complex numbers; sinusoidal steady-state circuits and phasors; impedances; frequency response of linear circuits and Bode plots; characteristics of the non-ideal operational amplifier; amplifiers and active filters using the operational amplifier; advanced topics in junction diodes; junction capacitance; diode small signal models; photodetectors and LEDs; analysis and design of diode circuits; MOSFET device operation and small-signal models; analysis and design of transistor amplifiers; basic MOS amplifier configurations. Associated laboratory work.

Prerequisites: ES-0003 or EE-0020

courses.title: Linear Systems
courses.desc: Continuous and discrete signals including phasors; continuous and discrete systems and their realizations using differential and difference equations; continuous and discrete convolution and correlation; unilateral and bilateral Laplace transforms; continuous time Fourier transform; continuous time Fourier series; discrete time Fourier transform; sampling theory; unilateral and bilateral Z transform. Computational exercises focusing on problems in control and signal processing. Recommendations: EE 21, MATH 70, and MATH 51.

courses.title: Probabilistic Systems Analysis
courses.desc:
Development of analytical tools for the modeling and analysis of random phenomena with application to problems across a range of engineering and applied science disciplines. Probability theory, sample and event spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, conditional probability, expectations and conditional expectations, and derived distributions. Sums of random variables, moment generating functions, central limit theorem, laws of large numbers. Statistical analysis methods including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals and nonparametric methods. Undergraduates may not take both EE 0024 and EE 0104 for degree credit.
Prerequisite: Math 0042 or equivalent

sections.req: Math 0042 or equivalent or Graduate Student

courses.title: Senior Design Project II - Part 2
courses.desc: Continuation of the design/research activities planned, initiated, and evaluated in EE97. Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Undergraduate Internship In Electrical Engineering
courses.desc: Supervised internships at suitable locations in industry and government. Jobs offered on basis of availability. Term paper required. Credit not given retroactively. Prior arrangements necessary.

courses.title: Design Of Medical Instrumentation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as BME 100.) An introduction to the design principles of medical instrumentation and simple biomedical signal analysis. Topics include analysis of the instrument and subject as a linear system, characteristics of various biological signals, design of transducers, modern implementation of A/D conversion, analog and digital filters, instrumentation amplifiers, patient isolation, and battery powered equipment.

sections.req: Completion of BME 10, EE 21, ME 31 or graduate standing

courses.title: Optimization in Deep Learning
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 130) Key optimization techniques in deep learning. Topics include gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, momentums, initialization, learning rate adaptation, normalizations, regularization, activations, second-order methods, and meta-learning. Application in deep learning tasks via mini-projects.

sections.req: MATH 0042 and MATH 0070 and one of (EE 0024, EE 0104, or MATH 0165), or graduate standing

courses.title: Physics of Solar Cells
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ MSE 111) Physics of photovoltaic cells including physics of semiconductors in photovoltaic devices, physical models of solar cell operation, characteristics and design of common types of solar cells, and approaches to increasing solar ceil efficiency.
Recommendations: MATH 42, MATH 51, EE 18, PHYS 42/43, or instructor permission

courses.title: Nanophotonics
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BME 115). Engineering, physics, and applications of nanophotonic structures. Wave propagation through optical waveguides, waveguide systems, and nanostructures. Optical mode theory and numerical modeling. Coupled mode theory. Design and analysis of optical modulators, resonators, interferometers, switching networks, and phased arrays. Research paper discussions about state-of-the-art nanophotonic devices and applications in telecommunications, biomedical devices, modern computing, and quantum information systems.
Recommendations: EE18 or ES15 or PHY42

courses.title: Computer Architecture
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ CS 146) Modern computer architecture, starting from caches and memory systems, basic 5-stage pipelines and progressing to out-of-order superscalar processors, multicore processors, and heterogeneous processors. Techniques to maximize single-thread performance within the constraints of memory technology, power consumption, and the inherent instruction-level parallelism of applications.
Recommendations: an undergraduate computer organization class such as EE25 or CS40

courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 111). Fundamental issues in operating system design. Concurrent processes: synchronization, sharing, deadlock, scheduling. Relevant hardware properties of uniprocessor and multiprocessor computer systems.

sections.note: Students looking to enroll in Operating Systems should enroll in CS 111-01.

courses.title: Machine Learning via Sequential Interaction
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 128) Introduction of machine learning as a sequential and interactive game technically referred to as 'online learning'. In online learning, the learner aims to minimize the regret: loss incurred for not playing the best strategy (in hindsight) averaged over time. This framework generalizes the traditional statistical learning set-up in a non-trivial manner to cases where the examples are not independent, are supplied only sequentially, and possibly in an adversarial manner. Topics include: general set-up of sequential learning with examples, online convex and online linear optimization, online-to-batch conversion, multi-armed bandits, contextual bandits, practical algorithms and their analysis with provable guarantees. Connections with and extensions to reinforcement learning will be highlighted. Prior programming experience is recommended.

sections.req: MATH 0070 and (EE 0024 or EE 0104 or MATH 0165) or graduate student

courses.title: Trusted and Responsible AI
courses.desc: Introduction to security and privacy concerns of modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include robust AI, adversarial attacks and defense, fair AI, explainable AI (XAI), privacy-preserving machine learning, trustworthy large language model (LLM), and AI system security. Explorations of individualized areas of interest within the context of the course material.

sections.req: EE 143 or CS 131 or CS 135 or graduate standing

courses.title: Introduction to RFID and IoT
courses.desc:
Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) Systems and technologies, scientific principles, and management structures that support them. Identification, evaluation and categorization of RFID System components with respect to industry standards. Suitability for various industries and applications, and relation to the business needs of multiple industries and their career planning. Role of RFID in the advancements of the
Internet of Things (IoT) and explore IoT applications and future trends.

courses.title: Parallel Computing
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 122) Programming modern parallel computer architectures, especially GPUs and multi-core CPUs. Rationale for modern multi-core CPUs. Challenges of multi-threaded programming. High-performance software taking advantage of hardware caches, cache coherency, memory systems and parallel computation. Recommendations: EE 25 or CS 40.

courses.title: Digital IC Design
courses.desc: Full design of a custom integrated circuit. Register-transfer-level (RTL) design using Verilog hardware description language (HDL). Design integration in an Arm-based system on chip (SoC) architecture. Floorplanning, place & route, and signoff steps to achieve timing closure based on design specifications. Gate-level simulation and physical verification of design rule checks and layout vs schematic comparison. Generation of GDSII files for manufacturing.

sections.req: Completion of EE 25 or EE 103 or graduate standing

courses.title: Wearable System Design
courses.desc: Advanced project-based learning experience centered around the design of wearable systems for health monitoring applications with foci in four fundamental areas: (1) battery and power management, (2) physiological sensors/transducers, (3) analog signal interface and acquisition, and (4) wireless system design and trade-offs. Labs and projects motivated by real-world clinical challenges provided by collaborators in industry and the local clinical and public health community. Students work in small teams to execute a substantial project.

sections.req: Completion of EE 20, ES 4 or Graduate Standing in EE, CompE, or BME

courses.title: Product & Market Design - Imagination & Creativity
courses.desc:
Iterative design process for creativity and innovation to harness product life cycle market growth. How to form models for impact and innovation, articulation and expression to tell a story, how to overcome challenges and obstacles for decision-making, how to learn from others and teams, and how to discern the societal and cultural context. Topics include: exploration of organizational dynamics, opportunities, ideas and concepts, prototype solutions, interaction with stakeholders, creating value, leadership and
teams.

courses.desc:
