courses.title: Foundations in Financial Accounting and Corporate Finance
courses.desc: An introductory course to corporate finance from the perspective of the chief financial officer (CFO). The first part of the course deals with financial planning and budgeting, financial analysis, and short-term financial management. The second part of the course develops a valuation framework for making investment decisions (capital budgeting) for new equipment, the launch of new products, mergers and acquisitions and LBOs... and the funding/financing decisions to be coordinated with those investment decisions. Special attention is given to the cost of capital and valuing stocks, bonds, convertible and preferred.

courses.title: International Financial Management
courses.desc: This course develops a conceptual framework within which the key financial decisions faced by multinational corporations can be analyzed. The traditional themes of corporate finance, including working capital management, capital budgeting, mergers and acquisitions, and funding strategies, are revisited in the context of volatile exchange rates, different regulatory environments and segmented capital markets. Focus on foreign exchange risk management including the appropriate use of new hedging instruments such as currency options, swaps, and derivatives. Case studies emphasize how international financial management should be integrated with corporate strategy and operating decisions. Open to students who have completed B200 or equivalent.

courses.title: Global Private Equity: From Money In to Money Out
courses.desc: This course provides a comprehensive examination of the role of private equity in global finance. It is intended to equip students with an analytical framework for assessing the industry and its key participants and to develop practical skills to support possible investment careers. The course is experiential by design and will be structured around two team-based projects that will engaged students directly in critical dimensions of the private equity finance process: fund development, investment analysis and decision-making. The course will cover the full spectrum of issues relevant to a globally oriented private equity firm from the structure of partnership agreements, through capital acquisition, deal sourcing, investment analysis, deal structuring, and exit. The course approach is intended to unite disciplinary rigor in financial and investment analysis with globally applied practices.

courses.title: The Future of Work
courses.desc: This seminar explores how and why the nature of work has changed dramatically in recent years and what this means for future career patterns. The course has four learning objectives: Provide students with an understanding of key drivers shaping work such as globalization and organizational and technological innovations. 2) Offer students a critical comprehension of how the relationship between workers and management is changing and how this impacts work and company competitiveness. 3) Enable students to assess a range of approaches to improving the nature of work such as skills development and training, programs for reducing race and gender inequality in the workplace, initiatives for improving work-life balance, as well as programs for talent development. 4) Building on the material in the course students should develop concrete strategies to further develop their own careers and preferred management style.

courses.title: Field Studies in Global Consulting
courses.desc: The goal of this course is to provide an introduction to consulting as it is practiced worldwide and across sectors. Students will achieve this goal by undertaking a consulting engagement for a real-world client. The first part of the course will include an introduction to and practice in the essential skills that form the core of professional development for consultants at top-level firms. Students will then put these skills to the test by completing a team consulting project for a sponsoring organization. Open to students who have completed B200 and/or B291 (or similar courses). Class size will be limited by the number of projects confirmed by external sponsors with a maximum of five projects, or twenty five students, being accepted. Input for the project grade will come primarily from the client project; team self- evaluations will be reflected in individual final grades. Course requires application. Contact the instructor or the TA for more information.

sections.note: Students enrolling in EIB B237 in Spring 2027 must be available for an in-person, pre-session intensive workshop that will take place between January 11 through 15, 2027.

courses.title: Sustainable Business Dynamics
courses.desc: Advances in technology, emergent social issues and pressing environment challenges are elevating the importance of corporate sustainability. Independent of the chosen designation (CSR, corporate responsibility, ESG…) an array of stakeholders (including NGOs, employees, consumers, communities, investors, and the planet) are expanding the boundaries of responsibility and elevating expectations for corporate executives. This course provides students with an understanding of the nomenclature, frameworks, and analytical tools needed to effectively integrate sustainability and responsibility into the management of a corporation.

courses.title: Sustainable Finance and Investment
courses.desc: Designed for students with prior coursework and/or practice in finance and investments and interested in understanding the effects of environmental, social, and governance factors on financial decision-making. These include risks posed to the firm and its stakeholders resulting from such factors, as well as risks posed by the firm to its extended stakeholders. The course is structured as an intermediated seminar, i.e. sessions will be facilitated by lecture slides with active engagement expected. The course will examine key themes and developments in regulation, financial reporting, sustainability assessment (or ratings), investment analysis, and capital sourcing across a range of financial markets and asset types, including public equities, public debt, private equity, and infrastructure. Across asset types, key themes include climate risks and financing climate transition, blended capital and innovations in development finance, and fintech, financial inclusion and democratization. Central to the course design is to examine financial strategies and vehicles as tools to advance sustainability and impact objectives whether at the investor, state, or multinational level. To this end, it will introduce and leverage a variety of analytic tools to understand the basic decision models of sustainable and impact investing.

courses.title: Corporate Sustainability in the Age of Globalization
courses.desc: The context for business and society is changing in (at least) four ways: globalization and a lack of global governance; increasing relevance of ESG (environment, social and governance) challenges; rising scale and scope of corporate activities; digitalization and datafication. These changes create new challenges as well as opportunities for business but also for their stakeholders. Stakeholders as diverse as investors, employees, the media, NGOs, and customers often have strong views on how corporations should address these new issues.

courses.title: Business and Political Risk in a Polarized World
courses.desc:
Global firms increasingly face complex political environments marked by polarization,
regulatory fragmentation, and the erosion of liberal economic norms. “Divisive times” —
from populist nationalism to green industrial policy rivalries — amplify corporate
political risk. This course examines how multinational firms assess and respond to these
risks.

In this course we explore how companies navigate regulatory divergence between the EU
and the U.S., handle the politicization of ESG and DEI, and respond to sanctions,
conflict, and trade disputes. The course combines theoretical frameworks from
international business and comparative political economy with real-world corporate
cases. Emphasis is placed on managerial decision-making under uncertainty, business
risk, reputational challenges, and stakeholder pressures. Students will engage in case
discussion, debates, and short analytical memos to apply insights to practice. The goal is
to equip students with the analytical and ethical tools to manage political risk
strategically and responsibly in an era of polarization.

courses.title: Impact Investing
courses.desc: Impact investments are investments made with the intention to generate positive, measurable social and environmental impact alongside a financial return. As such, they challenge the perspective that social and environmental problems could only be addressed by government, multilaterals, and philanthropy and that market investments should only seek financial returns. As the world faces unprecedented challenges, the impact investing market plays a critical role in providing much needed capital and strategic partnerships to help address the world’s most pressing social and environmental problems. Social issues include access to health care, housing, education, clean water, financial inclusion, and safe work conditions. Environmental challenges include not only climate change, but also biodiversity and sustainable agriculture. This class will focus on impact investing, discerning how it fits among other investing strategies in the broader sustainable investing ecosystem. We will discuss concepts including SRI, ESG, and UN SDGs, debate what is and what is not impact investing, and we will evaluate important tools and resources to measure and manage the social and environmental impact of investments. The format is interactive with a combination of case studies, workshops, lecture, and guest speakers. Goals include: developing fluency on the broader sustainable investing ecosystem, which includes SRI, ESG, UN SDGs, thematic, and impact investing strategies; understanding key characteristics of impact investments and tools to recognize “green-washing” or “impact-washing”; learning the basics of impact management, including industry frameworks, impact measurement tools, different investment vehicles, and best practices.

courses.title: Leadership: Building Teams, Organizations, and Shaping Your Path
courses.desc: This course explores the fundamental aspects of managing and leading people including: managing one-on-one relationships; influencing team behavior; and motivating and aligning people behind a common vision. It also examines the challenges and tradeoffs in creating a meaningful personal leadership path, especially in the early stages of your career. The course pedagogy is case-method discussion, drawing primarily on cases from the private sector, supplemented with comparative material from the public sector and civil society. This course will provide you with a number of critical concepts and competencies that will be useful in both the short term and long term. It will help you to make the transition from an individual contributor to a manager and, over time, build a career of increasing responsibility as a leader.

courses.title: Econometrics
courses.desc: This course introduces students to the primary tools of quantitative data analysis employed in the study of economic and social relationships. It equips students for independent econometric research and for critical reading of empirical research papers. The course covers ordinary least squares, probit, fixed effects, two-stage least squares and weighted least squares regression methods, and the problems of omitted variables, measurement error, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, and autocorrelation. Prerequisites include familiarity with (1) basic probability and statistics (EIB B206 or B205 or B206 equivalency exams), and (2) basic concepts of functions and derivatives (EIB E210m or an introductory calculus course).

courses.title: International Trade and Investment
courses.desc: This course investigates why nations trade, what they trade, and the distribution of the gains and the political economy from trade. Topics include trade and economic growth, technology, the product cycle, multinationals, international labor integration, tariffs, regional economic integration, dumping and international competitiveness of firms and nations. Special attention is given to analyzing the effects of various policy instruments. Open to students who have completed E211, or with instructor’s permission.

courses.title: Development Economics: Macroeconomic Perspectives
courses.desc: This course provides an introduction to several central themes in development economics. The organizing framework is pro-poor economic growth. By combining economic models and case studies, one can draw lessons regarding what approaches have worked to alleviate poverty. The course also pays particular attention to situations that have led to economic crises, and develops models of macroeconomic management and structural adjustment. Lectures and assignments presume a background in economics at the introductory level. Open to students who have completed E201 or equivalent.

courses.title: Development Economics: Micro Perspectives
courses.desc: This course teaches students how to use microeconomic theory and econometric skills to analyze issues in low-income countries, develop policy interventions to address those issues, and measure the impact of such interventions in a rigorous empirical manner. It then addresses the issues that constrain and support development, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa: health and education, labor, agriculture, financial services, and institutions. Open to students who have completed E211 or an intermediate microeconomic theory course. E213 is strongly recommended.

courses.title: Engineering Management - Technology and SaaS Organizations
courses.desc:
Organization of companies and engineering groups. Financial fluency, including time value of money, return on investment, income and cash flow statements, and balance sheets. Management of people and organizations. Project and program management techniques and tools. Management of research, development, and design. Operations management, including manufacturing operations and supply chains. 
Students may receive credit for either EM 51 or CEE 62/EM 62, but not both.

courses.title: Technical & Managerial Communication
courses.desc: Written and oral communications in the business setting. Written communications including technical reports and papers, memoranda, and electronic communications. Design and delivery of effective presentations. Informal communication styles and techniques. Communication across cultures.

courses.title: Engineering Leadership
courses.desc: Development of knowledge, skills, and mindset essential for leading programs and teams in a business organization. Topics include understanding personalities of self and others, emotional intelligence, creating high performance teams, influencing without authority, managing conflict, fostering creativity, creating shared visions, and organizational change. Communicating to inspire. Cultural differences in leadership style. Ethical considerations.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CEE 62) Economics and management of civil and environmental engineering systems throughout the project life cycle. Topics include contracts, project delivery, construction project organizations, time value of money, life cycle cost analysis, project scheduling, cost estimation, earned value management, and environmental permitting. Students may receive credit for either EM 51 or CEE 62/EM 62, but not both.

courses.title: Business in Action
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as EN 120 and TML 120) Examination of how business impacts the world. Exploration of different types of business and evolving roles and functions within business. Consideration of social, cultural, organizational, ethical, and technological factors affecting business organizations. Focus on the importance of purpose-driven, human-centered leadership.

sections.note: First year students welcome.

courses.title: Management Of Innovation
courses.desc:
Knowledge and skill development for students who aspire to lead and
manage innovation initiatives in technology based companies. Technology strategy and its role in the overall business strategy of commercial firms. Role of innovation in entrepreneurial ventures and established firms. Skills to present new product development proposals to senior management and/or prospective investors.

sections.note:
This course focuses on change management, emphasizing the distinction between leading and managing. I begin with the premise that the majority of our students are managers on the cusp of leadership, but are unsure and uncertain about which next steps in their leadership development are required.This approach fosters critical thinking and problem-solving, core components of active learning and professional development. We start and end with leadership guru John Kotter’s notion that great leaders live in the world of change; managers deal with the complexities and intricacies of such change. sections.note: Alongside reading, we will write our own novels with an emphasis on process, experimenting with multiple premises and beginnings, to be shared in a supportive workshop setting. Through generative exercises, journaling assignments, and self-reflections, we will work toward a final portfolio that includes the first thirty pages of a novel, as well as a roadmap for writing beyond the class. Note: The course is designed for students starting a novel from scratch. If you’re currently writing a novel and would prefer to build on it for this class, email simon.han@tufts.edu prior to enrollment to be considered for an alternative track.

courses.title: Writing Poetry: Advanced
courses.desc: An advanced course for students who have taken one or more semesters of ENG 6 or have equivalent poetry workshop experience. Focus on developing a sustained practice, project, and/or collection of poems. Prerequisites: One semester of ENG 6; ENG 1 and 2 or completion of the College Writing Requirement. Recommendations: Two semesters of ENG 6 or equivalent poetry workshop experience.

sections.req: Requires the completion of English 0006 and college writing requirement

courses.title: British & Irish Lit, Romantic to Post-Colonial
courses.desc: Survey of British and Irish poetry, fiction, nonfiction prose, and drama from the Romantic era of social and political revolution in the late 18th century to Post-Colonial modernity in the 20th century. Aesthetic experiment and formal innovation in a diverse selection of works in the context of persistent themes, emerging cultural trends, and challenges to the status quo. Evolving ideas about the function of art in society and in response to historical transformation.

sections.note: Fulfills English major survey requirement.

courses.title: Dissent and Democracy: American Literature to 1900
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ AMER 47 & CVS 31) Survey of multicultural early American literature. Democracy, dissent, and debate about fundamental issues such as race, gender, individual freedom, religion, economic inequality, immigration, human beings’ relationship with the earth. Works by Frederick Douglass, Henry David Thoreau, and Harriet Beecher Stowe, and important voices often ignored: letters by Chinese merchants, Latinx cuentos, Lakota protest against anti-Indian racism, Black abolitionists’ militance, a rabbi’s stand against anti-Semitism. Two field trips.

sections.note: Fulfills English major survey requirement.

courses.title: Asian American Writers
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as WGSS 36) Introduction to twentieth-century Asian American literature and culture. Major themes and topics include immigration, diversity, the relation between ethnicity and literature, minority experience, alienation from the English language, intergenerational conflict. Examples are drawn from representative prose narratives, poetry, and plays.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Literature Of The American Sixties
courses.desc: Interdisciplinary examination of literature produced in and about the American Sixties. Readings associated with the Beat and Black Arts movements, New Journalism, second-wave feminism, anti-war activism, psychedelic and blues-folk poetry, and popular culture. Attention to experimentation with literary forms, the incorporation of non-literary discourses, and connections among literature, music, and other arts. Comparative reading of seemingly disparate works, including SCUM Manifesto, Soul on Ice, The Whole Earth Catalog, Play It as It Lays, The Bluest Eye, In Cold Blood, and The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test. Exploration of how these works challenge familiar interpretations of the period and how their formal and narrative innovations helped shape contemporary autofiction and writing concerned with identity. Authors may include Thomas Pynchon, Bob Dylan, Joan Didion, Chuang Hua, Alice Walker, and Toni Morrison.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Faulkner
courses.desc: A study of major novels, focusing on the authors' careers and creative lives and on the environments -- cultural and psychological -- that influenced their work.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Elizabethan Bestsellers
courses.desc: Examines some of the most commercially successful forms of Elizabethan literature made possible by the rise of the printing press and of permanent public theaters. Includes a range of genres and forms of literature, such as poetry and plays. Covers works by major Elizabethan writers alongside those of lesser-known figures. Popular themes may include sex, violence, love, adventure, magic, humor, crime, xenophobia, and imperialist fantasies.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Literature of Migration: Past and Present
courses.desc: A survey of migration literature from the 16th century to the present, with emphasis on the English Renaissance. Explores intersection of migration history and literary history in the longue durée. Poems of exiles, Mediterranean romances, voyage dramas, utopian fictions, refugee narratives, graphic novels. Focus on close reading and critical analysis of literary texts. Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement. Fulfills pre-1860 requirement for English majors.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Un-American Activities
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CVS 63) How leftist and liberal politics have shaped popular culture in the United States. Left's responses to characterizations of it as "un-American." Relations between politics and popular culture, from 1940s to present. Development of youth culture and its effects on radical politics. How class intersects with race, gender, and sexuality. Emphasis on film, theater, and television, with attention to relevant literary texts. Offered fall 2002 and alternate years thereafter.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Film Noir And The American Tradition
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/FMS 54) Introductory course in film noir as a distinctively American genre. Attention to its literary, historical, and social contexts; its implication in the popularization of psychoanalysis; its particular interest for psychoanalytic criticism; its importance as a site of cultural anxieties centering on sexuality, gender, and race. Readings may include novels (by authors such as Hawthorne, James, and Baldwin), theoretical essays, and works in cinema studies. Films may include works by Wilder, Preminger, Hawks, Welles, Vidor, Tourneur, Dmytryk, Mann, Lang, Kubrick, Aldrich, and Scorsese.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Feminism in 20th century U.S. Literature and Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as WGSS 89) How the postwar U.S. women’s movement for equality, born of the mid-twentieth century antiwar and civil rights movements, made civic, legal and ethical challenges that are expressed in literature and film, in mass and high cultures, and in women’s experiences across race, class, ethnic, and sexual lines. Explores the effect of second wave feminism on discourses of gender and women’s sexuality using novels, poetry, essays and films with a view to understanding that forms of knowing are gendered; not universal but culturally constructed, contextual, mutable. Questions how feminism is postmodern; speculates how postmodernism is in part a feminist production; how the postmodern fits with recognitions about gender and liberations of sex and sexualities in the postwar U.S. women’s movement. Authors include: Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Toni Morrison, Audre Lorde, Alix Kates Shulman, Anne Sexton, Sylvia Plath, Adrienne Rich, Chuang Hua, Valerie Solanas. No prerequisites.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: New Topics - South Asian Diasporic Lit.
courses.desc: New or experimental courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to all interested undergraduates. Please see semester listings on SIS or English Department website for specific course descriptions: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/.

sections.note:
This course will question how a broad range of South Asian writers from the United States, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, interrogate questions of dispersal and migration to explore the global dynamics of the diaspora. We will look at how the writings we read deploy a diasporic critique as a mode of refusal — of belonging, nationalism, colonialism, heteronormativity, assimilation and model minoritization. And we will look at the possibilities and impasses that are opened up by South Asian diasporic literature as a mode of resistance. Authors may include Bapsi Sidhwa, Salman Rushdie, Anita Desai, Amitav Ghosh, Arundhati Roy, Taslima Nasrim, Micheal Ondaatje, Avni Doshi and more. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: New Topics - How to Read a Poem
courses.desc: New or experimental courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to all interested undergraduates. Please see semester listings on SIS or English Department website for specific course descriptions: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/.

sections.note:
Contemporary poets draw on a long history of poetic traditions and devices, often subverting them to surprise us or make us perceive the world differently. But how can we spot these techniques, and why should we care about such things? This course provides students with practical tools for reading poetry – not only to identify dactylic hexameter in a rap song, to appreciate an internal rhyme, or to talk confidently about an abstract conceptual poem, but to judge for themselves why poetry might (still) be necessary for thinking and feeling in our present moment of ecological devastation, fascism, and extreme inequality. A sonnet about a jail cell; an ode to a Hotpoint dishwasher; an elegy for extinct fly larvae; a collectively-authored poetic manifesto: how can we “tune in” to such poems, and how might they change us? No prior studies in poetry are necessary. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: New Topics - Literary Roots of Modern World
courses.desc: New or experimental courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to all interested undergraduates. Please see semester listings on SIS or English Department website for specific course descriptions: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/.

sections.note: This course engages with key literary texts from antiquity through the early modern period. We will begin with some of the earliest works in the Western traditions, the biblical cycle of stories surrounding King David and Homer’s Odyssey. We will then read other classical texts, works by Sophocles, Aristophanes and Virgil, before we move forward to a set of works from the early modern period, beginning with Sir Thomas More’s Utopia, an important work of both political theory and literary play. After discussing Machiavelli’s comedy Mandragola and two plays by Shakespeare, we will conclude with John Milton’s epic Paradise Lost, which can be read as a kind of summation of the classical and biblical inheritance. The class does not function as a survey; the literary landscape is too complex and varied to even sample effectively in a single semester. Rather, it is designed to serve as a series of glimpses into the roots of the modern literary tradition.

courses.desc: Practical experience in professional settings relevant to the study of literature, such as teaching, publishing, editing, public relations, librarianship, and other related fields. Students identify their own opportunities to integrate academic study with real- world training. Specific expectations for journal keeping, reflection paper, or other written components will be determined on an individual basis depending on credits assigned and other factors. Department approval required. Internships do not count toward the requirements for the English major or minor.

courses.title: The Sublime: Nature, Art, Film, Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ILVS 121) The sublime as an aesthetic category; the relationship between literature and other kinds of art (painting and film, especially); aesthetic responses to nature and art.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: James Joyce's Ulysses
courses.desc:
Examination of one of modernism's major works and its critical legacy. In addition to the novel itself, readings will include related studies in modernist poetics and literary theory.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 REQUIRED or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement. Recommended that the student already have taken either ENG 20,21,22, or 23.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Scenes of Revision
courses.desc: Examination of revision in African American literature within the contexts of enslavement, surveillance, material scarcity, and racial violence during slavery and Reconstruction. Analysis of texts revised, sometimes repeatedly, by authors including Phillis Wheatley, John Marrant, William Wells Brown, Hannah Bond, and Frances Ellen Watkins Harper. Attention to the material effects of revision and questions of authorship, agency, print culture, and archival recovery. Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Psychoanalysis and Cinema
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ ILVS 180 and FMS 180) Advanced seminar in the relation between psychoanalytic theory and the theory and practice of cinema. Focus on major psychoanalytic writings (primarily by Freud, Lacan, and Žižek) and important work in psychoanalytic film theory in relation to cinematic texts. Requirements: English major, FMS major, or permission of instructor.

sections.note:

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: New Seminar - Disordering the World
courses.desc:
New or experimental seminar format courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for seminar titles and descriptions offered in a given semester:
http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommended: Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note:
This course introduces students to the fields of critical race and disability studies. We will read contemporary African American literature and cultural production to interrogate how racial slavery and colonial genocide have shaped contemporary disability politics—specifically our ability to see pain, address illness, and negotiate capacity. Together, we will discover how disability is shaped, regulated, and disciplined through cultural expectations of racial, sexual, and gendered normalcy. This course reads varied literatures and cultural forms including black queer psychiatric survival literature, indigenous poetry, black trans carceral critique, and experimental film against definitions of disabled embodiment produced within the wellness industry, psychiatry and medicine, welfare policy, and eugenicist discourse. Reading black queer, chronically ill, and neurodivergent voices, this course attempts to reorganize our understanding of human need and human suffering from the position of bodies differently abled and marked for reform. Students will develop mad black and feminist analyses of disability and develop skills in close reading, critical thinking, and argumentative writing. Content warning: this course deals with sensitive topics related to mental health. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: New Seminar - Marxism & Literature
courses.desc:
New or experimental seminar format courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for seminar titles and descriptions offered in a given semester:
http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommended: Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note:
Post Marxism is having a revival. But far from the cliché of a theory glorifying the white male factory worker, much new Marxist scholarship attends to the way capitalism depends on social hierarchies of race, gender, class, and ability. This course offers students a fresh approach to Marxist studies to think about how economic transformations shape our literature, media, and culture. Studying contemporary fiction, poetry, film, and a play by Bertolt Brecht, we’ll begin with well-known Marxist literary and cultural critics (Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall, Fredric Jameson), before moving to read a range of global and non-Western Marxist thinkers (Raquel Gutiérrez Aguilar, Jairus Banaji, Aijaz Ahmad) alongside new cultural accounts of the gigwork economy, deindustrialization, and migrant care work (Sianne Ngai, Alessandra Mezzadri, Annie McClanahan). If you’re curious about Marxism but not sure where to start, this is the course for you. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement

courses.title: New Seminar - It’s Alive! Frankenstein Redux
courses.desc:
New or experimental seminar format courses offered on an ad hoc basis. Open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for seminar titles and descriptions offered in a given semester:
http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommended: Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note:
Since Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published in 1818, it has become one of the most widely adapted and reinvented novels in the English language. Starting with the original text (later revised), we will read a selection of the many works that have kept Victor Frankenstein and the Being he made out of scavenged parts alive as a global meme. From the first stage production in 1823 (a musical!) to contemporary reimaginings in literature and film across genres, we will consider how the questions Shelley’s novel asks about what it means to be human are rearticulated in new social and political as well as aesthetic terms. Along with some critical writing that situates the novel within particular interpretative frames, literary texts may include Shelley Jackson’s hypertext Patchwork Girl (1995); Laurie Sheck’s experimental A Monster’s Notes (2012); Ahmed Saadawi’s wartime Frankenstein in Baghdad (2013); Victor LaValle’s sci-fi graphic Destroyer (2017); Rachel Feder’s autocritical Harvester of Hearts (2018); and Jeanette Winterson’s queer Frankisstein: A Love Story (2019). Films may include the 1910 Edison Studios short; James Whale’s 1931 and 1935 classics; Mel Brooks’ parodic Young Frankenstein (1974); adaptations by Kenneth Branaugh (1994) and Guillermo del Toro (2025); and Yorgos Lanthimos’s 2023 remaking of Alasdair Gray’s 1992 postmodern satire, Poor Things.

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

Department permission required. One Directed Independent Study may be counted towards the English major or minor. Prerequisites: ENG 1 and 2 or fulfillment of the College Writing Requirement.

Required of all graduate students currently in classes; those who have finished coursework are welcome to attend.

courses.title: Engineering Psychology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PSY 53). Survey of the applied areas of psychology that have proven useful in the design of equipment for human use and in the design of human-machine systems. Emphasis on how humans process information and how psychological science can further inform each stage of information processing.

sections.note:
Estimated Textbook Cost: $0.00 
Must be declared ENP/HFP or HFE major
sections.req: PSY 1 or CSHD 1Engineering Psychology major OR Human Factors Psychology OR Human Factors Engineering major

courses.title: Methods for Human Factors Engineering
courses.desc:
Qualitative and quantitative methods and techniques used in human factors engineering research. Usability testing, structured observation, questionnaire design, focus group design, psychophysical methods, signal detection theory, and field studies. Examples of good and bad methods/techniques.

Recommendations: PSY53

courses.title: Project Study In Human Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as BME 120 and PSY 120.) A senior-level project design (capstone course), led by faculty from engineering and psychology as well as outside lecturers. Students participate in team fashion in human-factors design problems set by industry sponsors. Professional-level work is required, including report preparation and presentations. Timely lectures supplement the projects.

sections.req: Completion of (ENP 53 or PSY 53), ENP 64, ENP 161, and senior standing

courses.title: Internship In Engineering Psychology
courses.desc:
A mentored preprofessional experience in engineering psychology at an off-site organization. The internship must conform to all the requirements of the School of Engineering internship programs. The engineering psychology program will grant course credit for internships if the following conditions are met: 1) The student has junior or senior standing and has declared a major in engineering psychology. 2) The student has submitted a written internship proposal that has been approved prior to the semester in which the internship will be performed. No internships with course credit will be approved once the semester of the internship has started. 3) A faculty mentor in engineering psychology holds supervisory and technical control of any work that receives credit. 4) The student submits a written report that is to be evaluated by the faculty adviser and the outside institutional supervisor. Work of a proprietary nature cannot be used as a basis for the granting of course credit.
Recommendations: Junior or Senior standing or permission of instructor.

instructors: Anil Saigal, Briana Bouchard, Chris Rogers, Daniel Hannon, Dave Bryan Miller, Erica Kemmerling, Gary Leisk, Hoda Koushyar, Igor Sokolov, James Intriligator, Jason Rife, Jeffrey Guasto, Kristen Bethke Wendell, Luisa Chiesa, Marc S. Hodes, Mark L Kachanov, Markus Peter Nemitz, Michael Wiklund, Robert D. White, Trevion Henderson

courses.title: Assistive Technology Innovations
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as OTS 108) Assistive Technology Innovations focuses on the amazing clinical applications of assistive technology to empower people with disabilities in accessing their world, increasing participation, affording greater inclusion, improving independence and optimizing quality of life. Emerging and innovative technologies are showcased and discussed via online modules, in person demonstrations, and multimedia instructional materials. Students critically review research and innovative approaches to improving activity performance and participation across the lifespan through the application of assistive technologies. Assistive technology, universal design and emerging practice areas in the field such as augmented reality, virtual reality, digital fabrication (such as 3D printing, laser cutting), app development, mainstream accessibility features, and alternative access technologies will be addressed.

courses.title: Medical Technology Development
courses.desc:
Medical technology development and healthcare delivery. Human anatomy, medical conditions, roles of clinicians, and effect of medical care environments on medical care quality. User interfaces of diagnostic, therapeutic, and monitoring technologies. Design of medical devices to optimize medical care, user satisfaction, and patient safety. Visits to clinical care environments. Guest lectures by clinicians. Individual and group projects structured around real world problems. 
Recommendations: Junior Standing

sections.req: ME, HFE, HFP or ENP grads or undergrads (including certificate students)

courses.title: Use-Related Risk Management
courses.desc: Analysis of potential harm caused by user interaction of technology in various domains including medical, consumer, industrial products. Fundamentals of use error (human error). Identifying opportunities for use error and their likelihood and potential to cause serious harm or death. Methods for identifying root causes of use errors. Residual risk analysis. Rationales for product design acceptance in view of residual risk and societal tolerance for risk. Applications to human factors engineering, biomedical engineering, mechanical engineering, software development, and industrial design. Governmental expectations and industrial standards on risk management. Focus placed on medical technology. Prior coursework in human factors engineering preferred but not necessary.

courses.title: Engineering Forensics
courses.desc: Prevention of recurrence for high-profile accidents in transportation and related industries. Accident-investigation methods, discovery of system-safety faults, and identification of user-interface design errors. Case studies with emphasis on individual analysis and presentation. Site visits and guest lectures. Recommendations: PSY 53, ENP 64 and junior standing.

instructors: Andrew M Liu, Divya C Chandra
sections.req: ME, HFE, HFP or ENP grads or undergrads (including certificate students)

courses.title: Ergonomics in Design
courses.desc: Topics related to the domain of physical ergonomics with emphasis on the quality of fit between humans and the things they interact with on a job site, in sports, or at home. Applications drawn from aspects of human-made environments and designed products. Extensive in-class activities, group work, and collaborative discussion. Project experiences involving analysis of real-life scenarios. Anthropometry, functional anatomy, ergonomics, body mechanics, and human factors research methods. Guest lectures with local industry and professionals. Recommendations: Junior, Senior or Graduate Standing

sections.req: (Completion of ENP 64 and Junior standing), or Senior Standing

courses.title: Human Factor Product Design
courses.desc:
Material relevant in consumer product design, biomedical engineering, architectural design, and machine design. Topics include design methodologies, user feedback techniques, performance measurements, sensory evaluation techniques, creative design, and prototyping. Extensive individual and group project design work. Emphasis on designing and creativity.
Recommendations: ENP 53, ENP 64 and junior standing

sections.req: ME, HFE, HFP or ENP grads or undergrads (including certificate students)

courses.title: Human-machine System Design
courses.desc:
Techniques for man-machine system designs in which cognitive and dynamic aspects are of major importance. Applications to computer-interface design, auto/semiautomated systems, biomedical systems, and others. Topics include information processing, decision making, reaction times, and signal detection theory. Individual and group projects, laboratory demonstrations.

Recommendations: ENP 64 and senior standing, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Analytical Methods In Human Factors Engineering
courses.desc:
Quantitative and qualitative analysis methods applied in human factors engineering. Longitudinal data analysis, root cause analysis, inter-rater reliability analysis, utility analysis, usability analysis, heuristic review, and applications of machine learning to human factors.

Recommendations: ENP 162 or graduate standing.

courses.title: Applied Behavioral Statistics for Engineering
courses.desc: Behavioral statistics for human factors and applied behavioral research. Parametric, nonparametric, descriptive and inferential concepts. Small n and case study designs, factor analysis and power analysis. Use of modern statistical software package(s). Applications to product design and development, human performance, and survey methods.

courses.title: Industrial Design
courses.desc: History and current state of industrial design, the industrial design process, and industrial design principles. Application of industrial design for user needs and expectations. Product safety, efficacy and consumer satisfaction. Recommendations: Junior standing

courses.title: Computer Interface Design
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BME 166.) This hands-on course challenges students to design computer-based products and systems that are easy to learn and use. Lectures cover the user interface-design process, basic design principles, and design evaluation methods. In-class exercises and projects reinforce the students' understanding of the lecture material and provide practical design experience. Students use computer-based prototyping tools to model and demonstrate their design solutions. Frequent guest lectures by user-interface design specialists from industry.
Recommendations: EN 1, 2, and junior standing, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Master's Project
courses.desc: Completion of a project under the guidance of a faculty advisor. Proposal must be approved by faculty advisor and graduate director. Each project must address a substantive human factors engineering problem. Students are required to make an oral presentation of their project work. Enrollment is limited to students in the Human Factors Engineering Master of Science program.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 10) Theory and practice of leadership. Alignment of actions with goals and intentions. Connection of life experience and strengths to leadership approach.

Examination of global brands and application of marketing concepts and strategy to personal brands and companies.

courses.desc:

Rapid ideation workshops for novel solutions and innovations. Tools to stimulate brainstorming and creativity. This class is designed for undergraduate students, particularly Freshmen and Sophomores, who have not taken an ENT core course and are interested in learning more about innovation and entrepreneurship.

courses.title: Business in Action
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as EM 120 and TML 120) Examination of how business impacts the world. Exploration of different types of business and evolving roles and functions within business. Each student surveys their own skills, interests, assets and resources, selects a target market segment and associated customer problem, and creates and optionally launches a small business built around their own hobbies or professional skills. Primary market research, iterative solution development, marketing and sales, basics of small business finance, and legal and accounting considerations. By the end of the course, students will have created a real business they can launch and run.

sections.note: First year students welcome

courses.title: Art Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: Cultivate professional practices and methods that support creative career development. Weekly readings, lectures, discussions, assignments and visitors address topics related to professional artistic development including: goal setting, artist writing, networking & community building, promotion, documentation, grants & residencies, business planning, navigating non-profits, museums and galleries, etc. Develop professional artistic objectives within a community of peers.

Common fabrication techniques including foamboard, 3D printing, laser cutting, electronics, and AI-assisted programming. courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 180 & CVS 170) Integrates and applies concepts from adult development and learning, leader(ship) development, and organizational behavior to build capacity for social change. courses.title: Introduction to Environmental Studies
courses.desc: A case study approach to integrating the natural and social sciences with the arts and the humanities when exploring environmental challenges. Draws on both major Western thinkers and indigenous, global, and emerging environmental thinkers.

courses.title: Environmental Studies Lecture Series
courses.desc: Tied to the Environmental Studies Lunch and Learn lecture series featuring presentations on environmental topics by speakers from government, industry, academia, and non-profit organizations. Opportunity to broaden knowledge beyond the curriculum, explore career paths, meet other faculty and students, and network with the speakers. Students submit short writings before and after each talk. Detailed information about speakers and a full schedule can be found on the Environment Studies website. Mandatory pass/fail.

sections.note: The Speaker roster will be published here: https://as.tufts.edu/environmentalstudies/news-events/hoch-cunningham-lecture-series

courses.title: Environmental History of U.S.
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 21) Introduction to historical study of Americans' relationship with the natural world. Examines how natural forces shaped human history, and how humans altered their environments. Topics include climate, food systems, energy use, urbanization, warfare, environmental movements, consumerism, war, technological innovation, migration, political ideologies, and social and economic structures.

courses.title: Public Health Engineering
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CH 10, ENV 0027 and CEE 0052). An introduction to public health engineering. Elements of waterborne disease control, hazardous materials management, occupational health and safety, and environmental interventions. Applications to environmental engineering and environmental engineering science.

courses.title: Children, Nature, and the Development of Earth Stewards
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 34)Programs and methods being used around the world to connect children and teens to the natural world and nourish their development as earth stewards. Forest schools, wilderness programs, environmental education, urban gardening, children’s books related to earth stewardship, and teen protests for climate action. By permission of instructor, open to graduate students as CSHD 234

courses.title: Imagining the Environment in German Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-Listed as GER 182). How German culture engages with environmental challenges, focusing on themes such as sustainability, pollution and waste, radioactivity, climate change, and the relationship between humans and animals. Readings may include Alexander von Humboldt, Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, Rainer Maria Rilke, Theodor Storm, Franz Kafka, Rolf Dieter Brinkmann, Marlen Haushofer, Christa Wolf, W. G. Sebald, Ilja Trojanow, and Esther Kinsky. In German. Recommendations: GER 121 or consent.

courses.title: Special Topics - Clothing, Sustainability and Global Implications
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: What are the implications of our shopping choices, and how can we use our power as consumers, as community members, and as (future) business leaders to bring about a more equitable and sustainable world? Through the lens of something we all buy and use—clothing—this course will examine the relationship between culture, consumerism, business, and sustainability. Specifically, what are the implications of the global fashion system in terms of the environment, poverty, and sustainable development? How can we improve this picture? And who should lead the way?

courses.title: Special Topics - Native Am & Indigenous Environ
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
Full Title: Native American & Indigenous Environmentalisms
Class Description: This mid-level interdisciplinary course examines Native American and Indigenous approaches to land caretaking and ecological justice, culminating in an independent research project. Topics covered include:  Native American and Indigenous philosophies of land relationality; traditional ecological knowledges; relationships to western environmentalism; and political, social, and cultural mobilization.

courses.title: Special Topics - Media and the Environment
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
Students may choose lower level section (ENV 95-03) or upper level section (ENV 195-01). The upper level includes an additional research project. 

As conceptions of humanity’s relationship to nature have evolved, so too have the ways that people use media to represent the environment. We will look closely at how movies and other popular media have depicted nonhuman nature, and examine how audiovisual media have been used within the environmental movement, from the conservation efforts of the mid-20th century to the increasingly urgent efforts of activists in the era of climate change. We will read work by prominent scholars in ecocriticism, and view a wide range of media, looking at narrative, documentary, and experimental practices.

courses.title: Environmental Internship

courses.desc: Exploration of environmental fieldwork— how to gather, analyze and communicate data— in the natural and social sciences. Coverage includes Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Work with community clients to ask questions based on environmental concerns. Collect and interpret relevant data and report findings to stakeholders. Fieldwork will range from forests and urban areas to archival sources, maps, databases, surveys, and interviews. One laboratory session per week plus one discussion period. No pre-requisites.

courses.title: Environmental Policy - U.S. Challenges and Solutions
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 194) Overview of environmental policy focusing initially on the United States experience, then linking to global environmental policy-making. Introduction to the ways in which environmental policies are made in the United States and abroad including major actors, key decisions, and future challenges.

courses.title: Games For Environmental Futures
courses.desc: Games as representations of socioecological systems and as tools for exploring barriers and solutions to systemic change. Concepts from model thinking, game design, and behavioral sciences will be combined to consider how playful engagement can shift discussions and spur action on contemporary environmental challenges such as biodiversity loss, air/water quality, and climate resilience.

courses.title: Occupational & Environmental Health
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CEE 158.) An examination of current topics in the area of occupational and environmental health, with particular emphasis on the types of materials that produce human health effects. Both clinical and epidemiologic data will be used to assess the public health importance of environmental pollutants and to evaluate the effectiveness of control strategies.
Recommendations: Senior Standing or consent of instructor

courses.title: Environmental Health & Justice
courses.desc: Environmental health and environmental justice principles globally and in the US; strong emphasis on marginalized populations and communities in low- and middle-income countries. Major current challenges in environmental health as they relate to environmental justice. Topics may include solid waste disposal, electronic waste (e-waste), mining of natural resources, sanitation, water resources, and the climate crisis.

courses.title: Environmental Law
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CEE 207 and UEP 207) Analysis of environmental law and natural resource management at the federal, Tribal, state and local levels of government. The course is designed for those planing careers in environmental science, land use planning and environmental management and should be of value to others interested in learning about the structure of the nation's primary pollution statues and mechanisms for managing and protecting natural resources.

courses.title: Practicing in Food Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ANTH159) Project-based course designed to integrate academic learning with application in a range of food systems settings. Focused observation exercise culminating in a jointly produced useable report for a community partner. Emphasis will be on balance between process and product. Readings, discussion, and field research will be split between the specific content focus of the group project and general issues arising from planning and carrying out interdisciplinary team projects; developing productive relationships with communities, clients, and stakeholders; addressing ethical concerns in collaborative and public research. Preference will be given to students who have declared the Food Systems and Nutrition minor or the Food Systems, Nutrition and Environment major.

courses.title: Corporate Management Of Environmental Issues

(Cross-listed as CEE 265 & UEP 265 ) Students in this course will explore the ways corporations interact with the environment, with the goal of understanding the processes, pitfalls, and tools for preventing/addressing environmental issues or disasters.
