courses.title: Experimental College - Ferment Like a Scientist
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: How to Ferment Like a Scientist

Do you often find yourself in the kitchen, making a delicious loaf of bread, and wondering what went wrong? There’s a scientific explanation as to why! 

In many culinary cases, understanding the biochemical background of cooking can improve your baking outcomes. In this course, you’ll approach fermentation from an interdisciplinary lens, as we cover the science, anthropology, nutrition, and sustainability of fermentation, along with an introduction to common fermented foods. Then, you’ll choose a fermented food product to sustain through hypothesis-driven research design. For example, will changing your sourdough starter’s flour content alter the yeast’s feeding cycle? At the end of the course, you’ll share your food product with your peers to spur a collective conversation about its flavor profile, your scientific findings, and its anthropological impact. In this course, you’ll connect the way organisms such as bacteria and yeast undergo complex biochemical pathways to the creation of nourishing, informed recipes and rituals celebrated across many cultures. 

INSTRUCTORS: Gabriella Floro and Nina Fitzgerald are doctoral students in the Chemistry department at Tufts. Both have taught courses in bioanalytical chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Their research focuses on RNA modifications. Outside the lab, they are both passionate about cooking and baking.

courses.title: Experimental College - Journey to the Moon
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Journey to the Moon - From the Moon Knowledge

How far is it to the moon, and what can we learn from all the rocks we brought back?

On the eve of humankind’s return to the moon with Project Artemis, this class looks back over 50 years to the six successful Apollo missions that landed on the Moon and brought back hundreds of pounds of rocks. 

We will explore all the Apollo missions and how the data brought back by astronauts (and a single scientist) shaped our ideas of how the Moon, Earth, and other worlds formed. We will also learn about the importance of the Moon to Earth systems and explore the history of lunar observations, from ancient stories to Galileo’s first telescopic observations in the 17th century. 

Our investigations will culminate in a measurement of the distance to the Moon and an examination of Moon rocks acquired by Apollo astronauts. While we will focus mostly on lunar science and the Apollo missions, we will also discuss the politics, cost, mythology and conspiracies that surround the Moon. Like the Apollo missions themselves, this class is part adventure, part politics, and part science.

INSTRUCTOR: Andrew West is an astronomer and educator who has been teaching at Tufts since 2016. As a lecturer in the Chemistry department, he has taught several thousand Tufts undergraduates in the Big Bang to Humankind course. In 2023, he began teaching in the Tufts Prison Initiative (TUPIT) and has now taught introductory college-level astronomy to incarcerated students at medium and maximum-security prisons in Massachusetts. His research focuses on the smallest stars in the Galaxy (called red dwarfs), which he uses to understand the movement, structure and evolution of the Milky Way (and the stars themselves).

courses.title: Experimental College - Reel Journalism
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Reel Journalism: Hollywood, the Media & the Art of Storytelling

For nearly a century, Hollywood has been fascinated by journalism—the reporter racing a deadline, the editor deciding what the public needs to know, the source risking everything to tell the truth. This course explores that fascination across thirteen films and nearly a hundred years of American moviemaking, from screwball newspaper comedies to scathing satires to investigative dramas that changed how we think about the press.

Each week, students will watch a film on their own and in class we will take a closer look—from the perspective of moviemaking and from the viewpoint of journalism. What worked, what didn’t, and why? What was true, what wasn’t, and did it make a difference? It will be like a news event: we won’t know exactly what will happen, but informed discussion will lead us to interesting places.

INSTRUCTOR: Neal Shapiro (A80) has spent more than 40 years at the center of American journalism—as a producer at ABC News, Executive Producer of Dateline NBC, and President of NBC News, where he led the country’s most-watched news division through September 11, the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and multiple presidential elections. He went on to lead The WNET Group, the nation’s largest public media organization, for nearly two decades. He has been a film lover even longer—dating to his undergraduate days at Tufts, where three courses in the Experimental College made him a lifelong movie lover and critic. He edited The Tufts Observer, and reported for The New York Times and The Boston Globe. For more than 20 years he has hosted and written Reel Thirteen, WNET’s weekly film series. He has taught journalism and lectured at Tufts and many other universities.

courses.title: Experimental College - Wu-Tang Clan: A History
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Wu-Tang Clan: A History

Wu-Tang Clan enters its 35th anniversary as one of hip-hop’s most enduring cultural forces. This course treats them as a living case study in oral tradition—tracing the Caribbean, African American, and Native/Indigenous roots that shaped the group, and the mothers and women whose presence runs through their story, alongside the Shaw Brothers’ kung-fu films that gave the group its name and philosophy. Each class doubles as a historical study and writing workshop: students freewrite, explicate lyrics as poetry, and build community through discussion, becoming a “clan” of their own. By midterm, students begin a final project recovering their own family’s unwritten history.

INSTRUCTOR: Toni “Bee” Brooks is a poet, educator, and civic strategist. In 2011, she became the first woman elected Poet Populist of Cambridge, and in 2016 its inaugural Poetry Ambassador. Her oral history was featured in Harvard's Woodberry Poetry Room Initiative honoring Helene Johnson. She co-authored the article, “Reading and Teaching Phillis Wheatley Peters in Boston” published in Early American Literature. A GrubStreet Teaching Fellow (2024–2025), she is founder of Poets in the Garden, hosted at Longfellow House.

courses.title: Experimental College - The Artist Reader
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Artist Reader: Artmaking as Literary Interpretation

Have you ever stopped to marvel at the miracle that is reading? How can this be expressed in art?

This hybrid art/literature course proposes that reading is a profoundly creative act—that reading is art. In this course, we will ask why it is that readers do not get more credit for their share in making literary experiences. We will question a history that privileges authors, critics, and other gatekeepers over other readers. We will read and write about reading: its phenomenology and the “reader’s share” in crafting aesthetic meaning from text. We will also read ourselves as readers in texts from William Blake, Haruki Murakami, and Jorge Luis Borges, alongside Susannah Clarke’s Piranesi and Susan Howe’s My Emily Dickinson. Most importantly, we will show our reading by painting, drawing, and printmaking, so we can share our interpretations with one another. 

INSTRUCTOR: John Lehman (AG26) is an artist, writer, and educator whose multidisciplinary art has drawn from literature ranging from Shakespeare to Beowulf, Japanese wood-block storytelling to surrealist fiction. He received an Interdisciplinary PhD from Tufts blending Studio Art (drawing, painting, printmaking) and Comparative Literature. He also received an MFA from The School of the Museum of Fine Arts, an MA in English from Middlebury College, and a Master of Arts in Teaching from Brandeis University. His five years studying Haruki Murakami’s novel The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle culminated in a year-long solo exhibition entitled In the Well of the Wind-Up Bird at Tufts’ Tisch Library that consisted of over 300-hundred individual works of art.

courses.title: Experimental College - Mass Surveillance & the Law
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Search and Seizure: Mass Surveillance and the Law

How is mass surveillance affecting our lives? What role does the Fourth Amendment play in constraining surveillance by the government and by private corporations?

New technologies have placed vast surveillance capabilities in the hands of governments and private corporations. Your phone gives a comprehensive account of nearly everywhere you’ve ever been. Facial recognition technology threatens to identify you any time you step outside your front door. The U.S. Constitution provides several important legal frameworks for protecting your privacy from the prying eyes of government officials, but those constitutional provisions stand at a crossroads as courts, high and low, grapple with how to adapt old doctrines to new technologies. In this course we will examine the origin of constitutional search and seizure protections and explore the possibilities and perils of new surveillance technologies.

INSTRUCTORS: Julianna McCorkle is a criminal defense attorney employed by the Committee for Public Counsel Services—the state’s public defender agency—to represent indigent clients in Massachusetts state courts. Earlier in her career she worked as a public defender in the state of New Hampshire, clerked at the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois in Chicago, and taught in prisons and jails in New York state. She holds a JD from the University of Chicago. 

Mitchell Kosht is a public interest litigator at Thomas Oakley PLLC. His practice areas include appellate criminal defense, police accountability, public records litigation, and asylum. Before joining Thomas Oakley PLLC, he clerked at the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island and the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts. He received a JD from Northeastern University and a Master of Theological Studies from Harvard Divinity School.

courses.title: Experimental College - Material Futures
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Material Futures: What Should Tomorrow Be Made Of?

How are new materials created? Where will the materials of the future come from, and what superpowers could they have? 

In this course, we’ll explore how designers, scientists, and engineers are reimagining the materials that shape our everyday lives, from materials with extraordinary inherent properties like silk, to those that can interact with their surroundings. Through case studies, hands-on experiments, and visual exploration, you’ll discover emerging materials and their possibilities, limitations, and potential to address real-world challenges. You’ll learn to think like a material innovator: identify an opportunity, imagine a new material-based solution, define its functionality, and bring your idea to life through visualizations and/or tangible prototypes. You’ll develop a material innovation concept to solve a specific problem and explore how it could make a meaningful difference for people and the planet.

No prior experience required, just curiosity about what the world could be made of.

INSTRUCTOR: Shonglin Gaekwad (AG26) is an interdisciplinary materials innovator and designer whose work explores the intersection of materials engineering, biodesign, textiles, and product innovation. Her practice is grounded in the belief that meaningful and impactful material innovation emerges when scientific experimentation and creative thinking inform one another. She received an Interdisciplinary PhD from the Biomedical Engineering Department at Tufts, where her research focused on transforming textile waste into next-generation biomaterials and developing advanced silk-based materials. She is an inventor on two patent applications related to silk-based materials derived from textile waste. Prior to her doctoral research, she earned a Master’s in Design for the Fashion System from Politecnico di Milano, Italy. Her experience working in the New York fashion industry with renowned designers Zac Posen and Phillip Lim, in product development, fabric R&D, and materials sourcing, gave her insight into how one of the world's most resource-intensive industries approaches materials.

courses.title: Experimental College - State Secrets & Journalism
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: State Secrets: Using a Journalist’s Tools to Crack Open Government

How does your government really operate—and how do you know who is really running things behind the scenes?

Through a blend of civics education, writing instruction, and political theory, students will use the tools of journalism to answer those weighty questions, exploring the nuts and bolts of state government, and learning how to hold those in power to account. This course is suitable for anyone who wants a deeper relationship with their elected officials, whether you plan to report on them, lobby them on an issue, campaign to join their ranks, or even just decide whether to vote for them. Over the course of the semester, students will learn how to utilize FOIA (Freedom of Information Act), analyze campaign finance contributions, parse polls, and sharpen their writing skills for public presentation. Students will read and author news coverage, policy memos, public records requests, and political profiles.

Students will also benefit from Platoff and Gross’ rich rolodex of the state’s most influential thought leaders, political players, and veteran journalists—many of whom have worked in the state’s power centers for decades.

INSTRUCTORS: Samantha Gross is a politics reporter in the State House bureau at the Boston Globe. She joined the Globe in 2022 from the Miami Herald, where she won a Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News. She is a three-time finalist for the Toner Prize in political reporting. She studied journalism at Boston University, where she was the editor-in-chief of the Daily Free Press. She currently serves as the vice chair of the paper’s alumni board.

Emma Platoff is the senior enterprise reporter and an assistant metro editor at the Boston Globe. She started her career at the Texas Tribune in Austin, is a three-time finalist for the Toner Prize in political reporting, and has shared in several national Edward R. Murrow awards. A graduate of Yale College, she is a former managing editor of the Yale Daily News.

courses.title: Experimental College - Intellectual Property Law
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Understanding Intellectual Property Law

Intellectual property is all around us—from the software on your phone and the design of your sneakers to the music in your playlists and the brands you trust. Understanding Intellectual Property Law reveals how legal rules quietly govern the music you stream, the products you buy, and the features of your phone.
 
This course offers an introduction to how patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets function in everyday life. Across the semester, you'll uncover how intellectual property shapes global business and the products around us. Through student presentations and weekly quizzes, students will learn to identify these forms of intellectual property in common products, digital services, and media, while examining who owns creative work and how legal protections impact businesses and consumers.

INSTRUCTOR: James Coe is Senior Counsel for Intellectual Property at Keurig Dr Pepper, where he manages the company’s global patent portfolio and advises R&D and product teams on patent strategy, innovation processes, and IP risk. He previously served as General Counsel of a venture capital-backed startup in the field of additive manufacturing, and before that as Chief Patent Counsel for the Americas region of a multinational corporation. James has managed the development of patent portfolios in a variety of technologies and industries, and has advised clients on IP strategy development and policies. He is a graduate of Boston University School of Law and holds a MS in Electrical Engineering from Columbia University.

courses.title: Experimental College - The Design of Good Taste
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Design of Good Taste

In an age of infinite choices, what do you choose to care about? How do we recognize something as ‘you’—and not just algorithmically excellent?

Your taste is your edge, what makes you you. Together, we’ll explore how taste—shaped by culture, aesthetics, and intention—can set your work apart across fields from design ¿to code to art and beyond. We will define your visual sensibility by coupling subjective introspection with the objective Gestalt Principles of Perception. Students will learn to examine their influences, sharpen their worldview, and begin designing taste as a creative tool for meaning and distinction. Throughout the semester, you’ll build on your own evolving sense of taste through a Cabinet of (tasteful) Curiosities curated week by week.

Each class introduces examples drawn from across culture and history, alongside stories from the instructors’ work in brand, fashion, and experience design. We will share the weekly contributions to the Cabinet of Curiosities, and culminate in a final curation, synthesis, and rationale of taste, shared with the class. Because in a world of infinite options, to curate what you care about is what defines you.

INSTRUCTOR: Ludo Cestarelli is a Senior Brand Designer at Other Tomorrows, crafting identities for brands across industries such as hospitality, food, and aviation. She was previously a designer for the robotics company Piaggio Fast Forward and is a student of Japanese woodworking.

courses.title: Experimental College - Paranormal Writing Workshop
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Paranormal Writing Workshop: Ghost Hunting as Creative Practice

As writers, what can we learn from the process of paranormal investigation? Can embarking on our own ghost hunting projects reveal something to us about the nature of writing? How do the tools of investigation—electronic voice phenomenon, movement sensors, photography, historical/archival research, etc.—mimic tools of writing, adaptation, narrative, and artistic meaning making? 

This writing workshop/seminar will explore the relationship between artistic methodologies and paranormal investigation. We will become amateur ghost hunters through research and mimicry. We will go searching for spirits in the field. We will deep dive into both art/writing/cultural theory about ghosts but also art/writing that performs a ghost hunting methodology from the sacred to the profane to the silly. We will take in the foundational paranormal genre in Film & TV. Through a parallel paranormal investigation and writing project, field work, close-reading and discussion, and creative peer-to-peer workshop, we will synthesize the practices of paranormal investigation and writing as thoroughly as possible, until they become potentially unrecognizable from each other. Furthermore, what animates the desire to find evidence or proof of the after life? What about this desire mimics or mirrors our own artistic desires? What are the dangers of this mode of searching?

INSTRUCTOR: Brian Dang (they/she), or simply “b,” is a Vietnamese/Chinese poet/playwright and teaching artist based in Providence, RI. Their plays are a mixture of devised and scripted elements, often about the political domestic. Brian was a resident playwright at Parley (Seattle), a 2021 Tennessee Williams Scholar at the Sewanee Writers’ Conference, and a 2023 Lambda Fellow. Her plays include Grandmother/Bathtub (Theater Mu New Eyes Festival, Yale Cabaret, O’Neill Finalist ’25, Sparkfest Finalist ‘24) and This time (Undermain Fund for New Work, O’Neill Finalist ‘22, Many Voices Fellowship Semi-Finalist ‘22). They are currently a 2025-26 Core Apprentice at the Playwrights’ Center and a Creative Writing Mentor at New Urban Arts. Their poetry work includes 49 words I wish I could write in my family’s language, a collaborative translation project. Learn more at https://brianeatswords.com/

courses.title: Experimental College - Fandom: Economics of Attention
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Fandom, Inc.: The Platform Economics of Attention

Why does the algorithm seem to know you’re going to love that book, that band, or that reality show…before you do? 

Fandom feels organic, but it isn’t: every community that forms around a book, a band, or a reality-TV cast is built by the platforms that host it, the studios and publishers that profit from it, and the fans whose attention is the product being sold. This course treats fandom as a case study in platform economics and media strategy, tracking three case studies whose platform architectures couldn’t be more different—Heated Rivalry and BookTok’s open algorithm, BTS and HYBE’s owned Weverse ecosystem, and Love Island’s broadcast-plus-live-vote model—to ask who profits when we fall for something, and why. No fandom membership required.

INSTRUCTOR: Courtney Elston is a Technical Product Manager for AI Content Discovery at Audible, where she builds the recommendation and discovery systems used by millions of listeners, and serves as the company’s in-house romance and BookTok subject-matter expert. She previously built BookCrush, a discovery platform for romance readers, and holds an MBA from MIT Sloan.

courses.title: Experimental College - The Fallen Woman
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Fallen Woman: From the Bible to Bridgerton 

What do Eve and the biblical fall of “Man” have to do with Bridgerton? Or with the cultural debate that pits Beyoncé against Taylor Swift? How do these modern discourses around gender, sex, and race echo popular nineteenth-century literary tropes?

This course calls into question how capitalism and colonialism work to uphold and reinforce racialized and gendered conceptions of “virtue,” “purity,” and nationalism. We will look at how the “fallen woman”—a figure tied most prominently with the Victorian era— has been and continues to be reinscribed in contemporary culture even as the term itself has faded. We will study texts, including a novel, film, magazine articles, and more, about the fallen woman, race and racism, and colonial history, among other topics. This class will also follow debates that are still forming in today’s political and social climate in order to examine the persistence of nineteenth-century ideologies. 

INSTRUCTOR: Gillian Wood is a PhD candidate in the Tufts English Department specializing in nineteenth-century British literature. Her scholarship focuses on race and gender studies, the African diaspora, Caribbean history, and memory studies. Her dissertation explores the ways in which the popular nineteenth-century figure of the “fallen woman” is entangled with developing ideologies around race, gender, and nationhood. In addition to teaching first-year writing at Tufts for the past three years, Gillian served as a graduate fellow in the GIFT program, and holds an MA in English from Tufts.

courses.title: Experimental College - Korea: KPop, Film & Culture
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Korea Brand: Understanding KPop, Film, and Culture of the Two Koreas

Korea has become one of the most popular tourist destinations among young people today. KPop Demon Hunters, Squid Game, BTS, Korean food, Kbeauty, and the North Korean nuclear crisis continue to maintain Korea’s position as a transnational social media trope. Most recently, South Korea sits at the nexus of shipbuilding, defense, and AI, which is boosting the stock market, and is becoming technologically indispensable in multiple “arms races” (SK Hynix, Samsung, Hanwha Aerospace, HD Hyundai, LG Energy Solution, etc.). We will examine the rise of Korea as a recognizable brand in the thriving global market for Korean technology, music, film, cosmetics, food, and eSports. 

This course complicates the story behind the circulation of these popular technoscapes, foregrounding the colonial period, national division, and the rest of a very tumultuous twentieth century which led to Korea’s emergence as a global leader in the twenty-first century. Then we will move beyond the binary of Korea and the West undergirding old cultural flows, and consider the positionality of the Korea brand as both postcolonial and transnational. 

INSTRUCTOR: Ellie Choi writes on modern Korea, colonial Pyongyang, and contemporary Korean (food) media. She has also published prolifically on colonial Korea and interwar Korean intellectual history on issues of political collaboration and colonial spatiality. She has taught at Cornell, Smith, Yale, Dartmouth, and Brown. She has a PhD from Harvard in modern Korean history and literature.

courses.title: Experimental College - Food Media
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: An Insider's Guide to the World of Food Media.

The rise and evolution of food media over the last three decades has directly impacted every aspect of how we interact with food: from what, when, and where we eat, to how we connect with our plates and our planet. This course will be a wide-ranging survey of the past, present, and future of food media. We will analyze the theory behind this influential force at the nexus of information and entertainment, but our journey will be rooted in real-life practice. Your guide has a career that has been nearly as varied as food media itself, which is continually changing as it feeds our appetites and shapes how we look at the world. Food media encompasses a variety of formats across the wider media landscape. We’ll explore important skills including food writing, recipe writing, and food styling and photography, and we’ll go behind the scenes to explore food storytelling in books, newspapers, magazines, radio, podcasts, television, film, the Internet, and social media. We’ll analyze how each media form feeds, or is fed by, our culture’s current obsession with food. 

INSTRUCTOR: Denise Drower Swidey (A90) is an Emmy- and James Beard-nominated producer of national TV cooking shows as well as a chef, food writer, food stylist, and cooking instructor. She is the supervising producer of the James Beard-nominated PBS show The Food Flirts with the Brass Sisters, which she helped create. She is also a graduate of the Culinary Institute of America.

courses.title: Experimental College - Tufts Unplugged
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Tufts Unplugged: Connection Beyond Screens

This course meets on Feb. 5, Feb. 26, March 12, April 2. 

If you weren’t looking at a screen, what would you like to be doing? Explore Boston neighborhoods with a few friends? Share a home-cooked meal? Go birding in the woods? Do you miss “analog” activities or have skills to share - baking, knitting, songwriting, card games? 

The ExCollege is creating Tufts Unplugged as a pilot in Spring 2027 to give students a time and space to connect and explore without screens and technology. We will meet 4 times, set our phones aside, and try out some analog skills that build connection and an understanding of the community around us. This can be anything from journaling to hiking, art-making to games. We will ponder what we’ve gained and lost in the age of smart phones, and build time into our week to reflect. At the end of the course, students will present an artifact they created in relation to their unplugged experience. 

Come to an optional introductory meeting on Friday, Nov. 13 at 3:00pm to see what it’s all about. We will have hands-on activities and snacks, and we want to hear what you’re looking for in an unplugged course. Sign up for the meeting here: [https://tinyurl.com/tuftsunplugged]

Meeting sessions will be team taught and built around these themes:
- Learn (or share) “analog” tech-free skills
- Create community through shared activities
- Explore the Boston area - neighborhoods, food, museums, history
- Connect to nature

courses.title: Experimental College - Thriving After Tufts
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios

sections.note:
COURSE: Thriving After Tufts: Money, Career, and Network

This course will meet in the second half of the semester on March 9, March 30, April 6, April 13, April 20, and April 27.

This six-week course will help students to create a tangible, executable blueprint for their journey toward financial independence that will benefit them for decades to come. We will focus on the three key pillars of creating financial growth and stability: Money, Career, and Network. Students will leave with a personal financial dashboard, a five-year career blueprint, a mapped and activated professional network, and a working understanding of how these three pillars converge and compound over time.

INSTRUCTOR: Meena Thever (J’00) has spent 25 years working on Wall Street, first in investment banking before moving into private equity. She is the Founder & CEO of Wealth Is Female. An author, speaker, board member and entrepreneur, she was recently named a 2026 Women Innovators Award Honoree by Westfair Business Journal. Her book is set to launch in May 2027. She earned her BA in Economics from Tufts, a Masters in Public Policy from the Harvard Kennedy School, and an MBA from The Wharton School. She is also a Fulbright Scholar. She currently serves as a member of the Tufts University Board of Trustees.

courses.title: Experimental College - Camp: Bad Taste, Cult Classics
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Camp: Bad Taste, Humor, and Cult-Classics

“Camp isn’t about tie-dying t-shirts at summer camp. Rather, camp has everything to do with basking in the fabulousness, irony, and humor of being extra.” But is that all there is to Camp, to media’s raunchy inside jokes, to bad taste, to creating a cult-classic? Why are so many “campy” films set at summer camp? This course is dedicated to exploring the aesthetics of humor and horror of “campy” media. Through activities based in an imaginary summer camp, we explore what exactly “bad” taste is and who decides the fate of a piece of media on the spectrum of high or low-brow entertainment. From contemporary pieces like Lady Gaga’s music videos and the queens of RuPaul’s Drag Race, to the classic worlds of The Rocky Horror Show and John Waters, analysis happens when we turn out the cabin lights. Media is discussed via fireside chats, after pranks have been played, and during a long day of arts and crafts. Welcome, campers! There’s a lot to see here. But… watch your step. 

INSTRUCTOR: Jo Michael Rezes (they/them) is an award-winning theatremaker, scholar, AEA actor, and educator based in Greater Boston. They hold a Ph.D. in Theatre and Performance Studies from Tufts University, and their research examines camp, sensory culture, food, disability, and the cultural afterlives of HIV/AIDS across performance and media. Rezes has taught at Tufts University, Boston College, Emerson College, and Harvard University and currently serves as Associate Director of Education & Institutional Learning at The Theater Offensive. Their creative and scholarly work centers queer and transgender performance, fabulously grotesque aesthetics, and inclusive approaches to theatre-making and pedagogy.

courses.title: Experimental College - Brickology: Thinking in Lego
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Brickology: Thinking in LEGO

Have you ever wanted to ditch the instruction manual of a LEGO set and build from your imagination? 

In this course, you will get to explore the magic that is LEGO and the many forms it can take. Together, we will dive into LEGO art, puzzle boxes, Rubik’s cubes, and more. We will also explore the cultural relevance of the toy bricks since its creation in 1932, discussing the various choices the company has made along the way. There will be discussion of the engineering of a LEGO brick, marketing and branding, sustainability efforts, media, and controversy. As a critical part of this course, you will have the freedom to build your own creations. This course will culminate in a final project where you will use LEGO as an expression. 

INSTRUCTOR: Elizabeth Chin is a senior majoring in Biomedical Engineering.

courses.title: Experimental College - The Psychology of Survivor
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Psychology of Survivor: Chaos, Paranoia, Betrayal

What happens to the human psyche when people are stripped of comfort and stability, as well as forced to compete for both survival and social belonging? 

Using Survivor: Cagayan (Season 28) as a 13-episode case study, this course will psychoanalyze the contestants as they fight to get to the end of 39 days of deprivation, instability, and manipulation. Each week, students will watch one episode and apply a new psychological lens, gradually building a versatile toolbox for critical analysis. Challenges, structured debate, and creative analysis will turn the classroom into a low-stakes laboratory. This course is not just a psychology course, but an invitation to think critically about social situations. No psychology background or Survivor knowledge is required.

INSTRUCTOR: Sofia Qureshi is a senior majoring in Engineering Psychology.

courses.title: Experimental College - The DJ in Modern Culture
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Behind the Decks: THE DJ IN MODERN CULTURE

How do DJs create collective experiences? 

This course will examine the social and economic forces shaping DJ culture, from identity and community to nightlife, branding, and entrepreneurship. Students will trace the development of DJ culture from disco, Jamaican sound systems, hip-hop, house, and techno to festivals, streaming platforms, social media, and artificial intelligence. Through readings, case studies, listening exercises, technical demonstrations, and hands-on workshops, students explore DJing through historical, cultural, psychological, technological, and economic perspectives. Students will learn the fundamentals of mixing, electronic music history, and the nightlife industry. No prior DJ experience or equipment is required!

INSTRUCTORS: Thomas Gesick is a senior majoring in Quantitative Economics. 
Aaron Lai is a senior majoring in Economics.

courses.title: Experimental College - Sociopolitics of Horror
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Sociopolitics of the Horror Adaptation

What does Ronald Reagan have to do with American Psycho? How did suburbanization create
the slasher movie?

Horror, as both a literary and movie genre, has long served as a creative tool to mask real societal fears and anxieties behind supernatural monsters, unseen killers, and alien invasions. This course explores the way that horror—particularly through the transformation from literary work to visual media (either through direct adaptation or inspiration)—is a reflection of contemporary sociopolitical norms and tensions. The differences in characterization, setting, themes, and plot between works of horror literature and their visual offshoots highlight the way that our world continues to change, and documents how our relationships with the things we fear change with it.

INSTRUCTOR: Max Lerner is a senior majoring in English.

courses.title: Experimental College - How Bread Changed History
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Bread: How One Food Changed History

How did a mixture of flour, water, salt, and yeast build empires, start wars, and become the core
of global religions? 

Ever since it was invented, human civilization and bread have risen together. We will explore human history from the wild grass gatherers of the Fertile Crescent to the mechanical innovations of the industrial loaf, and ultimately to the modern artisanal sourdough revival. Along the way, we will learn practical truths about the human condition and gain critical business skills through gamified group projects and presentations. Students will investigate how technology, religion, class, and globalization are baked into the food that changed the world.

INSTRUCTOR: Owen Liao is a senior majoring in Electrical Engineering.

courses.title: Experimental College - Politics of Entertainment
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Politics of Entertainment

Why is the French national football team made up of mostly players from African immigrant backgrounds? Why are some countries banned from the Eurovision Song Contest due to conflict but not others? 

Political decisions do not only happen in parliament or electorally, but also in institutions that are a part of your everyday life. International sporting events, the music industry, and popular culture all garner millions of viewers, crafting target audiences with similar interests. However, entertainment does not exist within a vacuum, with issues surrounding identity and nationality playing a large role in the modern era of globalization. In this course, we will examine how major global cultural events reinforce political life and coincide with political headlines occurring at the same time. Split into units on sports, music, and social media, students will begin to understand politics from more than just what happens between politicians, and instead can identify how the pop culture and media they consume are influenced by groups of people vying for power and resources.

INSTRUCTOR: Alex Fial is a student majoring in Political Science and History.

COURSE: Conscious Nourishment: Embodying Intentional Foodways to Transform Our Self, Soil, and Society

Have you ever had a meal that felt sacred?

This course invites students to engage with food through reflective observation and community practice as a means of evolving our collective psyche. Beginning with the contemporary American food-scape, we will observe the habits and assumptions that have come to define our relationship with consumption. We will then encounter broader modes of nourishment through Indigenous foodways, Ayurveda, and Zen Buddhist culinary tradition. Along the way, students will engage with food as a practice of presence, wonder, creation, and interconnection, to transform our daily digestion into the sacred. Cooking and eating will take center stage in our conscious nourishment!

INSTRUCTOR: Julian Staeva-Vieira is a senior majoring in Interdisciplinary Studies: Conscious Nourishment (Food Systems, Sociology, and Religion).

courses.title: Experimental College - Bad PR/Misrepresenting Animals
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Bad PR: Media's Mispresentation of Animals

How much do you really know about Jumbo the elephant? 

Each week, roughly 250 families on undergraduate tours of Tufts University learn that Jumbo was a noble circus elephant who died in a blaze of glory, sacrificing himself to save a baby elephant crossing the train tracks. This story is almost certainly false. P.T. Barnum invented it to make Jumbo a hero and, ultimately, to sell more circus tickets. This anecdote captures how media gravitates toward hyperbole, exaggeration, and misinformation to attract discussion and attention. Animals are constantly subject to this kind of misrepresentation across many forms of media, whether from news headlines, movies, social media discourse, or even scientific studies. This course aims to explore, and ultimately reframe, how we see animals when being presented with a single narrative. We will examine several animal species through biological, historical, and anthropological lenses to understand the true nature of each species and challenge how media has incorrectly framed public perception of these animals.

INSTRUCTOR: Silas Summers is a senior majoring in Psychology/Biology and Anthropology.

Ann blends her research on the ways young climate activists manage emotions around climate change with the programming she runs for the Office of Sustainability. This half-semester course will serve a dual role during what can be a daunting period in the thesis-writing process. It will provide students with tools to move from researching to writing confidently and tackle large scale revision. It will also provide a regular writing community for accountability and advice. This course focuses primarily on writing, and students should expect to make weekly writing progress toward their theses.
 
INSTRUCTOR: Hannah Weildon is the Assistant Director of Writing Support at the Tufts, where she coordinates the Writing Fellows Program and provides individual writing support to students. Hannah received her PhD in English at Tufts and has previously taught writing and writing pedagogy in the First Year Writing Program and Experimental College as well as literature at Emerson College, Norwich University, and the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. She enjoys helping students and tutors alike build positive relationships with the writing process and find empowerment through peer-to-peer collaboration.

courses.title: Experimental College - Financial Literacy
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Ever thought, “Why doesn’t someone teach a class about how to handle all that adult financial stuff?” Well, you are in luck. Paychecks, budgets, taxes, savings, credit cards, loans, and more…what does it all mean and where to begin? In this course we will discuss all the pieces that make up a personal financial life and how they interact with one another, and how policy and laws (pulled from the headlines) can have an impact on individuals and families. The goal of this class is not to make you a financial expert, but to provide a basic toolkit to set you up to make thoughtful and informed decisions as you move forward.

INSTRUCTOR: Christopher R. Di Fronzo CFP® is the Director of Career Services and oversees the advising team in the Tufts Career Center. Prior to this he was the Director of the Tufts Finance Initiative and worked with students interested in finance and consulting. He began his career in software at The MathWorks and, after several years, transitioned into the finance industry. Before returning to Tufts as the inaugural Director of the Tufts Finance Initiative, he was the Managing Director of a private wealth advisory group in Rhode Island. He formerly held his Series 7, 66 and 24 and continues to hold his Certified Financial Planner TM designation through the CFP® Board. Considers the long history of woven objects alongside contemporary artists, designers and crafts people as makers and thinkers. Builds a virtual, collective, interactive weaving of information that brings together: histories, mythologies, economics, science, environmental impact, technology, and identity politics to help understand the complicated and intimate role cloth has and continues to play in human existence. Work on found looms, frame looms and backstrap looms and use traditional and non-traditional weaving materials and practices to develop a corporal knowledge of the techniques.

Examines natural dye as a material, ecological, and cultural practice through sustained studio work in a fiber garden setting. Using the SMFA Dye & Fiber Garden as a primary material resource, students explore plant-based dye processes from cultivation and harvest through dye extraction, fiber preparation, and application. Emphasis is placed on seasonal cycles, sustainable material systems, and place-responsive making. Technical workshops introduce historical and contemporary natural dye methods while supporting individual material research and experimentation. Students produce dyed fibers and yardage for use in independent studio projects, with opportunities for collaborative work connected to the garden’s ongoing care and sustainability. courses.title: Art of the Moving Image - Sophomore and Junior
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 51 & TPS 20) Exploration of cinema's basic aesthetic characteristics: its stylistic features, such as editing, cinematography, and sound, as well as its major narrative and non-narrative forms: mainstream and avant-garde, fiction and non-fiction, narrative and non-narrative, black-and-white and color, silent and sound. Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

courses.title: Television History
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with TPS 24) Examination of the introduction and development of U.S. television during the network era (40s-90s). Development of television (in the U.S. and within a global context) from its conception through its industrial, technical, aesthetic, and textual development to understand how American broadcast television emerged as a dominant cultural force around the world. Explore how specific analytical concepts in television studies develop. Learn and practice how media theory takes on historical research. Fulfills the FMS media history requirement.

courses.title: A Cultural History of the Internet
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 37) The internet as cultural and historical phenomenon and the power structures embedded in digital platforms. Internet development from early computational ideas to digital culture and interactive media. Foundational technologies including the Jacquard Loom and Babbage’s Analytical Engine, the emergence of networked computing and World Wide Web, and the explosion of online communities. Focus on internet culture: memes, digital art, remix culture, early social platforms, and interactive web-based games and artworks, from net.art experiments to Flash animations and viral browser games. Concludes with YouTube and the foundations of contemporary social media, when user-generated content became a dominant force in global media. The internet’s impact on media production, storytelling, and cultural identity.

courses.title: Introduction to Film and Media Production
courses.desc: Tools and techniques necessary to create stories for film, television, and the internet. Focus on how to effectively use the camera, set lights, record sound, and edit. Emphasis on learning both film style and scene building in preparation for more advanced film and video production courses. Recommended for first- and second-year students.

sections.note: Lab fee will be collected in class for equipment accessories. 4 Credits.

courses.title: Producing for Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 151) Explores the art and practice of producing for film through individual media projects while also joining the production team of a new professional film. Hands-on practice and exposure to the full production cycle: development, budgeting, fundraising, contracts and legal documents, scheduling, location management, post-production, marketing, festival strategy, and distribution. Broader questions of access to the industry, audience impact, and environmental and financial sustainability. Builds practical skills for launching future projects and a deeper understanding of film as a collaborative medium. Prerequisites: FMS 0010.

courses.title: Intermediate Film & Media Production
courses.desc: Advanced study of filmmaking through the collaborative production of a short narrative movie based on an optioned script. Preproduction includes script breakdown, location scouting, casting, and storyboarding. During production, students gain experience directing, shooting, setting lights, and recording sound for part of the script. Postproduction includes collaborative editing, mixing/mastering audio, and color grading. Prerequisites: FMS 0010.

sections.note: 4 Credits

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 79). Workshop in the craft of writing short films. Emphasis on visual storytelling and developing characters. Development of short film ideas from premise to screenplay. Focus on finding one's voice and discovering possibilities for creative expression afforded by film medium. Weekly script development activities and discussion of student work accompany screenings and analysis of short films from around the world. Prerequisites: FMS 0001

courses.title: Screenwriting: Features
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 178) Development of feature film ideas, from initial concept and premise to screenplay. Weekly discussions and writing activities emphasize developing an individual voice through visual storytelling, dramatic structure, and character development. Screenings and analysis of innovative films and produced screenplays that challenge convention complement discussion of student work. Development of the overall story for a film and completion of the first act of a screenplay. Prerequisites: FMS 0001.

courses.title: Acting for the Camera
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 52) Performance based acting course that teaches techniques to make emotional connections and create nuanced, truthful performances on camera. Work with filmed monologues, scenes, commercials, and workshops with casting professionals. Learn how to use information such as platform, director, genre, and creatives to determine how to approach performance. Focus on acting techniques, character development and emotionally connecting to material with a small portion of the course addressing the "business of acting" which will include union membership, auditioning, and creating reels.

courses.title: Dance & the Hollywood Musical
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with DNC 85) The role of dance in the film musical genre over the past century. Explores how bodies, movement vocabulary, and choreography can reinforce, oppose, and/or comment on contemporary society and our “collective” cultural identity. How do parallel developments in cinema and art impact the way we view dance? How are race, gender, and nationality portrayed? How do we define and view this genre today? Viewings, readings, movement experiences, discussions, and independent projects. Focus on developing literacy and critical research skills in dance. No previous dance or film background required. Recommendation: Art History and/or critical studies course in the arts.

courses.title: Dance on Camera
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/DNC 77 & DNC 177 & ILVS 29) Inter-disciplinary course designed for any dancer, artist or student interested in film & video production with dance or movement as a medium. Participants will take dance and movement concepts outside of studio walls and into the community through site-specific collaborative video projects. Through storyboarding, shooting, editing, and choreographing/directing, students will learn basic video production techniques and advanced camera work in this hands-on course. Development of movement ideas as well as non-linear editing skills will be explored. Work culminates in end of semester public screening and online video sharing. Open to all. No dance or film/video experience necessary.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENG 7) Introductory practice in various forms of journalistic writing including news, profile, feature, and investigative stories. Study of published works, ethical considerations, and current challenges to the field, and workshop of stories-in-progress. courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENG 11 & CVS 41) Advanced practice in journalistic writing with a focus on longform narrative, including features, profiles, and other magazine-style forms. Development of journalistic skills through analyzing published works, reporting and writing original stories on subjects of personal and academic interest, and developing work in a collaborative workshop setting. courses.title: Art and Business of Crafting Media Campaigns
courses.desc: Theory and practice of creating commercial content. Writing, producing, directing, and pitching various forms of short-form videos. Exploration of how commercial filmmaking shapes our culture, through a combination of lectures, screenings, and hands-on projects, including producing content such as television commercials, political ads, "brand videos," and corporate or non-profit narratives.

courses.title: Film Noir And The American Tradition
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ENG 88) Introductory course in film noir as a distinctively American genre. Attention to its literary, historical, and social contexts; its implication in the popularization of psychoanalysis; its particular interest for psychoanalytic criticism; its importance as a site of cultural anxieties centering on sexuality, gender, and race. Readings may include novels (by authors such as Hawthorne, James, and Baldwin), theoretical essays, and works in cinema studies. Films may include works by Wilder, Preminger, Hawks, Welles, Vidor, Tourneur, Dmytryk, Mann, Lang, Kubrick, Aldrich, and Scorsese.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 REQUIRED or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Film and the Avant-Garde
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 58, ILVS 187, HAA 159, FMS 185, HAA 49, VMS 185 and VMS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. Avant-garde filmmakers beginning in the 1920s, such as Fernand Leger and Marcel Duchamp, as well as filmmakers from cross-media movements such as Dada and Surrealism. Postwar artists in the United States who reworked prewar avant-garde film genres and pioneered new ones, including lyrical and collage film. Structural film of the 1960s and the pluralism of avant-garde film since the 1970s. Historical conditions and theories that shaped these developments, and the use of avant-garde film by feminists and other artists for socio-political critique. Lower level version of FMS 0185.

sections.note: Students may choose lower level section (FMS 58) or upper level section (FMS 185). The upper level includes an additional research project. Weekly recitation/screening is required.
Weekly recitation/screening is required.

courses.title: African American Theatre And Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as AFR 48 and TPS 18). A broad historical survey of plays and films by African Americans. Comparison of cinematic and theatrical representations. Relation of African American aesthetics to broader American, European, and Pan-African forms. Historical evaluation and comparison of images created by African Americans and those established in the mainstream milieu. (May be taken at 100 level for graduate credit with consent.)

courses.title: Russian & East European Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 86, RUS 81 & ILCS 81) Examination of a series of masterpieces by filmmakers from "the other Europe": the Soviet Union/Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and the former Yugoslav territories. Explores the role of film in terms of its artistic achievements and social commentary: As a tool in the transition to the new Soviet order; as an alternative means of expression during censorship; and, more recently, as a corrective tool in fragile new democracies and a voice of protest fighting against new forms of oppression. No prerequisites. In English.

courses.title: Laughter, Politics, Media: Francophone Perspective
courses.desc: Humor as both entertainment and critique across Francophone stand-up, film, television, comics, and digital culture, from café-théâtre and political satire to roasts, Netflix specials and online memes. How comedy challenges, reinforces, or plays with social norms around class, gender, sexuality, race, and postcolonial belonging; the controversies it sparks over cancel culture, censorship, and freedom of expression, and the shifting line between satire and offense. The role of media industries, platforms, and audiences in shaping comic voices, with particular attention to contrasts between Francophone and U.S. contexts. Analysis of comedy as a cultural form that reflects and reshapes debates about power, identity, and spectatorship. In English.

courses.title: Italian Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ITAL75.) Exploration of Italian cinema from WWII to the present, with special attention to the historical background against which films were produced, circulated and discussed. Study of intellectual movements like neorealism and modernism, but also popular genres like comedy and the spaghetti western. Screenings (with English subtitles) from directors like De Sica, Fellini, Sorrentino, and Rohrwacher. Readings may include topics such as political theory, gender, crime, colonialism, ethics, and ecology. In English.

courses.title: Japanese Film
courses.desc: (Cross-list w/ JPN 80)Survey of important Japanese films, including internationally renowned works by the "masters," Mizoguchi, Ozu, and Kurosawa; the '60s avant-garde cinema of Oshima and Shinoda; and some innovative works by contemporary filmmakers such as Itami and Morita. Understanding Japanese cinema in relation to Western cultural hegemony. Taught in English. Napier.Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/grall/japanese/.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ GER 85) survey of German cinema, from its striking and influential achievements in the Weimar Republic, through its role under Hitler and its decline in the postwar period, to the remarkable phenomenon of New German Cinema in the sixties and seventies and the developments of the contemporary period. courses.title: Special Topics - Media and the Environment
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Students may choose lower level section (FMS 94-01) or upper level section (FMS 194-01). The upper level includes an additional research project. 

As conceptions of humanity’s relationship to nature have evolved, so too have the ways that people use media to represent the environment. We will look closely at how movies and other popular media have depicted nonhuman nature, and examine how audiovisual media have been used within the environmental movement, from the conservation efforts of the mid-20th century to the increasingly urgent efforts of activists in the era of climate change. We will read work by prominent scholars in ecocriticism, and view a wide range of media, looking at narrative, documentary, and experimental practices.

courses.title: Special Topics - New Waves in Global Film
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: The course focuses on the 1960s and the subsequent four decades and explores the vibrant era of international “new waves” which in the globalized world brought to the surface new voices and diverse cinematic visions. While analyzing the established film industries of the Western world, we will also discuss the emerging cinemas of the Global South. We will map out connections, examine different aesthetic approaches, discuss the pushback against Hollywood, and consider film as a medium inviting personal reflection, artistic exploration and social transformation.

courses.title: Special Topics - Women and Gender on TV
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Students may choose lower-level section (FMS 94-05) or upper-level section (FMS 194-02). The upper level includes an additional research project. 

From Soaps to Streaming: Women and Gender on TV. Whether depicting the housewife of early sitcoms or iconic characters like Mary Tyler Moore, Leslie Knope, and Olivia Pope, television has played an influential role in women’s lives and engaged with gender politics. Because of its historical placement in the domestic sphere, TV has long been understood as a "feminized" medium. Yet, it also functions as a crucial site where women’s stories are told, and where gender, sexuality, race, and class are negotiated, contested, and reimagined. Throughout the course, we will consider questions such as: How have television texts represented women? In what genres have women dominated? Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE) in collaboration with the Film and Media Studies Program (FMS), this four-part film series invites Tufts students to examine the themes of individualism and nonconformity through screenings of landmark films drawn from a range of historical periods, political contexts, and cinematic traditions. Each session features a full-length film paired with faculty framing and guided discussion, allowing participants to analyze how individuals navigate the tension between personal conscience and collective pressure, and how political and social institutions respond to dissent. The series asks participants to think critically about moral independence, civic responsibility, and the costs and consequences of resisting conformity. Popcorn and pizza will be served. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are interested in exploring contested ideas, competing loyalties, and acts of principled resistance that shape public life. Faculty and staff are also welcome to join.

courses.title: Film and the Avant-Garde
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 187, HAA 159, FMS 58, HAA 49, VMS 185, VMS 58 & ILVS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. As conceptions of humanity’s relationship to nature have evolved, so too have the ways that people use media to represent the environment. We will look closely at how movies and other popular media have depicted nonhuman nature, and examine how audiovisual media have been used within the environmental movement, from the conservation efforts of the mid-20th century to the increasingly urgent efforts of activists in the era of climate change. We will read work by prominent scholars in ecocriticism, and view a wide range of media, looking at narrative, documentary, and experimental practices.

courses.title: The Grail Quest in Medieval French Literature
courses.desc: Literary evolution of the Grail from its pagan Celtic origins to its elusive role in the twelfth-century novel by Chrétien de Troyes, its thirteenth-century Christianization in the trilogy by Robert de Boron, and its exaltation in the anonymous Quest of the Holy Grail. In parallel readings the sins of Perceval and Lancelot will bar their way to the full vision of the Grail, provoke the birth of Galahad, lead to warfare based on the adultery with Guinevere, and in the anonymous Death of King Arthur, point to the dramatic end of Camelot. In English. Cross-listed as MDVL 22.

sections.note:
In Perceval by Chrétien de Troyes, the Grail, thought to be a pagan Celtic symbol, first appears in the Arthurian world. When its import eludes the naïve protagonist, the mystery is withdrawn from sight. The object – Christianized in the trilogy by Robert de Boron (Joseph of Arimathea, Merlin, Perceval) – then inspires the knightly Quest of the Holy Grail. Perceval and Bors the Younger are admitted to its presence after many trials, whereas Lancelot’s adulterous affair with Queen Guinevere, recounted in Chrétien’s Knight of the Cart, bars his way. Only Galahad, born expressly for the purpose, will fulfill the deepest aspirations of the quest. Gawain, nephew of the sovereign, prods his uncle into two wars against Lancelot in The Death of King Arthur; Mordred, the king’s illegitimate son, strives to take the royal realm by force. Son and father perish at each other’s hand in open battle, thus marking the dramatic end of Camelot. Cinematic adaptations will be viewed in tandem with the novels cited above. Class discussions; three low-
stakes quizzes; one take-home essay. Fulfills the French Culture Option, the Related Field requirement for French Majors, and the Humanities requirement for Engineers; counts toward the International Relations Major and the Interdisciplinary Minor in Medieval Studies. No prerequisites; conducted in English.

sections.note: Humor as both entertainment and critique across Francophone stand-up, film, television, comics, and digital culture, from café-théâtre and political satire to roasts, Netflix specials and online memes. How comedy challenges, reinforces, or plays with social norms around class, gender, sexuality, race, and postcolonial belonging; the controversies it sparks over cancel culture, censorship, and freedom of expression, and the shifting line between satire and offense. courses.desc: Cultural studies course examining contemporary graphic novels and historical comics from the Francophone world— including North Africa, the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, France/Belgium, Vietnam, and Québec. Analysis of key graphic novels and their receptions, exploring how visual narratives engage with themes such as colonial history, migration, memory, gender, sexuality, disability, and racial representation. Emphasis on the unique hybrid form of “bandes dessinées” (comic strips) in shaping conversations about identity, ideology, and power across Francophone societies. Discussion topics include (post)colonialism, Orientalism, antisemitism, feminism, and queer thought, with emphasis on aesthetic, political, and economic dimensions of the genre. In French. Recommendations: 2 courses taught in French above FR22.

courses.title: French for International Relations
courses.desc: Advanced French language course equipping students with the skills and cultural knowledge to communicate in the world of international diplomacy, politics, and global affairs. Analysis of historic speeches and discussions of global issues like climate change, trade agreements, and soft power. Prepares students for future careers in international organizations, diplomacy, and journalism. Recommendation: Two courses above French 22 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc:
(Conducted in French.) Guided individual study of an approved topic in French literature or civilization. No more than three credits in Independent Study may be counted toward the major. Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: One 100-level literature course and permission of instructor.

courses.title: International Supply Chains: Connecting the Developed and Developing Worlds
courses.desc:
International Supply Chains: Connecting the Developed and Developing Worlds: This course is about managing the growing flow of business between countries, especially the supply chains that interconnect economies. Supply chains are especially dynamic today—performance demands on companies are steadily rising, geopolitical risks abound, and digital technology offers new choices about how to deliver to customers and how to control the chain.

You will learn how to create, negotiate, and manage supply chains. The course operates at two levels. One is the global context: the forces that shape new supply networks, the elements that determine which ones succeed, and the particular challenges of operating in the developing world. The second is the operating level: how companies decide where to source, the partners they need, and where and how to build and control these supply networks.

The tools of the course range from hard analytics and decision-making models to soft skills in aligning incentives and conflict resolution. The course covers a great range of industries—from commodities to basic manufactures to high tech—as well as services and goods.

courses.title: Negotiating Leadership
courses.desc: Negotiating Leadership: This course explores the nature of leadership in the international business and organizational contexts. A key premise of the course is that leadership is an exercise in negotiation. To lead is to negotiate. The course will examine three key dimensions of the leadership life cycle: 1) the acquisition of leadership power, 2) the use of this power, and 3) the preservation and inevitable loss of this power. You will study a wide range of leadership theories and practices (American and international), examine failed leadership examples, and discuss the role of values, ethics, gender, and culture.

courses.title: Managerial Economics
courses.desc: This course introduces management issues from the perspective of economics. The focus is on the strategic responses a firm can make regarding both its internal organization and its external interaction with both consumers and other firms. You will learn how economic analysis can aid the understanding and improve the design of organizational structure and the development of competitive strategies, whether the organization is a for-profit firm or a nonprofit enterprise.

courses.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
courses.desc: Mergers and Acquisitions: This course reviews the structuring, negotiation, and implementation of cross-border merger and acquisition transactions. It takes into account the applicable issues of international law and national practice. The course discusses alternative forms of transaction structure and the underlying tax and legal considerations related to choosing particular approaches. You will analyze different forms of acquisition agreements, review the role and application of key transactional concepts, and analyze how these concepts are addressed in the context of specific transactions. You will review the typical areas of negotiation in the acquisition of private and public companies and evaluate how these negotiations are affected by international regulatory, legal, and fiscal considerations. Finally, you will review trends in deal terms, drawing on recent transactions involving North American, European, and Asian companies.

courses.title: Clinical Implications of Basic Research
courses.desc: This journal club course for MD/PhD students is organized around the “Clinical Implications of Basic Research” column published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Students read a primary paper(s) highlighted in the column or one that is similar to those highlighted and discuss the work. The primary goal of this required course, which meets for one hour every other week, is to encourage and teach students to continually ask how basic research can impact clinical medicine. The format also encourages students to sharpen their communication skills in a relaxed atmosphere.

courses.title: Mammalian Genetics
courses.desc: The course reviews the genetic principles that apply to mammals, including genetic mechanisms of sex determination, genetic imprinting, and mitochondrial inheritance. Attention is focused on the ways in which mutation is manifested in disease phenotypes in humans, and the methodologies that are currently used to perform genetic analysis of mammals.

courses.title: PhD Degree Only
courses.desc: Students enroll in this course when they receive permission to write and defend their theses from their thesis committees. This course represents the effort in the final preparation of the doctoral thesis. A grade of “S” is automatically awarded upon completion of the thesis.

courses.title: Elementary German II
courses.desc: Continuation of GER 0001. Focus on written and oral communication about everyday topics. Insights into cultural topics of German speaking countries. Continued study of basic grammar while practicing speaking, listening/understanding, reading, and writing. Prerequisite: GER 0001 or equivalent. Students may not earn credit for GER 2 if GER 01/2 has already been taken.

courses.title: Intermediate German II
courses.desc:
Authentic readings, films, and audio materials from a variety of genres and time periods. Development of reading and writing skills to enhance cultural awareness and cross-cultural understanding. Continued practice of intermediate grammar. Emphasis on broadening the vocabulary base and increasing the complexity of texts. One additional weekly practice session to improve speaking facility and reinforce and expand class material. Prerequisite: GER 0003 or equivalent.
Students may not earn credit for GER 4 if GER 3/4 has already been taken.

courses.title: Composition and Conversation II
courses.desc: Emphasis on fluency and accuracy in speaking German. Continued practice in writing. Introduction of more complex structures and vocabulary. Authentic materials cover current issues from the German-speaking countries. Film materials and texts from both journalistic and literary genres. Use of the Internet for independent student research. One additional weekly practice session to improve speaking facility and reinforce and expand class material. Prerequisite: GER 0021 or equivalent.

courses.title: Berlin: An Excursion to Modernity
courses.desc: Investigation of the co-emergence of metropolitan Berlin and modernist art and thinking from the early twentieth century to the present. Themes include utopian/dystopian urbanity, the relation between art and propaganda, the politics of memory, the aesthetics of terrorism as well as the creative force of cultural hybridity. Emphasis on literature, film, and visual culture, supplemented by readings in philosophy, (cultural) history, and urban studies. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: German Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ FMS 79) survey of German cinema, from its striking and influential achievements in the Weimar Republic, through its role under Hitler and its decline in the postwar period, to the remarkable phenomenon of New German Cinema in the sixties and seventies and the developments of the contemporary period. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Special Topics - Culture Under Totalitarianism
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for current course descriptions.

sections.note: After World War II and at the beginning of the Cold War, political philosopher Hannah Arendt recognized National Socialist German and Stalinist Soviet Union as totalitarian; a new form of government that was simultaneously modern and barbaric, incredibly terrifying and violent but also rationally organized and socially bureaucratic. This course will focus on the role of culture and cultural production as both support and subversion of these totalitarian societies, investigating and interpreting works of art, literature, film, music, architecture, etc. produced under these regimes. We will learn about how cultural producers navigated their own (often politically informed) aesthetics and ethics within the strictures of totalitarian censorship.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 107.)Broad foundation of Geographic Information Systems theory, capabilities, technology, and applications. Topics include GIS data discovery, data structure and management; principles of cartographic visualization; and basic spatial analysis and modeling. Assignments concentrate on applying concepts covered in lectures and class exercises to term projects in each student's fields of interest.
