courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LEAD 275) Geographical Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods and their applications. Topics include GIS data structures, geodesy, cartography and spatial analysis using rasters and vectors. Includes extensive laboratory exercises using ArcGIS. Final project using GIS to apply student interests.

courses.title: Advanced Geographical Information Systems
courses.desc: Spatial analysis methods including raster analysis, suitability analysis, spatiotemporal statistics, geostatistics and network analysis. Laboratory exercises include automation using ArcPy and Model Builder using ArcGIS. Topics in database management including SQL and UML. Group or individual projects based on students’ interests. For students from any discipline with an interest in advanced geospatial modeling and spatial analysis applications. Prerequisites: GIS 201 or department permission.

courses.title: Spatial Statistics
courses.desc: First course on spatial data analysis. Global and local spatial autocorrelation statistics, cluster analysis, principal component analysis, point patterns, interpolation, hotspot analysis, and space time analysis. A variety of regression techniques for spatial data including spatial, autologistic and geographically weighted regressions. Introduction of open source software including Geoda, and R. Prerequisites: An introductory statistics course or its equivalent; GIS 201 or department permission.

sections.note: Interested juniors or seniors must contact instructor for permission to enroll.

courses.title: Leadership and Negotiation Year-Long Lab
courses.desc: The aim of this year-long lab is to link the leadership and negotiation skills introduced in the first residency and subsequent terms to the strategies and practices of GMAP students themselves. Our hope is that armed with the knowledge of their own leadership styles and negotiation strategies, they will leave Fletcher with a firm set of goals and action steps that will assist them in achieving their vision of a meaningful career.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.
instructors: Diana V Chigas, Diane Ryan, Eileen F Babbitt

courses.title: Policy Memo Development
courses.desc: The Policy Memo represents the culmination of knowledge and skills gained during the Policy Lab which takes place during the March Residency. While the outcome of the Policy Lab is a policy pitch where students address a policy problem or opportunity delivered through a TED-Style talk, the Policy Memo is a written document that analyzes the same theme they explored in the Policy Lab. The Policy Memo outlines current policy gaps (backed by evidence) and proposes policy recommendations (also backed by evidence) in light of their chosen policy theme.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: Global Economic Governance: Sustainable Trade and Investment
courses.desc: Focuses on the relationship between globalization in the form of international flows of trade and investment, and sustainability, including climate change, other environmental policy, development, health, and other areas of non-commercial public policy. It explores the ways in which international law addresses these issues through legislative techniques, including special exceptions as well as integrative rules, through dispute settlement, and through international organizations. It provides an opportunity to examine forms and strategies of leadership in settings with multiple concerns and multiple horizontal and vertical nodes of authority.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: International Security Simulation
courses.desc: The red team simulation is a scenario driven exercise focused on building better plans through groupthink mitigation, cultural empathy, and alternative future analysis tools and methods. Scenarios come from real world international conflict areas and are developed by subject matter experts in that area.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: The Role of Force in the 21st Century International Security and Conflict Environment
courses.desc: Examines the political, economic, military and ethical factors affecting the use and utility of military force in international relations today. It aims to provide both theoretical foundation and the tools needed to analyze current security challenges confronting the United States and other countries. Topics addressed (may) include debates about grand strategy, military transformation and force structure,; theories of practice and coercion; theories and practice of crisis and post-crisis management; the causes of terrorism; nuclear, biological and chemical weapons (NBC) proliferation and counter-proliferation strategies; dynamics of military occupations, counterinsurgencies, and “nation building”; and the security implications of epidemic disease, border controls and demographic trends.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: Policy Lab
courses.desc:
The Policy Lab will cover critical steps in the policy development process including assessment, problem analysis, objectives setting, solutions development, and stakeholder engagement. We will introduce the stages and data requirements of policy design. At each step, students will apply the process to a case study, and, ultimately, to a challenge of their choosing.

The course will culminate in students applying policy development processes to a real-world challenge that they wish to address. Individually, they will conduct primary and secondary research to understand the challenge context and its root causes. They will complete the course with a well-designed solution (public policy proposal, business plan, or project charter), and will present this solution through a policy pitch.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: Public Policy Formulation and Practice
courses.desc: Examines how public policies are designed, implemented, and evaluated. This course explores both the theory and practice of the policy process with the level of analysis being at the national level and including comparative analysis in a global context. The course provides a conceptual framework for creating public policies and uses real cases of policies from different settings and contexts from the real-world public challenges - such as climate change housing, public health, digital transformation- in order to build skills of framing the values behind policy design decisions, examining the root causes of policy problems, stakeholder engagement, developing policy recommendations based on evidence and analysis, and evaluating policy solutions from diverse stakeholder perspectives.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: Qualifying Exam
courses.desc: Students present and defend a proposal for research consisting of a statement of an original research problem in which a scientific question is asked and the experimental approach to answering the question is explained in a written proposal. The proposal is presented orally to the faculty.

courses.title: Scientific Writing
courses.desc: This six-week course is designed to introduce students to basic scientific writing skills and can be useful for graduate students preparing for qualifying examinations. Participants will review the general principles of clear, persuasive writing and will apply these principles to writing for a scientific audience. Particular emphasis will be placed on conveying the significance of your research, outlining the aims, and discussing the results for scientific papers and grant proposals. While this is not a qualifying exam preparatory course, applying the principles of this course will help improve your scientific writing in your exam and beyond. Most class time will be spent discussing student scientific writing. The goal of the course is to encourage active and open interaction among students. Note that, in order to focus on the techniques of scientific writing, in-class discussion and critiques will not address scientific methodology or interpretations of results.

courses.title: Laboratory Rotations
courses.desc: 8-10 week laboratory rotations for first-year students are designed to provide experience with experimental design and theoretical aspects of the diverse research problems under investigation in various laboratories.

courses.title: Research Presentations
courses.desc: Students present progress reports on their research for questions and constructive criticism as well as gain experience in presenting data and leading discussion.

courses.title: Graduate Seminar
courses.desc: Visiting speakers from the Boston community and beyond present their scientific research to all members of the program, including faculty, students, and post-doctoral fellows.

sections.req: Grad Seminar must be taken every term, along with Grad Research (or Rotations), Research Presentations, and Journal Club (for 4 years, 3 for MD/PhD).

courses.title: Journal Club
courses.desc: Students select articles from the current literature, analyze their significance, and present them for discussion in a seminar group.

sections.req: Journal Club must be taken every Fall & Spring for 4 years (3 for MD/PhDs), along with Grad Research (or Rotations), Grad Seminar, and Research Presentations.

courses.title: Book Arts: Chapter 1
courses.desc: Learn the basics of building a book and how the design of its structure informs a narrative. In class demonstrations will include book binding from Western and Eastern traditions. Students are encouraged to develop personal projects that explore visual narratives through the form of the book. Project assignments focus on experimentation in text and image relationships and the design of the page. Trips to the SMFA library to study from our wide collection of contemporary artist’s books will inform the students’ understanding of the place of this sculptural medium has in contemporary art and art publishing. Beginning level, open to all.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Signs & Symbols
courses.desc: The origin of language and meaning in the employment of signs, especially as these are manifested in graphic symbols and representations. Theories of signs (composed of a signifier and a signified, as defined by semiotics) in historic and contemporary settings, in both analog and digital forms. Readings and hands-on projects explore visual meaning, legibility, and the complexities of seeing.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Codex in Context: Artists Books
courses.desc: Overview of the contemporary artist’s book starting from the 1960s to today. A variety of genres of photobooks, visual literature, picture books, graphic novels, formal explorations, zines and other forms of printed ephemera by artists who are dedicated to making/designing democratic, cheap and accessible art objects is studied. Each meeting focuses on a different structural theme to help analyze books from the vast collection in the SMFA library. Students work on their own artist’s publication. One GRA course or the design and production of one book is required prior to this class.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Narrative in Sequential Art
courses.desc: Explore different structures of sequential art and examine how to create a successful narrative. Spanning comic strip art, graphic novels, children's picture books and storyboarding for film, create engaging stories in a variety of formats and mediums, with an emphasis on the personal. Analyze and exercise ways to pull emotions from a set of images. In-class workshops develop drawing skills, problem solving, editing and revising. Computer tools such as page layout and panel design will be covered, but much of the work will begin with the most analog of materials: pencil and paper, scissors and tape. Introductory level.

courses.title: Design for Social Change
courses.desc: Explore design as a catalyst for social change. Focus on marrying design to activism and examine established methodologies for developing and fostering a successful call to action. Create and disseminate engaging and beautiful messages and materials in service of promoting an idea or product. Design and implement a campaign; final deliverable forms will vary but may include posters, websites, or public art installations. Through lectures, in-class activities, and critiques, examine the role design and designers play in social activism, as well as strategies for research, ideation, prototyping, and testing design solutions. Class demos will cover Photoshop and Illustrator. Introductory level.

courses.desc: For artists from various disciplines who use text in their work and want to learn about typography as a mark making tool. Slide lectures and project assignments will ask students to work with self-generated expressive text. Project assignments will provide a structure for each student’s interest toward typography and text based artwork including narrative, architectural, performative and three-dimensional type. The computer will be our primary tool but not the only one. Bring your calligraphy, photography and drawing skills along. We will use Adobe CC as our main software applications. courses.title: Graphic Novel: History & Craft
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 135) Examine graphic novels in light of the cultural impact of the form--from seminal texts like Art Spiegelman’s ‘Maus’ through a range of mainstream and contemporary independent examples of graphic texts, including manga and webcomics. Investigate graphic memoir forms, such as Alison Bechdel’s ‘Fun Home’, and journalistic examples, like Joe Sacco’s ‘Palestine.’ Look at abstract comics, and, in the case of Ta-Nehisi Coates's ‘Black Panther,’ the influence of comics on cinematic culture. Assignments will be based in writing and/or studio art. Assignments include weekly prompts, in-class critical discussions of readings, completion of two multi-panel comics, and short presentation. Intermediate level.

courses.title: Web Art: Culture & Practice
courses.desc: Survey internet art culture, while learning skills to create your own visual stories and experimental web-based art. Study web design practices and tools, explore the relationship between UX (user experience) and storytelling. Combine vector forms, typography, animation, and simple interactions to create browser-based artworks for desktop and mobile screens, with the power to engage, inspire, entertain, subvert, and inform. Projects are inspired by Net Art, Post-Internet Art, and Interactive Documentary. This course will utilize the web builder platform Cargo, Visual Studio Code and some coding, though no prior experience is necessary. A basic understanding of Adobe CC is helpful.

courses.title: Artist Books: Idea to Object
courses.desc:
Mixed media class explores handmade artists’ books as visual poetry, narrative, document, conceptual space, memoir and museum. Binding and image-making demonstrations, workshops and assigned problems expand students’ awareness of artists’ books as contemporary vehicles for content and hands-on innovation. Explores the history/culture of artists’ books (ancient codex, medieval illuminated manuscripts, chap books, altered books); draws upon global traditions (Asian, Middle Eastern, Western). Hands-on technical instruction, presentations, visiting artists, readings and critiques. Previous bookmaking experience is not necessary but encouraged.
Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

Develop your style in word and image as you learn to blend these storytelling forms into the singular craft that is the Picture Book. Practice techniques in rhythm and pacing in fun group exercises to engage and delight the reader. Study the masters of the form as we explore the wide range of artistic mediums used in professional picture books today. Learn the ins and outs of the children’s book industry from pitching to printing and everything in between as you create one-of-a-kind books for varied audiences ranging from baby board books, classic children’s books, and early reader story books.

courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

Create story-based web art known as “interactive documentary”—documentary stories in the form of interactive web experiences. Explore non-linear storytelling, the relationship between story and user experience (UX), as well as concepts of community-driven co-creation. Formats and tools addressed include SCROLLYtelling, GSAP (GreenSock JS animation), and WebGL (3D in the browser). Designers, researchers, photographers, and filmmakers are invited to reimagine their work in this format. Readings will look at MIT's Open Documentary Lab, Katerina Cizek, the National Film Board of Canada, and more. An understanding of basic coding is recommended, as well as familiarity with Adobe CC or similar tools.

courses.title: Special Topics - Vibrant Matter: Visualizing Curatorial Idea
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

This class is co-located with VMS 193-06.

This course offers students insights into intertwined curatorial and exhibition design strategies related to the representation, interpretation, and conceptual imaging of world cultures and identity groups. We will focus on understanding curatorial work and examining exhibitions contemporaneously on display. Close looking through museum visits and critical thinking exercises will engage students with the materiality of created environments, to explore the complex entanglements of art objects within architecture and designed spaces. This process will teach students to contextualize displays by examining their relations to the history of art and art exhibitions, as well as to the history of collecting. Half the class will focus on academic work, the other half will focus on the studio practice of Exhibition Design to design spaces for selected art objects. 

Strong exhibitions are developed through inclusive processes that incorporate multiple voices and thoughtful scholarship translated into nuanced design elements. This requires pedagogical skill, awareness of art historical contexts and contemporary art dialogue, as well as an open mind to explore diverse points of view in creative ways. Cultural literacy and technical skills are called upon to develop relevant solutions to complex presentations of art and history to present objects in context. 

Students will work in teams to design their own exhibitions based on selected curatorial content. Final projects will be presented for discussion and evaluation. Creative Suite technical skills will be integrated into coursework to provide students with relevant tools for future professional preparation.

courses.title: Special Topics - Type in Motion
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

This course explores dynamic text methods, where the animated, interactive, and visual qualities of text design are highlighted. Through software and code, students will consider narrative and experimental approaches to working with kinetic and responsive text. The course will also review traditional text design and discuss what it means to adapt this practice, along with its established guidelines, within Extended Reality (XR) and to question what new rules might need to be explored in order to adapt text design for Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR). Relevant works, artists, and technologies will be explored through readings, lectures, and demos.

courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

Course examines branding as a cultural practice, focusing on nation branding, collective identity, and public image. Studio projects progress from defining voice through branding conflict, developing systems through logo design, challenging consistency through branding “illness,” to resolving conflicts through alternative brand guidelines. Explores culture jamming, “subvertising,” and speculative design. Emphasizes independent research, critical analysis, and experimentation with complex visual systems.

courses.title: Art of Empire: Assyria and Babylonia
courses.desc: Imperial arts of the Assyrian and Babylonian empires in the broader social and political contexts of the first millennium BCE. Topics may include: influence of Phoenician, Egyptian, and Greek cultures on imperial art; systems of cuneiform knowledge production; literary and mythological works; localized traditions that may have represented forms of anti-imperialist resistance; and major monuments and architecture of Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian Empires. Readings based on approaches from art history and archaeology, as well as critical engagement with scholarship on Assyrian and Babylonian art. Discussions and assignments focus on interpretative approaches and analyzing the works of art within their ancient socio-historical context.

courses.title: Classical Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 27, CLS 27, and ILVS 27.) Survey of ancient Greco-Roman civilization spanning c. 3,100 BCE to 565 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: sculpture, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, sociopolitical organization, and artistic technique. Examination of the development and collapse of the Bronze Age civilizations of the Aegean and Italy. Exploration of the evidence of cultural transformations driven by trade, colonization, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the city-state in archaic Greece and Italy, then to the Greek-speaking kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, and finally to the inclusion of the Latins, Etruscans, Greeks, Egyptians, and others within a single multicultural state: the Roman Empire. Assessment of the renegotiation of identities and historical narratives as polytheistic religions were supplanted by Christianity within the Roman state. Field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Renaissance Venice
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ HAA 134) Painting, sculpture, and architecture in the "most serene republic" of Venice, 1400-1600. Elite patrons, confraternal piety, wealth from the Levant, and a taste for pleasure provide some framing contexts for Venetian subject matter ranging from altarpieces to sensuous female nudes. Artists to be considered include Bellini, Giorgione, Titian, Sansovino, Palladio, and Tintoretto. (May be taken at 100 level with consent; see below.)

sections.note: No additional costs.

courses.title: Film and the Avant-Garde
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 187 & HAA 159 & FMS 58 & FMS 185 & VMS 185 & VMS 58 & ILVS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. Avant-garde filmmakers beginning in the 1920s, such as Fernand Leger and Marcel Duchamp, as well as filmmakers from cross-media movements such as Dada and Surrealism. Postwar artists in the United States who reworked prewar avant-garde film genres and pioneered new ones, including lyrical and collage film. Structural film of the 1960s and the pluralism of avant-garde film since the 1970s. Historical conditions and theories that shaped these developments, and the use of avant-garde film by feminists and other artists for socio-political critique. Lower level version of HAA 0159.

sections.note: Students may choose lower level section (HAA 49) or upper level section (HAA 159). The upper level includes an additional research project. Weekly recitation/screening is required.

courses.title: Aesthetics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as VMS 53 & PHIL 52) A survey of some fundamental problems in the philosophy of art: the nature of aesthetic judgment; the task of criticism, formalism, and formalist criticism; the idea of antiart; the concept of quality in a work of art; modernist vs. traditional art. The course will include writings in contemporary philosophy and criticism as well as works by philosophers such as Hume, Kant, Nietzsche, and Heidegger.

courses.title: Modernisms
courses.desc: Broad study of the histories and meanings of modern art from circa 1850 to 1950 with special attention to social and cultural shifts and related developments in form, technique, and media. Themes include art and political upheaval; the avant-gardes; craft and colonialism; primitivism and futurism; the representation of history, landscape, and the figure; non-objectivity, collage, and the readymade.

courses.desc: An in-depth understanding of how curators conceive, research, organize, and stage art exhibitions. Topics include explorations of the differences between a special exhibition and the installation of works from the permanent collection; how museums organize traveling exhibitions, single-artist exhibitions, and group shows; how curators work with living artists and artist-curators; curatorial choices in different kinds of museum spaces. courses.title: Collections Care And Preventive Conservation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 291) The chemical and physical nature of material culture, agents of deterioration, preventive conservation strategies and protocol, proper care and handling of artifacts, and the appropriate cleaning and maintenance of museum art objects and historic artifacts. Students learn to survey a collection, establish a basic Integrated Pest Management program, prepare ofr and respond to an emergency, execute a condition request, construct an artifact preservation plan, and establish safe exhibition and storage techniques. Trips to museums and conservation laboratories, and hands-on opportunities to learn about tools and equipment essential for documenting artifacts and monitoring the museum environment. Prerequisite: ED/HAA/HIST 285

courses.desc:
Learning the fundamental structures of Hebrew and its basic forms, as well as the necessary vocabulary for everyday conversations, reading and writing on a limited scale.

courses.desc:
Rapid oral review of structural principles. Written exercises. Reading and discussion based on selected materials from Hebrew literature. Conducted mainly in Hebrew. 
Recommendations: HEB 3 or equivalent.

courses.title: Conversation/composition
courses.desc:
Reading and discussing adapted literary and scientific works as well as articles from the press. Becoming familiar with synonyms as well as expressions and idioms. Exposure to the Hebrew currently used in pop culture and everyday conversation. Focusing on the different verbal structures including exceptions to the rules, and becoming familiar with various syntactical structures.

courses.title: Gender in Rabbinic Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as REL 88 and JS 88) Overview of the ways in which gender is used as an analytical tool in the study of rabbinic literature. Examines how rabbinic sources challenge the traditional understanding of the gender binary. Contrasts traditional historical questions about the roles of men and women in society with more contemporary approaches that view gender as socially constructed, contested, and fluid. In English. No prerequisites. No knowledge of Judaism or rabbinic literature is assumed. If taken at the 100-level: Extra assignments and class meetings in Hebrew.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as REL 184 & JS 180) Broad overview of the Zohar, the 13th-century foundational text of Kabbalah with roots in mysticism. courses.title: Empires and Nations
courses.desc: Empires and nations in world history. Forms of empires, the relationship between empires and nations, historical contextualization of the recent emergence of nation states. Strategies of rule in empires and nations, imperial and national ideologies; exploration of sovereignty, autonomy, and minority perspectives within empires and nations.

courses.title: Africa since 1800
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ AFR 14) Survey of African history from the early nineteenth century to the present. Themes may include religion and state formation, abolition of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, development of “legitimate commerce,” European colonization of Africa, Africa and the world wars, African nationalism and independence, decolonization and the Cold War, social and economic developments, regional conflicts and cooperation, sports, music, and culture.

courses.title: Global History of Christianity since the Middle Ages
courses.desc: (Cross listed w/ CST 37 and REL 64) Development of Christianity as a world movement from the early modern period to the present. Major themes include Protestant Reformations; expansions of Christianity through exploration, trade, conquest and mission; diversity and transformations of Christian traditions in colonial and post-colonial societies; global spread of evangelicalism and pentecostalism.

courses.title: Environmental History of United States
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 21) Introduction to historical study of Americans' relationship with the natural world. Examines how natural forces shaped human history, and how humans altered their environments. Topics include climate, food systems, energy use, urbanization, warfare, environmental movements, consumerism, war, technological innovation, migration, political ideologies, and social and economic structures.

courses.title: Us Foreign Relations Since 1900
courses.desc: The rise of the United States to global preeminence over the course of the twentieth century is a fundamental element of recent international history. This transition had a profound impact on global life as well as the United States itself. This course will trace those changes.

courses.title: Civil War, Race, and Reconstruction - Race and Reconstruction
courses.desc:
Explores the Civil War and Reconstruction Era and its centrality to U.S., African-
American, and global history. Topics include race, slavery, and resistance in the causes and consequences of the war; black, white, and indigenous military participation; the transition from slavery to freedom for men, women, and children; race, labor, and global capitalism; gender, kinship, and the transformation of plantation households; representations of the era in literature, film, and popular culture.

courses.title: Modern Chinese History
courses.desc:
The history of modern China from the dynamic seventeenth-century of the Ming
Dynasty to the social backlash against market economic reforms of the 1980s. Lectures and discussions provide a big picture survey of historical chronology and important historiographical debates in Chinese history, as well as opportunities for in-depth investigation into selected materials and topics that illuminate the everyday lives of Chinese people.

courses.title: History Of Ancient Rome
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 38) The history of ancient Rome, tracing Rome's rise from an insignificant Italian community to the ruler of the Mediterranean world, and ending with the transfer of the imperial capital to Constantinople in A.D. 330. Emphasis on the interaction of Rome with various foreign peoples, and examination of literary and documentary sources. Spring.

courses.title: Eastern Europe,19th-Century to the Present
courses.desc: Survey of Eastern Europe from the 19th century through the present, with a focus on the late Habsburg and Ottoman empires and their successor states in East-Central Europe and the Balkans. Topics may include the Habsburg and Ottoman empires and their collapse, the rise of nationalism, anti-Semitism, emigration from Eastern Europe, World War I and the creation of independent countries in East-Central Europe and the Balkans, interwar fascist regimes and Czechoslovakia’s experiment with democracy, World War II and the Holocaust, postwar ethnic cleansing, life under communism, the collapse of communism, the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, the expansion of the European Union, and the recent rise of illiberal governments in the region.

courses.title: Europe Since 1815
courses.desc: The forces that shaped and characterized the history of Eastern and Western Europe from the Congress of Vienna into the contemporary era. Topics include nationalism, ethnic consciousness, the Industrial Revolution, political ideologies, the development of nation-states, Great Power diplomacy, the impact of the "Eastern Question," the disruptions of the First and Second World Wars, and the current conditions of the European states.

courses.title: Continent in Conflict, Europe 1914-2000
courses.desc: European society and politics in the turbulent twentieth century, 1914-2000. Primary source readings privilege eyewitness accounts of the world wars, fascism, Stalinism, the Holocaust, life in the communist bloc, European withdrawal from overseas empires, the revolutions of 1989, tensions over immigration and migration, emergence of the European Union.

courses.title: Great Britain And The British Empire
courses.desc: The growth of British world power after the loss of America in the late 18th century, and its domestic social, economic, and political context. War, patriotism, and the popular culture of imperialism. Decolonization, immigration, and the search for a post-imperial identity after the Second World War.

courses.title: Thinking Through Race in the French Atlantic
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FR 72) Examination of how race has been invented, contested, and reimagined across the Francophone Atlantic. Inquiry into various forms of racial thinking from its institutionalization in the eighteenth century to its alleged disappearance in the mid-twentieth century. Materials include recent scholarship as well as archival sources such as political declarations, literary texts, scientific experiments, photographs, and films. In English

courses.title: Special Topics, Europe - Jewish History: Med. to Modern
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: This course surveys the history of the Jewish people from the Late Second Temple period through the mid-twentieth century. We begin by examining the origins of rabbinic Judaism and Jewish life under Christian and Muslim rule. We then analyze the profound ruptures of the modern era, investigating the impacts of political emancipation, religious reform, and Western nationalism, culminating in the Holocaust and the establishment of the modern state of Israel. Through close analysis of primary source texts, students will understand how the modern Jewish world developed out of its pre-modern foundations.

courses.title: Special Topics - The True Believer
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information. http://ase.tufts.edu/history

sections.note:
This is going to be a very interactive, thought provoking, and hopefully enjoyable class in which we are going to read The True Believer by Eric Hoffer and Address Unknown by Kressman Taylor. We will talk about what forges mass movements and fabricated realities and think about how individuals are at times willing to subsume their personal wills into a group will/dynamic. No previous experience in history is expected. The course is 1 shu (credit) and will be very much discussion based.

The core text, The True Believer, was written in 1951 and we will discuss how that influences Hoffer's perspective as well as some of his ideas and vocabulary, some of which will seem a bit problematic. However, the core of what Hoffer argues reflects a series of ideas and perspectives that I think are still valuable and will provide you with a mode of understanding and interpretation that you will be able to apply, as an additional lens, to your work in a wide array of other classes include history, philosophy, IR, political science, economics, education, and more. Address Unknown is a work of fiction set during the 1930s and features letters between someone in the US and someone in
Germany. The text reflects many of the themes we will address the Hoffer. Work for the class will be a light reading load and then discussion board posts. My hope is to have every Thursday an interesting discussion that allows us to think about how human beings see themselves and the world around them using Hoffer to help us focus our
discussion.

courses.title: Special Topics - Life & Times of Thornton W. Burgess
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information. http://ase.tufts.edu/history

sections.note:
The year 2024 will mark 150 years since the birth of Thornton W. Burgess, conservationist and children’s
author. Through reading and discussion of his autobiography, two biographies, and of course a sampling of
the 100s of stories he crafted during his lifetime, we will learn about Burgess’s life in Sandwich and Hampden,
Massachusetts, the extraordinary characters he created to help bring nature to life for young readers, and his
lifelong mission to show us that we are all stewards of the natural world around us.

courses.title: Foundation Seminars, World/Transregional - The Great Crisis
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: Three critical eras-the Great Depression, World War II, and the start of the Cold War-constitute a hinge moment in the global history of the 20th Century. However, historians commonly treat each as separate epochs. Emphasizing new historical perspectives and methodologies this course will explore the three as one interrelated crisis. Big interlocking questions about ideology, the shape of society, the individual, and the composition of the international system were argued with means ranging from propaganda to total war. The outcomes of these disputes left the outlines of the world we live in today. By repositioning our understanding of these vital events, the course explores how different styles and methods of writing history can lead to new understandings of well-known historical events. We will also critically discuss how historical research can support different assertions on the same issue. Students will also learn the basics of historical analysis, research and writing through weekly assignments. Beyond basics of craft, a goal of the course is to expose them to the plural nature of history and historical debate.

courses.title: Foundation Seminars, North America - Gender and Containment in Post WW II America
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Gender and Containment in Post-WWII America is rooted in the era from the mid-1940s through the early 1960s
when there was deep concern about containing the spread of Communism and the threat of nuclear War. This course
will take a different tack. It will look at how concerns about containment shaped home, family, and gender roles. It
will look at a range of topics, including: the crisis of masculinity; the feminine mystique; race, gender and the
American Dream, and girlhood in the 1950s. Readings will include historians’ analyses of family and coming of age
in the 1950s; memoirs that give us the voices of women who grew up in the 1950s; and works of fiction that reached
a 1950s popular audience. The class will also go to the Tufts archives to look at student newspapers, yearbooks, and
other documents to examine the ways that Tufts students navigated this era of containment.

courses.title: Foundation Seminars, Europe - Imperial Britain
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: “The Lost Generation.” “The Long Weekend.” “The Roaring Twenties.” “The Hungry Thirties.” “The Age of Appeasement.” Britain between the end of the First World War and the beginning of the Second wears many historical hats with little consensus about their broader meaning and how they fit together. This foundation seminar will embrace these interpretive disagreements in order to answer one of the most important questions of the twentieth century: in a period of intense political, economic, social, cultural, and technological change, was this the era when Britain and its Empire truly became “modern”? Topics to be examined in this seminar will include: anti-colonial and independence movements in Ireland, India, and beyond; the impact of mass democracy on gender and class politics; the foundation of the BBC and the birth of mass culture; the Great Depression and the roots of deindustrialization; race-thinking, Social Darwinism and British fascism; rearmament and the Munich Crisis; and the rise of Winston Churchill. Students will analyze a variety of primary sources, including political speeches and manifestos, government reports, public opinion polling, cultural and social criticism, newsreels, ethnographic research, life-writing, and letters. We will also read recent scholarship from established and emerging historians of the period.

courses.title: Modern East Africa
courses.desc: Seminar on East African history from the early nineteenth century to the close of the twentieth century, encompassing the three modern states of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Themes may include racial and ethnic formation, state and class formation, slavery and resistance, colonialism and resistance, nationalism, citizenship, gender, religion, trade, war, democratization, and regional integration.

courses.title: Industrial America And Urban Society: The Progressive Era To The Great Depression - Progress Era to the Great Depression
courses.desc: The nation's transformation: industrial and urban growth after Reconstruction, public debate over the country's destiny, responses to inequality, social change, mass culture, and the politics of reform and renewal.

courses.title: Evangelicalism in America
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CVS 130, AMER 121 and REL 121) History of evangelical Christianity in North America from the 17th century to the present. Attention to issues of theology, race, class, gender, culture, politics and globalization. Consideration of relationships among evangelicalism, fundamentalism and pentecostalism. 
Recommended: One lower level course in the history of Christianity (REL 12 or 63) or one lower level course in American religious history (REL 42, 47, 48, 49), OR permission of the instructor

courses.title: Women and Gender in East Asian Tradition
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/WGSS 141) How women made history and how history made women. An international and comparative study of women and gender in traditional Chinese, Japanese, and Korean societies from the seventh to the nineteenth centuries. Women’s multiple roles in political, economic, legal, social, intellectual, and literary history.

courses.title: Contemporary South Asia
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ DHP P262) Organized along both historical and thematic lines, the course surveys politics, economy, and society in late colonial India and offers a comparative historical analysis of state structures and political processes in post-colonial South Asia, particularly India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Among the themes considered are the reasons for the partition of 1947, the nature of the colonial legacy, the origins of democracy and military authoritarianism, history of development, the shifting balance between central and regional power, the ongoing clash between so-called secular and religiously informed ideologies, and the impact on interstate relations in the subcontinent.

courses.title: Greeks And Barbarians
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CLS 143). Exploration of the unsettling and stimulating cross-cultural encounters of Greeks with other peoples of the ancient world, leading both to the Greeks' discovery of themselves-the formulation of a Greek "cultural identity"-and to expanding knowledge of the wider world. Attention to contacts and conflicts with Cretans, Trojans, Phoenicians, Egyptians, and Romans, with emphasis on the seminal, two-century-long, encounter of the Greek city-states with the mighty Persian Empire. Sources include the accounts of Greek poets, historians, explorers, and playwrights, documents from the Persian Empire, and images of ancient artifacts and sites such as Athens, Persepolis, and Alexandria.
Recommendations: CLS 31 or 37.

courses.title: Passion, Power, & Piety: The Voices of Byzantium
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CLS 109) Evolution of Byzantine history and literature through the voices of the Byzantines themselves, in their histories, novels, hagiographies, the great heroic epic Digenes Akrites (the Two-Blood Border Lord), the amusing if somewhat ribald Amazing Tale of Quadrupeds, and others, from the 4th century AD to the end of the empire. How Byzantine literature draws from Greek, Roman, Christian, Near Eastern, Islamic, and Judaic influences to construct a new identity, a world view neither "Eastern" nor "Western" but rather a complex fusion.

courses.title: Empresses, Saints, & Scholars: The Women Of Byzantium - Empresses Saints & Scholars:
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 110). Examination of the themes of political legitimacy, spirituality, education, gender roles, the spread of Byzantine culture, and the evolution of Christian theology through a careful study of the lives of various women of the Byzantine world. This will include examination of the lives of women of the Byzantine Empire, Southeastern Europe, Russia, Western Europe, the kingdoms of Armenia and the Ottoman Empire.

courses.title: Ethnicity and Religion in 19th and 20th C. Russia
courses.desc: Seminar examining ethnic and religious diversity in the Russian Empire and Soviet Union. Explores state policies for managing diversity and creating cohesive forms of Russian/Soviet identity, as well as the experiences of non-Russian minorities, including Ukrainians, Jews, Muslims, Georgians, and Chechens. Topics include the expansion of the Russian empire; Russification in the late Tsarist period; nationalist movements during the revolutions of 1917; Soviet anti-religious campaigns and religious life in the USSR; Soviet nationalities policies; late Imperial and Soviet conceptions of race; and the rise of nationalist movements in the late Soviet period and their role in the collapse of the USSR.

courses.title: Modern European Intellectual History - Modern Eur.intellectual
courses.desc: An intellectual history of modern Europe from the mid-nineteenth to the early twenty-first centuries as framed within the competing and complementary legacies of the enlightenment and romantic movements. Investigates the histories of socialism, psychoanalytic theory, nationalism and internationalism, pacifism, futurism and fascism, feminism, existentialism, and decolonization. Ends with ecocriticism and questions about ethics and ideas in the European Union. Readings will include Marx, Kollontai, Freud, Tolstoy, Benjamin, Beauvoir, Fanon, and others.

courses.title: Advanced Special Topics, North America - Black Power / Red Power
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note: Class Description: Heeding recent scholars' calls to place Black Studies and Native American and Indigenous Studies in more active dialogue with each other, this seminar examines the Black Power and Red Power movements. Students will engage both primary and secondary sources and attend to the ways in which these movements rejected the possibility of Black and Indigenous incorporation into the American polity and instead called for self-determination and political autonomy. Rather than limiting our consideration of Black Power and Red Power to the late 1960s and 1970s, we will take a “long movement” approach to thinking about these movements. Broad topics covered will include sovereignty and self-determination, and and community control, revolutionary violence and self-defense, gender and sexuality, and solidarity.

courses.title: Advanced Special Topics, Europe - Napoleon & Napoleonic World
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: Napoleon was born in Corsica the year it was annexed to France and died, in exile, on the remote British island of Saint Helena. In between, he won decisive victories for the Revolutionary army and ended the French Revolution; revolutionized much of European legal, political and social life and tried to create a new European dynasty; re-imposed slavery in the French Empire and triggered the most brutal phase of the Haitian Revolution; devastated Europe through unprecedented warfare; removed several long-standing restrictions on religion; accelerated the break-up of the Spanish Empire; ended his career in defeat and influenced aspiring empire-builders for many years after his death. None of this was done alone, and so the focus of the course will be on the Napoleonic world, broadly construed.

courses.title: Introduction to Geospatial Humanities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 175, CLS 125, and UEP 103) Geographic Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods, and technology for applications in the humanities in past and present settings. Topics include GIS data creation and data structures, geodesy, spatial analysis, and cartographic visualization. Includes extensive laboratory exercises to apply concepts presented in the lectures using a variety of GIS software and tools. Assignments concentrate on application of concepts covered in lectures and exercises and include a final project that applies GIS to each student’s field of interest.

courses.title: Independent Study, World/transregional - The Gill Fellows
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: The Gerald Gill Fellowship supports engaged scholarship on questions of race and democracy, broadly defined. The Gerald Gill Fellows serve as ambassadors of engaged scholarship and active citizenship on campus. In 2023-24, as part of a new university initiative, the Gerald Gill Fellowship will focus on African American and Afro-Native public history and memory at Tufts. This year's Gill Fellows will support a university-wide project to examine Tufts’ relationship to the history of slavery, colonialism, and Afro-Native communities. This project will build on the foundational work of Gerald R. Gill, professor of African American history from 1980-2007; the scholarly research and public programming of the African American Trail Project; and the ongoing work of Tufts Digital Collections and Archives, in concert with local community partners.

courses.title: Research Seminar, World & Transregional History - Travel Writing and History
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This research seminar examines the literary roots of historiography. Travel accounts and their major influence in shaping historiography, from Marco Polo to colonial reports, to travelogues and journalism today. The focus is on how cross-cultural encounters and exchanges shaped historiography, revolutionary writing and political philosophy in Europe and how narrative style and description still shapes historical text. Travel descriptions of Europe, the New World, Persia, India and China and Africa, some integrated into later historical texts are used as primary sources. Sources including text, early maps, photographs, and documentary film are analyzed. Oral presentations, discussion and a research paper. Sources are analyzed for views of the "other'', views of the world, post-colonial issues of representation, Orientalist discourse, expressions of racism, sexism, imperialism, and colonialism.

courses.title: Research Seminar, Latin America - The Cold War Era in Latin Amer
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
This research seminar examines the complex and varied dialectic of revolution
and counterrevolution during the ‘Cold War’ era in Latin America. The political
temperature of Latin America in the decades from the 1950’s to the 1990’s was
hardly “cold”; rather, these were decades of ardent idealism, democratic
struggle, and revolutionary mobilization, but also of brutal military coups and
state-sponsored repression of workers, peasants, students, and journalists. A
post-WWII economic downturn and the persistence of extreme poverty form the
backdrop of these increasingly violent political struggles. Through shared
readings, discussions and independent research, students will gain both a broad
and deep perspective on this era in Latin American history. They will learn of
the role of U.S. agents and influence in this period, but more importantly, they
will come to appreciate how Latin Americans’ own economic and political
experiences and histories informed their ‘Cold War’ languages, ideologies,
affiliations, and actions. The ultimate goal of the seminar is for students to
produce an original research paper on a topic of their own choosing having to do
with this tumultuous era in Latin American history. The class as a group will
work together through feedback, encouragement, structured deadlines and peer
review.

courses.title: Research Seminar, North America - Early Amer & The Atlantic Worl
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
This research seminar examines early America in the broadest possible sense. Though Britain's American colonies are at its
core, our readings, discussions, and research projects will consider them in the context of the Atlantic World, Native America,
and French, Spanish, and Dutch colonization; the chronology will range from the sixteenth to the early nineteenth centuries.
Students will research and write a substantial paper, on a topic of their choosing, within these broad parameters.

courses.title: Research Seminar, North America - Family Histories & American Cu
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Explores diverse experiences of family and kinship in U.S. history, especially in the context of racial
slavery, Indian removal, and transnational migration. Contextualizes the recent groundswell in
scholarly approaches to family history, as well as the popularization of DNA testing and genealogical
research in American culture. Allows students to develop skills and perspective necessary for
the production of scholarly research based on family histories, including their own. Readings will
include family histories, micro-histories, and memoir.

courses.title: Colloquium in European History - Books, Manuscripts, Material
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: A history of books, reading, and writing in medieval and early modern Europe. Examines manuscripts and printed books as material objects and explores their social and cultural meanings. Works closely with Tisch Library Special Collections to introduce students to manuscript studies and engage with a range of manuscripts and early printed books. Covers a variety of historical approaches in the vibrant field of book history. Main topics include: manuscript culture and the history of manuscript production; religious manuscripts; illuminated manuscripts; maps; calendars; the invention of print and the spread of the book trade; the impact of print culture; the material culture of reading, writing, and print; women as scribes, authors, illuminators, printers, and readers; the globalization of printing and the book trade; and shifting approaches to studying medieval manuscripts and early printed books.

courses.title: Colloquium in Middle Eastern History - War & Society in Middle East
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
Wars do not merely destroy societies; they remake them. They create new states, new refugees, new forms of citizenship, new humanitarian institutions, and new collective memories. This seminar examines the social history of war in the modern Middle East from the First World War to the ongoing war in Gaza. Rather than approaching war through campaigns, diplomacy, or military strategy alone, it asks how wars transformed societies and how ordinary people experienced these transformations.

Drawing on history, anthropology, sociology, geography, memory studies, legal studies, and genocide studies, the seminar explores war as a social process. It examines mobilization, displacement, occupation, humanitarianism, gender, disability, veteranhood, urban destruction, reconstruction, and memory across six major conflicts: the First World War, the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, the June 1967 War, the Lebanese Civil War, the Iran-Iraq War, and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Throughout the semester, students will work with an unusually diverse range of sources, including military archives, soldiers' letters, oral histories, memoirs, humanitarian reports, photographs, films, maps, legal documents, epidemiological studies, and digital evidence. The seminar emphasizes comparative analysis, asking how similar social processes recur across different conflicts while remaining attentive to the historical specificity of each case.

Rather than treating Middle Eastern wars as exceptional, the course places them in dialogue with broader debates in the social history of war, historical sociology, and genocide studies. Students will examine both classic historiographical interventions and recent interdisciplinary scholarship while developing their own comparative research projects.

courses.title: Revolutions: Theories and Histories
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as DHP H246) Revolutions have been responsible for some of the greatest political, social, economic, and cultural changes in human history. But what is a revolution? What sort of change does it induce, and what are its causes? What leads a revolution to fail? This course explores the history and meaning of revolutions by taking a theoretical and comparative historical approach. Students will first explore different sociological theories of revolution before studying a series of case studies in order to develop their own views about how to define and understand revolutions. The course is intended to provide students a framework through which to understand revolutions, as well as to encourage them to apply these frameworks to various historical and contemporary case studies.

courses.title: Exhibition Planning
courses.desc: Practical foundation for exhibition planning. Development of core ideas, learning outcomes, and experiential aims of museum exhibitions. Exploration of the relationship between interpretation, design, and project management through ideation, text writing, diagramming, budgeting, and scheduling. Taught through case studies, site visits, and guest speakers.

courses.title: Material Culture - The Meaning of Things: Interpr
courses.desc: The interpretation of past societies and cultures through artifactual material, and the problems involved in presenting these interpretations to contemporary audiences. The course draws on modes of analysis developed in social history, archaeology, anthropology, folklore, and material culture studies, with an emphasis on New England between the precontact period and the urban industrial present. Fall.

courses.title: Collections Care And Preventive Conservation - Collect Care & Preser
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HAA 288) The chemical and physical nature of material culture, agents of deterioration, preventive conservation strategies and protocol, proper care and handling of artifacts, and the appropriate cleaning and maintenance of museum art objects and historic artifacts. Students learn to survey a collection, establish a basic Integrated Pest Management program, prepare ofr and respond to an emergency, execute a condition request, construct an artifact preservation plan, and establish safe exhibition and storage techniques. Trips to museums and conservation laboratories, and hands-on opportunities to learn about tools and equipment essential for documenting artifacts and monitoring the museum environment. Prerequisite: ED/HAA/HIST 285

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HAA 289 and ED 284.) 125-hour museum internship gives students firsthand experience in museum work. The student, in collaboration with the academic and site supervisors, arranges the internship, following the protocol described in the Museum Studies Internship Handbook. Students may not do internships where they have worked or volunteered. Prerequisites: A minimum of three Museum Studies courses, one of which must be FAH/HIST/ED0285, must be completed before beginning the internship

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 63 & ARB 63) A survey of the composition, structure, history, and importance of the Arabian Nights, the famous tales narrated by Shahrazad during 1001 nights, with selected reading of the most important tales. The dissemination of the tales and their transmission to other regions of the world including their impact on other cultures as reflected in writing, art, and film.

courses.title: Russian & East European Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 86, RUS 81, & FMS 65) Examination of a series of masterpieces by filmmakers from "the other Europe": the Soviet Union/Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and the former Yugoslav territories. Explores the role of film in terms of its artistic achievements and social commentary: As a tool in the transition to the new Soviet order; as an alternative means of expression during censorship; and, more recently, as a corrective tool in fragile new democracies and a voice of protest fighting against new forms of oppression. No prerequisites. In English.

courses.title: Special Topics - Culture Under Totalitarianism
courses.desc: Special topics in the humanities. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: After World War II and at the beginning of the Cold War, political philosopher Hannah Arendt recognized National Socialist German and Stalinist Soviet Union as totalitarian; a new form of government that was simultaneously modern and barbaric, incredibly terrifying and violent but also rationally organized and socially bureaucratic. courses.title: Public International Law
courses.desc: This course will offer an introduction to the international legal system’s principal subfields, including international dispute resolution, the law of state responsibility, the use of force and counter-terrorism, the law of war, international criminal law, human rights, and jurisdiction and immunities. Time permitting; we may also cover selected issues in arms control, international environmental law, and international economic law. We will also explore how these subfields relate to domestic law, focusing on the U.S. legal system as the primary example. Open to students who have completed L200 or equivalent.

courses.title: Freedom of Speech
courses.desc: This seminar is an introduction to freedom of speech. It is intended for students with no legal background who study in all academic disciplines and fields of study. Its aim is to familiarize students with classical as well as contemporary reasons for and against protecting speech in various settings. The debate over these issues is timeless, raising profound questions concerning moral and political philosophy, culture, history, psychology and other disciplines. These arguments have been resolved differently from one age to another and from one legal system to another, embracing national governments as well as international organizations. But the competing values transcend any legal system and are much the same in each.

courses.title: International Criminal Justice
courses.desc: Following a long fallow period after Nuremberg, the demand for accountability for mass atrocities in the 1990s and since has catalyzed the creation of a range of mechanisms of international criminal justice. This course explores the contours of international criminal law and the institutions that apply it. We will consider the scope and boundaries of the core international crimes - genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes - and the range of actors potentially liable for those violations. In so doing, we will examine the application of this body of law through international courts, such as the International Criminal Court and the UN tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia, hybrid or special courts, such as those in Sierra Leone and Cambodia, and domestic courts exercising universal jurisdiction. The course will examine the reach and limits of these bodies in confronting impunity, the tension between state sovereignty and international criminal justice, and the problem of selectivity.

courses.title: Actors in Global Governance
courses.desc: This seminar is designed to explore in a comparative mode various actors in global governance: global organizations, regional organizations, groupings of states, non-governmental organizations, private sector actors, and networks. The first part of the seminar is devoted to theoretical, institutional, and legal issues. Each student then develops and presents to the class an outline for a “Reform Report” on an institution of their choice, taking stock of its performance and offering a vision for the future. Based on feedback from the class, constituted as the ‘senior management group’ of the institution, the report is finalized and submitted as the major assignment for the course.

courses.title: Selected Issues in Law of the Sea
courses.desc: This course explores current issues implicating the Law of the Sea (and in particular the United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea and related treaties). It explores the interaction of an international legal regime with the challenges posed by geography, climate change, history, military rivalry, trade and politics, and in turn how an international legal regime can itself influence the course of national conduct, whether through negotiation, adjudication or “lawfare”. We will explore the ongoing tension between freedom of the seas and sovereign rights and regulation, in contexts ranging from current political-military rivalries and criminal conduct at sea to the exploitation and management of marine resources and preservation of the ocean environment. We will also discuss how the ambivalent attitudes of leading military and commercial powers affect the rule of law in the oceanic context. The course uses current challenges in the South China Sea and the Arctic as a vehicle for consideration of certain of these topics.

courses.title: Conflict Management Tools for International Organizations
courses.desc: Looks at peace operations both as instruments for the management of conflict, and as a lens for understanding major issues in contemporary international affairs. Combining a thematic and case study approach, we consider the law, politics and doctrine of peacekeeping. Select cases are examined to draw out recurring themes and dilemmas, such as sovereignty v. intervention, peace v. justice and the UN v. regional organizations. In addition to lectures and structured discussion, the format of the course includes student presentations and a simulation exercise.

courses.title: Sustainable Development and Global Human Rights
courses.desc: In an age of multiple crises for international law and relations and for multilateral institutions, it is essential to deepen the study of the relevance and function of international law to the shared challenges of coexistence, development and survival of human communities. This course on Sustainable Development and Global Human Rights (SD-GHR) is framed to focus attention on the role of human rights and its mechanisms globally in complementing the contemporary challenge of sustainable development. An emphasis in the course will be on illustrating how the norms and mechanisms of international human rights law and sustainable development coexist around five themes: data and digital participation; hunger; water; health and knowledge management; and reduction of violence and access to remedies.

courses.title: Global Health Law
courses.desc: Global health law is a complex field of international law that intersects with public health institutions and norms, international trade, food safety, animal welfare, armed conflict, and international security. This course introduces students to the key institutions, theory, and practices of global health law, critically examining a range of issues extending from the prevention and control of disease outbreaks, epidemics and pandemics, through to addressing harmful international trade practices, food and animal welfare standards, access to medicines, the protection of healthcare workers and facilities during armed conflict, biological weapons, and emerging technologies such as genetic sequencing. Students will also learn to critically evaluate the diversity of international legal tools and approaches from soft law instruments like guidelines and frameworks to more formalized international treaties and hard law instruments, before then participating in a mock intergovernmental negotiation at the end of the course to apply the knowledge and skills they have learned. The course has been designed to be accessible for both international law students as well as those who may not have a legal background.

courses.title: International Business Transactions
courses.desc: This course is an introduction to the law of international business transactions. It is designed to be accessible to students with diverse academic backgrounds, legal or otherwise. The course is divided into seven parts. Part 1 provides a general introduction to basic legal categories and taxonomies, such as private-public law, substantive-procedural law, and choice of law. Part 2 focuses on specific international business contracts and instruments, covering international sales contracts, letters of credit, commercial terms, and project finance. Part 3 addresses the role of the public sector in international business transactions. This involves considering the role of the State both as a contractor through State-owned enterprises or in investment contracts, and as a regulator in areas such as taxation, corruption, competition, and intellectual property. Part 4 presents regimes of international law relevant to international business, such as trade and investment law. Part 5 features corporate social responsibility as an essential ingredient of business transactions. Part 6 considers the settlement of international disputes, covering litigation, commercial arbitration, and investment arbitration. Finally, Part 7 relates to the enforcement of judgments and arbitral awards related to international business transactions. Class discussions will include examples from both global-north and global-south jurisdictions.

courses.title: International Arbitration
courses.desc: International arbitration is one of the most widely used mechanisms of dispute resolution across legal systems, industries, and geographical regions. This module provides an introduction to international arbitration, from the formation of the arbitration agreement to the enforcement of arbitral awards. The focus of the module lies in international commercial arbitration. The module begins with a general description of the legal frameworks applicable to international arbitral proceedings. It then addresses three key moments in an arbitration. The first moment is the period preceding the arbitral proceedings. This part of the module highlights the design of the arbitration agreement, considering its elements and validity requirements. It also conveys drafting techniques for effective arbitration clauses. The second part of the module covers the conduct of the arbitral proceedings. It provides an overview of the main stages of an arbitration, from the constitution of the arbitral tribunal through the production of an arbitral award. In this context, students will engage with a broad range of topics, including the ethical duties of arbitrators, transparency, the taking of evidence, and interim measures of protection. The third moment is the period that follows the end of the arbitral proceedings. Students will learn about the annulment, recognition, and enforcement of arbitral awards, with examples from a myriad of jurisdictions from both the global north and the global south. The final session of the module provides a general overview of the use of arbitration in the settlement of disputes between foreign investors and States. Students will recognize the peculiarities of investor-State arbitration and how it differs from international commercial arbitration.

courses.title: International Financial and Fiscal Law
courses.desc: This course is intended to introduce students to the legal and regulatory context of international finance. It covers selected domestic and international aspects of (i) corporate law relating to finance, (ii) bank financing and regulation, (iii) securities financing and market regulation and (iv) insolvency law. It also addresses the process of innovation in international financial law, with coverage of emerging market debt, swaps and other derivatives, privatizations, and securitization. These topics will be reviewed from the standpoint of domestic law of the United States and other selected jurisdictions, as well as from the standpoint of applicable international law and practice.

courses.title: Law and Development
courses.desc: This seminar examines the role of law and legal systems in the economic and social development of developing nations, emerging markets, and countries in transition. It explores how law may both inhibit and foster change and the ways that legal institutions may be organized to achieve national goals. It first considers the nature of law, the nature of development, and the theoretical relationships of law to the development process. It then explores the links between law and development through case studies on land tenure, foreign investment, environment, governance, constitutionalism, corruption, judicial reform, enterprise organization, and the rule of law.

courses.title: International Law and the Middle East Conflict
courses.desc: The Middle East conflict (encompassing Israel-Palestine and related regional conflicts) is among the most contested subjects in contemporary international law and international relations. The conflict has raised competing legal claims relating to territory, colonization, self-determination, use of force, humanitarian law, security, occupation, apartheid, genocide, and human rights. This course will engage in legal analysis of these claims, focusing on identifying relevant legal rules, understanding interpretative arguments regarding the meaning of those rules, and evaluating the application of those legal rules to salient facts.

courses.title: Classical Archaeology - Civilizations of Mediterranean
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 27, HAA 19, and CLS 27). Survey of ancient Greco-Roman civilization spanning c. 3,100 BCE to 565 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: sculpture, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, sociopolitical organization, and artistic technique. Examination of the development and collapse of the Bronze Age civilizations of the Aegean and Italy. Exploration of the evidence of cultural transformations driven by trade, colonization, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the city-state in archaic Greece and Italy, then to the Greek-speaking kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, and finally to the inclusion of the Latins, Etruscans, Greeks, Egyptians, and others within a single multicultural state: the Roman Empire. Assessment of the renegotiation of identities and historical narratives as polytheistic religions were supplanted by Christianity within the Roman state. Field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Ancient China, Korea, & Japan
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 28 & ARCH 28) Survey of the ancient cultures of China, Korea, and Japan from g . 2,100 BCE to 907 CE. Archaeological analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: social rituals, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Excursions into sociopolitical organization, religion, diplomacy, philosophy, writing systems, and artistic technique. Evidence of cultural transformations and renegotiations of identity driven by trade, colonization, diplomacy, and territorial expansion leading first to the development of the state in ancient China, and finally to the evolution of a world system that interconnected the kingdoms and peoples of East Asia, as well as the many cultures linked by the Silk Routes: from the Yangshao culture to the Shang state, the first unification of China under the Qin emperor, to the Han and Tang periods, Gojoseon, Goguryeo, then the Jomon, Yayoi, and Kofun period Japan. Includes a field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.title: Dance on Camera
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/FMS 27 & DNC 177 & DNC 77 ) Inter-disciplinary course designed for any dancer, artist or student interested in film & video production with dance or movement as a medium. Participants will take dance and movement concepts outside of studio walls and into the community through site-specific collaborative video projects. Through storyboarding, shooting, editing, and choreographing/directing, students will learn basic video production techniques and advanced camera work in this hands-on course. Development of movement ideas as well as non-linear editing skills will be explored. Work culminates in end of semester public screening and online video sharing. Open to all. No dance or film/video experience necessary.

courses.title: Art of the Moving Image - Sophomore and Junior
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 1 & TPS 20) Exploration of cinema's basic aesthetic characteristics: its stylistic features, such as editing, cinematography, and sound, as well as its major narrative and non-narrative forms: mainstream and avant-garde, fiction and non-fiction, narrative and non-narrative, black-and-white and color, silent and sound. Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

sections.note: Twice weekly recitation/screening is required. This section is for sophomores and juniors; all others with instructor permission.
