courses.title: Film and the Avant-Garde
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 58, ILVS 187, HAA 159, FMS 185, HAA 49, VMS 185 and VMS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. Avant-garde filmmakers beginning in the 1920s, such as Fernand Leger and Marcel Duchamp, as well as filmmakers from cross-media movements such as Dada and Surrealism. Postwar artists in the United States who reworked prewar avant-garde film genres and pioneered new ones, including lyrical and collage film. Structural film of the 1960s and the pluralism of avant-garde film since the 1970s. Historical conditions and theories that shaped these developments, and the use of avant-garde film by feminists and other artists for socio-political critique. Lower level version of ILVS 0187.

sections.note: Students may choose lower level section (ILVS 58) or upper level section (ILVS 187). The upper level includes an additional research project. Weekly recitation/screening is required.
Weekly recitation/screening is required.

courses.title: Arabian Nights
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARB 63 & ILCS 68) A survey of the composition, structure, history, and importance of the Arabian Nights, the famous tales narrated by Shahrazad during 1001 nights, with selected reading of the most important tales. The dissemination of the tales and their transmission to other regions of the world including their impact on other cultures as reflected in writing, art, and film.

courses.title: Russian & East European Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILCS 81, RUS 81, & FMS 65) Examination of a series of masterpieces by filmmakers from "the other Europe": the Soviet Union/Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and the former Yugoslav territories. Explores the role of film in terms of its artistic achievements and social commentary: As a tool in the transition to the new Soviet order; as an alternative means of expression during censorship; and, more recently, as a corrective tool in fragile new democracies and a voice of protest fighting against new forms of oppression. No prerequisites. In English.

courses.title: Special Topics - Asian American Poetry
courses.desc: Please see Departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: Class Description: Poetry in English has been written by Asian Americans for a century and a half in this country, even if the term ”Asian American” itself dates from the late 1960s. This course will be a broad survey of various styles of Asian American poetry in English from the late nineteenth century to the present, with an emphasis on more “experimental” writing in recent decades. Students will learn how to close-read poems but always with an eye to the broader political, historical, and social contexts of the writing, which are themselves reflected in the poetry’s aesthetics. No prior knowledge of poetry required.

courses.title: Visualizing Colonialism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 117, ILCS 175 and CST 10). An overview of the intersection between visual culture and the conditions of colonialism and postcoloniality. Readings and viewings on representations of the non-Western world in colonial-era painting and photography, leading to an examination of the history of colonial cinema, and to later postcolonial visualizations of the colonial period. The development of cinemas of anti colonial resistance, and persisting effects of colonialism and empire in contemporary global visual cultures, including contemporary arts and new media. Materials drawn from a variety of regional contexts, with special emphasis on the Arab world. Secondary readings drawn from anti-colonial theorists and postcolonial studies. In English.

courses.title: Haruki Murakami and World Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JPN 118). Comparative study of Haruki Murakami’s literature in the context of World Literature. How some Western writers’ works have shaped Murakami’s work. How literature travels the globe, breaking national boundaries. The writers to be examined may include, besides Murakami, Kurt Vonnegut, Raymond Chandler, Raymond Carver, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Franz Kafka, Gabriel Garcia Marquez, and Dostoevsky. Freud, Girard, Karatani, Nietzsche, Damrosch, and others, provide theoretical insights. Taught in English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: The Sublime: Nature, Art, Film, Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ENG 120) The sublime as an aesthetic category; the relationship between literature and other kinds of art (painting and film, especially); aesthetic responses to nature and art.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Graphic Novel: History & Craft
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as GRA 135) Examine graphic novels in light of the cultural impact of the form--from seminal texts like Art Spiegelman’s ‘Maus’ through a range of mainstream and contemporary independent examples of graphic texts, including manga and webcomics. Investigate graphic memoir forms, such as Alison Bechdel’s ‘Fun Home’, and journalistic examples, like Joe Sacco’s ‘Palestine.’ Look at abstract comics, and, in the case of Ta-Nehisi Coates's ‘Black Panther,’ the influence of comics on cinematic culture. Assignments will be based in writing and/or studio art. Assignments include weekly prompts, in-class critical discussions of readings, completion of two multi-panel comics, and short presentation. Intermediate level.

courses.title: Who Owns the Past? Art, Heritage, and Global Conflicts
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HAA 164 and CVS 119) Cultural heritage as a subject of identity and ownership. History of museum collections and preservation programs in the context of nationalism and colonialism and the aftermath of these developments on the basis of selected case studies from different parts of the world. From heritage and the process of nation-building to the debate on heritage in the Anthropocene era.

sections.note: No additional costs.

courses.title: Psychoanalysis And Cultural Criticism
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ ENG 180) Advanced seminar in the relation between Lacanian psychoanalytic theory and contemporary literary and cultural analysis. Focus on various essays from Lacan's Écrits and several of his seminars, with additional readings in literary theory selected from the works of authors including Jane Gallop, Slavoj ¿i¿ek, Judith Butler, Alenka Zupancic, Diana Fuss, Leo Bersani, and Joan Copjec.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 REQUIRED or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement. Recommended that the student already have taken either ENG 20,21,22, or 23.

courses.title: Mapping Constellations of Italian Culture
courses.desc: Explorations of Italian culture from the Middle Ages to the Enlightenment through literature, art, and historical perspectives. Topics may include identity, nature, satire, and cultural responses to scientific and social change. Engage with diverse media and ideas, developing critical thinking and communication skills. Interdisciplinary approach highlights the connections between cultural works and societal shifts, offering insights into how they shaped Italy’s evolving identity. In Italian. Prerequisite: ITAL 21, ITAL 22, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Dante’s Purgatorio & Paradiso
courses.desc: An intensive study of Dante's Purgatorio and Paradiso, read in English translation with facing Italian text. No prerequisites.

sections.note:
Reading in prose translation (with facing Italian text), we shall follow Dante's journey up the mountain of Purgatory and then through Heaven's spheres. Hope is the guiding force within the Purgatorio; the Paradiso strives to depict a realm that lies beyond the reach of human words. Occasional outside readings, as assigned. Class discussions; three low-stakes quizzes; one take-home essay. Counts toward the Major in Italian Studies, the Minor in Italian, the Italian Culture Option, the International Relations Major, and the Interdisciplinary Minor in Medieval Studies; satisfies the Related Field requirement for French majors, and the Humanities or the Social Science requirement for Engineers. No prerequisites. (N.B.: No prior course on Inferno required.) Conducted in English.

The role of fashion in shaping personal and collective identities, with attention to beauty standards, body politics, and gender expression. Traditional Italian textile and garment production and contemporary fashion systems, with particular attention to environmental sustainability, labor equity, social justice, wellness, and self-representation. Course materials may include visual media, fashion journalism, documentaries, exhibition catalogs, and scholarly sources. In English. No prerequisites.

Discovery of a multidimensional picture of the unique socio-cultural environment that shaped the identity of the modern-day Russian-speaking Jews from the former Soviet Union through literary works, visual media, popular songs, works of art, and theater performances, translated into English from Russian and Yiddish. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Gender in Rabbinic Literature

Examines how rabbinic sources challenge the traditional understanding of the gender binary. Contrasts traditional historical questions about the roles of men and women in society with more contemporary approaches that view gender as socially constructed, contested, and fluid. In English. No prerequisites. No knowledge of Judaism or rabbinic literature is assumed. If taken at the 100-level: Extra assignments and class meetings in Hebrew.

courses.title: Special Topics - Jewish History: Med. to Modern
courses.desc: Courses on selected themes and authors in Hebrew literature and in Jewish literature translated from various languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Yiddish, Spanyol, German, Russian), including both classical and modern authors; and on selected subjects, such as Ladino language and culture and Israeli film. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course surveys the history of the Jewish people from the Late Second Temple period through the mid-twentieth century. We begin by examining the origins of rabbinic Judaism and Jewish life under Christian and Muslim rule. We then analyze the profound ruptures of the modern era, investigating the impacts of political emancipation, religious reform, and Western nationalism, culminating in the Holocaust and the establishment of the modern state of Israel. Through close analysis of primary source texts, students will understand how the modern Jewish world developed out of its pre-modern foundations.

courses.title: Directed Study - Convivencia vs. Reconquista
courses.desc: Guided independent study of an approved topic. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: What was the relationship like between Jews, Christians, and Muslims in medieval Spain? For nearly a century, in the wake of the debate between Américo Castro and Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz over the nature of Spanish identity, scholars have been torn between the concepts of convivencia and reconquista. Is Spanish identity the product of the mixing of Jews, Christians, and Muslims or does it predate the Arab invasion of 711, retaining an essentially Visigothic character? Students will read in translation excerpts of each scholar’s seminal work – España en su historia and España: un enigma histórico – and contemporary scholarship on Jewish-Christian-Muslim relations in medieval Spain.

courses.title: Special Topics - Judaic Studies - International Law & Israel-Hamas War
courses.desc: For advanced and graduate students.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course explores the international legal arena surrounding the Israeli case more broadly and the Israel-Hamas War in particular. The first section begins with a broad introduction to the Israeli-Palestinian arena, setting the stage that led to the Israel-Hamas War. This section includes a discussion of concepts and definitions used in the course. The second section focuses on the international legal system. Beginning with the first codifying of legal principles for modern warfare at the end of the 19th century, it takes us through the establishment of the United Nations, the Geneva Conventions, and the legal definitions of concepts like war crimes, terrorism, crimes against humanity, and genocide. The third section focuses on the evolution of the war between Israel and Hamas since October of 2023. Each week covers a different facet of the war and its relation to international law, including the October 7th attack, Israeli attacks in Gaza, humanitarian aid in Gaza, regional spirals of violence, the international court system, and the legal aspects of proposed day-after plans. By the end of the course, students will have a clear understanding of which questions should be asked with regards to each development in the war, granting them tools to analyze these developments.

courses.title: Special Topics - Judaic Studies - Protest & Mobilization Israel
courses.desc: For advanced and graduate students.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
This course applies a social movement perspective and analysis of collective action to the Israeli social and political scene. The aim is to examine the diverse movements that have shaped the country’s social, religious, and ethnic conflicts, situating these in a comparative setting and examining which are unique to the Israeli experience and which are more common cross-nationally. 
The course is divided into three parts: part one, Introduction to Social Movements and Contentious Politics, provides an overview of the theoretical foundations of social movement theory. Part two, Israel: A Movement Society, explores the development of a range of movements which have shaped Israeli society since the pre-state era. Part three, Between War and Peace, focuses on the different types of mobilization that have developed around the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Throughout the course students will be challenged to consider the shared patterns of mobilization reflected across cases, the connections between the development of Israeli social movements past and present, and the cumulative impact of the emergence of these movements on the shape of Israeli political institutions, governance, and society. The course has no prerequisites, however students are expected to come to class having done the readings and be prepared to actively engage in discussion.

courses.title: Developing Sustainable Communities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 284 and UEP 284.) Explores the many challenges of achieving sustainable development at local, regional, national and international levels. Investigates the theory of sustainable development, as well as the tools, strategies, and the contexts needed to move towards the ecological integrity, economic security, empowerment, responsibility, and social well-being characteristic of sustainable communities. Case studies drawn from the U.S. and overseas.

courses.title: The Laws, Policies, Politics & Ethics of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion
courses.desc: This course we will explore the history and ethics of law and policy as it applies to issues related to diversity, equity and inclusion. Additionally, we will examine the various policies and laws in existence as they relate to DEI issues in employment, education and health, and how policies solve or exacerbate existing problems. We will also build the skills needed to implement and enforce policies and regulations effectively.

courses.title: Negotiation, Mediation, And Conflict Resolution
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 230) Techniques of negotiation and mediation applied to a broad range of conflict situations from interpersonal differences to labor relations, environmental disputes, and international relations. Combines practice in basic methods with theoretical and applied aspects of conflict resolution.

courses.title: Research in Action
courses.desc: Introduction to the foundational principles and methodologies of program evaluation, emphasizing the development of comprehensive research proposals. Exploration of various evaluation models and study designs that effectively address problems of practice. Development of detailed proposals for program evaluation, equipping students with the skills to inform the development of new initiatives and interventions, raise awareness of organizational and/or societal problems of practice, and improve programs, services, and experiences within various contexts. Key topics include: formulating research questions; selecting appropriate evaluation designs; and developing data collection strategies.

courses.title: Research Methods and Design for Developmental
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 142) Introduction to research design and field and laboratory methods relevant to research in developmental science. Topics may include designs for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods research; measurement of behavior; reliability, validity, and generalizability of findings; and ethics. Analysis and evaluation of research studies and preparation of a literature review and a research proposal. Prerequisites: Senior or graduate status or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Graduate students only; undergraduates require instructor permission

courses.title: Interpreting and Communicating with Data
courses.desc: This course focuses on communication, visualization, and presentation of different types of data. The formats to be examined include written, graphical, and presentational methods. The focus is on how to create and design in each domain to best communicate information and ideas to a variety of audiences. This course will examine data communication as it relates to diversity, equity, and inclusion.

courses.title: Introductory Statistics for Developmental Science
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 140) Foundational statistics concepts and procedures including measures of central tendency and dispersion, relationships between continuous and categorical variables, and hypothesis specification and testing. Use of computer programs for analysis, data interpretation, and reporting results. Prerequisites: Junior, senior, or graduate status or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Introduction To Geographic Information Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as GIS 201) Introduces Geographical Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods and their applications. Topics include GIS data structures, geodesy, cartography and spatial analysis using rasters and vectors. Includes extensive laboratory exercises that apply concepts presented in the lectures using ArcGIS. The course will include a final project using GIS to apply student interests.

courses.title: Applied Regression Analysis for Developmental Science
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 249) This course covers the specification, conduct, and evaluation of various regression-based (general linear model) techniques used in developmental science and associated disciplines. Topics include models with continuous predictors, categorical predictors (including dummy codes), and interactions, as well as extensions of the general linear model such as logistic regression. Students must have a solid background in intermediate statistics, including analyses of variance. Prerequisite: CSHD 146 or equivalent intermediate statistics course with a focus on social and behavioral sciences.

courses.title: Language And Mind
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 3). Implications of recent work on language for our understanding of the human mind: consciousness, human intention, paradoxes, computers as models of mind, rules and conventions, metaphor. Readings drawn from classic and contemporary texts.

courses.title: Logic
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 33). An introduction to fundamental concepts of modern formal logic, including sentence logic, quantification theory, and identity. Emphasis on the application of formal methods to reasoning in philosophy, mathematics, and everyday affairs.

courses.title: Romance Linguistics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ML 96) Broad overview of linguistic complexity of the Romance languages, their relation to the greater Indo-European group, and their specific transformation over many centuries. Basic synchronic and diachronic linguistic description and analysis. Consideration of social, geographical, political, and cultural factors that hastened the fragmentation of Vulgar Latin and the development of its modern descendants, relation of language to cultural identity, and the advantages and disadvantages that this mosaic of languages poses for the European Union as well as Central and South American nations. In English. Recommendations: Knowledge of at least one Romance language (3 semesters) or instructor permission.

courses.title: Philosophy Of Language
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as PHIL 133). Examination of concepts fundamental to the nature of language and speech: reference, meaning, speech acts and linguistic competence, the syntax and semantics of natural languages. Philosophical views on these topics, including those of Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Quine, Grice, Chomsky, and others.
Recommendations: PHIL 2 and 33, or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Requires the completion of PHIL 33, or 103, plus one PHIL course, or graduate student.

courses.title: Development Of Language
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 155). Human language is examined as a form of communication and compared with animal signal systems. Other topics are phonological, syntactic, and semantic development; language, culture, and thought; language and social class; and language and bilingualism.

courses.title: Indo-european Linguistics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 170). Reconstruction of the Indo-European language family, including vocabulary, grammar, and poetics; principles of historical linguistics and the comparative method. Archaeology and history of the speakers of these languages. Survey of the family, with particular attention to development of Greek, Latin, English, and Sanskrit.

sections.req: Completion of GRK 0003 or LAT 0021 or LAT 0022 or SKT 3.

courses.title: Spanish For Heritage Learners
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as SPN 23) Development and expansion of reading and writing skills for students without formal training in the language but with ability to comprehend and speak Spanish because of their heritage. Study of grammar and stylistics, differences in regional dialectics, vocabulary expansion and effective communication based on literary and cultural readings. Conducted in Spanish.
Recommendations: SPN 21 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Childhood Across Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/AAST 62 and CSHD 62) Intermediate-level study of child development, with emphasis on cultural perspectives integrating psychological and anthropological theory. Children's development examined across cultures and in the context of the various social institutions and settings within which they live.

courses.title: Calculus Skills Workshop
courses.desc: Small group, active learning workshop that provides students with an extra resource while they are taking Math 32. Students are invited to sign up for this course after completing a diagnostic before Math 32 begins.

courses.title: Introductory Special Topics - Mathematical Reason and Model
courses.desc:
Content and prerequisites vary from semester to semester. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://math.tufts.edu
Recommendations: Engineering students are not permitted to take MATH 10 for credit.

courses.title: Symmetry
courses.desc:
A mathematical treatment of the symmetries of wallpaper patterns. The main goal is to prove that the symmetries of these patterns fall into seventeen distinct types. In addition, students will learn to identify the symmetries of given patterns (with special emphasis on the periodic drawings of M.C. Escher) and to draw such patterns.
Recommendations: High school geometry. Engineering students are not permitted to take MATH 16 for credit.

courses.title: The Mathematics Of Social Choice
courses.desc:
Introduction to mathematical methods for dealing with questions arising from social decision making. Topics vary but usually include ranking, determining the strength of, and choosing participants in multicandidate and two-candidate elections, and apportioning votes and rewards to candidates.
Recommendations: High school algebra. Engineering students are not permitted to take MATH 19 for credit.

courses.title: Introductory Statistics
courses.desc:
Descriptive data analysis, sampling and experimentation, basic probability rules, binomial and normal distributions, estimation, regression analysis, one and two sample hypothesis tests for means and proportions. The course may also include contingency table analysis, and nonparametric estimation. Applications from a wide range of disciplines.
Recommendations: High school algebra and geometry.

courses.title: Calculus I
courses.desc:
Differential and integral calculus: limits and continuity, the derivative and techniques of differentiation, extremal problems, related rates, the definite integral, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, derivatives and integrals of trigonometric functions, logarithmic and exponential functions.
Recommendations: High school geometry, algebra, and trigonometry. Students will receive an additional two credits (with grade) for passing MATH 32 after receiving credit for MATH 30. MATH 32 must be taken at Tufts and for a grade.

courses.title: Calculus II
courses.desc:
Applications of the integral, techniques of integration, separable differential equations, improper integrals. Sequences, series, convergence tests, Taylor series. Polar coordinates, complex numbers. Students may count only one of MATH 34 and MATH 36 for credit.
Recommendations: MATH 32.

courses.title: Calculus III
courses.desc: Vectors in two and three dimensions, applications of the derivative of vector-valued functions of a single variable. Functions of several variables, continuity, partial derivatives, the gradient, directional derivatives. Multiple integrals and their applications. Line integrals, Green's theorem, divergence theorem, Stokes’ theorem. Prerequisite: MATH 34 or 39.

courses.title: Differential Equations
courses.desc:
An introduction to linear differential equations with constant coefficients, linear algebra, and Laplace transforms.
Prerequisite: MATH 34. Recommendation: MATH 42.

courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CS 61.) Sets, relations and functions, logic and methods of proof, combinatorics, graphs and digraphs.
Recommendations: MATH 32 or COMP 11 or permission of instructor.

sections.note: Students looking to enroll in Discrete Mathematics should enroll in CS 61-01 or -02
Students looking to enroll in Discrete Mathematics should enroll in CS 61-01 or -02

courses.title: Number Theory
courses.desc: Introduction to number theory, including the Euclidean algorithm, congruences, primitive roots, and the law of quadratic reciprocity. Proof-writing required.

courses.title: Bridge to Higher Mathematics
courses.desc: Introduction to rigorous reasoning, applicable across all areas of mathematics, to prepare for proof-based courses at the 100 level. Writing proofs with precise reasoning and clear exposition required. Topics may include induction, functions and relations, combinatorics, modular arithmetic, graph theory, and convergence of sequences and series of real numbers.

courses.title: Linear Algebra
courses.desc: Introduction to the theory of vector spaces and linear transformations over the real or complex numbers, including linear independence, dimension, matrix multiplication, similarity and change of basis, inner products, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and some applications. Recommendations: MATH 34 or 39 or permission of instructor. Students may count only one of MATH 70 and MATH 72 for credit.

sections.req: Open to online CS or DS or MATH postbac, OR online CS or DS MS students

courses.title: Linear Algebra
courses.desc: Introduction to the theory of vector spaces and linear transformations over the real or complex numbers, including linear independence, dimension, matrix multiplication, similarity and change of basis, inner products, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and some applications. Recommendations: MATH 34 or 39 or permission of instructor. Students may count only one of MATH 70 and MATH 72 for credit.

courses.title: Mathematical Modeling And Computation
courses.desc: A survey of major techniques in the use of mathematics to model physical, biological, economic, and other systems; topics may include derivative-based optimization and sensitivity analysis, linear programming, graph algorithms, probabilistic modeling, Monte-Carlo methods, difference equations, and statistical data fitting. This course includes an introduction to computing using a high-level programming language, and studies the transformation of mathematical objects into computational algorithms. Prerequisites: (1) MATH 34 , 36, or 39, and (2) Math 70 or 72, or permission of instructor.Recommendations: MATH 34, MATH 36 or MATH 39, or consent.

courses.title: Mathematical Aspects of Data Analysis
courses.desc: Dimension reduction and data compression via principal component analysis, and the singular value decomposition; k-means clustering; clustering via diffusion on weighted graphs; support vector machines; tensor data analysis; kernel trick. Homework includes programming. Prerequisite: MATH 42, and MATH 70 or MATH 72. Some prior programming experience desirable, but not required.

sections.req: Open to online CS or DS or MATH postbac, OR online CS or DS MS students

courses.title: Numerical Linear Algebra
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CS 126) The two basic computational problems of linear algebra: solution of linear systems and computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Recommendations: MATH 70 or 72 and COMP 11.

courses.title: Complex Variables
courses.desc:
Introduction to the theory of analytic functions of a single complex variable, analytic functions, Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, residues, series expansions of analytic functions, conformal representation, entire and meromorphic functions, multivalued functions.
Recommendations: MATH 42 or 44, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Introduction to Analysis
courses.desc: An in-depth study of the real numbers and real-valued functions. The topology of the real line and completeness of the real numbers, sequences and series, limits and convergence, power series and Taylor series, continuity and differentiability, the Riemann integral, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Recommendations: Math 42 and Math 65. Students may not register for Math 134 after completing Math 135 or Math 136.

courses.title: Real Analysis I
courses.desc: An introduction to analysis. Metric spaces (with Euclidean spaces as the primary example), compactness, connectedness, continuity and uniform continuity, uniform convergence, the space of continuous functions on a compact set, contraction mapping lemma with applications. Recommendations: either MATH 0042 or 0044 and MATH 0065; or permission of instructor

courses.title: Real Analysis II
courses.desc: Applications of ideas from MATH 135 to further, in-depth study of functions on Euclidean spaces. Derivatives as linear maps, differentiable mappings, inverse and implicit function theorems. Further topics such as theory of the Riemann and Lebesgue integral, Hilbert spaces, and Fourier series. Recommendations: either MATH 0070 or 0072 and MATH 0135; or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Abstract Algebra I
courses.desc: An introduction to the basic concepts of abstract algebra, including theories of groups and possibly rings and fields. Some familiarity with proofs is recommended to succeed in the course." Prerequisite: MATH 70. Recommended: MATH Transition class. See department website for details.

courses.title: Abstract Algebra II
courses.desc: Further topics in groups and rings. Field extensions and Galois theory. Recommendations: Either MATH 0070 or 0072 and either MATH 0145 or 0245; or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
courses.desc: Upper-level course in ordinary differential equations from an applied point of view. Equilibria, limit cycles, and their stability. Saddle-node, pitchfork, transcritical, Hopf, and homoclinic bifurcations. Chaotic dynamics, strange attractors, and fractal dimension. Strong emphasis on examples from the natural sciences. Prerequisite: Math 42 or Math 44, and at least one of the following three: Math 51, Math 70, Math 72.

courses.title: Partial Differential Equations II
courses.desc: Introduction to the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations, including the method of characteristics, weak solutions, shocks and jump conditions, nonlinear wave equations, nonlinear diffusion and reaction-diffusion equations, applications to fluid dynamics. Prerequisite: MATH 155 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Probability
courses.desc:
Probability, conditional probability, random variables and distributions, expectation, special distributions, joint distributions, laws of large numbers, and the central limit theorem.
Prerequisite: MATH 34 or graduate standing.

courses.title: Statistics
courses.desc:
Statistical estimation, sampling distributions of estimators, hypothesis testing, regression, analysis of variance, and nonparametric methods.
Prerequisite: MATH 165 or EE 104 or graduate standing

courses.title: Statistics

courses.title: Stochastic Processes
courses.desc: Introduction to discrete-time and continuous-time stochastic processes and their applications. Topics include finite Markov chains (absorbing chains, ergodicity and convergence, reversibility, Monte Carlo methods and mixing times), countable state spaces (Poisson process, birth-and-death chains, branching processes, transience and recurrence), conditional expectation and martingales, optional sampling, and Brownian motion in one and several dimensions. Prerequisites: MATH 70 and either MATH 165 or EE 104. Recommendation: MATH 135 and some prior experience coding in a high-level language such as Python or Matlab.

sections.req: MATH 70 and either MATH 165 or EE 104 or graduate standing

courses.title: Algebraic Topology
courses.desc:
Applications of algebra to the study of topological objects, with emphasis on surfaces. Surfaces as manifolds, homotopy of curves, fundamental group, simple connectedness, covering spaces, genus, Euler Characteristic, orientability, and the classification of compact surfaces.
Recommendations: MATH 135 and 145.

courses.desc: Content and prerequisites vary from semester to semester. Topics covered in recent years have included mathematical neuroscience, Lie algebras, and nonlinear dynamics and chaos. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://math.tufts.edu

courses.desc: Attendance at department seminars and colloquia. May include research, teaching-based, and/or student-run seminars with significant math content and/or an outside speaker. Attendance at 10 seminars required for passing grade with up to two outside Tufts allowed if approved by instructor. Prerequisites: Graduate Standing or consent.

courses.title: Numerical Optimization
courses.desc:
Advanced numerical optimization with emphasis on modern first- and second-order algorithms, acceleration techniques, large-scale methods, and constrained optimization. Topics include gradient, proximal, mirror, and subgradient methods; heavy-ball and Nesterov acceleration; Newton and quasi-Newton methods; incremental and stochastic gradient methods and randomized coordinate descent; projected gradient descent and interior-point methods. Theoretical foundations and practical applications to real-world problems are emphasized. Programming experience required.
Prerequisites: MATH 128, MATH 225, and MATH 226.

courses.title: Complex Analysis
courses.desc:
Analytic functions, power series. Integration in the complex plane, Cauchy's integral theorem and formulas. Entire functions. Singularities. Conformal mapping, Riemann mapping theorem. 
Prerequisites: Math 135 and graduate standing; or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Algebra II
courses.desc:
Foundational results in commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, and
homological algebra. Prerequisites: Math 245; or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Partial Differential Equations II
courses.desc: Boundary-value problems of Sturm-Liouville type, separation of variables, special functions. Similarity solutions, transform methods, power-series solutions, the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya Theorem. Topics in functional analysis, including L^p spaces and derivatives and existence of weak solutions to second-order elliptic equations and linear evolution equations. Interior and boundary regularity. Topics in the calculus of variations. Other selected topics. Prerequisites: Math 255; or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Algebraic Topology II
courses.desc:
Homology, homological algebra, cohomology and Poincare duality. Group cohomology if time permits. 
Pre-requisite: Math 275 or 175 and graduate student or permission of instructor

courses.desc:
Students select articles from the current literature, analyze their significance, and present them for discussion in a seminar group. Students will learn how to
present a research article, make a research poster and present a scientific talk.

courses.title: Masters Thesis Research
courses.desc: These courses provide guided research on a topic suitable for a master’s thesis.

courses.title: Computerized Motion/Gait Analysis
courses.desc: The course will cover the planning of clinical trials; procedure of data acquisition, and interpretation of results. It will consist of didactic lectures and computer-based sessions at the Tufts/NESH Center for Human Performance. The course includes materials on NIH funded research projects, and students will learn how to conduct biomechanical trials themselves using the Lab’s equipment. Interested students will be able to participate in research projects with their results submitted for publication.

sections.req:
This course is limited to students admitted to the Master of Science in Biomedical Sciences Program.

External students are strictly prohibited from cross-registration in any MBS course.

courses.title: Bioethics for the Physician-Scientist
courses.desc: This course will cover the following topics: foundations of bioethics including the Nuremburg and Helsinki Codes; scientific misconduct including plagiarism, intellectual dishonesty, fraud, misuse of statistics, and protecting both complainants and respondents; the human treatment of animals in research; mentoring in both the laboratory and hospital, including respect for trainees, harassment issues, developing independence, and the mentor as role model; human volunteers, including informed consent; use of placebos; research on vulnerable populations including children, prisoners, pregnant women and their fetus, military personnel, students, economically/culturally disadvantaged, and the elderly; and stem cell research/cloning/regenerative medicine.

sections.req:
This course is limited to students admitted to the Master of Science in Biomedical Sciences Program.

External students are strictly prohibited from cross-registration in any MBS course.

courses.title: Bioethics for the Budding Clinician
courses.desc: This course will cover the following topics: foundations of bioethics including the Nuremburg and Helsinki Codes; conflicts of interest; patient rights; apologies in medicine; religion and medicine; death and dying; conception and birth; assisted reproductive technologies; new technologies, including telemedicine and robotic surgery; organ transplantation; and the ethics of clinical trials and genetic testing.

sections.req:
This course is limited to students admitted to the Master of Science in Biomedical Sciences Program.

External students are strictly prohibited from cross-registration in any MBS course.

courses.title: Critical Evaluation of the Clinical Literature
courses.desc: Modern medicine increasingly relies on sophisticated treatments and evidence-based decision-making. Whether evaluating novel therapeutics or identifying risk factors for disease prevention, stakeholders, including providers and policy makers, must be able to critically assess published evidence. In this journal club-style course, students will read and engage in guided discussions of a range of scientific and clinical literature, including basic science papers, clinical trials, metanalyses, and more. The course may include guest lectures covering a range of research topics, followed by journal club sessions in which students critically discuss papers relevant to these topics. Students will develop skills in evaluating study design, interpreting data, and understanding the broader context of research findings. Students will also develop their research presentation skills through leading a class discussion of a selected journal article. Specific topics covered will vary each year but will always include a range of different fields.

sections.req:
This course is limited to students admitted to the Master of Science in Biomedical Sciences Program.

External students are strictly prohibited from cross-registration in any MBS course.

courses.title: Mental Illness and its Pharmacologic Management
courses.desc:
Emotional disorders and mental illness are commonly encountered in medical practice by primary care physicians, internists, and most of the medical subspecialties. These disorders can present as the principal reason for seeking health care, or as components or consequences of other underlying medical disorders. The majority of such individuals are not referred for specialty treatment by psychiatrists, but rather are managed by their primary physicians. The principal objective of this course is to introduce MBS candidates -- the majority of whom will go on to become physicians involved in primary health care delivery -- to the fundamental features of emotional disorders and mental illnesses encountered in clinical medicine, and pharmacologic approaches to management of these disorders. The instructional strategy will involve integrated teaching by Tufts-affiliated physicians having extensive experience in clinical psychopharmacology, together with basic/clinical pharmacology instruction by the course director and other faculty with a focus on mechanisms of psychotropic drug action, principles of appropriate clinical use, and recognition of hazards and adverse reactions. 

The course will meet once each week for 12 weeks in the Spring semester for 90 minutes per session, for a total of 20 contact hours. The core topics will be:

-	The epidemiology of mental illness, and the relation to primary care medicine.
-	Anxiety and panic disorders
-	Anxiolytic and anti-panic drugs
-	Sleep disorders
-	Sedative-hypnotic medications
-	The clinical spectrum of depression and mood disorders
-	Antidepressant agents
-	Bipolar disorder and its treatment
-	Schizophrenia and other thought disorders
-	Medications used to treat schizophrenia
-	Substance abuse and its pharmacologic treatment
-	Complementary and alternative medicines
-	Genetics of mental illness and its pharmacologic treatment
-	Drug interactions in psychopharmacology
-	Topical review

courses.title: Immunotherapy of Cancer and Autoimmune Disease
courses.desc:
In the last few years we have seen a revolution in the treatment of cancer and autoimmune diseases - we cannot turn on the television or open a magazine or newspaper without seeing an ad for some new medication to treat a specific cancer or autoimmune disease. 

The reasons for this revolution in clinical treatment are clear - advances in “immunotherapy”: the manipulation of some component or arm of the immune response to treat disease. What are these advances? This course will explore this new and exciting area, relevant to both cancer and autoimmunity, discussing topics that include CAR-T cells and other T-cell products, therapeutic antibodies, and vaccines to prevent and treat cancer.

The goal of this course is to show that the principles that underlie the successful use of immunotherapy are an extension of the basic immunological concepts taught to students in their first-year immunology course.

courses.title: Cancer Biology and Molecular Oncology
courses.desc:
Advancements in understanding cancer biology continue at an impressive rate. Scientific findings lead to better stratification of disease based on molecular drivers, as well as improvements in targeted therapy. These scientific and clinical advancements have, unsurprisingly, lead to improvements in cancer patient morbidity and mortality. In other words, patients survive longer and adjuvant therapies are better tolerated. 

What are the scientific advances underpinning our deepening knowledge of cancer initiation and metastasis? What are the new, targeted therapies that have led to improved cancer patient survival? The answers to these two questions will be explored through both lecture and discussion of scientific literature and clinical data. We will explore both the concepts of signal transduction and gene expression that underlie the development of targeted therapies and is an extension of the basic cell biology and biochemistry concepts taught to students in first-year courses. The material presented complements, but does not overlap, the Immunotherapy elective. Where appropriate, connections to the Immunotherapy elective will be highlighted.

courses.title: The Developmental Origin Of Adult Diseases
courses.desc: Recent clinical and epidemiological studies reveal that changes in the maternal environment play a major role in the genesis of certain diseases in her fetus, and that these diseases manifest once the exposed fetus reaches adult life. The importance of this field of developmental pathogenesis is growing rapidly, and it is expected to become a major medical discipline. For example, nutritional deprivation during gestation, caused by famine, war and migrations increases the likelihood of the fetus developing hypertension and stroke if exposure to famine occurs during the 1st trimester. Fetuses exposed during the 2nd trimester have an increased propensity of developing diabetes and heart disease. Similarly, exposure to certain hormonally-active agents (also known as endocrine disruptors) such as pesticides during fetal and early postnatal development increase the propensity of developing breast cancer during adult life, as does exposure to the estrogen DES before the 13th week of development. Recently, disease susceptibilities (autism, behavioral deficits, cancer, diabetes, obesity, asthma) are also being linked with exposure to environmental toxins. In sum, the environment interacts with the developing organism to produce novel, at times impaired or disease-prone phenotypes. Thus, ecological developmental biology is becoming a medical discipline in the 21st century.

courses.title: Neuroscience
courses.desc:
This course will examine the basic principles of anatomy, physiology, and neurochemistry of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Topics will be covered to help develop an understanding of how neuronal communication underlies human brain function. The course will be taught as a mixture of lecture-based sessions and discussions of scientific journal articles on neurological cases. Lectures supplemented by discussion of clinical case studies will serve as an introduction to understanding of neurological disorders. Radiological images will be integrated where relevant within the course.

Specific topics covered will include gross brain and meninges, neuronal microenvironment, synaptic transmission, autonomic nervous system function, spinal reflexes, sensory processing, movement, sleep and wakefulness, hunger, thirst, caloric and body fluid homeostasis, emotion control, maintenance of balance, hearing, visual sensation and pertinent neurological disorders.

courses.title: Laboratory Techniques
courses.desc: Mastering the underlying laboratory techniques is imperative for the development of vaccines targeting both human and veterinary pathogens. This hands-on workshop eschews traditional lectures in favor of dedicated laboratory time. Participants will immerse themselves in practical exercises, honing their skills under expert guidance. From culturing E. coli to assessing immune responses, basic aspects of vaccine development will be explored through active experimentation. This experiential approach fosters a deeper understanding of the intricate processes involved in vaccine research, equipping participants with invaluable expertise to tackle real-world challenges in the field of pre-clinical drug development.

Designed to complement the medical microbiology curriculum, the course emphasizes experiential learning over traditional lectures. Students will engage in guided laboratory sessions that build core competencies in microbial culture, aseptic technique, diagnostic assays, and data interpretation. Through active experimentation and collaborative analysis, participants will gain confidence in handling microorganisms and understanding their relevance to infectious disease diagnosis and public health.

courses.desc:
This course is designed for students who specialize in another area to reimagine/recontextualize their work frame-by-frame through animation. Students will be introduced to a wide variety of animation techniques with special attention given to their multimedia possibilities. Students working in film, sculpture, painting, photography, performance, video, ceramics, drawing etc. will consider the possibilities for animating their work and learn the techniques necessary for integrating animation into their art practice. The course is aimed to help students who don't see themselves becoming animators as such, but who have an interest in finding ways to expand their current practice through animation. Special consideration will be given to installation concerns and alternative methods of presentation. Class time will be split between screenings, demonstrations, work time and field trips to view animation in public and/or gallery settings when possible. Through hands-on projects, design and rig 2D characters, mechanical elements, and cameras. Topics include performance-based animation such as walk cycles and lip syncing; motion for objects and camera based off of hierarchical parenting, controllers, automated keyframe interpolation, through the use of industry-standard plugins: Joystick and DUIK. An immersive, interdisciplinary, and collaborative course focused on developing technical and conceptual expertise in participatory research methodologies, community-based art practices, and the ethics of engagement. Partnering with a Boston-based nonprofit, students will co-design, co-create, implement, and reflect on impactful art projects. Students work alongside unhoused artists at Saint Francis House to co-create artworks that reflect shared stories of resilience, care, and belonging. The first four weeks emphasize context, ethics, and preparation; the remaining nine weeks center on collaborative making, critique, and public presentation. Through workshops, technical training, assignments, readings, and discussions, students will gain practical skills in conducting participatory research on social justice issues, using digital and analog tools to collect oral histories and interviews, applying fiber arts for community engagement, exploring performance art as a medium for empowerment and storytelling, and utilizing multimedia platforms to amplify engagement and documentation. This hands-on course prioritizes co-creation, collaborative knowledge production, and meaningful partnerships, preparing students to co-produce art projects that authentically represents community voices and concerns. Open to all skill levels. Locations: SMFA + Saint Francis House Art Studio (alternate visits).

courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course surveys the history of the Jewish people from the Late Second Temple period through the mid-twentieth century. We begin by examining the origins of rabbinic Judaism and Jewish life under Christian and Muslim rule. We then analyze the profound ruptures of the modern era, investigating the impacts of political emancipation, religious reform, and Western nationalism, culminating in the Holocaust and the establishment of the modern state of Israel. Through close analysis of primary source texts, students will understand how the modern Jewish world developed out of its pre-modern foundations.

Developing flows and transition to turbulence. Condensation and boiling heat transfer. Radiation and conjugate heat transfer involving radiation. Temperature and heat flux measurements. Numerical techniques.
Recommendations: ME 150 Thermal-Fluid Transport I or equivalent.

courses.title: Microfluidics
courses.desc:
Microscale fluid mechanics and mass transport. Microfluidic device design, fabrication, and experimental characterization. Hydraulic circuit analysis, electrokinetic flow, capillary effects, and multiphase flow. Brownian motion, diffusion, and dispersion. Applications including mixing and separations, cell sorting and chemotaxis, droplets and emulsions, and pumps and valves. Laboratory component including micro particle image velocimetry. Meets with ME 217. In no case may a student receive credit for both ME 155 and ME 217.
Prerequisites: ME 51 or ME 150 or graduate standing

courses.title: Power Generation Systems
courses.desc:
Design and engineering of electric power production systems. Thermal-mechanical principles of electrical energy conversion, cogeneration, and storage using fossil fuel, geothermal, hydroelectric, nuclear, ocean, solar thermal, and wind power sources. Direct generation using fuel cells and photovoltaics. Economic and environmental sustainability aspects.
Recommendations: Senior standing. ME 50 and ME 51 or equivalent thermal-fluids background with permission of instructor

courses.title: Data Science for Sustainability
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CEE 0132 and DS 143). Emerging topics in data science and statistical learning with applications to the three pillars of sustainability (environmental, economic, and social). Building, estimating and interpreting models used in energy and environmental decision-making with emphasis on social justice. Development of critical consumers and responsible producers of data-driven analysis through: learning a suite of data-driven modeling and prediction tools; building the programming and computing expertise to use those tools; and, developing the ability to formulate analyses to answer questions pertaining to sustainability.

sections.req: (ES 2, CS 10 or CS 11) and (ES 56, CEE 156, EE 24, EE 104, BME 141, MATH 166, or ME 102); OR graduate standing

courses.title: Structural Health Monitoring
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CEE 127) Vibration-based structural health monitoring including system identification of linear systems. Data acquisition, signal processing, modal identification, parameter estimation, and optimization.

sections.req: (ES 55 and (ES 56 or CEE 156)) or graduate standing

Development of governing equations, stiffness and load matrices for deformation and stress analysis. Work and energy theorems. Hands-on experience with industry-standard software and practical applications in structural engineering.
Recommendations: CEE 22 or ME 41 or consent of instructor

courses.title: Qualifying Exam
courses.desc: Students present and defend a proposal for research consisting of a statement of an original research problem in which a scientific question is asked and the experimental approach to answering the question is explained in a written proposal. The proposal is presented orally to the faculty.

courses.title: Animal Virology
courses.desc: Molecular aspects of viral replication and host-cell interactions are emphasized. Topics include virion structure; mechanisms of nucleic acid replication, transcription, and translation; virion assembly and release; genetics; mechanisms of transformation by oncogenic viruses; responses of the host to viral infection, tumor viruses and tumor cells; and mechanisms of persistent and slow virus infections. Prerequisites: a course in molecular biology or working knowledge of molecular techniques.

courses.title: Introduction to Infectious Diseases
courses.desc: This course is comprised of three integrated components; a Medical Microbiology Tutorial designed to introduce students to pathogens and pathophysiology of infectious diseases, Infectious Diseases Problem-Based Learning designed to introduce students to clinical cases, and a Teaching Clinic designed to expose students to real clinical cases and treatment options.

sections.req: Course restricted to First Year MERGE_ID and Inflammation students.

courses.title: Laboratory Rotations
courses.desc: 8-10 week laboratory rotations for first-year students are designed to provide experience with experimental design and theoretical aspects of the diverse research problems under investigation in various laboratories.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Microbiology O
courses.desc: This collection of lectures of four trending topics in Microbiology is offered in odd years.

courses.title: Graduate Seminar
courses.desc: Visiting speakers present their scientific research to all members of the program, including faculty, students, and post-doctoral fellows.

sections.req: In the Fall & Spring, Grad Seminar must be taken with Grad Research (or Rotations), and Journal Club (through year 4 for PhDs and year 3 for MD/PhDs).

courses.title: Journal Club
courses.desc: These courses provide in-depth study and discussion of specific topics involving the critical review of current literature in a small group format. Given by faculty and graduate students (years two through four) and attended by all program members.

sections.req: Journal Club must be taken every Fall & Spring (through year 4 for PhDs, year 3 for MDPHDs), along with Grad Research (or Rotations) and Grad Seminar.

courses.title: Graduate Research
courses.desc: These courses provide guided research on a topic suitable for a doctoral thesis.

sections.req: Grad Research must be taken every Fall and Spring along with Seminar, and Journal Club (through year 4 for PhDs, year 3 for MDPhDs)

courses.title: Advanced Ethics for Scientists
courses.desc: This course is a discussion/seminar course that treats selected topics related to ethical behavior in scientific work. Topics covered include fraud, plagiarism, data selection and analysis, record keeping, animal welfare, personnel issues, genetic screening and gene therapy, and conflict of interest. Enrollment is restricted to third and fourth year graduate students.

courses.title: PhD Degree Only
courses.desc: Students enroll in this course when they receive permission to write and defend their theses from their thesis committees. This course represents the effort in the final preparation of the doctoral thesis. A grade of “S” is automatically awarded upon completion of the thesis.

courses.title: Physics of Solar Cells
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ EE 114) Physics of photovoltaic cells including physics of semiconductors in photovoltaic devices, physical models of solar cell operation, characteristics and design of common types of solar cells, and approaches to increasing solar ceil efficiency.
Recommendations: MATH 42, MATH 51, EE 18, PHYS 42/43, or instructor permission

courses.title: Instrumental Analysis
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CHEM 141) Theory, operation, and application of principal instruments used in chemical analysis and research. Selected special topics such as molecular, atomic, and mass spectroscopies; electrochemistry; and chromatography. Designed to acquaint the student with modern laboratory techniques used in all areas of chemistry. Student-designed projects incorporating analytical metrics of precision, accuracy, selectivity, and sensitivity as well as experimental design and hypothesis development that relate theory to experimental data. Recommendations: CHEM 31, 41 or 43, and 51, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed with BME 154) Fundamental concepts of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine (scaffolds, stem cells and bioreactors); progress with specific tissue systems; applications for tissue engineering; and current state-of-the art of tissue regeneration. Additional topics: transport phenomena and mechanical regulation of stem cell function, with focus on mechanisms of mechanotransduction. Course independent of, but complementary to, BME 153.
Recommendations: Junior standing, BIO 13, CHEM 51, PHYS 11, ES 9, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Finite Element Analysis
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ME 177 & CEE 105). Finite element analysis of problems important in structural engineering. Overview of direct stiffness method. Discretization of continuum to finite elements for approximate solution of complex engineering problems. Development of governing equations, stiffness and load matrices for deformation and stress analysis. Work and energy theorems. Hands-on experience with industry-standard software and practical applications in structural engineering.
Recommendations: CEE 22 or ME 41 or consent of instructor

courses.title: Manufacturing Processes And Materials Technology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ ME 110) A study of traditional and nontraditional manufacturing processes related to processing of metals, ceramics, and polymers, including computer-aided manufacturing. Topics include properties and behavior of materials, selection of materials and processes subject to surface finish, tolerance, design, and economic constraints.
Recommendations: ME 11.

courses.title: Composite Materials
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ME 116 & CHBE 116) Fundamentals of design, manufacture, and analysis of composite materials. Fiber materials such as glass, kevlar and carbon fibers along with state-of-the-art thermoplastic and thermoset matrix materials. Rules of mixtures (ROM) to calculate transverse isotropic properties in laminae. Classical Lamination Theory (CLT) and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to calculate stress and strains in laminates. Case studies in aerospace. Hands-on experiences, such as vacuum bagging to manufacture and test composites. Team project.

courses.title: Introduction to Metals
courses.desc: Basic vocabulary of wearable art and sculptural expression in non-ferrous metals. Through a series of demos and projects, learn basic metalsmithing skills including sawing, filing, soldering, forming, and finishing, and use them to create three-dimensional art pieces. Through historic and contemporary examples, learn essential skills for creating works of art in non-ferrous metals.

courses.desc: Introduction to historical practices in metals to understand the potential for contemporary applications in body adornment and the decorative arts. courses.desc: Within an artistic practice, The Multiple allows you to reproduce specific objects or designs that are available to a wider audience and more affordable than a one-of-a-kind piece. Examines the historical and applied context of examples of multiples and small series editions in all kinds of materials and types of production. courses.desc: Designed for intermediate to advanced students as an in-depth exploration of the use of color within jewelry and metalworking. Covers traditional surface treatments such as patinas and enameling and the potential to make and incorporate colorful, non-metal objects and materials using fabrication-based setting techniques. Create finished pieces of jewelry and objects that exhibit an understanding of color’s expressive and symbolic qualities. Prerequisite: MTL 0113 or MTL 0116.

courses.title: Introduction to Music Theory and Musicianship
courses.desc: Exploration of the basics of music theory, including notation, rhythm, scales, intervals, chords, and form. Introduction to ear training, sight singing, and keyboard skills. Musical systems both inside and outside Western notated tradition covered.

Scholarships are available for Music, Sound, and Culture majors or minors, financial aid recipients, and ensemble members. Applications are due the first week of each semester.

courses.title: Sound and Structure II
courses.desc:
An integrated approach to music theory and analysis, with focus on advanced harmonic resources, formal and dramatic organization, and issues of perception and interpretation. Emphasis on creative activities and large projects. Development of aural skills such as sight singing and dictation. Ear training lab required. Prerequisite:
MUS 11, placement through the Music Theory Assessment (offered every Fall), or consent of department theory coordinator.

courses.title: Introduction to Theory and Analysis Of Popular Music
courses.desc: Study of the structure and forms used in popular music through score analysis, transcription, and aural skills. Focus includes the innovation and development within specific genres, as well as their shared common practices. Genres studied will include: rhythm and blues, soul, funk, hip-hop, rock, folk, musical theater numbers, and ballads from the 30's -50's. Prerequisite: MUS 5 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Writing About Music
courses.desc: Introduction to the art and craft of writing about music. Exploration of genres and development of techniques for writing effectively for a broad audience. Learning to write about music to refine skills in listening and to develop a deeper understanding of the role of arts criticism as such, its purpose and its benefits to us as individuals and as a society. Prerequisites: English 1 and 2 or completion of college writing requirement..

sections.req: Requires the completion of ENG 0001 and ENG 0002 or ENG 0003 and ENG 0004 or equivalent(s) and A&S, or ENG 0001 and SOE

courses.title: American Music
courses.desc: A historical and cultural overview of American art music from the founding of the United States to the present day with close readings of representative works. Intended for undergraduate music majors.

courses.title: History of Rock 'n' Roll
courses.desc: An examination of sociocultural meaning and musical structure in rock 'n' roll and related idioms of popular music. Emergence of the idiom in context of the history of American music. Connections among various styles and major artists. Impact of technology and the music industry.

courses.title: History of Jazz
courses.desc: History of jazz from its origins to the present day, examining various styles including Dixieland, swing, bop, modal, free-jazz, Latin jazz, and fusion. Emphasis placed on social, cultural, and historical contexts of the African American experience from which jazz emerged, and its influence on global cultures. Exploration will include live performance examples and opportunities.

courses.title: Music and War in History and Memory
courses.desc: Exploration of the relationships among music, armed conflict, history, and cultural memory from the nineteenth century to the present. Topics include music and nationalism; music on the battlefield; resistance, survival, and protest; and postwar commemoration. Global case studies, including the two World Wars, the Rwandan genocide, the Colombian armed conflict, and the war in Ukraine, examine how societies use music to prepare for and wage war, protest violence, remember trauma, rebuild communities, and construct and contest national mythologies. No prerequisites.

courses.title: African Musical Arts
courses.desc: Variety of musical expressions including the traditional, neo-traditional, and contemporary mass mediated popular music (Afro-Pop/Afrobeats). Social context of the music process, music and historical narratives, music and religious ritual, court music traditions, contemporary issues in Afro-Pop, and various aspects of performance practices. Hands-on activities, guest speakers/artists, and audio-visual recordings.

courses.title: Soundworlds of North Africa
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 82) Anthropology of music approach to North African soundworlds—the sonic spaces where music, culture, and social action intersect. Centering the voices of North African scholars, musicians, and listeners of the contemporary Maghreb region (Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara, and their borderlands and diasporas). Topics may include the role of music in Amazigh rights and Sahrawi independence movements, spaces of Islamic-Jewish convergence, ritual healing and the recuperation of sub-Saharan heritages, traumas of migration, the Arab Spring, and mythmaking about North Africa by foreign and local powers. How to relate anthropological and social theory to public and “hidden” meanings embedded in the sounds of diverse musical genres.

courses.desc: A critical overview of the production, reception, and circulation of East and Southeast Asian pop music. How different musical movements and genres are crafted and how pop music conveys ideas of social changes and cultural identity.

courses.title: Composer of The Year - Charles Ives - Unity and Disso
courses.desc: A study of an important composer. Focus on significant works in the context of the composer's life and times.

sections.note: Charles Ives challenged the norms of late 19th and early 20th century composition to create music that continues to inspire composers and improvisors of our time – from John Adams and Tania León to Bill Frissell and The Grateful Dead. This course examines the life and music of Ives and emphasizes the unique ways Ives’ music addresses ideas of community, memory, and place, and the musical practices of polyrhythm, dissonance, and spatial perception. No prerequisites or prior musical training required.

courses.title: Computer Tools For Musicians
courses.desc: (formerly Music 64) Using computer technology to compose, arrange, synthesize, transcribe, orchestrate, mix, and publish music. Tools to be covered include Sibelius, Reason, Kontakt, and Digital Performer. Students will complete several creative projects using music hardware and software. Prerequisites: Music performance and/or composition experience, ability to read music, facility at the keyboard, familiarity with the Macintosh operating system. Registration by permission only.

courses.title: Electronics for Music
courses.desc: Fundamental concepts of electricity and electronics; application to musical contexts and professional settings. Calculation and measurement of important electrical quantities; choosing electrical components based on circuit requirements. Assembling cables, prototypes, and breadboard circuits; troubleshooting; soldering electrical connections. Culminates with building a small audio device.

courses.title: Jazz Theory
courses.desc: Harmonic and melodic techniques of jazz and popular music. Extended chords (ninths, elevenths, thirteenths) and substitutions; modulations and free melodic treatment of dissonance. Song forms. Written exercises and analysis; emphasis on student composition. Continuation of aural and keyboard skills. Recommendations: MUS 12 or instructor consent.

courses.title: Orchestration
courses.desc:
Ranges, tone qualities, and expressiveness of instruments and voices. Students learn how to orchestrate songs and piano scores or reduce the size of a larger score. Special individual projects reflecting student interest.
Recommendations: MUS 11 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Contemporary Composition
courses.desc:
A project-oriented course with emphasis on the creative experience. Lectures on significant composers; attendance at concerts of contemporary music.
Recommendations: MUS 11 or permission of instructor

courses.title: Conducting
courses.desc: Vocal and instrumental conducting, stressing baton techniques and score reading. Preparation of vocal, orchestral, band, and other instrumental ensembles for conducting with the assistance of Tufts performing groups. Recommendations: MUS 11 (Sound and Structure) or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Boston Soundscapes
courses.desc: Explores the soundscapes of Boston and Greater Boston and how residents and institutions construct ideas of home and community through music. Case studies include Chinatown, Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, the South End, and East Boston, with attention to cultural centers, places of worship, jazz clubs, pubs, parades, festivals, protests, and street performance. Questions of social identity, racial inequities, urban policy, and residents' tactics to claim cultural spaces are considered. Attendance at local musical events is encouraged. Through a semester-long, library-supported research project, a collaborative ArcGIS StoryMap documenting public musical life in the Boston area is developed. Cross-listed with Civic Studies and Anthropology

courses.title: Social Justice, Advocacy, and Music
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 175) The role of music in movements for social change and in models of advocacy in scholarship, research, educational programming, and communities. Case studies include the role of music in the Civil Rights movement and LGBTQ+ advocacy in the US, and in the struggle against apartheid in South Africa. Using music as a tool for activism, and the role of music in developing successful social justice initiatives. No prerequisite.

courses.title: Music, Trance, & Consciousness
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ANTH 156) Cross-cultural approaches to relationships between music and altered states of consciousness, ranging from high-arousal trance states in healing rituals to low-arousal, individual experiences of deep listening. Ethnographic case studies of music-driven spirit possession, mysticism, shamanism, rave culture, and mobile individual listening practices from Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Interdisciplinary approach with material from ethnomusicology, anthropology, psychology, religious studies, and neuroscience.

courses.title: Fieldwork Methods in Music, Sound, and Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 154) Experiential and critical approach to ethnographic field research in the arts and humanities. Hands-on learning assignments in project design, participant-observation, field note taking, interview techniques, audio-visual documentation, and ethnographic writing. Ethics of knowledge production, complexities of self-other relations, and awareness of implicit bias. Decolonial, collaborative, and multimodal methodologies. Strategies for creating written, visual, and multimedia representations of music, sound, and embodied cultural expressions, and their entanglements with social issues. Recommendations: Major or minor in Anthropology or in Music, Sound, and Culture, or graduate standing, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Digital Methods for Music Scholarship
courses.desc: Introduction to core digital methods for music research, specifically close reading and encoding using the Music Encoding Initiative (MEI) schema. Hands-on experience in creating, manipulating, and encoding music and textual content, applying historical, cultural, and/or bibliographic research methods to develop a collaborative digital project. Designed as a humanities lab: students will have in-class time to learn, experiment, and create together. Assigned readings will offer grounding in music research and digital humanities methods (MEI, close reading, digital editions), with additional readings related to the semester topic. Please see the class notes below for information on the specific theme and digital project chosen for the given semester, as well as any prerequisites.

instructors: Anna E. Kijas, Melinda Latour O'Brien

courses.title: Settling Scores: Screen Music Theory and Analysis
courses.desc: Analytical approaches to music in film, television, music video, and video games. Traditional methods (tonal design, thematic structure, topic theory) alongside recent perspectives (transformational harmony, timbre, rhythm and meter, embodiment). Audiovisual scores, leitmotif and memory, trailer music, film scores in concert, and interactivity and player agency in game music. Emphasis on transcription by ear and development of original analytical methodologies. Recommendations: MUS 0012 or 0017, graduate standing, or instructor consent.
