courses.title: Graduate Painting & Drawing Practicum
courses.desc: Designed to assist graduate students with a range of studio issues related to painting drawing and the intersection and overlap between these two modes of working. Course designed for both committed students in painting and drawing and those who are interested in integrating these discourses and discipline into their practices, regardless of media. Discussion of drawing or painting assumes the use of and interest in diverse tools and diverse outcomes from canvas and paper to digital and temporal to textual and referential. Assist in the advancement of skill building for artists already versed in painting and drawing and offer introductions to the media for those new to their use. Equal emphasis will be given to technical, formal and conceptual concerns. Individual meetings with the faculty regarding student’s independent projects and group discussions and critiques.

courses.title: Painting Foundation
courses.desc: Introduction to materials and methods of painting. Learn basic properties of paint; obtain broad understanding of color, shape, structure and space. Examine the world around you; capture and respond to it in paint. Subject matter includes objects, landscapes, people and places; exploring students’ own ideas and reacting to the current moment. Classes consist of demonstrations, discussion, painting exercises that build upon one another over the semester. Students gain comfort and familiarity with the language of painting by reading about and responding to contemporary painting/painters, and critiquing/discussing each other’s work. Open to all levels.

courses.title: Disrupted Realism
courses.desc: Interpret and distort ‘realism’ using psychology, insight, and revelation. Include emotion, impulses, and memory as you respond to the subjectivity and sensations of your experience. Students research contemporary artists working in this vein. They learn new painting techniques, and use multiple perceptions and methods (drawing, photography, video, and digital image manipulation) to develop images. Demonstrations, one-on-one instruction, and generous easel time. Develop and express personal vision by reinterpreting realism. Previous painting experience helpful. Open to all levels.

courses.title: Contemporary Portrait
courses.desc: Designed to help students understand and express the complex landscape of the human head. Look at a variety of contemporary portrait artists; explore many solutions to how to paint people. Students will learn to identify, mix, and apply color using both observational and emotional skin tones. Group critiques provide opportunities for creative problem solving. Directed exercises; time to work on your own projects. Class designed around heavy body paints (oils or acrylics), also open to experimentation with other media. Both virtual and in person participation (depending upon access) are welcome.

Hone ideas through iteration, inquiry, and group dialog. Open to abstraction, representation, and combinations thereof. Intermediate class open to all levels; previous painting experience is helpful.

courses.desc:

Students engage with real-world challenges related to healthcare delivery, policy, environment and climate, and structural inequities, while developing skills in critical thinking, evidence-informed decision-making, and communication. The course emphasizes belonging, helping students consider how they will contribute to public health in ways that are thoughtful, responsible, and grounded in advancing health equity.

courses.title: Research Methods in Public Health
courses.desc: Research Methods in Public Health is designed to acquaint public health students with the process of conducting public health research. The major objective of the course is to understand the nuts and bolts of conducting public health inquiry and research, emphasizing qualitative, community-engaged, and quantitative methods and use of a geographic information system (GIS) relevant to research. We will build on the concepts learned in the introductory courses of biostatistics, epidemiology, and other related courses to address biomedical and public health issues through rigorous research and evaluation methods. The course is intended to be a survey course of some of the major issues and tasks involved with conducting public health research. Emphasis is placed on identifying which methods are most appropriate for answering a specific research question and on preparing students for doing independent work in their Integrative Learning Experience.

courses.title: Cancer Epidemiology and Prevention
courses.desc: Cancer epidemiology is the study of causes of cancer in human populations; understanding what causes cancer is critical to reducing the burden of cancer through prevention. Cancer is a disease that develops over many years and risk factors can impact initiation and/or progression of cancer. Challenges to understanding which risk factors are causally related to cancer include understanding the biological pathways and relevant time periods of exposure.

courses.title: Heat, Housing, and Health: Climate Resilience in a Changing World
courses.desc:
Extreme heat is a predictable - and preventable - public health risk, especially for residents who are unsheltered, living in substandard housing, older, medically fragile, or socially isolated. Students learn about systems that reduce repeated heat stress through proactive planning, targeted outreach, and reliable access to cooling and hydration supports. Students learn how heat risk concentrates by neighborhood and vulnerability. Students gain insight into how various cities have designed their heat-response workflows, as well as training for how to work with municipal and community partners as collaborative consultants on related issues.

This is a fully asynchronous course (self-directed with opportunities for live, online interaction with the Course Instructor). It is intended as a standalone course, but also serves to prepare students for PH 0235 Heat, Housing, and Health: Immersive Experience.

courses.title: Heat, Housing, and Health: Immersive Experience
courses.desc: Extreme heat is a predictable - and preventable - public health risk, especially for residents who are unsheltered, living in substandard housing, older, medically fragile, or socially isolated. This course supports cities in building “heat stability” for vulnerable populations: systems that reduce repeated heat stress through proactive planning, targeted outreach, and reliable access to cooling and hydration supports. Students learn how heat risk concentrates by neighborhood and vulnerability, and how to design realistic heat-response workflows. During the 3-day intensive, students work with municipal and community partners to assess on-the-ground barriers (hours, transportation, messaging, trust) and co-build a practical response plan.

courses.desc: Environmental epidemiology is the study of how environmental exposures affect human health. Students in Environmental Epidemiology will learn to critically evaluate environmental epidemiology literature, design environmental epidemiological studies, and apply the methods of environmental epidemiology to real-world problems. Students will delve into methods and principles of environmental epidemiology, including exposure assessment, conceptual challenges in the analysis of temporally and spatially patterned data, and specification of consequential research questions.

courses.title: Strategies for Public Health Advocacy
courses.desc:
This course explores the role public health practitioners can play in advocating for programs and policies to improve the public’s health and examines strategies and techniques to promote the funding of public health programs and the adoption of public health policies through legislation or regulation. It first introduces the concept of advocacy and its relationship to the practice of public health. It then reviews the theory and practice of community organizing, including basic organizing philosophy, building coalitions, community empowerment, and basic strategies for community change. It then covers the public policy making process, the role of public opinion in public policy formation, the role of the news media in setting the policy agenda and in framing issues, the role of marketing and public relations in shaping public opinion, and the influence of lobbying at the federal, state, and local levels. Students learn basic skills in community organizing, grassroots mobilization, policy analysis, media advocacy, and legislative lobbying. 

Classes include lectures and discussions, class exercises, and discussions of advocacy case studies, and culminate in a mock state legislative hearing in which students must advocate for or against a public health policy proposal. Throughout the semester, students will follow a specific piece of federal, state, or local legislation, attending committee hearings, legislative sessions, and meetings of public health advocates and community members. Students will prepare framing memos, press releases, op-eds, and legislative testimony relating to an assigned policy issue.

courses.title: Implementation Science: Global Perspectives
courses.desc:
Implementation science aims to accelerate the adoption, scale-up, and impact of evidence-based public health interventions, as new evidence-based interventions take an average of 17 years to be incorporated into routine practice. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), challenges related to implementation are even more profound. Due to limitations in financial resources, skilled health personnel, and infrastructure, evidence-based interventions discovered decades ago - including many vaccines, diagnostic tests, treatment regimens, and mental health counseling strategies - are often not widely implemented in a manner that achieves public health impact for the world’s most vulnerable populations.

This course serves as an introduction to implementation science, through the lens of public health and healthcare delivery challenges faced by vulnerable populations in global settings. The curriculum will cover core implementation science theories, models, frameworks, and approaches for: (1) measuring and identifying gaps in care delivery (e.g., care cascades, delay studies, standardized patient studies); (2) assessing patient or client preferences (e.g., preference methods); (3) developing, adapting, and integrating interventions (e.g., human-centered design, ADAPT-ITT); (4) development of multicomponent implementation strategies (e.g., implementation mapping); (5) hybrid effectiveness-implementation randomized trials; and (6) measurement of implementation outcomes (e.g., the RE-AIM framework). These theories, models, frameworks, and approaches will be taught through their applications in studies in global settings, on issues like global mental health, HIV, tuberculosis, maternal and infant mortality, chronic diseases, parasitic disease elimination, and antimicrobial resistance. We will also have a special session examining strategies for assessing implementation of novel technologies in LMICs. Assignments will ask students to apply theories, models, frameworks, and approaches to major challenges in global public health and healthcare delivery.

courses.desc: This course takes an ecological approach to health. The determinants of individual health can range from individual actions to broad social and environmental conditions. Although interventions can be directed at the individual (for example, helping patients adhere to a low-fat dietary regimen) or to the population as a whole (such as mandating seat belt use) an objective of public health practice is often to encourage people to adopt behaviors that will improve their health status. courses.title: Analysis of Multilevel and Longitudinal Data
courses.desc: Multilevel and longitudinal study designs have become commonplace in public health, biomedical sciences, and medicine. Ignoring the correlative structure of the responses in the analysis leads to invalid tests and erroneous conclusions. This course presents corrective statistical methods that include linear and generalized linear mixed models, repeated measures analysis of variance, generalized estimating equations, and hazards regression models. Each method is discussed in a practical in-depth manner by emphasizing parallels with more familiar regression models and is illustrated by analyzing data using statistical software. The course not only provides guidelines for selecting an appropriate analytical approach but also provides a sound interpretation of the results.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 14) An introduction to moral judgment--and the reasoning it is based on--by a detailed study of current issues such as abortion, vegetarianism, and responsibility for war crimes, and the application to such problems of ethical theories, such as egoism, utilitarianism, and the doctrine of rights.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 30, REL 30 and CVS 54 ) Major religious, philosophical, and scientific thinkers from the 16th to the 20th centuries whose influence led to the eclipse of the medieval worldview and the emergence of a modern one, as well as critics of European Modernity: Luther, Descartes, Copernicus, Kant, Hegel, Darwin, Nietzsche, Freud, Sartre, De Beauvoir, Fanon, and Ghandi.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LING 33). An introduction to fundamental concepts of modern formal logic, including sentence logic, quantification theory, and identity. Emphasis on the application of formal methods to reasoning in philosophy, mathematics, and everyday affairs.

courses.title: Knowing And Being
courses.desc: Introduction to epistemology and metaphysics. Typical topics: truth and relativism, what really exists, what we can know, space and time, existence in fiction, the essence of things, God.

courses.title: Paradoxes and Dilemmas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 40) Introduction to fundamental themes in logic, epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. Paradoxes and dilemmas are frequently associated with moments of crisis and groundbreaking developments in the history of philosophy, as they lead to questions about basic presuppositions. Analysis of famous cases in the history of Western thought from Antiquity to the present including Meno’s paradox (knowledge), Zeno’s paradoxes (space, time, motion, and the infinite), the Euthyphro dilemma (justification), the liar paradox (truth), the Heap (vagueness), the Ship of Theseus (identity), Antigone (moral conflict), the voting paradox (choice), and the prisoner’s dilemma (action).

courses.title: Justice, Equality, And Liberty - Justice, Equality, And Liberty
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 43) An introduction to the central concepts and problems in the foundations of political order, including the nature of the state, rights, justice, equality, representation, property, law, and coercion. Readings from classic and contemporary thinkers.

courses.title: Aesthetics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as VMS 53 & HAA 59) A survey of some fundamental problems in the philosophy of art: the nature of aesthetic judgment; the task of criticism, formalism, and formalist criticism; the idea of antiart; the concept of quality in a work of art; modernist vs. traditional art. The course will include writings in contemporary philosophy and criticism as well as works by philosophers such as Hume, Kant, Nietzsche, and Heidegger.

Course description: This is a course in epistemology, which is the theory of knowledge and justified belief. We will critically examine opposing views about what rationality requires of us. More specifically, we will consider these four topics:

1. Uniqueness vs. Permissivism (Is there just one conclusion that you are rationally required to draw in response to a given collection of evidence, or can a range of different beliefs be equally and fully rational? We will consider examples involving jurors, detectives, and scientists.) 

2. Internalism vs. Externalism (Which facts determine whether your belief is justified or not? Is being rational wholly a matter of what’s going on inside your own mind? For instance, suppose you form your beliefs through a process like “trusting your gut” without having any idea why that belief-forming method might reliably lead to the truth. Or suppose you trust the prediction made by an algorithm or a fortune teller. Does it make a difference in determining the extent of your rationality whether the process by which you formed your belief is in fact reliable? The externalist thinks that it does. Or does it only matter how things appear from your own perspective? This is an internalist view.)

3. Evidentialism & Moral Encroachment (Is evidence for the truth of a proposition the only legitimate basis for believing that claim? What is the proper role of your moral obligations in determining what you ought to believe? For instance, can you be obligated to have more faith in a close friend than your evidence alone would support? Can moral considerations prohibit you from drawing conclusions that are supported by your evidence?)

4. The Authority of Epistemic Norms (If we are obligated to follow standards of rationality in forming beliefs, why is that? What is the source of that obligation and how do we explain it? For instance, is it because accurate beliefs are useful to us as we pursue our everyday goals? Or are we obligated to form rational beliefs regardless of whether it helps us or not? Furthermore, does the practice of assessing the rationality of others serve a valuable social function? For example, does blaming your friends for getting medical advice from social media help to facilitate the sharing of accurate information?)

courses.title: Special Topics - Love and Sexuality
courses.desc: Special Topics. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Course description: Love is a controversial topic for many reasons; one of them is that four traditions of love in the West differ in defining love at its best. They are: The Platonic tradition (Plato, his student Aristotle, and Neo- Platonism), the Christian tradition (mysticism, Catholicism and Protestantism), the Romantic tradition (Medieval Courtly Love, Shakespeare, Romanticism in Philosophy, Literature and Music), and the Realistic Tradition (Epicureanism, Schopenhauer, Freud and the current psychological and scientific research on love). Through a study of these four traditions of love in the West, the course addresses current confusion about the nature of love and about love’s relationship with both friendship and sexuality. The course aims at clarifying our thinking about these matters and at furthering our understanding of forms of love that are not immediately associated with romantic love. Apart from philosophic texts, the course exemplifies these four traditions in literature, poetry, plays, movies, music and the current sex industry. Following the inquiry into the nature of love, various views of the nature of sexuality are introduced and evaluated to complete the in-depth investigation of the nature and relationships of these two powerful yet mysterious forces in human life.

Focus on independent projects that utilize print media to create installations, posters, publications, performance, video, props, and clothing. Project proposal, research methods of production and materials, weekly studio practice, and meeting with the instructor to discuss ideas and motivations. Individual and group meetings support the conceptual and technical development of projects. Most appropriate for intermediate to advanced students working with print media who can source materials and work across studios as needed.

In addition to etching basics (hard ground, soft ground, and aquatint), special attention will be paid to a broad array of intaglio applications: found objects, collagraph approaches, alternative plates (non-etched), collage, and monoprint techniques. Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE), this weekly series invites Tufts students to explore politics and culture by reading controversial books and articles, engaging with faculty discussants and guest speakers, and discussing sensitive political, economic, and social issues with depth, humility, and courage. Each week, participants will encounter sophisticated arguments associated with a diversity of ideological, religious, and cultural worldviews. Lunch will be provided, and seats are limited. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are intellectually curious and want to deepen their understanding of contentious and consequential public affairs and policy issues. The series is also open to faculty and staff attendees.

courses.title: Workshop in Political Science - Alexis de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE), this weekly workshop will undertake a close reading of Alexis de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America. Participants will examine the work in its historical context and assess its relevance to American politics and civic life nearly two centuries after its publication. Discussions will explore Tocqueville’s observations of nineteenth-century American society, including his accounts of “equality of conditions,” “tyranny of the majority,” and “self-interest properly understood,” as well as the relationships among the state, civil associations, and religion. The group will consider what these ideas reveal about the enduring tensions among liberty, equality, and democratic governance. The group will be facilitated by Shani Agarwal Hood, CEVIHE Program Manager, and Oscar Gonzalez, AG27, with faculty and other guest facilitators leading selected sessions. Students from all disciplines and majors are welcome. Members of the Tufts community who are not registered for credit may attend as observers, subject to available space, and should contact CEVIHE for more information.

courses.title: Workshop in Political Science - Individualism and Nonconformity in Film
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
Class Dates: Thursday, 2/11, 2/18. 3/11, and 4/8

This class is scheduled in the OPEN session. Dates for registration and add/drop are dynamically dated commensurate with the length of the class. Students may add this class through 2/18/27 can drop without record through 3/4/27, and can withdraw through 3/1/27. Refund deadlines can be found at https://students.tufts.edu/financial-services/billing/tuition-refund-policy

Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE) in collaboration with the Film and Media Studies Program (FMS), this four-part film series invites Tufts students to examine the themes of individualism and nonconformity through screenings of landmark films drawn from a range of historical periods, political contexts, and cinematic traditions. Each session features a full-length film paired with faculty framing and guided discussion, allowing participants to analyze how individuals navigate the tension between personal conscience and collective pressure, and how political and social institutions respond to dissent. The series asks participants to think critically about moral independence, civic responsibility, and the costs and consequences of resisting conformity. Popcorn and pizza will be served. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are interested in exploring contested ideas, competing loyalties, and acts of principled resistance that shape public life. Faculty and staff are also welcome to join.

courses.title: Introduction To Comparative Politics
courses.desc: Theories and evidence in comparative politics, preparing students for upper-level courses that focus on specific regions, countries, and themes. The rise and fall of democracy in selected countries from different regions such as Western Europe, Eastern Europe and Russia, East Asia, South Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America.

courses.title: Western Political Thought II
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 42 and CVS 52.) Central concepts of modern political thought. The views of those writers who challenged the dominance of Christianity: Machiavelli, Descartes, Hobbes, and others. Some of the main transformations of political thinking that characterized the Enlightenment: the possibility of scientific thinking and reasoning as the basis for human freedom. Nietzsche's critique of the Enlightenment, and the ability to find political principles that are genuinely true or liberating.

courses.title: Justice , Equality, And Liberty
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 43.) An introduction to the central concepts and problems in the foundations of political order, including the nature of the state, rights, justice, equality, representation, property, law, and coercion. Readings from classic and contemporary thinkers.

courses.title: Introduction To International Relations
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 61) Examination of several conceptual designs intended to make order out of the essential anarchy in international relations, from a theoretical assessment of the nation-state and the nature of national power to an exploration of behavior among nation-states, including the ultimate problem of war and peace and an appraisal of the factors that give an age its particular characteristics.

courses.title: Future of Global Institutions (EPIIC)
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 81) Education for Public Inquiry and International Citizenship (EPIIC) explores the role of global institutions in contemporary world affairs, beginning with a critical examination of theoretical concepts and debates about global institutions and global governance. Origins of the UN in the aftermath of the Second World War. Overview of the African Union and other regional organizations. Leadership role of executive heads of international organizations, especially the UN Secretary-General. Appraises the substantive work of global institutions on peace and security, sustainable development, human rights, the rule of law, humanitarian affairs, and the environment.

sections.note:
The Future of Institutions: The Politics of the Past: Memory and Historical Narrative

“The ways in which the memories of past events are interpreted, misinterpreted, or even manipulated in public discourse create the context that shapes international relations.” -- from Power and the Past: Collective Memory and International Relations
 
How do people(s) construct a sense of the past, and what are the implications of how that history is told? Can there be shared cultural knowledge when there are competing narratives, especially as a result of traumatic events? Why do some pasts triumph, while others fail, and how do those decisions affect future decisions and power relations? This class will explore the connections between the cultural, political and historical aspects of memory, as well as the connections between representation and social experience.

This year marks the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Declaration of Independence, a set of ideas that became a transformative, global event. How has the memorialization of those ideals manifested in today’s partisan politics? Rwanda faces a bifurcation between those that continue to be defined by the 1994 genocide and those ready to be defined by the country’s current accomplishments. Memory attached to land is a powerful driver, from Israel/Palestine to the Field of Blackbirds to the legacies of partition in South Asia. What some call “memoryscapes” are often deep-seated historical, cultural and emotional attachments driven by violence, displacement, dispossession. 

What is a national memory? How are national and international events memorialized and how are those memorials experienced by current and future generations? 
 
What is the influence of collective and/or competing memories on foreign policy formation? How is the cultural made political? How are historical narratives being used from Ireland to Russia to define territorial boundaries? 
 
This yearlong class is organized with frequent guest lecturers where students have the opportunity to organize and enact an international symposium.

courses.title: Fieldwork In Politics
courses.desc: Internship placements with such employers as legislators, campaigns, news media, lobbies, law firms, and administrative agencies. Twelve to fifteen hours of work per week. Written assignments, with supporting readings, on organizational structure, goals and strategies, and occupational socialization.

sections.req: PS (11 or 21, 41 or 42 or 61) and any two PS courses

courses.title: The Presidency And The Executive Branch
courses.desc:
Study of the constitutional development of the presidential office, its power, prestige, and functions, as well as the influences of the person occupying that office. Major emphasis is on the process of policy formulation in the executive branch. Analysis of the president's relations with his staff, the bureaucracy, the Congress, the press, and the public.
Recommendations: Sophomore standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Political Science Research Methods
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CVS 148). The study of quantitative methods for investigating political issues and policy controversies. Focuses on collecting, analyzing, and presenting data. Emphasizes hands-on training that provides useful skills for academic and professional settings. Topics covered include: measurement, hypothesis development, survey design, experiments, content analysis, significance tests, correlation, and regression. No prior statistics background necessary. Prerequisites: PS 11, 21, 41, 42, or 61. A methodologically focused course.

sections.req: Completion of any Political Science Foundation Course: PS 11, 12, 41, 42, or 61 or Political Science first year tutorials: PS 2, 3 or 4, or CVS 20

courses.title: Political Psychology
courses.desc: Employs social and cognitive psychological theories to examine politics. Focuses on the roles of thought, emotion, behavior, institutional design, and the linkages between them in shaping political outcomes. Topics may include information processing, rationality, emotions, personality, stereotyping, prejudice, intergroup conflict, and altruism. Most coursework emphasizes politics in the United States, though the material speaks to political science broadly. Methodological-focus with emphasis on the use of experiments in political science research.

courses.title: Seminar: Policymaking Under Separation of Powers
courses.desc: Advanced seminar on policymaking in each branch of government in the United States, including the legislative process, presidential unilateralism, bureaucratic rule-making, and federal court rulings. While each branch can unilaterally influence policy, they can also frustrate other branches’ policymaking efforts. Prerequisites: Junior standing or instructor consent. Recommendations: PS 0011

courses.title: Topics in American Politics - Social Movts & Amer. Pol Inst.
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Social movements are important drivers of institutional change. The American constitutional system influences how these movements emerge – and whether or not they are successful. In this class, we explore theories of how social movement mobilization, followed by an overview of the American political system, focusing on the intersections between movements and institutions in multiple venues. We conclude with an analysis of movement-state interactions from the 1960s to present, focusing on how progressive and conservative movements have reshaped the political order through the party system, tracing movement-state development from the Civil Rights Movement to the MAGA and Democratic Socialist movements of the 2020s. Students will engage with scholarship from sociology, political science, and history in this fast-paced and rigorous course that asks students to consider how change occurs in the American political system. The final product of this course is a 15-20-page original research paper on a case of the student’s interest, including a research presentation to the class.

courses.title: Seminar: Power And Politics In China
courses.desc:
Advanced seminar on sources of political power and resistance in post-Mao Chinese politics. Debates in recent research over state strength, origins of political reform, development of civil society, prospects for democratization, corruption, censorship, religion, and protest.Please see departmental website for specific details.
Prerequisites: PS 126 or HIST 41, or permission of instructor.

sections.note: This course examines how democracies confront both perennial and acute challenges to their institutions and principles. Themes include theories of democratic origins and survival, the role of civil society and the media in times of crisis, and patterns of protest and collaboration. Cases include countries from around the world and across time, but there is a particular focus on the contemporary United States

courses.title: Topics In Comparative Politics - Demo. & Development in Asia
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Examines the core questions about democracy and development in the Asia-Pacific region. Cases covered include Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Indonesia, the Philippines, and India. Topics include state formation, democratization, elections, political parties, presidential and parliamentary systems, civil society, ethnic conflict, democratic backsliding, strategies of economic development, welfare states, economic inequality, climate change, migration, and relationship between democracy and development.

courses.title: Topics In Comparative Politics - Protest & Mobilization Israel
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
This course applies a social movement perspective and analysis of collective action to the Israeli social and political scene. The aim is to examine the diverse movements that have shaped the country’s social, religious, and ethnic conflicts, situating these in a comparative setting and examining which are unique to the Israeli experience and which are more common cross-nationally. 
The course is divided into three parts: part one, Introduction to Social Movements and Contentious Politics, provides an overview of the theoretical foundations of social movement theory. Part two, Israel: A Movement Society, explores the development of a range of movements which have shaped Israeli society since the pre-state era. Part three, Between War and Peace, focuses on the different types of mobilization that have developed around the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Throughout the course students will be challenged to consider the shared patterns of mobilization reflected across cases, the connections between the development of Israeli social movements past and present, and the cumulative impact of the emergence of these movements on the shape of Israeli political institutions, governance, and society. The course has no prerequisites, however students are expected to come to class having done the readings and be prepared to actively engage in discussion.

courses.title: Seminar: Political Thought of Montesquieu
courses.desc:
Examination of Montesquieu's political thought through his comparative analysis of political regimes in his major work, Spirit of Laws. Topics include the principles that guide tyranny, monarchy, and republican government, the principle of separation of powers, the meaning of political liberty, the impact of commerce on political life, the relation of mores to laws, and the character of Montesquieu's liberalism. His other works, The Persian Letters or Considerations on the Greatness of the Romans and Their Decline, will also be considered.Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: Sophomore standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar: Hannah Arendt
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 118 & JS 157) Hannah Arendt (1906-1975) personally experienced some of the great events of the 20th Century, interacted with many famous contemporaries, and offered challenging arguments about totalitarianism and democracy, migration and human rights, Jewishness and Israel, modernity and science, feminism, activism, and the role of intellectuals. Critical discussion of her texts, her life, and her context. Comparison of her ideas to those of other thinkers and issues of the present.

sections.req: Requires the completion of one PHIL course or graduate standing

courses.title: Topics In Political Thought - Medieval Christian Politcal Thought
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course will explore the political thought of Latin Christendom during the high and late Middle Ages, from c. 1050 to c. 1550. Political thought during this period was shaped by the recovery of Roman law, the transmission of Greek and Arabic texts to western Europe, persistent conflict between church and empire, the development of modern European state structures, and global encounters across the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Through engagement with the core political genres of the era: mirrors for princes, summae, commentaries, and legal treatises, students will consider fundamental debates concerning: the relationship between civil and ecclesiastical power; the sources of law; public office; tyranny; theories of universal empire; and international law.

courses.title: Topics In Political Thought - Literary Roots of Modern World
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course engages with key literary texts from antiquity through the early modern period. We will begin with some of the earliest works in the Western traditions, the biblical cycle of stories surrounding King David and Homer’s Odyssey. We will then read other classical texts, works by Sophocles, Aristophanes and Virgil, before we move forward to a set of works from the early modern period, beginning with Sir Thomas More’s Utopia, an important work of both political theory and literary play. After discussing Machiavelli’s comedy Mandragola and two plays by Shakespeare, we will conclude with John Milton’s epic Paradise Lost, which can be read as a kind of summation of the classical and biblical inheritance. The class does not function as a survey; the literary landscape is too complex and varied to even sample effectively in a single semester. Rather, it is designed to serve as a series of glimpses into the roots of the modern literary tradition.

courses.title: Cyber-Security & Cyber-Warfare
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 28) An interdisciplinary analysis of cybersecurity and cyberwar in the United States and other countries. Policymaking and intelligence aspects of cybersecurity and political science and the technical constraints of computer networks and software. Exploit methods including packet analysis, password cracking, social engineering, reconnaissance, and malware analysis. State-backed and non-state actors engaged in cyber-espionage, counterintelligence, deterrence, and offensive cyber-operations. Prerequisites: Political Science 61 or Computer Science 11.

courses.title: Migration, Refugees, And Citizenship In A Globalized World
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 167) Analysis of the causes and consequences of modern population movements that have occurred around the world since the late twentieth century, and recipient states' reactions to it. Topics include the political, economic, social, and security determinants of refugee and migration flows; the political and social responses of receiving governments and societies; the security and crime-related issues and concerns engendered by international migration; changing conceptions of citizenship and nationality in receiving states; the role played by the international institutions in influencing state policies towards refugees and immigrants, and the moral and ethical issues for public policy posed by international population movements. Cases examined are drawn from throughout the world, with particular emphasis on Europe and the United States.

courses.title: Seminar: Better Than The Truth: Extra-Factual Information in International Politics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 165) Examines the sources, manipulation and consequences of unverified and unverifiable information – such as rumors, myths, propaganda, and conspiracy theories – in international politics, with a particular focus on the influence of such information on the formulation and conduct of foreign and defense policy. Prerequisites: PS 61 and senior standing.

sections.req: Prior completion of PS 61 and Senior Standing

courses.title: Topics In International Relations - Masc., Politics & Modern War
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: How do images of masculinity and male socialization shape everyday politics, the militarization of states and societies, and the conduct of war? This methodologically focused course examines the influence of ideas and norms of masculinity on contemporary politics and modern warfare. It tackles a wide range of topics, from political competition and sports to scientific research on the biological and social foundations of aggression, overconfidence, risk acceptance and group violence. We will consider evolving norms of masculinity in American political culture from the Cold War through the contemporary era of America First, as well as the social and political forces behind the development of missile technologies and the national security state. Along the way, we will examine public opinion and domestic support for war, debates over military conscription and battlefield effectiveness and the politics of disability and post-traumatic stress disorder. Although the course draws on research across disciplines and subfields, our discussions will repeatedly return to questions in International Relations. Recommendations: PS-61 and sophomore standing.

courses.title: Topics In International Relations - Dictators, Generals & War
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Why do dictators go to war, and how does authoritarian rule shape the way wars are fought? This course examines the domestic politics of war and peace in authoritarian regimes, exploring how political institutions, regime survival, civil-military relations, bureaucracies, economic interests, and leaders’ individual characteristics shape decisions about the use of force. Along the way, we will consider whether democracies and dictatorships behave differently in international politics, why some autocrats are more constrained than others, how dictators build and manage their militaries, and what authoritarian politics can tell us about risk-taking, nuclear weapons and the conduct of war. Recommendation PS-61.

courses.title: Topics In International Relations - An Introduction to AI Safety
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
An Introduction to AI Safety: Rewards, Risks, and Responses 

This course focuses on issues of AI safety and governance and adopts a socio-political approach to the promise and perils of AI development and deployment. We will explore what AI is, what it can do at present, and what is driving its advancement; identify who are the key players and what are their interests; and unpack the benefits that may accrue from AI as well as the political, economic, social, and security risks it—and its uses by humans—may pose. We will also examine potential responses to AI risks; discuss putative trade-offs between risks and rewards and related ethical issues; and identify methods for bolstering resilience should risks become active threats. This course assumes no prior knowledge of AI and no training in computer science, machine learning, or other related discipline.

courses.title: Topics In International Relations - Int. Law & Israel-Hamas War
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course explores the international legal arena surrounding the Israeli case more broadly and the Israel-Hamas War in particular. The first section begins with a broad introduction to the Israeli-Palestinian arena, setting the stage that led to the Israel-Hamas War. This section includes a discussion of concepts and definitions used in the course. The second section focuses on the international legal system. Beginning with the first codifying of legal principles for modern warfare at the end of the 19th century, it takes us through the establishment of the United Nations, the Geneva Conventions, and the legal definitions of concepts like war crimes, terrorism, crimes against humanity, and genocide. The third section focuses on the evolution of the war between Israel and Hamas since October of 2023. Each week covers a different facet of the war and its relation to international law, including the October 7th attack, Israeli attacks in Gaza, humanitarian aid in Gaza, regional spirals of violence, the international court system, and the legal aspects of proposed day-after plans. By the end of the course, students will have a clear understanding of which questions should be asked with regards to each development in the war, granting them tools to analyze these developments.

sections.note: This senior seminar focuses on the foreign policies of a number of emerging candidates for regional power in the Middle East (Russia, Turkey, Iran, Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia) in the context of a potential retreat of American hegemony. It combines four main elements: a review of the burgeoning theoretical literature on mid-level power dynamics; an investigation of the linkage between domestic factors – particularly competing conceptions of identity – and foreign policy in each country; a chronological survey of each country's security policy; and in-depth analyses of the emerging dynamics between them. courses.title: Seminar In Psychology - Wired to Value: The Neuroscience of Reading Others
courses.desc: Contemporary problems in selected areas of psychology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: The social inclination of humankind, including our fundamental ability to correctly interpret and evaluate other people, is tightly linked to the value individuals imbue on experiences related to other individuals. In this upper-level seminar we will examine how a neurobiological mechanism, the reward circuitry, manifests in such social contexts. Students will investigate up-to-date functional models of the reward circuitry, refresh their knowledge on theories of motivation, and through in-depth discussions review contemporary evidence for the critical role the reward system plays in our ability to evaluate others—to the point that it biases judgments and leads to phenomena such as in group preference. This course has been approved to count as an elective for the Biopsych or CBS major (Part IIIA) in S27. Requires: Any 10- or 20-level PSY course, or PSY 103, or graduate standing (PSY 13 or PSY 25 or PSY 103 would be ideal).

courses.title: Seminar In Psychology - Belonging, Equity, & Education
courses.desc: Contemporary problems in selected areas of psychology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This seminar examines educational inequality through a social psychological lens, focusing on how identity, power, and institutional contexts shape student experiences and outcomes. Students explore the historical foundations of inequality in U.S. education alongside contemporary issues such as school funding, segregation, access to opportunity, and institutional practices that shape educational experiences. Drawing on theories of social identity, bias, schemas, and group processes, the course analyzes classroom dynamics, discrimination, peer relations, social hierarchies, belonging, mental health, and representation across educational contexts, including STEM. An intersectional approach—engaging frameworks such as Critical Race Theory, queer theory, disability studies, and related critical perspectives—guides analysis of how race, gender, sexuality, class, and ability intersect to influence educational experiences. The course also integrates perspectives from organizational and educational psychology to examine how institutions, relationships, and learning environments shape motivation, well-being, and access to support. Requires: Any 10- or 20-level course in PSY or graduate standing.
sections.req: Requires the completion of any PSY 10 level course or any PSY 20 level course or graduate standing.

courses.title: Seminar In Psychology - Psychoneuroimmunology
courses.desc: Contemporary problems in selected areas of psychology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Why can't you think as clearly when you're sick? How can some bacterial infections cause rapid-onset psychosis? Why would first trimester influenza drive a 7x increased risk for offspring schizophrenia? Why does COVID in the elderly increase the risk of Alzheimer's onset? Cutting edge research questions often occur at the boundaries of systems once incorrectly thought to be separate, like the nervous system and the immune system. This course introduces relatively new neuroscience field, Psychoneuroimmunology, that blurs the boundaries among psychiatry, neurology, and immunology. This course has been approved to count as an elective for the Biopsych or CBS major (Part IIIA) in S27. Requires: PSY 12 or PSY 25 or PSY 103

courses.title: Seminar In Psychology - Biological Basis of Violence
courses.desc: Contemporary problems in selected areas of psychology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Ever wondered what caused a nasty act of aggression? This seminar explores the hidden forces behind some of our most surprising behaviors -aggression and violence. The course begins with an overview of genetics, neurons, and the brain/nervous system. We build on contemporary methodologies in clinical, social, cognitive, developmental, and behavioral neuroscience to help explain why brazen behaviors sometimes occur. The course then emphasizes recognized reciprocal relationships between experiential factors and the nervous system, starting with how the brain coordinates highly complex social behaviors like aggression and violence in the moment. We will then consider influences on longer timescales and how they bias these consequential patterns of neural activity. From there, we consider how the brain continually reorganizes itself over the lifespan, helping explain the diverse range of human behaviors. This course has been approved to count as an elective for the Biopsych or CBS major (Part IIIA) in S27. Requires: PSY 25 or 26 or 103

The goal of this course is to help graduate students integrate neurobiology and its methods with behavioral and motivational issues in psychology. We will cover the essentials of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and neurochemistry and use that information to understand current theories and experiments on the biological bases of sexual behavior and sexual differentiation, hunger and body weight control, and learning and memory. Readings will include texts in neuroscience and original literature in physiological psychology. We will discuss the readings and in these discussions I will take into account the varying levels of familiarity with this literature and the different interests of the students. This heterogeneity can be an asset in a seminar and lead to the uncovering of some interesting alternative perspectives. During the semester each student will pick one topic in physiological psychology to research in depth and write a paper on that subject. courses.title: Rigorous and Reproducible Research Practices
courses.desc:
This course will provide graduate students with an overview of contemporary debates and practical solutions to conducting rigorous, reproducible quantitative research. In addition to learning what rigor and reproducibility actually mean, we'll discuss the whys and hows of statistical inference and transparent research practices (e.g., sample size planning, preregistration, sharing data and materials), and best practices for reporting and evaluating research. We'll also consider thorny issues surrounding conducting and evaluating replication research, giving and responding to scientific criticism, and the everyday incentives that shape scientists' behavior. Students will come away having developed a principled understanding of relevant concepts and a set of concrete tools for producing and consuming high quality science.

courses.title: Introduction to Studies in Race, Colonialism, and Diaspora
courses.desc: Introduction to the study of race, colonialism, and diaspora within and beyond the United States. Examines the major themes and interdisciplinary approaches across these intersecting fields: Africana studies, Native American studies, Colonialism studies, Latinx studies, Asian American studies, and American studies. Materials span the Americas, Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and Europe . Provides opportunities for place-based study of the historical and cultural impact of slavery, colonialism, and diaspora on greater Boston.

courses.title: Introduction to Asian American Studies
courses.desc: Histories of East, South, and Southeast Asian migration and settlement in the United States from the late 18th century to the present. Heterogeneous histories, cultural productions, and contemporary issues that shape the field through historical analysis, memoir, art, film, and digital media. Topics include labor migration, community formation, U.S. imperialism, legal exclusion, racial segregation, gender and sexuality, cultural representation, and political resistance. Explores the shifting meanings of “Asian American” over time, employing transnational and diasporic frameworks to situate Asian American history within broader histories of race, gender, and empire.

courses.title: Introduction to American Studies
courses.desc: Rethinking the concepts “America” and “American” to explore foundational myths and images, counter archives, and undocumented (forgotten, erased) knowledges. Using various media (historical documents, literary, legal and scholarly texts, visual and aural media, material artifacts, archival ephemera) and the broad interdisciplinary methods of the field of American studies to excavate the historical, ideological, and structural underpinnings of the “American” project. Situating the history and politics of the United States within broader hemispheric and global contexts.

Full Title: Native American & Indigenous Environmentalisms
Class Description: This mid-level interdisciplinary course examines Native American and Indigenous approaches to land caretaking and ecological justice, culminating in an independent research project. Topics covered include:  Native American and Indigenous philosophies of land relationality; traditional ecological knowledges; relationships to western environmentalism; and political, social, and cultural mobilization.

courses.title: Special Topics - Asian American Poetry
courses.desc: Mid-level courses open to undergraduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Class Description: Poetry in English has been written by Asian Americans for a century and a half in this country, even if the term ”Asian American” itself dates from the late 1960s. This course will be a broad survey of various styles of Asian American poetry in English from the late nineteenth century to the present, with an emphasis on more “experimental” writing in recent decades. Students will learn how to close-read poems but always with an eye to the broader political, historical, and social contexts of the writing, which are themselves reflected in the poetry’s aesthetics. No prior knowledge of poetry required.

courses.title: Special Topics - No City on a Hill: Race and Boston
courses.desc: Mid-level courses open to undergraduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
Concentrating on our vibrant and complex metropolitan Boston region, this course critically considers the relationship between racialization and the urban built environment in the modern United States. Pairing classroom study with student-driven research and engagement across urban sites, we will investigate how racial formation, racism, and racialized resistance have shaped the fundamental fabric of Greater Boston.
Our work will span urban and environmental studies; cultural history and politics; artistic expression and performance; and critical theory, among many fields. Geographically, we will consider various locales, including but not limited to Boston's downtown core; Chinatown; Roxbury and Jamaica Plain; suburban districts; and Indigenous tribal territories. We will also ask how communities around Boston have influenced the development and circulation of critical race theories and politics, within this region and well beyond. Through these inquiries, we will foreground an intersectional, relational approach to race and space — one that does not try to read fixed or independent racial categories onto the city, but instead highlights the urban processes and experiences of racialization connecting diasporic European, African, Asian, and Indigenous life in greater Boston.
Our classroom studies will build a nuanced, interdisciplinary understanding of key questions and topics. Throughout the semester, students will then elaborate and shape that learning with site-specific research at chosen sites around Boston, and will incorporate their own metropolitan lived experiences into what we study.

courses.title: Special Topics - South Asian Diasporic Literature
courses.desc: Mid-level courses open to undergraduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
This course will question how a broad range of South Asian writers from the United States, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, interrogate questions of dispersal and migration to explore the global dynamics of the diaspora. We will look at how the writings we read deploy a diasporic critique as a mode of refusal — of belonging, nationalism, colonialism, heteronormativity, assimilation and model minoritization. And we will look at the possibilities and impasses that are opened up by South Asian diasporic literature as a mode of resistance. Authors may include Bapsi Sidhwa, Salman Rushdie, Anita Desai, Amitav Ghosh, Arundhati Roy, Taslima Nasrim, Micheal Ondaatje, Avni Doshi and more. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Palestinians & Israelis: Ethnographies of Justice
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ANTH 143 and CST 143) Ethnographic approaches to the study of Palestinians and Israelis with various legal statuses and cultural and religious backgrounds; migrants in Israel; Palestinian refugees in the Middle East and beyond. Comparative analysis based on concepts of race, colonialism, diaspora, and indigeneity. Analysis of mobilizations for justice for Palestinians and Israelis, primarily but not exclusively in the Middle East.

courses.title: Racial Capitalism & Settler Colonialism in the US
courses.desc: Historical and cultural analysis of US capitalism as a set of economic, cultural, and ideological systems. Emphasis on Black Studies and Native Studies approaches to the study of capitalism, race, and colonialism as related structures. How enslavement and racialization made capitalist development possible in the United States (and beyond). The role territorial dispossession and settler colonialism have played in the expansion of capitalist relations in the US. How capitalism shapes the relationships between diverse human and more-than-human beings. Prerequisite: RCD 50 or instructor permission.

courses.title: In the Flesh: Race, Performance, Sex, and Skin
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as SMFA 135 and TPS 135) Seminar on theatre and dance performance, sculpture, and new media about how skin obscures or reveals race, gender, and sexuality. Builds on the "theory in the flesh," based on the material lives of minoritized bodies, advocated by women of color feminism. Focus on performances where skin is a site of oppressive history and liberation, the limits and possibilities of embodied knowledge, and the co-constitutive social forces of race, gender, sex, sexuality, and nation. Artists studied may include Kara Walker, Narcisister, Regina José Galindo, Jeremy O’Harris, and Xandra Ibarra. Prerequisites: RCD 050, TPS 001, or TPS 002.

courses.title: Special Topics Research Seminar - Strong Feelings
courses.desc: Upper-level special topics course offered by RCD faculty members drawing on their current research. See current listings at https://as.tufts.edu/rcd/.

sections.note:
FULL TITLE: Strong Feelings: Affect, Race and Performance Studies

Feelings are instructive; consider what comes to the body when you read "fear, joy, shame, disgust, ugliness, paranoia, guilt”. Feelings and sensations teach us about attachment and transformation, and yet until recent times, they have remained a largely understudied field in the humanities. This course will attune to the intersection of affect studies, performance studies, and aesthetic theory, particularly as each field relates to conditions of power across difference. We will consider diverse artistic media that model the aesthetics of sensation as well as teach us how feeling is curated through form. Course includes attending live performance. Authors include José Esteban Muñoz, Sianne Ngai, Leticia Alvarado, Cathy Park Hong and Eve Sedgwick, among others. Graduate Level Seminar in TPS, Open to advanced undergraduates. Instructor/department permission needed.

courses.title: Special Topics - Black Power/Red Power
courses.desc: Upper-level courses open to advanced undergraduate students and graduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Class Description: Heeding recent scholars' calls to place Black Studies and Native American and Indigenous Studies in more active dialogue with each other, this seminar examines the Black Power and Red Power movements. Students will engage both primary and secondary sources and attend to the ways in which these movements rejected the possibility of Black and Indigenous incorporation into the American polity and instead called for self-determination and political autonomy. Rather than limiting our consideration of Black Power and Red Power to the late 1960s and 1970s, we will take a “long movement” approach to thinking about these movements. Broad topics covered will include sovereignty and self-determination, and and community control, revolutionary violence and self-defense, gender and sexuality, and solidarity.

courses.title: Special Topics - Scenes of Revision
courses.desc: Upper-level courses open to advanced undergraduate students and graduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Examination of revision in African American literature within the contexts of enslavement, surveillance, material scarcity, and racial violence during slavery and Reconstruction. Analysis of texts revised, sometimes repeatedly, by authors including Phillis Wheatley, John Marrant, William Wells Brown, Hannah Bond, and Frances Ellen Watkins Harper. Attention to the material effects of revision and questions of authorship, agency, print culture, and archival recovery. Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Special Topics - Disordering the World
courses.desc: Upper-level courses open to advanced undergraduate students and graduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
This course introduces students to the fields of critical race and disability studies. We will read contemporary African American literature and cultural production to interrogate how racial slavery and colonial genocide have shaped contemporary disability politics—specifically our ability to see pain, address illness, and negotiate capacity. Together, we will discover how disability is shaped, regulated, and disciplined through cultural expectations of racial, sexual, and gendered normalcy. This course reads varied literatures and cultural forms including black queer psychiatric survival literature, indigenous poetry, black trans carceral critique, and experimental film against definitions of disabled embodiment produced within the wellness industry, psychiatry and medicine, welfare policy, and eugenicist discourse. Reading black queer, chronically ill, and neurodivergent voices, this course attempts to reorganize our understanding of human need and human suffering from the position of bodies differently abled and marked for reform. Students will develop mad black and feminist analyses of disability and develop skills in close reading, critical thinking, and argumentative writing. Content warning: this course deals with sensitive topics related to mental health. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 59) Study of the origins of Christianity and the evolution of its earliest beliefs and practices, as reflected in the writings ultimately selected for its canon. Jesus and his interpreters, Paul and his letters, beginnings of the church, interaction between Christians and their jewish and Greco-Roman enviroments, women's paticipation in the shaping of early Christian history. courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 16) Introduction to the philosophical analysis of major religious concepts, such as God, human nature, freedom of will, immortality, and the problem of evil, through a study of representative types of religious philosophies.

courses.title: Gurus, Cults, and Utopias
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 34) Introduction to the study of modern and contemporary New Religious Movements (NRMs) in specific regional contexts (South Asia, the United States, and Japan) and as a global phenomenon. Explores central questions in the study of religion around charismatic leadership, sect formation, utopianism, social mobility, gender, and violence. Influential 20th-century theories of religion and recent critical analyses of transnational, new age, esoteric, and alternative spiritualities.

courses.title: Global History of Christianity since the Middle Ages
courses.desc: (Cross listed w/ CST 37 and HIST 15) Development of Christianity as a world movement from the early modern period to the present. Major themes include Protestant Reformations; expansions of Christianity through exploration, trade, conquest and mission; diversity and transformations of Christian traditions in colonial and post-colonial societies; global spread of evangelicalism and pentecostalism.

courses.title: Gender in Rabbinic Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 88 and HEB 62) Overview of the ways in which gender is used as an analytical tool in the study of rabbinic literature. Examines how rabbinic sources challenge the traditional understanding of the gender binary. Contrasts traditional historical questions about the roles of men and women in society with more contemporary approaches that view gender as socially constructed, contested, and fluid. In English. No prerequisites. No knowledge of Judaism or rabbinic literature is assumed. If taken at the 100-level: Extra assignments and class meetings in Hebrew.

courses.title: Readings in the Study of Religion - Religion and Technology
courses.desc: The academic study of religion through scholarly-theoretical texts, lectures, and films. Topics include theory of ritual and myth, history of the field of religion, anthropology, political philosophy, and current events that intersect with the study of religion. Prerequisite: Must have taken at least one class in the Religion Department at Tufts.

sections.note: 1-credit reading group. We will meet five times over the course of the semester, to read and discuss contemporary scholarship in the study of religion. This Spring, REL 98 includes visiting speakers and focuses on the intersection of religion and technology/AI: 1) religion, ethics, and algorithmic dating practices, 2) technology in Africana religions, and 3) AI-driven religious apocalypticism. Specific dates TBD.

courses.title: Sacred Spaces, Contested Places
courses.desc: An exploration of religion as emplaced, embodied, material and spatial. What makes some places sacred? What is the relationship between place and religious experience? Why do some sacred sites become scenes of conflict? Discussion of religious geography, spatial politics, environment and pilgrimage, with selected case studies from Jewish, Christian, Native American, Hindu, Buddhist, and Muslim traditions.

courses.title: Evangelicalism in America
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CVS 130, AMER 121, HIST 126) History of evangelical Christianity in North America from the 17th century to the present. Attention to issues of theology, race, class, gender, culture, politics and globalization. Consideration of relationships among evangelicalism, fundamentalism and pentecostalism. 
Recommended: One lower level course in the history of Christianity (REL 12 or 63) or one lower level course in American religious history (REL 42, 47, 48, 49), OR permission of the instructor

courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Ancient Christianity
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ WGSS 160 and CLS 159) Examination of gender and sexuality in the ancient Mediterranean, with special attention to how issues of gender and sexuality are treated in the New Testament, in early Church Fathers, Hebrew Bible, martyrdom accounts, and hagiography (saints’ lives). Consideration of pre-Christian sexual ethics and the structure of the family in Mediterranean patriarchal cultures (in this
case Greeks, Romans, and Judeans) and discussion of the sexual ethics found in the writings of figures like Pythagoras, Plato, and the Stoics. Discussion of how early Christians (second through the fifth centuries CE) simultaneously reinscribe traditional gender roles and notions of sexuality, and also subvert these roles and ideas. Consideration of the conflict over the right of women to hold
positions of authority and alternative avenues of power such as renouncing sexuality & marriage, and voluntary martyrdom. The rise of sexual renunciation as a central feature of ascetic Christianity and attention to the ways that women and men strive to shed the trappings of “this mortal coil” by denying sexuality full-stop.

courses.title: Introduction to the Zohar
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 180 & HEB 179) Broad overview of the Zohar, the 13th-century foundational text of Kabbalah with roots in mysticism. Expiration of the Zohar and its enduring influence on Jewish thought and life, through various lenses: literary, theological, mystical, and artistic. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Romance Linguistics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LING 96) Broad overview of linguistic complexity of the Romance languages, their relation to the greater Indo-European group, and their specific transformation over many centuries. Basic synchronic and diachronic linguistic description and analysis. Consideration of social, geographical, political, and cultural factors that hastened the fragmentation of Vulgar Latin and the development of its modern descendants, relation of language to cultural identity, and the advantages and disadvantages that this mosaic of languages poses for the European Union as well as Central and South American nations. courses.title: Elementary Russian
courses.desc: Continued introduction to the fundamentals of Russian. Focus on developing active speaking, reading, and listening skills. Students gain a solid understanding of Russian grammar and develop basic writing skills. Upon completion of the course, students can talk about their families and hometowns, biographies and plans for the future, and make purchases and order food. Students learn about Russian culture through short readings, songs, and videos. Recommended: Russian 1 or placement exam and permission of instructor. Students may not earn credit for RUS 02 if RUS 01/2 has already been taken.

courses.title: Intermediate Russian
courses.desc: Continued expansion of speaking, reading, writing, and listening skills. Emphasis on vocabulary development. Videos, recordings, and more extended readings enhance the student’s understanding of Russian culture. Compositions and oral presentations. Recommended: Russian 3 or placement exam and permission of instructor.

courses.title: Contemporary Russian Culture
courses.desc: Exploration of Russian culture through literature, film, the media, and the arts from the era of "stagnation" to glasnost, perestroika, and the post-Soviet period. The destruction and reconstruction of cultural and political canons and myths: the Stalinist legacy and reevaluation of Soviet history; the revival of religion and nationalism; social dislocation: the problems of youth, the generation gap, and women's issues; the breaking of taboos and the dark side of freedom--violence, crime, pornography, and neofascism; the liberalization and commercialization of art. All readings and films are in English. Course may be taken at 100 level with additional hour and readings in Russian.

courses.title: Russian-Jewish Experience: Revolts and Returns
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 79) Exploration of 19th to 21st century Russian Jewry through survey of literature, memoirs, film, and art. Jewish cultural history in Russia and USSR from the creative experiences of Russian Jews in the context of various historical periods. Discovery of a multidimensional picture of the unique socio-cultural environment that shaped the identity of the modern-day Russian-speaking Jews from the former Soviet Union through literary works, visual media, popular songs, works of art, and theater performances, translated into English from Russian and Yiddish. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Russian & East European Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 86, ILCS 81, & FMS 65) Examination of a series of masterpieces by filmmakers from "the other Europe": the Soviet Union/Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and the former Yugoslav territories. Explores the role of film in terms of its artistic achievements and social commentary: As a tool in the transition to the new Soviet order; as an alternative means of expression during censorship; and, more recently, as a corrective tool in fragile new democracies and a voice of protest fighting against new forms of oppression. No prerequisites. In English.

courses.title: Special Topics - Culture Under Totalitarianism
courses.desc: Courses on selected themes and authors given in English. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: After World War II and at the beginning of the Cold War, political philosopher Hannah Arendt recognized National Socialist German and Stalinist Soviet Union as totalitarian; a new form of government that was simultaneously modern and barbaric, incredibly terrifying and violent but also rationally organized and socially bureaucratic. This course will focus on the role of culture and cultural production as both support and subversion of these totalitarian societies, investigating and interpreting works of art, literature, film, music, architecture, etc. produced under these regimes. We will learn about how cultural producers navigated their own (often politically informed) aesthetics and ethics within the strictures of totalitarian censorship.

courses.desc:
Explores objects as form, material, and content. Examines relationships between objects, everyday experience, and understandings of the past. Considers the presence, performance, and cultural significance of objects. Investigates processes and techniques related to the use, mass production, and sourcing of objects. Produce multiple works using assigned objects as source material. No prior sculpture experience necessary. 

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Material Matters!
courses.desc: Explore sculpture with nontraditional materials and processes. Experiment with a new material every two weeks while engaging with recent scholarship in material culture studies and theory. In-class demonstrations and discussions will guide individual experiments and projects by using the properties of the provided materials as a point of departure. Students will gain insight into contemporary issues in sculpture while testing material limits and meanings in their own work. No previous experience in sculpture is required. Open to all.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Performing Objects
courses.desc:
Investigate the role that the object plays in performance. From prop to stage to costume to relic, sculpture and performance are closely linked disciplines where body and object inform one another to create meaning. Explore various manifestations and hybrid forms through self-directed projects, critiques, readings, discussions, field trips and introduction to the work of contemporary working artists in the field.

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

sections.note: Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

courses.title: Advanced Sculpture Projects
courses.desc:
Advanced Sculpture Projects is a studio and seminar course designed for self-directed students working on an advanced level. Seminars will include topic-based lectures, weekly readings, viewings, field trips and critiques. Students will present two self-directed finished works for critique and three research-based presentations.

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

Builds on foundational woodworking skills through intermediate and advanced studio projects using wood as a primary material. Students develop self-directed work supported by demonstrations, technical workshops, critiques, and discussions. Emphasis is placed on material intelligence, structural thinking, and project planning through processes such as advanced joinery, structural systems, carving and shaping, and hybrid material approaches. Projects support increased scale, complexity, and conceptual rigor across sculptural and object-based practices.

courses.desc: See departmental website for details.
