Introduces steel fabrication and welding as foundational processes for sculptural practice. Students develop skills in metal preparation, cutting, grinding, welding, cold connections, structural design, fabrication, and safe Welding Shop practices. Projects emphasize material behavior, structural problem-solving, planning, joining, and construction. Successful completion provides foundational Welding Shop training and prepares students for continued fabrication-based work. Introductory level. No prior welding or metal fabrication experience required.

courses.title: Special Topics - Introduction to Woodworking
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Enrollment is limited to SMFA students only until November 30 at 10am.

Examines foundational woodworking processes through hands-on studio practice using both hand tools and machines. Introduces wood properties, material behavior, and basic fabrication strategies, including measuring, cutting, joinery, shaping, and surface treatment. Technical demonstrations and workshops support the development of safe tool use, structural thinking, and material literacy. Through a series of guided exercises and studio projects, students create objects of their own design using additive and subtractive processes. Lectures, discussions, and occasional field trips provide additional context for contemporary woodworking practices.

courses.title: BFA Capstone
courses.desc: Develop culminating art project that demonstrates artistic, conceptual, and technical learning achieved through undergraduate study. Participate in faculty-led interdisciplinary critique groups and technical workshops, advancing artistic practice and preparing projects for public exhibition. Learn installation strategies and professional gallery practices with TUAG staff. Develop exhibition proposals, project descriptions, artist statements, catalog production, and documentation materials within a supportive structure that strengthens each artist’s ability to articulate and advocate for their artwork. Bridge undergraduate study and life beyond school through professional public exhibition experience that prepares artists to navigate practices, expectations, and opportunities of the contemporary art world and related creative fields.

courses.title: In the Flesh: Race, Performance, Sex, and Skin
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 135) Seminar on theatre and dance performance, sculpture, and new media about how skin obscures or reveals race, gender, and sexuality. Builds on the "theory in the flesh," based on the material lives of minoritized bodies, advocated by women of color feminism. Focus on performances where skin is a site of oppressive history and liberation, the limits and possibilities of embodied knowledge, and the co-constitutive social forces of race, gender, sex, sexuality, and nation. Artists studied may include Kara Walker, Narcisister, Regina José Galindo, Jeremy O’Harris, and Xandra Ibarra. Prerequisites: RCD 050, TPS 001, or TPS 002.

courses.title: Interdisciplinary Practices
courses.desc: Studio and seminar course that investigates the role of painting and art in communicating and reflecting upon other topics including science and the humanities. Surveys methodologies for incorporating research into a creative practice and gives students time to develop their own processes for making creative work about a topic of their interest. Examines knowledge construction and encourages the integration of current research information into artistic discourse. Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Practicum for Studio Credit - Editorial Illustration in STEM
courses.desc: Supervised professional training, serving as a bridge between academic studio practice and client-based work. Develop an independent, cohesive body of artwork while engaging in the practical aspects of a career in the visual arts. See Class Notes for topic details.

sections.note:
Create an original, interpretive visual artwork that reflects ongoing scientific research at the School of Engineering. You will work in a client-based model with multiple labs, producing a portfolio of narrative, concept-driven pieces that translate scientific ideas into compelling visual forms. Students are expected to attend weekly meetings with Lab leaders and the faculty supervisor to complete 3 sets of assignments throughout the semester. Successfully completed artwork will be shared publicly whenever feasible, with clear credit to the student artist.

Open to 3rd year and above, students who are responsible, deliver work in a timely manner, and are open to feedback. Creative image makers across all media are welcome to apply via handshake with a portfolio of 5-10 images. Registration is based on the instructor’s approval.

courses.title: Post Baccalaureate Seminar
courses.desc: The Seminar is a mandatory core component of the curriculum for post-baccalaureate students, who take it both fall and spring semesters. Content is determined by the needs of the class and changes from fall to spring. The seminar includes professional presentations, student presentations, directed group discussions and writing projects, critiques of work, and visits to museums, galleries, collections, and other sites. We discuss the work and ideas of class members in the context of broad issues such as the role and purpose of art making, the practice of art as a career, and the perspectives currently under discussion in art criticism and theory. Emphasis is on group collaboration and peer support for individual artistic development. To keep discussion groups small, faculty lead separate seminar sections. (These groups occasionally hold meetings together.) Be ready to talk at the first class about your ideas and needs in your artwork, school, and prospective career, so that we can plan the semester's content.

courses.title: Post Baccalaureate Consultations
courses.desc: Individual critique sessions promote and foster abundant work and rapid progress by helping you deepen an understanding of your art, creative process, and work methods through focused critical feedback at regular intervals. Students meet individually with the instructor several times during the semester for critiques, to present works in progress, and to discuss emerging issues of individual interest. These consultations support and complement the work in the Post-Baccalaureate Seminar. Post-baccalaureate students are expected to actively seek individual critiques and consultation from their assigned faculty advisors and from faculty members teaching studio courses in which they are working.

courses.desc: One-on-one meetings with faculty and group meetings over the course of the semester to critique work, assess progress, and develop mentorship. Critique sessions promote and foster abundant work and rapid progress, deepening understanding of the creative process and work methods. Prior to 1st meeting, student must present a statement of intent, quantifying expected output, topics of interest and goals. At the end of the semester students summarize their work via an all class critique that includes a developed artists statement. Upper classmen and advanced students (MFA, Post-Baccalaureate, Diploma or Third and Fourth year BFA Students). Faculty permission required.

courses.title: Grad Group Critique
courses.desc: This course is designed to build and develop the verbal and written articulation critique skills among the first and second year graduate students in a group setting facilitated by a faculty member. Critique is an essential skill for students to develop. Graduate Group Critique is a forum in which the capability of each student to identify and articulate the concerns, issues and motivations that form the basis of their research and practice expands. Through focusing on the ability to articulate the concerns investigated and addressed through each individual student’s art work, in whichever form that may take, this course assists students in both preparing for their review boards and preparing for the defense of their thesis. All first and second year Master of Fine Arts students are required to take this course each semester.

courses.title: Intro. to Sociology: The Scientific Study of Society
courses.desc: Introduction to the systematic and scientific study of human social behavior. Topics include how history and social structure shape individuals’ daily interactions and experiences in the world, how individuals co-create social categories and cultural meanings together through interaction, and how human behavior varies across large and small groups. How societies maintain social control, set up stratification systems based on class, race, and gender, and regulate daily life through institutions such as families, schools, politics, and labor markets.

courses.title: Death & Dying
courses.desc: Death and dying as fundamentally social processes in contemporary society. How the end of life is socially managed in the United States, including the historical evolution of ideas about a “good death” and changing practices surrounding the treatment of the dead. Topics include social and cultural variations in death and dying; the influence of social location–such as race, class, gender, and inequality–on end-of-life experiences; the role of medical, legal, and bureaucratic authorities in classifying and defining causes of death; and the impact of social institutions, including family, law, medicine, and religion, on practices of dying, death, and mourning.

Individual faculty sponsor internships in their areas of expertise. Students must have an on-site supervisor, and complete a piece of meaningful scholarly work related to the internship area.Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: SOC 1 or 10, plus one additional course in sociology related to internship area. To be arranged by individual members of the department.

courses.title: Research Design and Interpretation
courses.desc: Introduction to common empirical research methods to understand and explain social phenomena. Crafting of sociological questions and designing research to answer them. Methods include surveys, experiments, ethnographic methods, in-depth interviewing, material-based research, and focus groups; addresses the strengths, limitations, and complexities of each approach. Application of methodology through interpretation and critical assessment of existing research to become skilled consumers of sociological research.

courses.title: Qualitative Research Methods
courses.desc: Advanced course specializing in qualitative methods (e.g., ethnographic observation and in-depth interviewing). Epistemological foundations of qualitative research design, sampling, and methods, including related ethical issues. Development of an original research project, including formulation of a researchable sociological question, review of the sociological literature, identification of field sites, development of consent forms and interview guides, completion of systematic observations and qualitative interviews, coding and analysis of data, and development of a clear sociological argument and final paper simulating a published academic journal article. Strongly recommended for students interested in conducting independent qualitative research (e.g., senior honors theses).

sections.req: Must have 2 sociology CoursesSociology Majors and Minors only

courses.title: Sociological Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 112) Examination of major theoretical traditions and their critical challenges in sociology. Explores diverse frameworks that address systems of power and oppression (e.g., racism, misogyny, capitalism, colonialism, adultism, and their intersections). Sociological discussions focusing on modernity, evolution of society, community and division, domination; approaches to highlighting past and contemporary social divisions and imagining social visions for alternative futures.

sections.req: Requires the completion of at least one Sociology course.Sociology Majors and Minors only

courses.title: Urban Sociology
courses.desc:
Sociology Cities as global phenomena, studied with classic texts on U.S. urban social life and transnational comparisons. Analysis of economic globalization, redevelopment, and landscape formation in cities. Case studies of local politics and planning, socioeconomic inequality, urban cultural change, and citizenship struggles.
Recommendations: SOC 1 or 10 or consent.

sections.note: Must have taken SOC 1 or 10 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Law and Society
courses.desc: Examines the connections and relationships between law and the social world using an interdisciplinary approach to understand the lived experience of law. Topics include legal institutions and the legal profession; law and social control; and law’s role in promoting or hindering social change.

courses.title: Race and the Criminal Justice System
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ CVS 122) Foundational concepts in the study of race, crime, and justice. Social construction and measurement of race and crime. Historical evolution of institutions of racial social control and rise of mass incarceration. Current practices in policing, courts, and punishment. Efforts to reform and transform the criminal justice system. 
Prerequisites: Sophomore standing and one sociology course, or permission of instructor

sections.note:
Social theory is one of the major intellectual traditions that informs the contemporary study of performance. This seminar combines select readings from classical sociological thought (Marx, Weber, Durkheim and others), with contemporary works of performance theory and analysis, such as those by Schechner, Phelan, Butler, and Muñoz. The seminar examines both theatrical concepts in works of social theory, and social theoretical perspectives on performance in both its aesthetic and off-stage forms.

This course is available to graduate students and upper-level undergraduates.

sections.note: This course is designed to examine the interrelated fields of tourism, gastronomy, and music in Latin America and Spain, focusing on the challenges and/or incitements these areas pose. Topics discussed include mass tourism in places such as Machu Picchu; ecotourism and its environmental damage in the Galapagos Islands; white-saviorism and voluntourism in Mexico; gentrification of quinoa and other indigenous foods; narcotraffic’s links to avocado production; sexism and rebellion in reggaeton and cultural appreciation vs. appropriation in music, and many other topics. The course includes an outside-classroom experiential project, zines, guest speakers, as well as variety of multimodal materials (films, articles, podcasts, videos, websites, and songs). Students must register for a recitation. Prerequisite: Spanish 21 or consent.

courses.title: Spanish Language through Culture II - ¡De cine!: Superando desafíos
courses.desc: Continued advanced grammar review begun in Spanish 021 with emphasis on written and oral expression. Compositions, oral reports and class discussions based on literary texts, films, and topics of general interest. Required weekly recitation session. Conducted in Spanish. Recommendations: Spanish 021, SPN 005, or consent.

courses.title: Spanish For Heritage Learners
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as LST 23) Development and expansion of reading and writing skills for students without formal training in the language but with ability to comprehend and speak Spanish because of their heritage. Study of grammar and stylistics, differences in regional dialectics, vocabulary expansion and effective communication based on literary and cultural readings. Conducted in Spanish.

courses.title: Diversidad: Identity & Dissent in Modern Spain
courses.desc: Exploration of cultural productions that shaped the history of Modern Spain from the 18th century to the present. Interdisciplinary approach to literary texts, films, songs, and visual works to examine Spain's diverse identities. Key questions include whether Spain can be considered a modern country and how modernity is reflected in its contemporary literary and cultural productions; whether religion remains a defining characteristic of modern Spain; and what non-canonical works reveal about equality and freedom in the country. Topics and literary movements may include the Enlightenment, Romanticism, Realism, Modernism, Generations of ‘98 & ‘27, immigration, and nationalism. Development of critical skills by analyzing diverse cultural forms to understand their historical significance and contemporary relevance. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

Spanish 22, Spanish 23, or consent of the instructor

courses.title: Latin America: Cultural Perspectives
courses.desc: Exploration of the cultural productions that have shaped key moments in the histories of Latin America and the Caribbean, from the early 20th century to the present. Interdisciplinary approach to literary texts, films, songs, and visual works to unpack the complexity of Latin American cultures and their ongoing transformations. Key questions include how identities are constructed and how they relate to literature, film, and the dynamics of cultural production and in what ways artistic movements and popular culture engage with these identities. Topics may include modernity, the Latin American literary boom, authoritarianism, the climate crisis, and indigeneity. Development of critical skills in analyzing diverse cultural forms to understand their historical significance and contemporary relevance. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Convivencia: Identity and Dissent in Early Modern Spain
courses.desc: Interdisciplinary study of cultural expression in Spain between the 11th and 17th centuries, a period of coexistence and intense exchange between Christians, Muslims, and Jews that culminated in the creation of a unified, monocultural Spain. Focus on key literary texts and corresponding cultural materials, like art, music, historical documents, to examine the beliefs underpinning major social and artistic developments of the era. Topics such as national identity, gender, religion as devotion and suppression, and models of love and beauty may be interwoven with an exploration of how the Catholic Kings’ concept of empire influenced the myth of Convivencia. Understanding of contemporary cultural forms and society by recognizing their origin in Spain’s past. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Spanish 22, Spanish 23, or consent of the instructor

courses.title: Latin America: Colonial (Dis)encounters
courses.desc:
Cultural, social, and political transformations from pre-Hispanic civilizations to the late 19th Century. Focus on colonial and post-colonial materials to explore how colonial legacies continue to shape our contemporary world. Topics may include indigenous worldviews, (often violent) encounters between European and Native American cultures, the imposition and adaptation of colonial structures, slavery and its
legacies, evangelization and syncretism, and literature's role in shaping and challenging colonial ideologies. Analysis of historical objects, connecting them to contemporary issues, to understand the ongoing relevance of colonial histories in modern societies. Development of cultural literacy skills by analyzing diverse forms to appreciate their historical significance and interconnectedness. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Health and Illness Through Literature in Spanish
courses.desc: Explores narrative and film in Spanish as tools to engage critically with health, illness, and care. Draws on the interdisciplinary fields of Health Humanities and Narrative Medicine. Examines representation of stigmatized illnesses such as cancer, HIV/AIDS, infectious diseases, and mental health to understand the influence of cultural, social, political, and economic contexts on health and wellbeing. Analysis of fiction, poetry, film, podcasts, visual representations, and graphic novels to develop critical thinking, empathetic listening, and close reading skills. Conducted in Spanish. Recommended: Two courses above SPN 22 or instructor permission.

courses.title: From Poets to Songwriters: Lit & Music in Spain
courses.desc:
The Silver Age of Spanish literature, the New Latin American Song, and the Catalan Nova Cançó inspired a generation of “cantautores” in Spain during the 1960s and 1970s. How singers and poets have carried on this tradition into the 21st century, blending literature and music to reflect Spain's historical, social, and cultural landscape over the past 75 years. Exploration of the role of songwriting with emphasis on original compositions, adaptations of literary classics, and the perspectives of recent generations.

Emphasis on historical contextualization to examine how the visual and literary renditions have fused with political events, both within Latin America and abroad, to construct these iconic figures. Students analyze how television narratives engage with issues such as social class, inequality, gender roles, sexuality, family, immigration, public institutions, and social change. Readings drawn from cultural studies, sociology, gender studies, and contemporary social and historical contexts provide analytical frameworks for interpreting the social realities represented on screen. courses.title: STS Reading Lab - AI Hype
courses.desc: Reading- and discussion-only course, intended to complement courses outside the STS curriculum. Discussion of readings from a list organized around rotating topics of interest. Topics vary by semester and may include energy, life, information, classification, power, and models. See STS website or SIS detail view for semester-specific information. Course but not topics may be repeated for credit.

sections.note:
AI is an industry, a suite of technologies, a cultural phenomenon, and – ultimately – a series of promises. Advocates and developers rely on grandiose claims in promoting the technologies and political arrangements on which they depend. Sometimes these are apocalyptic: fears of terrorism, or alien sentience. Sometimes these are utopian: curing cancer, or solving global warming. But whether focused on hope or doom, hype aims to influence how we (individually, and collectively) think about and respond to these technologies. How are we to understand these narratives? How do we evaluate claims made by those promoting AI? And what do such claims ‘do’?
This class will explore (and answer) each of those questions, by looking at how imagined technological futures shape our social and regulatory responses to those technologies in the present. Looking at both primary sources of AI hype, and critical evaluations of them, students will learn how to analyse, evaluate and respond to claims about not only algorithmic technologies, but promised futures more generally.

courses.title: Global Cities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 20 and UEP 20) Introductory-level urban anthropology class exploring cities as intersections of people, ideas, capital, and the physical environment. Themes include anthropological understandings of space and place-making; utopic and dystopic urban visions of the city; urban mobility; cities as nodes in global environments, economies, and networks of people and production; sensory experience and expressive culture in cities; urban "nature" (e.g., parks); difference and inequality in urban landscapes; the growth of urban populations and megacities; and tensions between the city as planned or conceptualized and the city as a lived experience.

courses.title: A Cultural History of the Internet
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 7) The internet as cultural and historical phenomenon and the power structures embedded in digital platforms. Internet development from early computational ideas to digital culture and interactive media. Foundational technologies including the Jacquard Loom and Babbage’s Analytical Engine, the emergence of networked computing and World Wide Web, and the explosion of online communities. Focus on internet culture: memes, digital art, remix culture, early social platforms, and interactive web-based games and artworks, from net.art experiments to Flash animations and viral browser games. Concludes with YouTube and the foundations of contemporary social media, when user-generated content became a dominant force in global media. The internet’s impact on media production, storytelling, and cultural identity.

courses.title: Introduction to AI and Society
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as AI 20 Introduction to how AI systems are developed, deployed, and managed in a broader societal context. Technical foundations relevant to discussions and critiques of AI systems. History of AI and computation and their roles in society, with a focus on social issues such as privacy, the environment, and labor. Technical foundations include principles of computing and programming such as data representation, problem decomposition, and algorithm design.

courses.title: Special Topics - Contraptions
courses.desc: See program website for details

sections.note: “Contraptions” are a weird kind of technology: they may work, but they don’t work right. This course is a workshop in the anthropology of technology, dedicated to exploring the figure of the contraption in social and cultural context. How do people decide that a technology is complicated, or too complicated for a particular use? Why do some technologies seem to barely work, and how do we know what it means for a technology to work in the first place? How do people respond emotionally to technologies, finding them funny, pathetic, or even liberatory? Topics will range from early anthropological debates about technical and social complexity to contemporary concerns about the programming behind AI agents. We’ll talk about how hacks, kludges, and workarounds of all kinds might change the way we think about how technology works and why it works the way it does. Alongside course readings and discussion, students will collaborate with a team from the School of Engineering to build and critique contraptions of their own.

courses.title: Special Topics - Fandom: Economics of Attention
courses.desc: See program website for details.

sections.note:
COURSE: Fandom, Inc.: The Platform Economics of Attention

Why does the algorithm seem to know you’re going to love that book, that band, or that reality show…before you do? 

Fandom feels organic, but it isn’t: every community that forms around a book, a band, or a reality-TV cast is built by the platforms that host it, the studios and publishers that profit from it, and the fans whose attention is the product being sold. This course treats fandom as a case study in platform economics and media strategy, tracking three case studies whose platform architectures couldn’t be more different—Heated Rivalry and BookTok’s open algorithm, BTS and HYBE’s owned Weverse ecosystem, and Love Island’s broadcast-plus-live-vote model—to ask who profits when we fall for something, and why. No fandom membership required.

INSTRUCTOR: Courtney Elston is a Technical Product Manager for AI Content Discovery at Audible, where she builds the recommendation and discovery systems used by millions of listeners, and serves as the company’s in-house romance and BookTok subject-matter expert. She previously built BookCrush, a discovery platform for romance readers, and holds an MBA from MIT Sloan.

courses.title: Technologies of Enchantment

Compares the design, use, and reception of techniques ranging from animal trapping to user experience design. Topics may include hunting, machine gambling, scams, advertising, magic, art, hospitality, persuasive design, behavioral addiction, and algorithmic recommender systems. courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 152 and WGSS 151) Theories and ethnographies of biopolitics and biopower. Reading of conceptual and ethnographic texts at the intersection of science, medicine, the state, and capital. Topics include neoliberal governmentality, hegemony of interventionist biotechnologies, bioethics, biosecurity and management of risk, biocapitalism, necropolitics, logics of social abandonment and disposability, political rights, and projects of biological and social enhancement.

courses.desc: Early performance rituals in Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Europe; the classical drama of Greece, Rome, and India; and the theatre of medieval Europe and Asia. Special attention paid to the ways theatre has challenged or supported the society that produced it and to how ethnicity, gender, sexuality, religion, class, and other social constructs have shaped performance, playwriting, and production. Relationship between these cultures and their theatres through a close examination of approximately twenty plays, related critical readings, research, presentations and discussions. May be taken before TPS 11 and/or TPS 12.

courses.title: The American Musical: Radical Acts and Adaptations
courses.desc: (Crosslisted w/ TPS 114 and MUS 20) Exploration of the American musical, most notably the “Broadway musical,” from the early 20th century to the present. Examination of musicals as products of their cultural moments, revealing American attitudes about race, gender, class, and ethnicity. Consideration of the established narratives, limited binaries, and systemic whiteness the American musical has traditionally embodied. Focus on innovative, even revolutionary, musicals and how they have evolved through adaptation and revival. Discussion of the musical as a global phenomenon and the impact of changing media technologies including social media on this dynamic, increasingly intercultural form. No prerequisite. Lower level of dual level course.

courses.title: African American Theatre And Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as AFR 48 and FMS 59). A broad historical survey of plays and films by African Americans. Comparison of cinematic and theatrical representations. Relation of African American aesthetics to broader American, European, and Pan-African forms. Historical evaluation and comparison of images created by African Americans and those established in the mainstream milieu. (May be taken at 100 level for graduate credit with consent.)

courses.title: Asian American Theatre And Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with AAST 19) Survey of the field of Asian American film and live performance from 1970s to the present, with emphasis on their exploration of cultural and racial difference, gender, sexuality, family, generational conflict, ethnicity, and identity. Weekly or bi-weekly film screenings required. (May be taken at 100-level for graduate credit with consent.)

courses.title: Art of the Moving Image - Sophomore and Junior
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 51 & FMS 1) Exploration of cinema's basic aesthetic characteristics: its stylistic features, such as editing, cinematography, and sound, as well as its major narrative and non-narrative forms: mainstream and avant-garde, fiction and non-fiction, narrative and non-narrative, black-and-white and color, silent and sound. Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

courses.title: Television History
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with FMS 6) Examination of the introduction and development of U.S. television during the network era (40s-90s). Development of television (in the U.S. and within a global context) from its conception through its industrial, technical, aesthetic, and textual development to understand how American broadcast television emerged as a dominant cultural force around the world. Explore how specific analytical concepts in television studies develop. Learn and practice how media theory takes on historical research. Fulfills the FMS media history requirement.

courses.title: Greek And Roman Comedy
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 56.) Study of plays of Aristophanes, Menander, Plautus, and Terence and the contexts in which they are performed. (May be taken at the 100-level.)

courses.title: Critical Drag
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/WGSS 1) Exploration of drag as a performance practice that aestheticizes gender for purposes such as entertainment, socio-political critique, and labor. Creation of individual drag personas and performances considering intersections of gender, nationality, race, class, and disability to understand the implications of putting gender on the body, on stage, and in everyday life. courses.title: Introduction To Acting
courses.desc: A basic course in acting aimed at enhancing self-confidence, oral expression, and creativity. Emphasis on concentration, motivation, and improvisation, and what it means to create a character and speak before an audience. Limit of eighteen students per section.

courses.title: Acting for the Camera
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 24) Performance based acting course that teaches techniques to make emotional connections and create nuanced, truthful performances on camera. Work with filmed monologues, scenes, commercials, and workshops with casting professionals. Learn how to use information such as platform, director, genre, and creatives to determine how to approach performance. Focus on acting techniques, character development and emotionally connecting to material with a small portion of the course addressing the "business of acting" which will include union membership, auditioning, and creating reels.

courses.title: Musical Theatre: Scene and Ensemble
courses.desc: A multi-layered, performance based approach to employing the singing voice in conjunction with scripted scenes to accomplish full, rich, and truthful acting. Develop an approach to understanding the internal life of a character using musical information, acting techniques, and embodiment within the context of a scene from the American Musical Theatre. Use mind, body, emotion, and voice to be present and connected with scene partners. Foster a versatile, flexible, vocal instrument, an open and curious musical mind, a generous and collaborative spirit when working with other artists, and the confidence that comes with repeated performance and growth.

courses.title: Voice And Speech - The Art Of Confident Expression
courses.desc: A course in persuasive communication designed to empower students to speak with confidence and fluency in any situation. courses.title: Public Speaking
courses.desc: Introductory course exploring the fundamentals of clear, confident, and effective communication in one-on-one and group settings. Development of tension management skills, good breathing habits, awareness of body language, and the ability to engage an audience through a series of practical exercises. Specific vocal work focuses on tone, variety of pitch, rate, volume, and articulation. Satisfies Humanities Requirement Fall 2006 and beyond.

courses.title: Stage Management

courses.title: Performance and Globalization
courses.desc: “Globalization” names the conditions that control cross-border flows and interdependence of capital, labor, media, ideology, and the desires that incite and impede them. These conditions are often set into motion by projects of empire building and the mission to occupy, extract, and exploit land, labor, resources, and culture. But sometimes the elements are unruly, subjects ungovernable, and culture too opaque to appropriate. Sometimes the itineraries initiated by global projects create strange encounters in the ocean or shadow economies at the border that were not the intention of the institutional effort. Performance can be a useful method to trace the complicated itineraries of globalization, to capture ongoing and multidirectional movements. Further, performance repertoires travel with globalization: languages, rituals, taste, recipes, etc. Performance is also a tool of empire building, securing power through embodied pedagogy, and by stripping subjugated people of communication and culture. This graduate seminar offers students an opportunity to follow a performance practice, form, or genre across borders, and to consider how performance and culture are transformed by shifting migrations, attachments, and proximities. Readings and assignments are designed to assist students in applying a variety of analytics to their area of focus.

sections.note:
FULL TITLE: Strong Feelings: Affect, Race and Performance Studies

Feelings are instructive; consider what comes to the body when you read "fear, joy, shame, disgust, ugliness, paranoia, guilt”. Feelings and sensations teach us about attachment and transformation, and yet until recent times, they have remained a largely understudied field in the humanities. This course will attune to the intersection of affect studies, performance studies, and aesthetic theory, particularly as each field relates to conditions of power across difference. We will consider diverse artistic media that model the aesthetics of sensation as well as teach us how feeling is curated through form. Course includes attending live performance. Authors include José Esteban Muñoz, Sianne Ngai, Leticia Alvarado, Cathy Park Hong and Eve Sedgwick, among others. Graduate Level Seminar in TPS, Open to advanced undergraduates. Instructor/department permission needed.

courses.title: Serving a Healthy Diet
courses.desc:
In a world of conflicting food messages, how do we know which foods are good for us? What is the evidence for why you might want to incorporate foods like leafy greens, beans and berries more often into the meals you prepare? How do you construct a menu that tastes good, meets the nutrient and health requirements for an individual or group, and is culturally appropriate and responsibly sourced? 
Planning and implementing healthy meals for customers, clients, family, and friends can pose a challenge. In this course we explore the relationship between diet and health by examining the habitual eating patterns, e.g., Mediterranean-style, vegetarian, etc., that have been shown to prevent chronic diet-related conditions such as heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. We learn about the nutritional components of the foods and beverages commonly present in these healthy eating patterns and to implement strategies that will help those we serve make better food choices. 

Course Objectives:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to
•	Describe healthful dietary patterns and summarize their common factors. 
•	Identify the healthful properties of foods, how to responsibly source those foods, and how preparation influences their properties.
•	Create a healthful dish based on principles of maximizing flavor while mitigating chronic disease risk.

instructors: Diane Louise McKay, Julia M. Appel

courses.title: Food is Medicine 101: Translating Evidence to Action
courses.desc:
The Food is Medicine 101 continuing education (CE) course aims to educate medical professionals on the critical link between nutrition and health and its application to the healthcare setting. This 1-hour course will provide definitions of Food is Medicine (FIM) and its related programs; context of FIM within the current state of chronic disease, healthcare costs, and health inequities; evidence-based information about interventions that integrate FIM into patient care; practical strategies for applying FIM in clinical settings; patient experiences; policy directions; and resources for further learning.
This is a continuing medical education module, intended for healthcare providers, including doctors, nurses, other health professionals who qualify for continuing ed credit from ACCME and/or ANCC (e.g. physician assistants, registered dietitians).

courses.title: Global Cities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 20 and ANTH 20) Introductory-level urban anthropology class exploring cities as intersections of people, ideas, capital, and the physical environment. Themes include anthropological understandings of space and place-making; utopic and dystopic urban visions of the city; urban mobility; cities as nodes in global environments, economies, and networks of people and production; sensory experience and expressive culture in cities; urban "nature" (e.g., parks); difference and inequality in urban landscapes; the growth of urban populations and megacities; and tensions between the city as planned or conceptualized and the city as a lived experience.

courses.title: Land Use Planning: Regulatory Tools and Techniques
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 201) Local government’s attempts to manage and control land use through the use of regulatory options such as zoning, subdivision control and other government-imposed restrictions on private property including more creative approaches including transfer of development rights, impact fees and development agreements. (Non-Regulatory controls are the focus of UEP 200 Land Use Planning: Nonregulaory Tools and Techniques). Review of differing state approaches to comprehensive planning and the connection between a plan and resulting actions; analysis of “regulatory takings” and related issues defining the breadth of local government power to shape land use decisions. Graduate standing or consent.

courses.title: Introduction to Geospatial Humanities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 175 and CLS 125) Geographic Information Systems (GIS) theory, methods, and technology for applications in the humanities in past and present settings. Topics include GIS data creation and data structures, geodesy, spatial analysis, and cartographic visualization. Includes extensive laboratory exercises to apply concepts presented in the lectures using a variety of GIS software and tools. Assignments concentrate on application of concepts covered in lectures and exercises and include a final project that applies GIS to each student’s field of interest.

courses.title: Transportation Planning
courses.desc: Course looks at major passenger transportation modes including walking, bicycling, transit and automobiles. Focus on the skills and tools needed to effectively plan transportation projects- both directly through planning skills and indirectly through managing consultants. Course is presented within the context of how transportation intersects with communities, including how transportation impacts neighborhoods, the elderly and disabled, the price of affordable housing, economic development and overall quality of life. "Hands-on" approach with many guest speakers and a final project that will integrate course-work with student's professional interests.

courses.title: Homelessness In America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 161 and CSHD 186) Multi-disciplinary course examining the social, economic, and political dimensions of homelessness in the United States. Overview of causes, historical responses, and current conditions. Analysis of housing and welfare policies, mental health and substance abuse issues, economic and employment concerns. Volunteer work at shelters and organizations addressing homelessness required.

courses.title: Community-Based Investing – Systems & Practice
courses.desc: The course will explore the core principles and practices of community-based investing. If we wish to address the growing wealth gap and ecological challenges of our times, we need to create the opportunity for communities to own and control their future. That means circulating investment dollars locally, transforming the governance structures that allocate capital so people most affected have the most say, and designing investment approaches that make wise use of blended capital—integrating debt, equity and grantmaking. Students will have an opportunity to apply these concepts in group projects by learning how to design, structure, raise and manage an impact investing fund dedicated to creating sustainable, resilient and inclusive local economies. The course will take a whole systems approach to place-based change, covering the role that many stakeholders play in contributing to community wealth building, including entrepreneurs, investors, philanthropy, anchor institutions, policymakers, professional service providers and community members.

courses.title: Blended Return: Impact Investing Measurement Tools and Processes
courses.desc: The course begins with an exploration of the correlation between values systems, measurement processes and the necessity to pursue efficiency for any values systems. The course reviews traditional financial return models to offer models for calculating blended return on investment for investors, firms, policy makers, ESG fund managers and others seeking tools to create informed choices for driving impact investment. Content ranges from an overview of traditional GRI reporting, ESG ratings criteria and rating systems to emerging tools for measuring impact at the local scale. The course will branch and allow students to critique and explore practical applications to impact measures within their own fields of interest. The course also explores existing and emerging metrics, data sets and the way impact is measured from the international level (UN SDGs) to the community level. Students will come away with the tools and information to identify risks and opportunities within portfolios, the skills to screen and value investments based on data, and an understanding of how to integrate ESG criteria into management and investment decisions.

courses.title: American Indian Policy, Planning, and Law
courses.desc: Contemporary policies and laws affecting American Indians in the United States. Reviews the history of U.S.–tribal relations and legal and planning issues in civil and criminal jurisdiction, as well as environmental and land-use regulation on and off the Reservation. Emphasis on the allocation of authority among tribal governments, the federal government, and state and local governments, with attention to planning implications.

courses.title: Urban Studies Capstone
courses.desc: Urban studies capstone project on an urban studies topic such as a research paper, an oral presentation, a video, a photographic exhibit, a fictional narrative, or other forms of study. Credit will be given at the discretion of a project committee consisting of two faculty members.

courses.title: Urban Design and Changing Suburbs
courses.desc:
Explores how planners, policy makers, and placemakers can reverse the negative impacts of suburbs by retrofitting them and creating more sustainable communities. Examines evolving challenges and narratives of the suburban landscape, physical and social. Traces the evolution of successive types of suburbs,
history of racial exclusion, and the rise of suburban poverty. Looks at current manifestations of sprawl. Students learn tools like Illustrator, InDesign, and SketchUp to create examples of transforming suburban environments into vibrant, sustainable, and connected communities.

courses.title: Land Use Planning: Regulatory Tools and Techniques
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 101) Local government’s attempts to manage and control land use through the use of regulatory options such as zoning, subdivision control and other government-imposed restrictions on private property including more creative approaches including transfer of development rights, impact fees and development agreements. (Non-Regulatory controls are the focus of UEP 200 Land Use Planning: Nonregulaory Tools and Techniques). Review of differing state approaches to comprehensive planning and the connection between a plan and resulting actions; analysis of “regulatory takings” and related issues defining the breadth of local government power to shape land use decisions. Graduate standing or consent.

courses.title: Planning for Low Impact Development and Green Infrastructure
courses.desc: The course is designed to present a comprehensive approach to site planning and development that incorporates low-impact development approaches and techniques. Also known as green infrastructure, low-impact development is a conservation-based site planning and design process that sets aside critical open space buffers, reduces impervious surfaces and concentrates development into appropriate “building envelopes”. It also includes a broad range of best management practices including green roofs, bioretention, rain gardens, vegetated swales, constructed wetlands, infiltration systems and alternative wastewater management systems.

courses.title: Environmental Law
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CEE 207 and ENV 109) This survey course explores the evolution of environmental and natural resource law and examines if, where, and how it addresses climate change among several other pressing environmental threats. The course also reveals the challenges presented by the intersection of environmental issues and our political process and the critical role played by planners and policy makers. The course is designed for those considering careers in environmental science or engineering, environmental management, and those looking to participate (professionally or personally) in the political or regulatory process related to environment and climate issues.

courses.title: Local Government Finance
courses.desc: Concepts, techniques, and laws relating to municipal finance. Detailed analysis of the tools available to local governments as they seek to raise revenues for the provision of traditional services, including property tax and fees (user and regulatory), but with emphasis on "new" strategies such as impact fees and development agreements. Trends toward "privatization" and the legal implications of transferring traditional municipal obligations to the private sector. Discussion of the policy implications found in "tax cap" states such as California and Massachusetts.

courses.title: Climate Change Policy, Planning And Action
courses.desc: Examination of climate change problem from perspective of scientific evidence, policy responses and media coverage. Sources of greenhouse gas emissions and a wide range of mitigation and adaptation measures are explored and assessed. Overview of climate change solutions being taken or planned by governments, communities, and institutions (both for profit and non-profit) and for major systems, e.g. transportation, buildings, and energy.

courses.title: Public Health and the Built Environment
courses.desc: The epidemics of asthma, diabetes, and obesity have focused new attention on the role played by suburban sprawl, transportation, and other built environment features on public health. This course will explore the linkages between the built environment and public health from a policy and planning perspective. Students will develop analytical skills to evaluate modern day public health and built environment challenges, including mapping tools, health impact assessments, and healthy planning and design.

courses.title: Negotiation, Mediation, And Conflict Resolution
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LEAD 254) Techniques of negotiation and mediation applied to a broad range of conflict situations from interpersonal differences to labor relations, environmental disputes, and international relations. Combines practice in basic methods with theoretical and applied aspects of conflict resolution.

courses.title: Environmental Life Cycle Assessment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as NUTR 331) Which is a more environmentally sustainable protein choice: chicken, tofu, or salmon? What processes in a food company’s supply chain should be targeted to reduce energy use and costs? How would shifting to nationally recommended diets impact the environment? These are a few examples of the myriad questions that can be addressed with life cycle assessment (LCA). LCA is a tool in the field of industrial ecology that quantifies the resource use and emissions of a product or system along its entire life cycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal. A central objective of this method is informing evidence-based decision-making toward sustainability by policy makers, NGOs, companies, and individuals. This course covers the intellectual foundations of LCA and provides hands-on experience applying the tool, with a focus on topics, data sources, and methodological issues relevant to food and agriculture. This is an intensive, project-based modeling course where you will learn new concepts, vocabulary, quantitative skills, and software. Prior experience managing and analyzing quantitative data in Microsoft Excel (or equivalent) is highly recommended. Please speak with the instructor if you are uncertain about your preparedness for the course.

courses.title: Food Systems Modeling and Analysis
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as NUTR 342) Agriculture and food industries are a subject of growing interest in terms of their resource requirements, ecological impacts, and sustainability. With a focus on local and regional food systems in the United States, this course will provide a foundation in some of the methods of modeling and analysis used to study food systems. We will address several types of approaches, generally building in complexity, starting with net balances of production and consumption and continuing through modeling carrying capacity, foodshed analyses, system dynamics, and integrated transdisciplinary modeling. Students will learn what types of questions are best addressed through modeling approaches, the methods used to conduct food systems models, and the data required to complete the analyses. In addition, they will have opportunities to conduct simple analyses through in-class exercises. Finally, students will learn how models might be relevant to the development of policy related to local and regional food systems or dietary changes to reduce environmental impact. Prerequisite: NUTR 0231: Fundamentals of GIS or an equivalent course with instructor’s consent and graduate standing or instructor consent.

sections.note: Boston Campus

courses.title: Economics of Food, Agriculture and Nutrition
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as NUTR 238) This course helps students explain, predict and evaluate change in consumer behavior, agricultural production and food businesses, government policies and nutritional outcomes. The first half is a gentle introduction to economic principles, using analytical diagrams to represent individual choices and interactions between people. The second half is data analysis, using Excel to construct charts and tables using downloadable data from a variety of sources about food, agriculture and nutrition in the U.S. and worldwide. Presentation and discussion in class is reinforced by weekly exercises followed by either exams or a course project, building skills needed for careers in nonprofit organizations, for-profit enterprises and government agencies. Our teaching blog with links to the open access textbook (Food Economics, published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2024) is here: https://sites.tufts.edu/foodeconomics.

courses.title: Teaching Democracy
courses.desc:
Teaching Democracy, a course in popular and participatory education, is part of UEP’s Co-Research/Co-Education (CoRE), offerings. As such, it brings students and community practitioners / activists into a shared learning space. It is geared for students who have already had experiences in popular and community-based education or who plan to be using these methods in the near future. Teaching Democracy (TD) introduces the purposes, uses and methods of participatory and popular education. It combines participatory classroom learning, reading, journaling, and practical
experience. It is especially relevant to those who do or want to incorporate community engagement, planning, and decision-making into their work / practice. Due to limited capacity, participation in the class is through an application process and requires the
approval of the faculty.

courses.title: Design Skills for Urban Planners: InDesign and SketchUp
courses.desc:
This course will provide the necessary tools and techniques required to display 2D and
3D information in a visually compelling and interesting format. Students
will learn the necessary workflow to skillfully utilize Adobe InDesign and Trimble
SketchUP.

courses.title: Economics For Planning And Policy Analysis
courses.desc:
Required core course for M.A. and M.P.P. students. Economic concepts and tools of analysis for graduate students interested in public policy and planning. The emphasis of this course will be on microeconomic policy tools, although some macroeconomic topics will also be covered. The course will discuss the economic theories and techniques that can inform current policy debates such as global climate change, health care, employment, and economic inequality. The class will also demonstrate the limitations of economic analysis in guiding policy making. Although prior coursework in economics is not required, students are required to have a solid understanding of college-level algebra. Waiver permitted for students with an undergraduate major or substantial work-related experience in economics subject to faculty approval.
Recommendations: College-level algebra

courses.title: Field Projects: Planning And Practice
courses.desc: (Required core course for MA UEPP, MS EPP, and MS Sustainability students only) This course strives to integrate theory and practice by providing students the opportunity to work on real-world challenges, while offering community and nonprofit organizations, cities and towns, private firms and public agencies research, analysis, and advice that enhances insight into priority issues and advances strategic objectives. The Field Projects course combines research, practical planning, and problem-solving, accompanied by the development of skills integrally connected to the projects themselves. Learning is supported through discussion and reflection among students, TAs, and instructors and skills workshops.

instructors: Christine Cousineau, Kari L. Hewitt, Kathryn K. Davies, Melissa Anne Peters, Penn S Loh
sections.req: UEP Majors or student enrolled in the Sustainability MS

courses.title: Program Evaluation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 247) Purposes for, and types and techniques of, program evaluation. Study of the evaluation process, including design, implementation, and dissemination, with focus on development of relevant data collection, analysis, and report-writing skills. Emphasis on learning to match individual programs with particular models of evaluation.

courses.title: Corporate Management Of Environmental Issues
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CEE 265 & ENV 265 ) Students in this course will explore the ways corporations interact with the environment, with the goal of understanding the processes, pitfalls, and tools for preventing/addressing environmental issues or disasters. Using case studies, students will critique the ways corporations have
managed real environmental challenges, and discuss the alternatives that may have been available. Students will also be introduced to approaches used by companies to envision and prepare for environmental problems. They will also focus on the perspectives of various stakeholders who have an interest in corporate environmental management, including shareholders, boards, corporate leaders, community members, governments, and activists/NGOs, and unravel the tensions that often exist among these groups.

courses.title: Sustainability Metrics And Decision Tools
courses.desc: (Required core course option for M.S. Sustainability) Governments, companies, institutions, and non-government organizations are making both internal and public commitments to greenhouse gas reduction and sustainability. Whether driven by regulatory or voluntary efforts, operationalizing these commitments effectively and consistently can be challenging. This course examines how sustainability targets are established, metrics are identified and tracked, and progress is reported and communicated in order to continue to inform decision-making for sustainable management. A range of topics and metrics will be covered, including greenhouse gas emissions, clean energy, waste, food systems, health outcomes, land use, transportation, resilience, and economic indicators, among others, as well as systems and tools for assessing and managing them. Students will learn how sustainability is measured by a variety of stakeholders, consider how progress is communicated, and how sustainability data inform their decision-making processes. This course will also begin to explore how ecological, environmental quality, and sustainability data combined with spatial data can provide important insights for understanding local economies, human health, climate risks, and resource consumption, and how approaches to data visualization can be used to address multi-faceted sustainability challenges.

courses.title: Policy Implementation and Innovation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LEAD 242) Seminar explores how policies, programs, and initiatives get translated into practice in public and nonprofit organizations through case studies and individual student projects. Reviews the challenges of implementation in light of concerns about accountability to multiple stakeholders and responsibility for achieving results. Explores strategies for innovative solutions to overcome implementation challenges including performance measurement, diffusion and adaptation of innovations, inter-organizational coordination and collaboration, and strategic framing.

sections.note: Non-UEP graduate students need permission from the instructor to enroll.

courses.title: Social Policy For Children And Families
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ CSHD 282) Intersection of child development and social policy. Case studies of processes through which social problems are defined, policies formulated and implemented. Models for analyzing existing and proposed policies and for interpreting program evaluation results. Topics may include child abuse and neglect, family leave, maternal and child public-health policy, child care, early-childhood education. Special attention to policies affecting disadvantaged and minority populations.

Upper level of dual-level course with expanded readings and more advanced assignments.

Recommendations: CSHD 1 or PSY 1.

courses.title: Developing Sustainable Communities
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 284 and LEAD 213.) Explores the many challenges of achieving sustainable development at local, regional, national and international levels. Focuses on improving the quality of people's lives, on disinvested communities, and on the inequitable distribution of income, wealth, and environmental hazards. Investigates the theory of sustainable development, as well as the tools, strategies, and the contexts needed to move towards the ecological integrity, economic security, empowerment, responsibility, and social well-being characteristic of sustainable communities. Case studies drawn from the U.S. and overseas.

courses.title: Sustainability Internship
courses.desc: Students in the MS in Sustainability course must complete a supervised Internship (of at least 150 hours) in an organization in a field related to environmental sustainability. In addition, students must prepare a detailed assessment of the sustainability challenge or challenges observed and/or engaged with during the internship that draws on their observations and insights as well as relevant scholarly literature in the field.

courses.title: Internship - Internship
courses.desc: The UEP internship enhances professional skills, allows the student to explore career options, broadens professional contacts, and provides a meaningful opportunity to work in a community. The student arranges the internship with an employing agency for a minimum of 150 hours of work. Additional requirements: completion of an internship agreement with the employing agency prior to beginning work; the supervisor's evaluation; the student's assessment of the experience.

courses.title: Histories of Film II: 1955-Present
courses.desc: (cross-listed as FMS 51) The two Histories of Film courses are sequential, one-semester courses that may be taken separately, but are created as a year-long inquiry into the history of the art of cinema. Constructed as a foundations course, we will examine the historical development of cinema from its inception in the late nineteenth century through the present. Presented through a broad historical, aesthetic, and critical framework, this course will introduce the student to the study of cinematic representation by focusing on the first half-century of its development in the fall and the second half-century of its development in the spring. By investigating the aesthetic, formal, and stylistic devices of film as well as its narrative codes and structures we will consider the evolution of its rich and complex language. Our study will focus on such noteworthy film movements as the early international avant-garde, German Expressionism, Soviet filmmaking of the 1920s, the classical studio Hollywood film (including genre and authorship studies), postwar cinemas in Japan and Italy, international New Wave cinemas of the 1960s, post-classical American cinema, World cinema, contemporary independent film practices, and more.

courses.title: Mapping “East Asias” in New England
courses.desc: Examines how various institutions in New England have collected and exhibited East Asian art and artifacts, focusing on the region’s major port cities in the 18th and 19th centuries as hubs of complex commercial, diplomatic, and cultural exchange between East and West. Explores the short-lived Chinese Museum in Boston, the development of Asian art collections at the Museum of Fine Arts and the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, the Harvard Art Museums’ role in shaping the field of Asian art history, and the newly opened Korean Collection at the Peabody Essex Museum. Activities outside the classroom include cultural artifacts housed and displayed in museums, the MFA Japanese Garden, Boston Korean War Memorials, and the MIT Public Art Collection. Archival research using primary and secondary sources.

courses.title: Roots of Contemporary Art
courses.desc: Art made since 1960, emphasizing developments that have shaped current practices. Weekly topics investigate art and activism; counter-cultures and the culture wars; experiments beyond the studio and gallery; histories of performance, assemblage, installation, and site-specificity. Reflection on the significance of minimalism, conceptualism, feminism, and environmental art, among other movements.

courses.title: Film and the Avant-Garde
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 187, HAA 159, FMS 58, HAA 49, VMS 185, FMS 185 & ILVS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. Avant-garde filmmakers beginning in the 1920s, such as Fernand Leger and Marcel Duchamp, as well as filmmakers from cross-media movements such as Dada and Surrealism. Postwar artists in the United States who reworked prewar avant-garde film genres and pioneered new ones, including lyrical and collage film. Structural film of the 1960s and the pluralism of avant-garde film since the 1970s. Historical conditions and theories that shaped these developments, and the use of avant-garde film by feminists and other artists for socio-political critique. Lower level version of VMS 0185.

sections.note: Students may choose lower level section (VMS 58) or upper level section (VMS 185). The upper level includes an additional research project. Weekly recitation/screening is required.
Weekly recitation/screening is required.

courses.title: Italian Fashion: Weaving Culture and Identity
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ITAL 78) Fashion in Italy from an interdisciplinary approach: historical, political, economic, cultural, and social aspects. Sartorial identity and its influence on the design, production, consumption, and global exportation of clothing and accessories. Cultural and economic significance of regional craftsmanship and artisanal traditions. The role of fashion in shaping personal and collective identities, with attention to beauty standards, body politics, and gender expression. Traditional Italian textile and garment production and contemporary fashion systems, with particular attention to environmental sustainability, labor equity, social justice, wellness, and self-representation. Course materials may include visual media, fashion journalism, documentaries, exhibition catalogs, and scholarly sources. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Special Topics - Media and the Environment
courses.desc: See departmental website for details

sections.note:
Students may choose lower level section (VMS 91-01) or upper level section (VMS 193-02). The upper level includes an additional research project.

As conceptions of humanity’s relationship to nature have evolved, so too have the ways that people use media to represent the environment. We will look closely at how movies and other popular media have depicted nonhuman nature, and examine how audiovisual media have been used within the environmental movement, from the conservation efforts of the mid-20th century to the increasingly urgent efforts of activists in the era of climate change. We will read work by prominent scholars in ecocriticism, and view a wide range of media, looking at narrative, documentary, and experimental practices.

courses.title: Queer World Cinema
courses.desc: Global historical and contemporary approaches to queer cinema, especially representations and expressions of gender and sexuality. Analysis of film and media works that challenge popular representations and critically engage with issues of intersectional identities spanning race, ethnicity, femininity, masculinity, heteronormativity, and LGBTQ+ identities. Examines systems of oppression , the work of feminist and queer activism, and contemporary LGBTQ+ cultures using cinema as a political tool and artistic form of expression.

courses.title: Art and the Home since 1900
courses.desc: Analysis of modern and contemporary artworks that address domestic cultures. Focus on sculpture, installation, and performance; comparisons with visual culture, furniture, crafts, and interior design. Western and non-Western examples, discussed through the lens of cultural studies, critical theory, feminism, postcolonial studies, and social art history. Relationship between private and public spheres; modernization and consumption; and nomadism and migration.

courses.title: Afro-Brazilian Diaspora at the MFA
courses.desc: Focuses on Afro-Brazilian artwork in the MFA Axelrod collection. Considers the history and historiography of Afro-Brazilian visual culture and art and its links to religion and popular culture. Looks at Afro-Brazilian and Afro-American art in comparative ways. Analysis of modes of display and how to approach works of art in a museum context. Classes at SMFA and MFA to examine original works.

courses.title: Icons of Latin America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as SPN 180) Examination of some revolutionary and political figures including Tupac Amaru, Malinche, Simón Bolívar, Emiliano Zapata, Che Guevara, and Eva Perón, and visual, cultural, and literary figures such as Frida Kahlo, Carmen Miranda, Diego Maradona, and Pablo Neruda. Exploration of myths, historical realities, and misconceptions associated with them. Emphasis on historical contextualization to examine how the visual and literary renditions have fused with political events, both within Latin America and abroad, to construct these iconic figures. Co-taught and conducted in Spanish. Prerequisite: two 30-level Spanish courses or consent of the instructor.
