courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 187, HAA 159, FMS 58, HAA 49, FMS 185, VMS 58, ILVS 58) The role of film within avant-garde art, primarily in Europe and North America. Avant-garde filmmakers beginning in the 1920s, such as Fernand Leger and Marcel Duchamp, as well as filmmakers from cross-media movements such as Dada and Surrealism. Postwar artists in the United States who reworked prewar avant-garde film genres and pioneered new ones, including lyrical and collage film. Structural film of the 1960s and the pluralism of avant-garde film since the 1970s. Historical conditions and theories that shaped these developments, and the use of avant-garde film by feminists and other artists for socio-political critique. Upper level version of FMS 0058; students do a research project.

sections.note: Students may choose lower level section (VMS 58) or upper level section (VMS 185). The upper level includes an additional research project. Weekly recitation/screening is required.
Weekly recitation/screening is required.

courses.title: Latin American Icons
courses.desc: The tempestuous history of Latin America has generated some of the most lasting historical and mythical figures in the world. From revolutionary and political figures such as Tupac Amaru, Malinche, Simón Bolivar, Emiliano Zapata, Che Guevara, and Eva Perón to visual, cultural and literary figures such as Frida Kahlo, Carmen Miranda, Diego Maradona, and Pablo Neruda, Latin American icons have become an integral part of the global cultural landscape. This class examines some of these figures to explore myths, historical realities, and misconceptions associated with them. Through a careful historical contextualization, we examine how the visual and literary renditions have fused with political events, both within Latin America and abroad, to construct these iconic figures. Conducted in Spanish. Prerequisite: two 30 level courses or consent.

courses.title: Special Topics - Agribusiness Dreamworlds
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: This course applies cultural anthropology and visual studies approaches to deconstruct the histories and ideals of agribusiness on a global level. We cover agriculture as a possible means for land occupation with colonial aims; theoretical aspirations to standardization, order, modularity, and control; university contributions to shaping modern agriculture; rural aesthetics and experiences as foundations for national, gender and racial identities; ideal cities and adventure parks informed by farming utopias. Also, we consider resistance and critiques of agribusiness models, including worker organizing and protest, worker expertise and rights, pluriversal approaches to farming, artistic responses and consumer awareness efforts.

courses.title: Special Topics - Media and the Environment
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Students may choose lower level section (VMS 91-01) or upper level section (VMS 193-02). The upper level includes an additional research project.

As conceptions of humanity’s relationship to nature have evolved, so too have the ways that people use media to represent the environment. We will look closely at how movies and other popular media have depicted nonhuman nature, and examine how audiovisual media have been used within the environmental movement, from the conservation efforts of the mid-20th century to the increasingly urgent efforts of activists in the era of climate change. We will read work by prominent scholars in ecocriticism, and view a wide range of media, looking at narrative, documentary, and experimental practices.

courses.title: Special Topics - Screening Paranoia
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: From worries about digital surveillance, to the widespread dissemination of misinformation, we live in a paranoid age. But technological anxiety and mistrust are hardly new to our culture. We will see how emerging technologies have been met with fear throughout history—from beliefs that early electronic media such as radio could contact other worlds, to contemporary concerns about how corporations and governments track our every behavior. We will trace how popular media such as film have represented paranoia, from 1950s science fiction to 1970s thrillers, and conclude by examining how paranoia is central to so much of today’s popular culture and political discourse.

courses.title: Special Topics - Modern, Contemporary Asian Art
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: This course introduces students to diverse practices of modern and contemporary art in East Asian countries, such as Japan, Korea, and China, and Southeast Asian countries including Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam. We will pay careful attention to a broad range of forms, styles, and media of art practices in the Asian region since 1945, exploring multilateral factors that have entailed the unprecedented changes in painting, sculpture, architecture, and the indefinable area that exists between them. The course also addresses related critical themes, such as the role of minorities, hybridity, and national/transnational identities, which help us develop a better understanding of shared values and aspirations, as well as the coexistence of diversity within the Asian modern and contemporary culture.

courses.title: Special Topics - Animalia and the Post-Human
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: Focus on art featuring non-human animals and other beings. Study a wide range of art and visual culture from the 18th¿through the 21st¿century through the theoretical lenses of Animal Studies, Ecocriticism and Posthumanist philosophies. Learn to approach making and viewing from the vantage point of non-human subjectivity. Case studies address how artists have approached relationships with the more-than-human world as objects of representation, as providers of materials, as resources and as co-creators and companions. Recommendations: Prior enrollment in HAA and/or VMS courses.

courses.title: Special Topics - Vibrant Matter: Visualizing Curatorial Idea
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:
Co-located with GRA 191-03

This course offers students insights into intertwined curatorial and exhibition design strategies related to the representation, interpretation, and conceptual imaging of world cultures and identity groups. We will focus on understanding curatorial work and examining exhibitions contemporaneously on display. Close looking through museum visits and critical thinking exercises will engage students with the materiality of created environments, to explore the complex entanglements of art objects within architecture and designed spaces. This process will teach students to contextualize displays by examining their relations to the history of art and art exhibitions, as well as to the history of collecting. Half the class will focus on academic work, the other half will focus on the studio practice of Exhibition Design to design spaces for selected art objects. 

Strong exhibitions are developed through inclusive processes that incorporate multiple voices and thoughtful scholarship translated into nuanced design elements. This requires pedagogical skill, awareness of art historical contexts and contemporary art dialogue, as well as an open mind to explore diverse points of view in creative ways. Cultural literacy and technical skills are called upon to develop relevant solutions to complex presentations of art and history to present objects in context. 

Students will work in teams to design their own exhibitions based on selected curatorial content. Final projects will be presented for discussion and evaluation. Creative Suite technical skills will be integrated into coursework to provide students with relevant tools for future professional preparation.

courses.title: Special Topics - Cultures of Collecting
courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note: This course explores different types of museums and their recent innovation through the 19th and early 21st centuries across various geographies. Our point of departure is to trace how museums become “public” institutions, how they collect, preserve, document, and exhibit objects. From this historical purview of the fundamentally Western practices, we will expand our discussion to critical discourses and various case studies— such as “Third-World biennials,” artist-run alternative spaces in Asia, and decolonizing endeavors of so-called “cultural peripheries.” We will also discuss contemporary expectations that “global” museums should function, as diversified platforms for cross-cultural exchanges and value creations.

courses.title: Critical Drag
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ TPS 41) Exploration of drag as a performance practice that aestheticizes gender for purposes such as entertainment, socio-political critique, and labor. Creation of individual drag personas and performances considering intersections of gender, nationality, race, class, and disability to understand the implications of putting gender on the body, on stage, and in everyday life. Workshops, short performances and critiques to curate performance resources and cultivate performance techniques, culminating in a public performance.

courses.title: Asian American Writers
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENG 36) Introduction to twentieth-century Asian American literature and culture. Major themes and topics include immigration, diversity, the relation between ethnicity and literature, minority experience, alienation from the English language, intergenerational conflict. Examples are drawn from representative prose narratives, poetry, and plays.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Introduction to Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies
courses.desc: (SPRING 2013 & BEYOND) (Cross-listed w/CVS 72). Interdisciplinary survey of major issues in the study of women, gender, and sexuality. Emphasizes intersections with race, class, ethnicity, culture and other categories of identity and difference, including a strong global or transnational perspective.

courses.title: Introduction To Queer Studies - Intro to Queer Studies
courses.desc: Introduction to the interdisciplinary field of queer studies through an examination of key texts and practices. Course will interrogate notions of normality; binary systems of sex, gender, and sexuality; and cultural representations of personhood, citizenship and family. It will examine the application of queer theory in fields such as economics, anthropology, literature, cultural studies, and film studies. Of particular concern will be ways gender and sexuality intersect with race, ethnicity, nationality, and class.

courses.title: Topics in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies - Drag Tech
courses.desc: New or one-time course offerings. See program website for specific details.

sections.note:
Unlock the secrets to creating a drag character that's not only fierce but also technically sound! In this immersive class, you'll dive deep into the tools, techniques, and strategies needed to bring your drag persona to life, from head to toe. Whether you're a seasoned drag performer or just starting out, this class will guide you through the crucial technical aspects that make a drag character stand out. By the end of the class, you’ll have all the tools you need to confidently create and execute a drag persona that’s as technically impressive as it is dazzling. Whether you're performing on stage, shooting a photoshoot, or just expressing yourself in your everyday life, you’ll be ready to slay with every detail!

Lab Fee $150. TDPS is committed to making our courses accessible to all and will assist students who need support with lab fees. Please email TDPS Associate Department Chair Linda Ross Girard for more information.

courses.title: Topics in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies - Women and Gender on TV
courses.desc: New or one-time course offerings. See program website for specific details.

sections.note:
Students may choose lower-level section (WGSS 85-26) or upper-level section (WGSS 185-94). The upper level includes an additional research project. 

From Soaps to Streaming: Women and Gender on TV. Whether depicting the housewife of early sitcoms or iconic characters like Mary Tyler Moore, Leslie Knope, and Olivia Pope, television has played an influential role in women’s lives and engaged with gender politics. Because of its historical placement in the domestic sphere, TV has long been understood as a "feminized" medium. Yet, it also functions as a crucial site where women’s stories are told, and where gender, sexuality, race, and class are negotiated, contested, and reimagined. Throughout the course, we will consider questions such as: How have television texts represented women? In what genres have women dominated? How have race and class intersected with gender on television? Students will use gender as a core framework to explore television’s technological evolution, from its origins as a domestic broadcast medium to the era of cord-cutting and streaming. We will examine how gender shapes discourses of taste and legitimacy, the reputations and branding of network, cable, and streaming platforms, industrial practices and modes of distribution, and audience practices, fandom, and consumer culture across historical eras. Through these topics, students will become familiar with television studies scholarship and develop skills in feminist media analysis to engage with television as a powerful system that shapes and influences gender at every turn.

courses.title: Feminism in 20th century U.S. Literature and Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENG 89) How the postwar U.S. women’s movement for equality, born of the mid-twentieth century antiwar and civil rights movements, made civic, legal and ethical challenges that are expressed in literature and film, in mass and high cultures, and in women’s experiences across race, class, ethnic, and sexual lines. Explores the effect of second wave feminism on discourses of gender and women’s sexuality using novels, poetry, essays and films with a view to understanding that forms of knowing are gendered; not universal but culturally constructed, contextual, mutable. Questions how feminism is postmodern; speculates how postmodernism is in part a feminist production; how the postmodern fits with recognitions about gender and liberations of sex and sexualities in the postwar U.S. women’s movement. Authors include: Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Toni Morrison, Audre Lorde, Alix Kates Shulman, Anne Sexton, Sylvia Plath, Adrienne Rich, Chuang Hua, Valerie Solanas. No prerequisites.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Internship
courses.desc: Gain experience, make connections, explore career opportunities working alongside individuals, agencies or organizations( private, non-profit, or government), political advocacy groups, or women's social movements that impact the lives of women.

courses.title: Sex and Money: Anthropology of Sex Work
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ANTH 147) Intersections between sex (and other forms of intimacy) and money (and other forms of exchange). Reading of ethnographies about sex workers and those who seek to regulate, profit from, or “help” them. How neoliberalism has shaped ways of earning a living throughout the world in ways that changed gender roles and intimate relationships. Topics include ethical concerns with studying sex workers; their relationships with family members, pimps, and clients; moral panics about “white slavery” and “sex trafficking;” the whore stigma; sex tourism; criminalization and legalization; transactional sex; and the eroticization of perceived racial difference.

courses.title: Biopolitics & the Body: Life, Power, Knowledge
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 152 and ANTH 152) Theories and ethnographies of biopolitics and biopower. What happens when biological life (including that of humans) becomes a site for power and management? Reading of conceptual and ethnographic texts at the intersection of science, medicine, the state, and capital. Topics include neoliberal governmentality, hegemony of interventionist biotechnologies, bioethics, biosecurity and management of risk, biocapitalism, necropolitics, logics of social abandonment and disposability, political rights, and projects of biological and social enhancement.

courses.title: Gender and Sexuality in Ancient Christianity
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as REL 160) Examination of gender and sexuality in the ancient Mediterranean, with special attention to how issues of gender and sexuality are treated in the New Testament, in early Church Fathers, Hebrew Bible, martyrdom accounts, and hagiography (saints’ lives). Consideration of pre-Christian sexual ethics and the structure of the family in Mediterranean patriarchal cultures (in this
case Greeks, Romans, and Judeans) and discussion of the sexual ethics found in the writings of figures like Pythagoras, Plato, and the Stoics. Discussion of how early Christians (second through the fifth centuries CE) simultaneously reinscribe traditional gender roles and notions of sexuality, and also subvert these roles and ideas. Consideration of the conflict over the right of women to hold
positions of authority and alternative avenues of power such as renouncing sexuality & marriage, and voluntary martyrdom. The rise of sexual renunciation as a central feature of ascetic Christianity and attention to the ways that women and men strive to shed the trappings of “this mortal coil” by denying sexuality full-stop.

courses.title: Gender, Work, And Politics In East Asia
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ PS 128) Gendered experiences of work in the East Asian economic "miracle." The state's role in creating, challenging, or mitigating gender considerations in work, the centrality of women's labor in development, and women's work as an international relations issue. Readings on factory, office, domestic, and sex work.

courses.title: Special Topics Seminar in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies - Social Theory and Performance
courses.desc:
New or one-time seminars on a variety of topics in the fields of Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies.
Recommendations may apply. See program website and specific course descriptions for details.

sections.note:
Social theory is one of the major intellectual traditions that informs the contemporary study of performance. This seminar combines select readings from classical sociological thought (Marx, Weber, Durkheim and others), with contemporary works of performance theory and analysis, such as those by Schechner, Phelan, Butler, and Muñoz. The seminar examines both theatrical concepts in works of social theory, and social theoretical perspectives on performance in both its aesthetic and off-stage forms.

This course is available to graduate students and upper-level undergraduates.

courses.title: Special Topics Seminar in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies - Marxism & Literature
courses.desc:
New or one-time seminars on a variety of topics in the fields of Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies.
Recommendations may apply. See program website and specific course descriptions for details.

sections.note:
Post Marxism is having a revival. But far from the cliché of a theory glorifying the white male factory worker, much new Marxist scholarship attends to the way capitalism depends on social hierarchies of race, gender, class, and ability. This course offers students a fresh approach to Marxist studies to think about how economic transformations shape our literature, media, and culture. Studying contemporary fiction, poetry, film, and a play by Bertolt Brecht, we’ll begin with well-known Marxist literary and cultural critics (Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall, Fredric Jameson), before moving to read a range of global and non-Western Marxist thinkers (Raquel Gutiérrez Aguilar, Jairus Banaji, Aijaz Ahmad) alongside new cultural accounts of the gigwork economy, deindustrialization, and migrant care work (Sianne Ngai, Alessandra Mezzadri, Annie McClanahan). If you’re curious about Marxism but not sure where to start, this is the course for you. 

Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement

courses.title: Special Topics Seminar in Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies - Violence, Pleasure, and Value(s)
courses.desc:
New or one-time seminars on a variety of topics in the fields of Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies.
Recommendations may apply. See program website and specific course descriptions for details.

sections.note: This upper-level seminar examines anthropological theories of value and will try to understand them on their own terms as well as apply them to thinking about the value(s) of pleasure, especially but not exclusively sexual pleasure, in relation to violence. We will spend the first five weeks of the semester reading anthropological approaches that center economic value, semiotic value, and their intersections, as well as approaches that define value as that in which people see as worthwhile to invest their time and energy. We will then spend the rest of the semester applying those ways of framing value to texts from a variety of disciplines (mostly by Black, Latina, and Latin American feminist, queer, and trans scholars and activists) that grapple with the co-existence of violence and pleasure, covering topics such as: BDSM, pornography and postpornography, sex work, femicide and transfemicide, and countersexuality.
